Md Shorfullslam Khan, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Jiban Bima Corporation Dhaka ------ Petitioner
vs.
Mustafa Hussain & anr ------ Opposite Parties"
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 8-8-87 and respectively passed in Title Appeal No.89 of 1987 by the learned Subordinate Judge and Judge, Commercial Court No.1 Dhaka dismissing the apple and affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-1-1987 and 2-2-87 respectively passed in Title Suit No.647 of 1985 by the learned Munsif, 4th Court, Dhaka decreeing the suit. 

2. The opposite party as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.647 of 1985 in the 4th Court of Munsif, Dhaka praying for decree declaring that he is continuing in his service as his dismissal was not made as per service rules of the corporation and also for a decree for all arrear pay; allowances due and payable to him with costs and also for any other for further relief as the court may deem fit and proper, contending that the order of dismissal dated 27-9-82 is not lawful in as much as the order of conviction dated 18-8-82 got its finality on 16-11-82 and that the corporation without any proceeding has passed the dismissal order. The defendant petitioner contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and asserting that the dismissal order was passed on due consideration by the proper authority, inasmuch as the Board of Directors of the Corporation in its duly held meeting for the purpose took resolution dismissing the plaintiff opposite party No.1 from service as he was found guilty of the charges brought against him by the Summary Martial Law Court and that the order of conviction and sentence dated 18-8-82 on review was modified in that the order of conviction was confirmed but the sentence was remitted and therefore the plaintiff opposite party's conviction having, been confirmed got finality and he was not prejudiced by the order of dismissal dated 27-9-82. The learned Munsif heard the matter and considering the materials on record decreed the suit in part declaring that the impugned order of dismissal dated 27-9-82 was premature, null and void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff and also declared that the plaintiff still is in his respective service. Being aggrieved the defendant No.1 filed Title Appeal No.89 of1987 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka, which on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.1, Dhaka by the impugned judgment and decree. The learned Subordinate Judge on due consideration of the materials on record affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif holding that the impugned order of dismissal dated 27-9-82 was passed before the conviction order dated 18-8-82 was made final on review by the Zonal Martial Law Authority on 16-11-82. 

3. Mr Md NuruIlah, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner Corporation submitted that the courts below erred in law in not considering the fact that the order of conviction has not been set aside by the review authority and, as such, the plaintiff opposite party has not been prejudiced in any way by the dismissal order dated 27-9-82 inasmuch as the said dismissal order was passed by the corporation based on the order of conviction passed by the Summary Martial Law Court. He further submits that the order of dismissal has been passed on the basis of a resolution taken by the competent authority of the Corporation as per service rules of the corporation. Mr. Nurullah then submits that the suit itself is not maintainable and the courts below erred in law in not holding that the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for want of prayer for consequential relief. The learned Advocate also submitted that the decree as passed being unenforceable is a nullity. 
4. Mr Nurullah in elaborating his submissions on the dismissal order referred to the provisions of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976 which is also applicable for the Corporation as adopted in the Service Rules of the Corporation and particularly to Rule 8 of the said rules which reads as:"8. Savings; Nothing in rule 6 or 7 shall apply to a case- a) where the accused is dismissed or removed from service or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction in a criminal charge; or b) where the authority competent to dismiss or remove the accused from service or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that, for reasons to be recorded in writing by that authority, it is not reasonably practicable to give the accused an opportunity of showing cause;" and submitted that the plaintiff petitioner was found guilty on the 'charges in SML case No.3( 46) of 1982 by the Summary Martial Law Court No.3 on the basis of a First Information Report filed with the Motijheel police station in Motijheel Police Station Case No.191(5) of 1982 and therefore convicted and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 2 years and fine of Taka 1,00,00.00 in default further Rigorous Imprisonment for 1 year more by its order dated 18-8-82 A copy of the said order was forwarded to the Corporation for taking necessary action and accordingly the Corporation in its Board meeting took resulting dismissing the plaintiff opposite party No.1 along with others, on the basis of the said conviction and the decision of the Corporation was communicated to the plaintiff opposite party by a letter dated 27-9-82 and the same has been made complying with the Rule 8(a) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976 quoted above, and there is no illegality or irregularity. He further submits that the order was reviewed by the Zonal Martial Law Administrator and by its order dated 16-11-82 confirmed the conviction but remitted the sentence and therefore the plaintiff remained a convict and therefore the order of dismissal has not prejudiced him in any way. He however candidly admitted that as per Martial Law Regulation-I of 1982 Sub-Regulation 3(3) the order of conviction dated 18-8-82 was subject to the review and in view of Sub-Regulation 3(5) such order gets finality only on review. Mr Sharful Islam, Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party, on the other hand, submitted that both the courts below have found the impugned dismissal order dated 27-9-82 as premature and hence declared as illegal and void and therefore this court in its revisional jurisdiction should not interfere with such finding. He submitted that the Courts below were just and right in declaring the order of dismissal as illegal since they have correctly found that the order of dismissal is a premature order inasmuch as before the order of conviction got its finality, the order of dismissal was passed. The order of conviction and sentence dated 18-8-82 was recommending in nature and only after review on 16-11-82 the said order got its finality and legality. The learned Advocate also took me through the office memorandum of the Establishment Division Cabinet Secretariat of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh being numbered as R-Vl/S-3/77-15 dated Dacca, the 5th February, 1977 "Subject. Removable from service of a Government servant on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction in a criminal offence," which contained that "if a government servant is convicted of a criminal offence it is not incumbent upon the authority, he should impose upon him a penalty of dismissal or removal or reduction relevant on the ground of his conviction. In each case, the authority will consider the conduct of the Government Servant which has led to his conviction and if it is of the opinion that the conduct is such that it calls for a penalty of dismissal or removal or reduction in rank, it may proceed to impose such penalty and submitted that the said memorandum is applicable in the case of the plaintiff opposite party inasmuch as the Government Servant's Rule 1976 has been adopted by the Corporation and that the Corporation has not taken any independent decision by itself and the dismissal order itself on the face of the record shows that the passing of the dismissal order is based only on the order of conviction dated 18-8-82. He submitted that the corporation ought to have proceeded against the plaintiff opposite party to satisfy itself, whether he is liable for dismissal under the Service Rules of the Corporation in the circumstances and thus the Corporation has acted illegally in issuing the impugned order of dismissal, which is also a pre-matured order. On this point the learned Advocate relied on the decision in the case of Helaluddin Ahmed vs. Bangladesh reported in 45 DLR (AD) 1 wherein their Lordships in the Appellate Division have observed that a close scrutiny of the Regulation-S of MLR No.1 of 1982 reveals that a review of the proceedings of a Martial Law Court is an "essential part" of the original proceeding which is unknown to the ordinary procedure of trial of criminal case under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Regulation 3(5) provides that any order by any Martial Law Court attains finality only upon review and order of a Martial Law Court is therefore merely tentative in nature so long it is not reviewed and an accused cannot be said to have derived any vested right from such order pending review and Regulation 3(2)(3) makes mandatory that all orders passed by Martial Law Court be reviewed. Considering the materials on record and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties and relying on the decision of 45 DLR (AD) 1 referred to above that an order of a Summary Martial Law Court gets its finality only on its review and the fact that the order of dismissal has been passed on the basis of the order of conviction passed by the Summary Martial Law Court before its review, I find substance in the submissions of Me. Shorful Islam Khan and I concur with the decision of the courts below on the issue and therefore I do not find any ground to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree declaring the order of dismissal dated 27-9-82 as null and void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff opposite party and that the plaintiffs till holds his service. 

6. The next contention of Mr M Nurullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner-Corporation, that the suit itself is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, since the plaintiff did not seek any consequential relief in the suit. In elaborating his submissions the learned Advocate submitted that from the plain reading of the plaint particularly paragraph 25 of the same, which runs as "The suit is for declaration and establishment of right admissible under the law and there being no prayer in the form of any mandatory injunction to direct the defendant petitioner to reinstate the plaintiff, the suit lacks prayer for consequential relief and the decree as passed is not executable or enforceable. The learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Manager, Personal Division vs. Md Sazaban Miah & others reported in 35 DLR 224 wherein his Lordship Syed Muhammad Hussain J, sitting in a Single Bench, held that "Omission to pray for consequential relief for enforcing declaratory decree renders it unenforceable   in law" and submitted that omission to pray for any   consequential relief for the purpose of enforcing a declatory decree would be hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the' impugned declaratory decree passed by the courts below is unenforceable and therefore is a nullity. He also referred to the decision of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (CPSLA) No.299/83 by which the aforesaid decision of 35 DLR has been upheld. Their Lordships in the Appellate Division observed that, "Since the plaintiff's prayer for declaration was not followed by any consequential relief the learned Judge committed no illegality in holding that the omission of prayer for any consequential relief for the purpose of enforcing declaratory decree was hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Judge has given cogent reason for his decisions and there is no reason to interfere with the same. The petition is dismissed." 

7. The learned Advocate submitted that the aforesaid decision of the Appellate Division has not been modified or changed till today and as such the same is binding on all. The learned Advocate also referred to the decision of the High Court Division in the case of Dhunat Degree College and others vs. Md Abdus Samad and others reported in 49 DLR 38 wherein his Lordship Syed Amirul Islam sitting in a Single Bench considering cases of this court held that in view of the proposition of law as laid down by the Appellate Division in CPSLA No.299/83 a simple declatory suit in a service matter is not maintainable without any prayer for consequential relief as it is hit by the provision to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. It is to be noted here in the judgment reported in 49 DLR 38 the number of CPSLA has been printed incorrectly as 229/1983 where as the correct number is CPSLA No.299/1983. Me Shorful Islam Khan, the learned Advocate submitted that there is no dispute that the decision of the Appellate Division is binding upon all but from the judgment of the case reported in 35 DLR 224 and the Judgment of C P S L A No.299/1983 it appears that the various decisions referred to in the case of Fazlul Karim vs. Agrani Bank, represented by the Chairman, Board of Directors, Agrani Bank and others reported in 45 DLR 375 namely, the decisions in the case of High Commissioner for India vs. 1M Lall reported in1948 AIR PC 121 which is also reported in 52 CWN 761 (PC); Yusuf Ali Khan vs. Province of Panjab reported in PW (1949) (Lah) 219; Ramesh Chandra Das vs. Province of Bengal reported in 57 CWN 767; Habib Khan vs. Federation of Pakistan reported in PW 1954 Sind 199; Province of East Bengal vs. Zahorul Huq reported in 7 DLR (Dac) 446; Province of East Pakistan vs. Mir Golam Sarwar reported in 13 DLR 341,' Province of East Pakistan vs. Abdul Latif Talukder reported in 22 DLR 589 have not been placed before their Lordships for consideration. But their Lordships in the case reported in 45 DLR 375 considered the aforesaid decisions and also the decision reported in 35 DLR 22.4 and then held that "Considering the . facts and circumstances of the present case we hold that the present suit for declaration is maintainable. "The learned Advocate referring to the decision in the case of Bangladesh Water Development Board vs. Syed Moazzem Hossain reported in 15 BLD (AD) 239 submitted that their Lordships have observed that, "A declaratory suit need not be confined within the terms of section 42 of Specific Relief Act which is meant for obtaining a specific relief. A declaration can be sought for various other matters as well." and in the instant case the relief sought for is a decree declaring the order of dismissal illegal and the plaintiff is in service and for arrears of pay and allowances as are due and payable to him and as the defendant corporation is a statutory body, it is obliged to honour the decision of court of law as is bound under the Constitution of the country. The learned Advocate taking me through prayer portion of the plaint, wherein the plaintiff has prayed for decree for declaring that the order of dismissal is not binding and that he is in continuous service and also for a decree for all arrears of pay and allowances, submitted that plaintiff prayed for decree for declaration together with consequential reliefs and therefore the suit is not hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and is maintainable. Further, he submits that neither in the written statements nor in the memo of appeal or in the revisional application, the petitioner has raised the question of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and, as such, the petitioner is not entitled to raise this question at this stage in revisional jurisdiction and in support of his contention referred to the case of Sarder Ahmed Ali vs. GM AU Boksb and ors reported in 37 DLR 7, wherein his Lordship Mr Justice Anwarul Hoque Chowdhury J sitting in a Single Bench has observed; Further, it is seen that even in the written statement of the defendant appellants before the trial Court no such objection as to the maintainability of the suit had been taken. No such issue was framed. The parties neither fought out the case on that basis except an issue to the effect as to "Whether the suit is maintainable in the present form "where it was not argued that the suit is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief and also that "There are authorities to show that when a person being the defendant did not take the plea in his written statement that the plaintiff's case should be dismissed, being hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Act, the defendant cannot on appeal or on revision be allowed to set out a new case which he did not make in his written statement as to the maintainability which need to have been agitated at the earliest possible opportunity, which was not done in the instant case and further I find that the suit was not hit by section 42 of the proviso as it was not a mere declaration but there were consequential relief to the extent it was capable of being asked at the time of institution of the suit by the plaintiff. Further, in a matter like this the finding whether the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is a finding of fact to be decided by the court initially and if the court proceeds with the suit finding no objection under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, higher courts on revision would be very reluctant to interfere, if court at the first instance had not exercised the discretion arbitrarily which however is not the case here." 

8. In the instant case it appears that the defendant-petitioners did not take any objection in their written statement to the effect that the suit is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and no specific issue has also been framed referring to aforesaid section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and further, neither in the memo of appeal nor in the revisional application the defendant appellant petitioner has taken any ground referring to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and in view of the fact that the plaintiff in his plaint has prayed, amongst others, for a declaration that he is in service and not dismissed and also for decree for all arrears of pay and allowances due and payable to the plaintiff and also relying on the aforesaid decisions I am of the opinion that the plaintiff has also prayed for consequential relief in the form of the prayer for decree for all arrears of pay and allowances due and payable and therefore the suit is maintainable and not hit by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

9. The 3rd contention of Mr Nurullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, is that the decree as passed is not enforceable and therefore a nullity. In support of his submissions the learned Advocate referred to the case of Gladstone, Wyllie & Co Ltd vs. Badsha Miah reported in 11 DLR 528 wherein their Lordships quoted a passage from the case of Andhra University vs. Koraia Durga Lakshmi Mancharam reported in AIR 1951 (Mad) 870 which runs as: "The learned District Judge has, on the other hand, appreciated the legal as well as the factual position, right from the standpoint of legal sense as well as common sense in holding that the declaration, if granted, would not, although ineffective to bring about the plaintiffs to office except on the good sense of the master, and is a futility but a valuable gain for the plaintiff. "The learned Advocate submitted that if the corporation refuses to honour the decision of the court the same cannot be executed and therefore such decree is a nullity. 

10. Mr Shorful Islam Khan, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, submitted that there is difference between the case referred to by Mr M Nurullah and in the instant case and in the aforesaid responded case the parties were private parties whereas in the present case the petitioner is a statutory corporation and, as such, it is obliged under the Constitution of the country to honour and implement any decision of a court of law. He further submitted that in the aforesaid reported case such decree has not been described as nullity but it has been said that the plaintiff gains valuable right. I find substance in the submissions of Mr Shorful Islam Khan. Further, in the reported case of 35 DLR 224 his Lordship has held that a declaratory decree passed in a case without any prayer for consequential relief is an "annuity". Therefore such decree is a gain or annuity for the plaintiff and the implementation is dependent against whom the decree is passed and in the instant case the defendant being a statutory corporation, there is no reason to believe that such corporation will not honour and implement the decision of the court of law. In the present case it seems that the courts below have considered the materials on record in detail and arrived at their decisions with reasoning and while passing the decree the learned courts below have refused the prayer of the plaintiff for arrears pay and allowances and confirmed the continuous service and hence no interference is called for. 
	
11. In the facts and circumstances of the case and for reasons stated above I do not find any illegality or error occasioning failure of justice in the impugned judgment and decree and therefore, I am not inclined to interfere with the same. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged with cost of Taka 2,000.00. The impugned judgment and decree are affirmed. Let the records of the courts below be sent down immediately. 

End.

vs.
Naziur Rahman ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saba J: In this Rule the order dated 30-7-97 passed by the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 105 of 1997 has been called in question. By this order the learned Assistant Judge returned the plaint to the filing Advocate for the plaintiffs for filing afresh with correct valuation of the suit.

2. Short facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that, the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the suit in the 3rd Court of the Assistant Judge, Dhaka for eviction of a monthly tenant, being Title Suit No. 105 of 1997, alleging, inter alia, that the defendant-opposite party was a monthly tenant under them and he defaulted in payment of rent regularly and hence the suit for his eviction. It appears that on the day of filing of the suit on 30-7-97 the learned Assistant Judge issued orders for issuing summons upon the defendant and at the same time he ordered for returning the plaint to the filing Advocate for refilling the same with correct valuation of the suit.

3. Mr AS Md Ramzan Khan the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the learned Assistant Judge erred in law in returning the plaint to the plaintiff-petitioners without recording any finding to the effect that the suit is not triable by him. Mr Khan further submits that the learned Assistant Judge erred in law in returning the plaint without holdings any enquiry to ascertain the correct valuation of the suit in terms of sections 8C and 8D of the Court fees Act and the same has occasioned failure of Justice.

4. No one appears to oppose the Rule. Mr Khan has placed before me the impugned order passed by the learned Assistant Judge. He has also referred to me the provision of section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure as well as section 8C and 8D of the Court-fees Act. In support of his same has contention Mr Khan has referred to me the case of Sola Bibi vs. Amiran Nessa and others reported in 5 BLT 117. Mr Khan has also referred to me the case of Rahmat Ali vs. Banares Silk Industries and another reported in 19 DLR 287, (Special Bench).

5. Section 8C of the Court-fees Act reads as follows:

"If the Court is of opinion that the subject-matter of any suit has been wrongly valued it may revise the valuation and determine the correct valuation and may hold such inquiry as it thinks fit for such purpose."

Section 8D(1) of the Court-fees Act reads as follows:

"For the purpose of an inquiry under section 8C the Court may depute, or issue a commission to any suitable person to make such local or other investigation as may be necessary and to report thereon to the Court. Such report and any evidence recorded by such person shall be evidence in the inquiry.

(2) The Court may, from time to time direct such party to suit as it thinks fit to deposit such sum as the Court thinks reasonable as the costs of the inquiry, and if the costs are not deposited within such time as the Court shall fix, may notwithstanding anything contained in any other Act dismiss the suit if such party is the plaintiff or the appellant and in any other case, may recover the cost as a public demand."

6. Mr Khan submits that having regard to the provisions of law regarding the valuation of the suit as envisaged by sections 8C and 8D of the Court- fees Act the learned Assistant Judge erred in law in returning the plaint to the filing Advocate of the plaintiffs without himself ascertaining the valuation of the suit by holding an inquiry in the matter either by himself or by any other person appointed by him in that behalf. Mr Khan next submits that the learned Assistant Judge also erred in law in pointing to the market-value of the suit property to be the guiding factor in determining the valuation of the suit ignoring the frame and scope of the suit and the occasioned failure of justice. In support of his contention Mr Khan has placed reliance on the case of Rahmat Ali VS. M/s Banares Silk Industries and another reported in 19 DLR 289 (Special Bench). In this case it has been held that the valuation of a suit for eviction of a monthly tenant is governed by section 7(XI) of the Court-fees Act and it has no reference to the market value of the suit property.

<u>7. On perusal of the provisions of sections 8C, 8D and 7(XI) of the Court- fees Act it is evident that the frame of the present suit for eviction of a monthly tenant provides an objective standard for valuation of the suit. I do not, therefore, find any justification on the part of the learned Assistant Judge to return the plaint to the filing Advocate without himself making an exercise to determine the correct and proper valuation of the suit, if the valuation of the suit made by the plaintiffs was considered improper and inadequate. Instead of doing so and asking the plaintiffs to pay proper court- fees that might be considered necessary in the facts of the case, the learned Assistant Judge returned the plaint to the filing Advocate with option to refile the same with the correct valuation of the suit.</u>

<u>8. Order VII rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides as follows:</u>

<u>"The plaint shall at any stage of the suit be returned to be presented to the court in which the suit should have been instituted."</u>

9. The learned Assistant Judge passed the impugned order for returning the plaint to the filing Advocate without finding that the suit was filed wrongly before him and he had no jurisdiction either pecuniary or financial, to entertain and try the same and, as such, it was being returned to the filing Advocate for presentation before the appropriate Court. Under such circumstances, the return of the plaint on the ground of improper or inadequate valuation of the suit appears to be totally misconceived and highly superficial. If it appeared to learned Assistant Judge that proper and adequate court-fees were not paid on proper valuation of the suit, he ought to have made in inquiry in the matter and determine the correct valuation of the suit in terms of sections 8C and 8D of the Court-fees Act. In that view of the matter, it must be held that the learned Assistant Judge passed the impugned order legally and arbitrarily ignoring the express provisions of law regarding the return of the plaint and the valuation of the suit.

10. For the reasons stated above, I find that the learned Assistant Judge erred in law in passing the impugned order illegally and arbitrarily and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners are accordingly sustained.

11. In the result, the Rule succeeds and it is made absolute without any order as to costs.

12. The impugned order date 30-7-97 passed by the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. lO5 of 1997 is set aside.

13. The learned Assistant Judge is directed to ascertain the proper valuation of the suit in accordance with law and then to proceed with the suit in pursuance thereof.

Let a copy of this order be communicated to the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for his information and necessary action.

End.

full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: In this Rule at instance of the petitioner M Mohsin Hossain legality of the notice dated 22-7-95 (Annexure-A) issued by the respondent No.4, Sub-Inspector of Police, Motijheel Police Station asking the petitioner to produce its documents is under challenge.

2. Learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submitted that though no investigation was pending against the petitioner he was illegally asked by respondent No.1 to produce his document under section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, as such, the notice is liable to be declared illegal.

<u>3. On going through notice dated 22-7-95 we find that respondent No. 5 MA Salam made a complaint with the Ministry of Home Affairs alleging that petitioner received sum of Taka 12,75,000.00 (Twelve lakh seventy-five thousand) only as advance from him by executing a bainapatra to sell RAJUK Plot No. 11(14) of Road No. 23, Block 3, Banani Dhaka. But due to dispute about the said property petitioner agreed to refund that said advance amount but ultimately did not do so and thus misappropriated the said amount cheating him and in connection with the said complaint petitioner was asked to produce his documents on 24-7-95. Petitioner stated in paragraph 4 of the petition that in compliance with the said notice he appeared before the respondent No. 4 and obtained 15 days' time and thereafter filed this case. On going through the said notice we find that there is no reference of any case in that notice in connection with which petitioner was asked to produce his documents. Section 160 of the Code of of Criminal Procedure authorises police officer to direct any person to appear before him in connection with investigation of a criminal case. Under clause (1) of subsection (1) of section 4 of the said Code investigation includes all the proceedings under the Code for the collection of evidence conducted by a police officer or by any person (other than a Magistrate) who is authorised by a Magistrate in this behalf. Thus it appears that investigation under section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure includes also an enquiry directed by the Magistrate. Since there is no reference as to any investigation or enquiry in the said notice we are of the view that the same has been issued by the respondent No. 4 in an un authorised manner.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. Impugned notice dated 22-7-95 is declared to have been issued without any lawful authority and of no legal effect.</u>

End.

Vs
