case_source: (From the judgment and order dated January 6, 1993 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 954 of 1991).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman, J.: Respondent No. 1 instituted Title Suit No. 122 of 1987 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Fourth Court Dhaka for a declaration that the order dismissing him from the post of Headmaster of the Post Office High School, Motijheel Dhaka-2 was illegal and not binding upon him. His case, in brief, is that in 1986 defendant No. 2, Mr. GM Delwar Hossain, the then Chairman of the Managing Committee of the Appellant School, requested him to allow his relation Rehana Yasmin, to appear in the SSC Examination, though she fared very badly in the test examination. In view of a decision of the School Committee the plaintiff could not allow that student to appear in the SSC Examination. On 11 January 1987 the plaintiff was illegally suspended from his service. He challenged the order of suspension by filing the above suit. By an order dated 15 August 1988 he was dismissed from service. After amending the plaint the plaintiff then challenged the order of dismissal. He asserted that the allegations of corruption and misappropriation, made against him, were false; that the enquiry committee did not hold that enquiry properly; that the Committee only asked him to answer four questions and it did not examine any witness or any paper in his presence. It was further urged that Mr. Harun-ur-Rashid Talukdar, the teacher representative in the enquiry committee, was absent on 7 April 1988, but the enquiry committee continued its proceeding without adjourning it and without giving a reasonable opportunity to the plaintiff to defend himself. No second show cause notice was served before passing the order of dismissal.

2. The case of the appellant, the school committee, is that the plaintiff, as the Headmaster, was the drawing and disbursing officer and was personally responsible for accounts of the school and he was to approve the audit report. From 3 January 1987 to 8 January 1987 the plaintiff was repeatedly asked by defendant No. 2 to issue a notice for holding an emergent meeting of the Managing Committee for discussion of accounts, but he did not pay any heed to that. Defendant No. 2, however, managed to issue a notice for holding an emergent meeting on 11 January 1987. The plaintiff received the notice duly on 10.1.87. He deliberately remained absent in the meeting held on 11.1.87, although he attended the school on that date. On review of the allegations made against the plaintiff the School committee unanimously decided to place him under suspension with effect from 12 January 1987. The plaintiff did not attend the school on 12 January 1987, but he engaged some goonda elements to disturb the law and order situation and academic atmosphere in the school. On a complaint the Officer-in-Charge of the Motijheel Police Station started a criminal case, No. 66 dated 12 January 1987 under section 406 of the Penal Code, against the Headmaster. The plaintiff did not make over the charge of the office of the Headmaster to the acting Headmaster, and ultimately on 14 January 1987 the locked almirahs of the Headmaster's office were opened in presence of a First Class Magistrate and other witnesses. An enquiry committee was set up with four members. The report of the enquiry committee revealed that the plaintiff misappropriated from the school fund a sum of Taka 94,754.75 paisa. The plaintiff was then dismissed from his service and that the order of dismissal was approved by the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education.

3. The trial Court dismissed the suit after finding that the plaintiff was given an opportunity to show cause and defend himself. On appeal the appellate court, however, decreed the suit. It found that on 28 February 1988 the plaintiff was only asked to answer to four questions, and he submitted his answers. No witness was examined by the school authority. The enquiry committee started its proceeding with Mr. Nurullah, the Headmaster of the New Model High School, as the teacher representative. Later on, in place of Mr. Nurullah, Mr. Harun-ur-Rashid was included in the enquiry committee as the teacher representative. The plaintiff was asked to appear before the enquiry committee on 7 April 1988 at 3:00 PM. As on that date Mr. Harun-ur-Rashid was absent, the appellate Court held that the enquiry committee ought to have, in law and equity, adjourned its proceeding to another date, but the defendants without fixing another date for enquiry committee obtained an ex pane report from the enquiry committee and dismissed the plaintiff. According to the appellate Court, the plaintiff did not get full opportunity to defend himself and, that though there was no provision in the Regulations for second show cause notice before dismissal the plaintiff ought to have been given, in interest of justice, a second show cause notice. The High Court Division upheld the judgment of the court of appeal below.

4. The appellant now contends that the High Court Division did not at all consider that the appellate Court reversed the decision of the trial Court without adverting to the reasonings of the trial Court; that the second show cause notice was not available to the plaintiff, not being a government servant; and that as there is no rule that in the absence of a member of the enquiry committee its proceeding should be automatically adjourned, the deliberations of the enquiry committee could not be questioned on the supposed violation of principles of natural justice.

<u>5. Taking a cue from a query from this Court whether the order of approval by the Board was challenged in the suit, the learned Counsel for the appellant raised a new plea that the plaintiffs failure to challenge the order of approval of the Board by appropriately amending the plaint would make the decree made by the appellate Court as inconsequential. He has cited two cases. In Bauribandhu Misra Vs. IG of Police and others AIR 1970 Orissa 213 where a new point, not mentioned in the petition, was allowed to be raised when accuracy of factual basis of statement was not disputed. In RJ Singh Vs. State of Delhi AIR 1971 (SC) 1552 (1553) a jurisdictional point as to whether the sanction for the prosecution was granted by the Government was allowed to be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court. The new plea need not be considered if the order of dismissal is found to be in order.</u>

6. The learned counsel for respondent No. 1 frankly concedes that the plaintiff was not entitled to a second show cause notice before the passing of the order of dismissal. He has, however, insisted that in the facts of the case the plaintiff was not given full opportunity to defend himself before the enquiry committee.

7. Regulation 14 of the Recognised Non-Government Secondary School Teachers (Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka) Terms and Conditions of Service Regulations, 1979 provides the following procedure.

"(1) When a teacher is to be proceeded against for offences specified in regulation 11, he shall be called upon by a notice to submit a written explanation within seven days as to why the penalty or penalties specified in the notice should not be imposed on him for the alleged offences and asking him if he desires to be heard in person.

(2) On receipt of the explanation from the teacher and his desire to be heard in person, the authority competent to impose penalty shall constitute a three member enquiry committee with a Chairman.

"Provided that at least one of the members of the Committee shall be from the teaching profession"

<u>8. By a notice dated 27 August 1987 the enquiry committee asked the plaintiff to give his reply to the charges within seven days. The plaintiff received the notice on 31 August 1987. On his prayer he was permitted on 15 September 1987 to examine the records. The plaintiff examined the records on four different dates between 22 September to 1 October 1987, and submitted his reply on 28 September 1987. Thereafter, the plaintiff was asked to appear before the enquiry committee on 7 April 1988 with relevant papers and make his submissions. On that date he wrote to the Chairman of the enquiry committee that as Mr. Harun-ur-Rashid Talukdar, the teacher-representative, was absent he thought it would not be proper for him to give any reply, and that in any case his reply would be found in his earlier reply, submitted on 28 October 1987 to the queries made by the committee, and that a copy of that reply was lying with the Chairman. It is to be noted that the plaintiff did not ask for any adjournment nor did he ask for personal hearing or examination of any witness. The finding of the committee was, therefore, necessarily to be made on the papers produced before the enquiry committee. In Bashir Ahmed Vs. Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation and others 44 DLR (AD) 267-270 where no witness was examined it was observed:</u>

<u>"The domestic tribunal is not a court to follow procedures of a trial or enquiry according to the Civil Procedure Code. In appropriate cases the domestic tribunal may arrive at a decision simply by questioning the accused and considering his explanation."</u>

9. The appellant has cited Project in Charge, Paruma (Eastern) Ltd. Vs. Aminur Rahman Khan and another 31 DLR 124 and the General Manager, Jamuna Oil Company Ltd. Vs. Golap Rahman & another 34 DLR (AD) 166 where the following provision in sub-section (7) of section 35 of the Industrial Relation Ordinance, 1969 came up for construction:

"If any member of the Labour Court is absent from or is otherwise unable to attend any sitting of the Court, the proceeding of the court may continue and the decision or award may be given in the absence of such member; and no act, proceeding, decision of the Court shall be invalid or called in question merely on the ground of such absence."

10. Because of the enabling provision, it was held in 31 DLR 124 that where the proceeding has already started with the required number of members and if thereafter there is any casual absence of any member, or if he ceases to be a member or is incapable of sitting in the Court further, the proceeding need not be stopped but it may be carried to its conclusion. In 34 DLR (AD) 166 it was similarly held that if, after the constitution of the Court, a member is absent from a sitting of the Court such absence will not invalidate the decision of the Court.

<u>11. In the aforementioned Regulation 14 for drawing proceedings there is no provision similar to sub-section (7) of section 35 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance 1969. However, as there is no provision imposing a legal obligation on a member of the enquiry committee to be present in all its sittings no legal consequence will follow from a member's failure to attend such a sitting. The enquiry committee will follow the ordinary rules of a committee meeting. Where a member fails to be present the committee may suo motu or on application by a party interested may adjourn its meeting or carry on its proceeding to its conclusion. Both the appellate Court and the High Court Division failed to consider that the procedure for enquiry as enjoined under Regulation 14 was complied with in this case. No principle of fair trial was violated. The enquiry committee was properly constituted. The vacancy in the place of Mr. Nurullah, the teacher-representative, was properly filled in. When the teacher-representative was not present the enquiry committee could have adjourned its hearing on the prayer of the plaintiff, but no such prayer was made. And there is no mandatory provision in the Regulations that in the absence of a member of the enquiry committee its meeting is to be adjourned.</u>

<u>12. Again, there is no rule or service condition that the order of dismissal could only be passed after a prior second show cause notice to the employee. The appellate Court, however, invoked the principles of equity of justice and held that when the teacher-representative was absent the meeting of the enquiry committee ought to have been adjourned, and that the plaintiff deserved a second show cause notice before the order of dismissal.</u>

<u>13. The reasonings of the appellate Court are flawed. The High Court Division ought to have disapproved such judicial latitudinarianism. The plaintiff had the full opportunity to examine the papers and place his case. He did not ask for any personal hearing, nor did he ask for examination of any witness or production of any document. The enquiry report, on the basis of papers and the plaintiffs answer to the committee's queries, was endorsed by, all the three members. The order of dismissal, based on that report, was approved by the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education. At the trial the plaintiff did not challenge the order of dismissal or its approval by the Board in the manner it was assailed at the appellate stage. There is no merit in the plaintiffs cause. The appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree of the trial Court are restored and those of the appellate Court and the High Court Division are set aside. No costs.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Mr. AKM Nurun Nabi Khan with Mr. Khurshed Alam, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
Mr. Md. Azizul Huq, Advocate ----- For the Opposite-Party.
parties:
Ajiran Nessa Bewa and others ----- Petitioners.
Vs.
Md. Abdul Mannan ----- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 29.5.85 passed by the learned Munsif, Sreebordi, in OC Execution Case No. 13 of 1984.

2. The opposite-party Md. Abdul Mannan a minor, through his father, filed a suit for permanent injunction against the petitioner No. 1 Ajiran Nessa Bewa and her three sons, the other petitioners and obtained an ex parte decree on 28.4.80 restraining the petitioners from permanently entering into the scheduled land. The opposite party subsequently file, the aforesaid execution case under Order 21, rule 32 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure alleging that the petitioners disobeyed the decree by forcibly entering into the schedule land on 15th Baishakh, 1389 BS (after about two years from the decree), erecting huts and planting trees.

3. The petitioners denied the allegations and contended that the petitioner No. 1 Ajiran Nessa had been in exclusive possession of the scheduled land since 26.3.46 when her husband transferred the land to her by a registered kabinnama of that date.

4. The learned Munsif allowed the execution case by the aforesaid judgment and his order runs as follows:

"that the instant execution case is allowed on contest against the judgment-debtor Nos. 1, 2, & 4 and ex parte against Judgment-debtor No. 3 without cost. The Judgment-debtor Nos. 1, 2 & 3 Ajirannessa, Amanullah, Azim Ali are directed to remove the said obstruction like houses, banana trees and bamboo jhar, etc. from the decreetal land of schedule No. 1 of the instant petition within 35 (thirty five) days from the order at their own cost. Otherwise the lands of schedule No. 2 of the instant petition under the ownership of Judgment-debtor Nos. 1, 2 & 3 named Ajirannessa, Amanullah, Azim Ali will be attached and to be sold in open auction directed and guided by the court and the decree holder to be compensated, with Tk. 5000.00 for his loss and sufferings from the attached property."

The moot question, therefore, before me is whether the learned Munsif can pass such order under the provision of Order 21, rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

5. Rule 31 contains five sub-rules and an illustration. It provides the mode of execution of "decree for specific performance, for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction."

6. In the case of a decree for an injunction, if the judgment-debtor willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced according to sub-rule 1 by his detention in the civil prison or by the attachment of his property or by both. Sub-rule 2 states as to how such detention and attachment will be effected in case of a decree passed against a corporation. Sub-rule 3 states that where attachment under sub-rule 1 or 2 has remained in force for one year and if the judgment-debtor has not obeyed the decree the attached property may be sold on the application of the decree-holder and out of the proceeds the Court may award compensation to the decree-holder. Sub-rule 4 states that if the decree is obeyed and costs of execution is paid or no application is made for sale at the end of one year of attachment or if made, is refused, the attachment shall cease. Sub-rule 5 states that in lieu of or addition to all or any of the aforesaid processes, the Court may direct that the act required to be done may be done at the cost of the judgment-debtor and the expenses incurred may be recovered as if they were included in the decree.

7. It appears from the above quoted order the learned Munsif directed the judgment-debtors to remove the alleged obstruction obviously under sub-rule s and in case of non-compliance thereof ordered: attachment and sale of their property and awarded compensation of Tk. 5,000.00 to the decree holder out of the sale proceeds apparently under sub-rules 1 and 3 respectively.

8. As to applicability of rule 32, there are two decisions of our Court, namely, 16 DLR 61 (Barhanuddin Ahmed Vs. Veda Brata Chakraborty) and 33 DLR 207 (Moyna Mia Vs. Haji Abdus Samad) holding different views and an obiter dictum in 13 DLR 531 (Saleh Ahmed Chowdhury Vs. Kabir Ahmed) expressing the same view as in the later decision. According to 16 DLR 61, sub-rule 1 of rule 32 is not applicable to a prohibitory decree when there is violation of it as "there remains no decree to be enforced" while according to 33 DLR 207, it is a "particular manner or method of enforcing an otherwise in executable prohibitory decree if it is violated". According to both the decisions, however, sub-rule 5 is applicable only to decree for mandatory injunction.

9. In view of these decisions holding different views, the issue raised in this case seems to me a piquant one and calls for elaborate discussion.

10. It is necessary at the outset to state briefly the object and scope of the Code of Civil Procedure. The object of the Code is to consolidate the law relating to Civil Procedure; but it is well-settled that the Code is not and cannot be exhaustive. The Code deals with procedural matters and not with substantive rights. The sections of the Code create jurisdiction while the Rules indicate the mode in which they are to be executed.

11. Section 38 of the Code, which creates the jurisdiction in case of execution of the decrees, is as follows:

"38. A decree may be executed either by the Court which passed it, or by the Court to which it is sent for execution." Order 21 containing 103 rules indicates the modes in which the decrees are to be executed obviously by the Court empowered under section 38.

12. It is now convenient to quote rule 32 as hereunder:

"32. Decree for specific performance, for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction:

(1) Where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution or conjugal rights, or for an injunction, has been passed, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced in the case of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction by his detention in the civil prison, or by the attachment of his property or by both.

(2) Where the party against whom a decree for specific performance or for an injunction has been passed is a corporation, the decree may be enforced by the attachment of the property of the corporation or, with the leave of the Court, by the detention in the civil prison of the directors or other principal officers thereof, or by both attachment and detention.

(3) Where any attachment under sub-rule (1) or sub-rule (2) has remained in force for one year, if the judgment-debtor has not obeyed the decree and the decree-holder has applied to have the attached property sold, such property may be sold; and out of the proceeds the Court may award to the decree-holder such compensation as it thinks fit, and shall pay the balance (if any) to the judgment-debtor on his application.

(4) Where the judgment-debtor has obeyed the decree and paid all costs of executing the same which he is bound to pay, or where, at the end of one year, from the date of the attachment, no application to have the property sold has been made, or if made has been refused, the attachment shall cease.

(5) Where a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction has not been obeyed, the Court may, in lieu of or in addition to all or any of the processes aforesaid, direct that the act required to be done may be done so far as practicable by the decree-holder or some other person appointed by the Court, at the cost of the judgment debtor, and upon the act being done the expenses incurred may be ascertained in such manner as the Court may direct and may be recovered as if they were included in the decree."

13. In 33 DLR 207 four reasons have been given in favor of applicability of sub-rule 1 of rule 32 in case of violation of a prohibitory decree. First reason is that rule 32 is a particular method of enforcing an otherwise in executable decree, if it is violated and this method of "enforcing" the decree have nothing to do with its "execution".

<u>14. I am afraid this is not the correct approach. According to rule 6 of Order 20 a decree "shall specify clearly the relief granted". The decree which requires execution for completing the relief so granted can only be executed under section 38 which gives jurisdiction to the Court to execute such decree according to the procedure as provided in Order 21. The question of enforcing a decree in wider sense is thus not contemplated in the Code. When there is violation of a prohibitory decree there remains as such no decree to be enforced in the said sense of execution. In fact, the violation is a fresh cause of action and the remedy lies in a separate suit.</u>

<u>15. Furthermore heading of Part II of the Code containing section 38 is "Execution" and the heading of Order 21 is "Execution of Decree and Orders". It is an acceptable rule that the heading of a chapter can be looked into as that can be regarded as preamble whose function is to explain ambiguity and may either restrict or extend its scope. So there is nothing like enforcing a decree which does not contain any relief which per se requires to be executed.</u>

16. Second reason which is also the view of the Indian High Courts is that to do what a person is prohibited from doing is just as much disobedience as if he fails to do what is directed to do.

17. Third reason is that rule 32 is a special penalty and is not a specific method of execution of a decree in terms of the decree.

18. I have already answered partly against these reasons. The second reason sounds good as a broad principle, but does not, as indicated by me, fit in with the provisions of the Code. The third reason is not also correct. Rule 32 like its other sister rules in the compartment of Order 21 provides mode of execution of certain decrees.

19. Fourth reason is based on the presumption that there must be procedure in the Code for punishing a judgment-debtor in case he violates a prohibitory decree, otherwise it will be practically useless to obtain a decree for permanent injunction. The Code, as already stated, is not and cannot be exhaustive. In all civilized countries, it is found, despite the best laws, residium of injustice will remain. Let us take the case of declaratory decree. Their effectiveness of execution depends on the good sense of the judgment-debtor. The decree-holder of a prohibitory decree, of course, has the remedy in a separate suit.

20. To understand rule 32, we must keep in view firstly, as to why three decrees, namely, for specific performance, for restitution of conjugal rights and for an injunction have been grouped together in sub-rule 1. They must be of similar nature. Nature of the first two being mandatory, the other must be of similar nature. Secondly, expression "failed to obey", "has not obeyed" and "has obeyed" used respectively in sub-rules 1, 3 and 4 and the expression "act required to be done" used in sub-rule 5 must have the same meaning as to obeying the decrees. To presume that sub-rules 1, 3 and 4 relate to both the decrees for prohibitory injunction and mandatory injunction and sub-rule 5 relates only to decree for mandatory injunction is to deprive these sub-rules of their plain meaning. Thirdly, the words "in lieu or in addition to all or any of the processes mentioned aforesaid" stated in sub-rule 5 which prescribes direct mode of execution indicates only those types of decrees for specific performance of contract and for injunction to which all the sub-rules can be made applicable or, in other words, all the five rules must be taken conjunctively. These five rules prescribed both indirect and direct modes of execution. As the decree for restitution of conjugal right cannot be executed in accordance with sub-rule 5, Order 21 has prescribed another mode of execution thereof in rule 33. Similarly, it has prescribed further direct mode of execution of decree for execution of document or endorsement of negotiable instrument in rule 34. Had it been the intention that Order 21 would apply to decree for prohibitory injunction, there should have been provision therein for direct mode of execution thereof like those decrees.

21. 13 DLR and 33 DLR 207 have followed some decisions of Indian High Courts. Those and other similar decisions chronologically are 1934 Cal. 402 (Hem Chandra Nashkar Vs. Narendra Nails Bose), 1938 Pat. 522 (Toon Lal Vs. Sanoo Lat), 1945 Oudh 81 (Prag Datt Vs. Keder Nath) 1950 Mad. 237 (Nail Chinnabba Chesty Vs. Chengalroyo Chesty), 1954 Nag. 245 (Arabrao Domajee Vs. Alma Ram Chowdhury), 1961 Mysore 268 (Gundila Manjappa Vs. Manjakke Shedthi), 1961 Punjab 547 (Murari Lal Vs. Nawal Kishore), 1969 AP 92 (Eveuru Venkata Subbayya Vs. Srieshti Veerayya) and 1969 Kerala 232 (Paul Vs. Cheeran Narayannan).

22. These decisions are based on the reasons as those of 33 DLR 207 and as such I need not reiterate my reasons for disagreeing with them.

23. Lastly, I shall point out impossibility in enforcing the decree for prohibitory injunction in case of violation thereof in the manner as provided in Order 21.

24. A decree is executed by a written application which is prescribed form being No. 6 of Appendix E of Schedule 1 to the Code. This form is in accordance with rule 11 of Order 21. If application for execution is filed within one year from the date of decree, it is executed without any notice to the judgment-debtor. Under rule 22 of Order 21 a judgment-debtor is entitled to get a show cause notice only when an application is filed after one year from the date of decree. The Code is silent about the procedure which will have to be adopted if the execution of the decree is to be dependent on subsequent act of the judgment-debtor disobeying the decree. This is significant. Such silence indicates that disobedience to decree as stated in rule 32 means, in the narrow sense, disobedience to the mandatory order which the decree contains itself.

<u>25. I, therefore, most respectfully differ with the decision in 13 DLR 531, 33 DLR 207 and like others. I agree with the decision in 16 DLR 61 that when a prohibitory injunction is violated, the remedy is not by putting the decree into execution, but by adopting other measures as provided by the law. As in the present case, the prohibitory injunction has been violated, the decree is not executable and the execution case is not maintainable for any of the remedies under rule 32 of Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

In the result, this rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated 29.5.85 passed by the learned Munsif, Sreebordi, in OC Execution Case No. 13 of 1984 is set aside and the execution case is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
AF Hasan Ariff with Zakir Hossain Munshi, Syed Golam Masud and ZA Mamun, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Rafiq-Ul Huq, AR Yousuf, M Nurullah and Mahmudul Islam-Amicus Curiae.
parties:
Mahboob Uddin Ahmed ------ Petitioner
vs.
Bangladesh Election Commissioner, and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
KM Hasan J: The Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondent No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned notification No. wbdm/wcs/Rvt mvs-29/98 2072 (H dated 15-4•98. as contained in Annexure-C to the writ petition should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the said notification should not be cancelled and rescinded. 

2. Since the matter raised a constitutional question of importance we asked Mr Rafiq-Ul Huq, Mr AR Yousuf, Mr M Nurullah and Mr M Mahmudul Islam, the learned senior' counsels of this Court to be present at the time of hearing and assist us in the mauer as amicus curiae. 

3. The General election to Parliament held in 1996 included a constituency in Barisal Division called constituency No. 125, Barisal 5. The polling took place on 12-6-96. The petitioner as well as some more candidates contested the election, but the principal contestants were the petitioner and late Dr Ehtesamul Hoq Nasim Biswas, son of former President, Abdur Rahman Biswas. It is stated by the petitioner that Dr Nasim Biswas was declared elected as a member of parliament, while the petitioner was shown to have secured the second position. After the gazette notification of the result of the constituency on 16-6-96 the petitioner filed an election petition before the Election Commission, Bangladesh Election Commission on 26-7-96 under Article 49 of the Representation of the People's Order 1972 (President's Order 155 of 1972), (Annexure-A). The gravamen of the petitioner, as stated in the election petition, is that he had been deprived of victory by corrupt practice. 

4. The election petition was duly forwarded to the District Judge and Election Tribunal, Barisal by the respondent No.1, the Bangladesh Election Commission, and it was registered as Election Case No. 5 of 1996. Subsequently when an election tribunal was constituted by the Government for Barisal District, it was transferred to the Barisal Divisional Election Tribunal where it was renumbered as Election Case No. 1 of 1997. 

5. On the death of the returned candidate, Dr Ehtesamul Hoq Nasim Biswas, on 12-3-98 a date for ex parte disposal was fixed on 15-4-98 by the tribunal. On that date two other candidates entered appearance and prayed- for time for submitting written statements, which was granted and 17-5-98 was fixed for filing written statement (Annexure-B). 

6. The Tribunal again fixed 7-6-98 for ex parte disposal of the petition. It is complained by the petitioner that the respondent No.1 Bangladesh Election Commission, knowing fully well that the Election Case is pending before the Tribunal, issued Election Schedule for holding by-election vide Notification No. wbdm/wcs-1/Rvt mvs-29/98/2072  dated 15-4-98, fixing '26-4-98 for filing nomination, 27-4-98 for scrutiny, 6-5-98 for withdrawal of candidature and 24-5-98 for poll. 

7. On 21-4••98 the petitioner through his learned Advocate issued notice upon the respondent No. 1 requesting to postpone the election of the constituency No. 125, Barisal 5 and not to hold it during the pendency of the aforementioned election petition (Annexures D. Dl and D2). It is alleged that the election schedule given by the respondent No. 1 is illegal and without lawful authority as an election case was filed before it by the petitioner, which was subsequently forwarded to the Election Tribunal. At present Divisional Election Tribunal is in seisin of the Election Case No.1 of 1997. 

8. It is further stated in the petition that on an identical issue in the unreported Writ Petition No. 3046 of 1996 the Rule was made absolute by the High Court Division on 25-8-96 by holding that for ends of justice, the bye-election shall remain stayed till the disposal of the election petition. A copy of the Judgment and order was produced before us. 

9. The• petitioner thought that if the by-election was allowed to be conducted, as per schedule, irreparable loss would have been caused to him and therefore he sought to intercept the progress of the by-election by invoking the writ jurisdiction of this Court. 

10. Mr AF Hasan Ariff, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that irrespective of the mandatory nature of Article 123(4) of the Constitution the same has been overridden by Article 125 because of a non obstanate clause in the latter Article, Therefore, the election contemplated under Article 123 should be kept in abeyance till-the tribunal gives its decision otherwise two members might be imbibed for the same seat. 

11. Mr AF Hasan Ariff submits that the election process does not always end with the declaration of the result. In case of a dispute it continues till the final disposal of the election dispute. The Bangladesh Constitution has recommended this in Article 125(b). This Article read with Articles 62 and 67 of the Representation of the People Order of 1972 (president's Order155 of 1972) gives the Tribunal power in an election dispute to declare the election of the returned candidate to be void, the petitioner or any other contesting candidate to have been duly elected or the election as a whole to be void and finally to communicate its decision, to the Commission for publication in the official gazette. If meanwhile ie before the disposal of the election petition the successful candidate dies and no other respondent except the contesting candidate remains to contest, the Tribunal may decide the case ex parte under Article 70 of the President's Order 155 of 1972. Therefore" after the death of Dr Ehtasamul Hoq Nasim Biswas, as the petitioner has filed an election case before the Tribunal and the next date is fixed on 7 -6-98 for ex parte decision, the election process is still continuing and a vested right of having the election petition decided has accrued to him. This right, according to him, has the Constitutional protection under Article 118(4) of the Constitution and cannot be taken away: It continues to exist till the election petition is finally settled. 

12. Mr Ariff further argues that if an election, contemplated under Article 123, is free from dispute it will be a complete election as it reaches a finality with gazette notification. But in case of pendency of an election dispute there will be no such finality and no vacancy will legally occur to the parliamentary seat of the disputed constituency till the dispute is settled finally. As a result without a seat being vacant there is no scope for Article 123 to become operative. 

13. Mr Ariff also urges that because of the poll result being challenged by the petitioner by an election petition the petitioner will be left helpless without any remedy if the by-election is held as per article 123(4) of the Constitution. Chapter V of the President's Order 155 of 1972 starting with Article 49 and ending with Article 72 deals with election dispute and provide law for different stages of Parliamentary Election. Therefore these provisions are required to be read with Article 125 of the Constitution dealing, among others, with election dispute. Article 125 of the Constitution, which relates to delimitation of the constituency, allotment of seats and election dispute has been provided with the protection of law under the Constitution and this protection shall automatically extend to the relevant provisions of President's Order 155 of 1972 dealing with election dispute. The petitioner's right to the seat in dispute is, therefore, protected by law as long as the dispute is not settled by the Tribunal. 

14. The next point canvassed by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the Election Commission has a mandate under the Constitution to resolve the election dispute. Articles 118, 119 and 123 of the Constitution when read together will show that the Election Commission is entrusted to conduct both general and by-election. Similarly, Article 125 read with Chapter V of the president's Order 155 of 1972 makes the Chief Election Commission the sole agent and the Tribunal only a machinery to resolve the election dispute. Since election dispute is a part of election process the Election Commission should not have abandoned the election disputed by announcing election schedule for holding by-election. Article 125 backed by a non obstante clause gives the Election Commission a mandate to resolve the election dispute first and not to bypass it and then, if necessary, hold the by election. The mandate gives Article 125 precedence over any other provision of the constitution whether mandatory or not. Therefore, the proposed bye-election of the Constituency 125, Barisal, 5 should not be held till the disposal of the election dispute. 

15. Mr Ariff submits that if the Election Commission is allowed to hold the by-election it will nave an adverse impact on other Articles of the Constitution and provisions of other laws relating to election dispute. For example: (a) if an election is held now in the disputed constituency under Article 123, before the election dispute is finally decided, it will amount to adjudication of the dispute by the Election Commission and the dismissal of the election dispute (b) it will bean affront to Article 125 of the Constitution, which being supported by a non obstante clause should prevail over all other Articles of the Constitution, Article 123 is neither out of the Constitution nor does it empower the Election Commission to decide the election petitions. Endorsed by the non obstante clause Article 125 of the Constitution will overrule the power entrusted to the Election Commission under Article 123 to hold election  and lastly, (c) holding of by-election, before the  election dispute is settled, will make the Tribunal subordinate to the Election Commission. It is true that the Tribunal, as the machinery for adjudication. of the election disputes, has been set out by the Election Commission, yet the Tribunals are not subordinate bodies to the Election Commission. Their jurisdiction is drawn from Article 125(b) of the Constitution and they are manned by subordinate judiciary who are in no way subordinate to the Election Commission. Being established by law the functions of the Tribunals should in no way be interfered with by the Election Commission. 

16. Mr Hassan Ariff submits that the respondent NO.1; the Election Commission has acted without any lawful authority by initiating the by- election in the constituency, 125 Barisal, 5 in respect of which the election petition filed by the petitioner is pending before the election Tribunal. The election petition being sub judice before an appropriate forum the Election Commission should not have preempted the final outcome of the election petition. 
17. Lastly, Mr. Ariff submits that dispute does not abate with the death of an election candidate. Articles 52 and 70 of the President's Order 155 of 1972 have taken care of such a situation. In this case with the filing of the election petition after the death of the successful candidate Article 70 has already taken effect. Therefore, the election dispute cannot be done away with. If death does not take away the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to adjudicate the election dispute the Election Commission cannot adjure the jurisdictional fact. Therefore the Election Commission is devoid of authority to hold election under Article 123. 

18. Expressing his agreement with the learned Counsel for the petitioner, Mr Rafiq-UI Huq, the learned Counsel, has submitted that a general bar has' been imposed on all the Articles of the Constitution by the non obstante clause in Article 125. This bar will include Article 123, though a mandatory provision. Therefore, while the election petition is pending the Election Commission should not have given the election schedule for the disputed constituency. In this connection he submits that the election process starts from filing of the nomination paper and continues till the disposal of the election petition. He further submits that Article 118 of the Constitution makes the Election Commission an   independent body, subordinate to none but subject to the Constitution only, Article 119 of the Constitution provides that in superintending, directing, controlling and conducting both presidential and parliamentary elections the Election Commission shall perform such functions as may be prescribed by the Constitution or by any other law. Therefore, in view of the non obstante clause in Article 125, it is incumbent upon the Election Commission to allow the election petition to proceed to its conclusion before an election schedule for by-election under Article 123 is given. The death of Doctor Ehtesamul Hoq Nasim Biswas, according to him, 'has only created a physical vacancy in Parliament, no constitutional or legal vacancy has occurred because of continuance of the election process. Article 70 of President's Order 155 of 1972 which deals with such situation clearly states that if before the conclusion of an election petition, a respondent dies and no other respondent remains to contest, the Tribunal shall decide the case ex parte. Lastly, for viewing the whole problem from the angle of finding the true intentions of the legislature, the learned Counsel urges us to apply the well known principle of harmonious interpretation. 

19. Mr AR Yousuf, the learned Counsel, agrees with Mr Rafiq-Ul Huq, concerning the vacancy of the seat and with both Mr Ariff and Mr Huq regarding the supremacy of Article 125 over Article 123. To enforce his argument further Mr Yousuf points out that Article 125 being a subsequent Article, it will prevail over Article 123. In his opinion, there is no legal vacancy because of the non obstante clause in Article 125 and pendency of the election dispute before the Tribunal. Therefore, he concludes that the election petition filed by the petitioner must be disposed of before the election is held. 

20. Me M Nurullah the learned Counsel, on the other hand, while differing with the concept that no legal or constitutional vacancy has occurred, ventured to find out what is meant by vacancy but found that it is neither defined in the Constitution nor in the President's Order 155 of 72. The definitive clause of our Constitution, Article 152, does not define vacancy. In his quest he checked the Indian Constitution also but he submits no definition of vacancy of a seat could be found there. According to him, the death of a candidate definitely creates a vacancy, both physical and legal in Parliament. 

21. Regarding the question, which one of the two mandatory Articles of the Constitution will prevail, Me Nurullah argues poignantly that Articles 123 and 125 deal with matters completely different from each other. While Article 123 refers to by-election in case of casual vacancy, Article 125 refers to election dispute. Sub-Article 124 of the Constitution provides that in case of a seat falling vacant otherwise than reason of the dissolution of Parliament an election shall be held within ninety days of the occurrence of the vacancy. This, according to Mr Nurullah, is a special feature in our Constitution and cannot be found in the Indian Constitution. Therefore, it is a mandate by the Constitution upon the Election Commission to hold election under Article 123. He finds that there is no apparent conflict between the two Articles as they relate to two different issues. Lastly, by referring to Article 124 of the Constitution Me Nurullah argues that this Article contemplates for securing the due constitution of Parliament' which, according to him, means a full Parliament and the absence of a single member indefinitely does not make a Parliament a full Parliament. There are three hundred seats, and none of them should remain vacant indefinitely and should be filled quickly in terms of the Constitution. He claims a Parliament cannot be filled by a dead man. 

22. According to Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel, the writ petition was filed out of fear that the by-election will defeat the petitioner's right This has led the petitioner to rely on the non obstante clause in Article 125 to obstruct the holding of the by-election so that his right to the seat which has fallen vacant by the death of Dr Ehtesamul Hoq Nasim Biswas is protected. Me Islam then argues that the presence of non obstante clause in an Article makes that Article prevalent over all the Articles of the Constitution only if there is a conflict. Such a situation may arise when two Articles relating to the same power conflict with each other. But when the two provisions relate to two different issues, as is the case between Article 123 and Article 124, there will be no conflict and no question of one prevailing over another will arise. But, he continues, that if ever an occasion arises when Articles 123 and 125 cannot be interpreted without a conflict then because of the non obstante clause Article 125 will prevail over Article 123. This may occur, if the candidate who has filed the election petition eventually gets a declaration that the election of the member who is declared successful is void and he himself had been duly elected. There will be two candidates representing the same constituency at the same time. One of them declared to be duly elected at the genera election and the other declared to have been elected at the by-election. Therefore, an impossible situation will arise. Then and then only, the learned Counsel submits that the non obstante clause will come into effect. In such a case by referring to Bindra's Interpretation of Statutes, 7th Edition page 567 he argues that an attempt should first be made for giving a harmonious interpretation. In this connection he also refers to the case of Abu Ala Maudoodi vs. Misbahul Islam Faruqul reported in 17 DLR (SC) 209 and some more cases reported in AIR 1921 (PC) 240, AIR 1955 (SC) 161 and 18 DLR (SC) 69. However, Me Islam categorically submits that in the instant case at this stage there is no scope for reading conflict between Articles 123 and Article 125. 

23. From the above it appears that the questions to be resolved by us, with reference to Article 123 and Article 125, arise in the instant case, due to the death of Doctor Ehtasamul Hoq Biswas, who was elected candidate from constituency, 125, Barisal, 5 in the last election. As the election of the deceased is under challenge before the Tribunal, the petitioner, to protect his right has filed this petition, challenging the impugned notification giving the election schedule. What troubles us in this writ petition is the confusion created by the aforementioned two mandatory provisions of the Constitution. Article 123 of the Constitution reads as follows: 
	Article 123, "(1)……………………. 
	Provided…………………….. 
	(2) ………………………….		 
	(3) ……………………				 
(4) An election to fill the seat of a member of Parliament which falls vacant otherwise than by reason of the dissolution of Parliament shall be held within ninety days of the occurrence of the vacancy. Provided that in a case where, in the opinion of the Chief Election Commissioner, it is not possible, for reasons of an act of God, to hold such election within the period specified in this clause, such election shall be held within ninety days following next after the last day of such period." 

24. The General Rule of interpretation is that if a provision contains direction respecting the time or modes of proceeding for exercise of power, there is at least a strong presumption that the power must be exercised in that time and mode. This time factor and mode of proceeding gives a provision a mandatory nature. Further the use of expression 'shall' in a provision, in general be always taken to be indicative of its mandatory nature, but not, if the neglect of the main object of the provision does not affect the validity of the acts done. In such a case the provision should be held to be directory. What we find in Articles 123 is not only the use of the expression 'shall' but also a time limit of ninety days, within which the election for a seat fallen vacant causally, is to be' held. Therefore there is little scope for controversy that this Article is not meant to be mandatory by the legislature. 

25. Let us now proceed heuristically to find out the implication of Article 125 which reads as follows: "Article 125, Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution: (a) the validity of any law relating to the delimitation of constituencies, or the allotment of seats to such constituencies, made or purporting to be made under Article 124, shall not be called in question in any court. 
(b) no election to the offices of President or to Parliament shall be called in question except by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as may be provided for by or under any law made by Parliament." 

26. From the above it appears that Articles 125(a) which deals with pre-election matters imposes a bar on any action in any court challenging the validity of any law relating to the delimitation of constituencies or the allotment of seats to such constituencies, and Article 125(b) which deals with post-election matter, puts a bar on any action in any court, questioning the election to the office of the President or to Parliament except by an election petition as may be provided by a law made by Parliament. 

27. This Article, as a whole armed with a non obstante clause imposes a blanket bar on litigative challenges to electoral steps taken by the Election Commission and its officers for carrying forward the process of election to its culmination in the formal declaration of the result. Based on Article'125 in Shah Alam's case reported in 41 DLR (AD) 68 a blanket bar has been clamped down upon litigative interference during the process of election. According to this decision the jurisdiction of Article 102 challenging any step in the process of election, including any order of the commission, can be exercised only on limited ground of coram non judice and malice. 

28. The question now arises whether the blanket bar provided in Article 125(b) applies uniformly to all the provisions of the 'Constitution? Is Article 123 covered by the embargo and if so, is Article 125 bar enough to restrain the Election Commission from holding the bye-election within ninety days from the date of occurrence of the casual vacancy? Should the Election Commission, clothed with the comprehensive function to hold election under Article 123 cancel the election schedule, which is already given and wait for the formal declaration of the result of the Election Petition by the Tribunal? 

29. We now reach the constitutional zone relating to the controversy regarding this case. The problem is prickly, calling for application of principles of interpretation to the relevant provisions of the Constitution and those of the President's Order 155 of 1972, which will avoid amomaly and assure justice. Article 125(b) which is pertinent for our purpose and deals with post election matter envisages the challenge to an election by a petition to be presented to such authority as Parliament may by law prescribe. Therefore, the scheme of Article 125(b) and the relevant provisions of President's Order 155 of 1972 should be implemented together, since they are integral to each other and the latter is intended to be nothing more but to include a set-off provisions which had to be passed in implementation of Part VII of the Constitution, dealing with election, and expressing provisions for carrying out the firm and veritable intention expressed in Article 125. 

30. The cardinal principle in interpreting the Constitution is that it should be read as a whole. In case of an apparent repugnancy between the provisions of the Constitution, it should be removed by interpretation. If the repugnancy is real the Court should harmonise them if possible. The court should not readily find inconsistency in the matter of interpretation of Constitution and Statutes. (Fazlul Kader Chowdhury vs. Md Abdul Haque 18 DLR (SC) 69 and Lutfar Rahman vs. Election Commission 27 DLR 278). It is upon the' court to try by interpretation to reconcile the conflict between two provisions, if any, and give effect to both provisions and the construction that render either of them inoperative should not be adopted except in the last resort (Bengal Immunity Co Lid vs. State of Bihar and others AIR 1995 (SC) 161). If such harmonious interpretation is not possible generally the latter provision will prevail over the earlier provision (Anower Hossain's case 41 DLR (AD) 165. It is also a cardinal principle of interpretation of a statue that where interpreting the law, the Court will take law as it finds the law and take every word in its ordinary meaning as expressly said in the Act itself. Legislature means what it says and does not mean what it does not say. 

31. Now if the matter in our hand, be looked at only from the point of view that the conferment of function to the Election Commission, under Article 125, is mandatory, and Article 125 has the power. to supersede all the Articles of the Constitution because of the non obstante clause, then there will be difficulty in giving a harmonious interpretation to Article 125 when read with Article 123. As we have stated above, the quest-ion that has always been agitating our mind is that what do the words 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution' in Article 125 mean. Is it wide enough to take away sweepingly constitutional Obligation of the Election Commission under Article 123 to hold by-election within ninety days of a seat falling casually vacant. 

32. A non obstante clause becomes effective, only if, there is a conflict between two provisions on the same subject matter or on the same issue. But here, there is no conflict between Article 123 and Article 125 of the Constitution. The two belong to different spheres, dealing with different subject matters and different powers. We have already found that Article 12.3 deals with conducting of election once a seat falls casually vacant, whereas Article 125 deals in both pre and post election matters. Clause (b) of Article 125, which is relevant in our case deals with post-election matter like election dispute and provides the forum where such disputes can be resolved. The non obstante clause in Article 125 limits its scope to pre election matters like delimitation of constituencies in the allotment of seats to such constitutencies as defined in clause (a) and post election matter like election dispute as stated in clause (b) of the Article and to any other provisions, if any, in the Constitution relating to the same subject matter. The framers of the Constitution while conferring Article 123 and Article 125 with two specific and separate powers did so with their eyes open and we are to read their intention from the plain words used in the two provisions. The use of non obstante clause in Article 125 does not, in our opinion, contemplate mechanical as opposed to an intelligent exercise of the power thereunder. The extent of the prohibition intended to be imposed is meant to be exercised upon the election dispute, the delimitation of constituencies or the allotments of seats to such constituencies only. The non obstante clause in Article 125 does not curtail obligation conferred upon the Election Commission under Article 123 of the Constitution to hold election. Therefore, both articles can be obeyed and effect can be given to without violating the mandatory nature of either, in the instant case holding of election by the Election Commission to the vacant seat will not stand in the way of given relief to the petitioner by the election Tribunal in the election petition. But we would like to remind that this opinion of ours will hold good as long as Articles 123 and 125 co-exist and do not come into direct conflict with each other. What will be the legal consequence if in course of following their separate and parallel existence the two articles come into conflict with each other, has been considered in a later paragraph. 

33. From the above we have DO doubt in our mind that the Election Commission has to hold election within ninety days from the date ora seat falling vacant casually. Ninety days being the period prescribed for holding the election cannot be extended or delayed in breach of mandatory provision of the Constitution, except in case of an act of God as provided in the proviso to Article 123. This proviso further highlights the mandatory nature of Article 123. The Article has to be held mandatory as the essence of our Constitution is democracy and the purpose of the framers of the Constitution was to fulfill democratic aspirations of the people. In view of the pervasive philosophy of democracy in our Constitution it shall be wrong even to infer that the framers of the Constitution did not apply their mind while framing the Constitution. 

34. This brings us to the next question, whether holding of election in constituency No.125, Barisal, 5 by the Election Commission under Article 123 of the' Constitution will deprive the petitioner of his legitimate right to a seat in Parliament if subsequently he is declared elected in the election petition. The petitioner need not be afraid of losing his right. Here we would like to repeat that the trend of interpretation of statute is not to find inconsistencies between the two provisions but to give a harmonious interpretation of the conflicting provisions to avoid ahead on clash, "If it is possible to avoid a conflict between two provisions of an enactment on a proper construction thereof, then it is the duty of the Court to so construe them that they are in harmony with each other". 

35. We have already wondered in a previous para what would be the legal consequence, if ever Articles 123 and 125 come into conflict. We do not discard the possibility of such a situation arising when a person is declared to be elected in. tile by-election and another is declared elected after the, conclusion of the election petition. Once an election dispute is finally settled, it reaches a point where the result in the election dispute converges with the result of the by-election and the two without assimilating causes a conflict between the provisions of Articles 123 and 125. At that point the non obstante clause becomes the determining factor. In our opinion, the non obstante clause will-then come into effect and in such a case, Article 125 will prevail over Article 123 and the person declared elected in the election dispute will automatically replace the candidate elected in the by-election. The Election Commission will have the full power and authority to give effect to this under section 21 of the General Clauses Act. The Election Commission having the power under the Constitution to make orders, Rules and by-laws, also has the power to add or amend orders, Rules and by-laws. Therefore, the Election Commission will not lack power to declare the candidate winning the election dispute, by gazette notification, as the candidate having the right to sit in the vacant seat in Parliament. The rationality behind this is that the conduct of by election by the Election Commission under Article 123 does not wipe out the dispute regarding the seat till it is finally settled. In the absence of a time limit it may or may not take long to settle an election dispute. But the six months' time limit provided in Article 57(b)of President's Order 155 of 1972 for the Tribunal to endeavour and expeditiously conclude an election dispute, being directory in nature, two years have already elapsed in the instant election petition, but no witness has yet been examined and the dispute still persists. In such a case where the dispute continues the elected candidate in a bye-election takes over the disputed seat with his eyes open. By participating in the bye-election and being elected he only accrues a right, subject to the result of the election petition. Even, Late Dr Ehtasamul Hoq Nasim Biswas was occupying the seat in the Parliament subject to this condition. As soon as the election dispute is settled, its result will take effect. The successful candidate in the election ceases to be a member of Parliament automatically and the successful candidate in the election dispute takes seat in Parliament. The seems to us to be the most cogent and harmonious interpretation of the two Articles in conflict 

36. Democracy is a Government by the people; Article 124 of the Constitution refers to the due constitution of Parliament, which means a full Parliament of three hundred members. In case of a seat remaining vacant indefinitely, Parliament will not be a full Parliament of three hundred members. With that in mind, in our opinion, the framers of the Constitution provided in Article 123 a time limit of ninety days for' holding of the election by the Election Commission. Therefore, the concept that as long as an election dispute is not disposed of, there is no vacancy in Parliament, is a wrong concept, Dr. Ehtesamul Hoq Nasim Biswas had also been sitting in a disputed seat in Parliament. His seat would have been lost if he were finally unseated in the election dispute. The same will be the position of a candidate who will be elected in the election held under Article 123. 

27. Another aspect that remains to be addressed by us is that if the petitioner now participates in the by-election and simultaneously follows the election dispute to its end what will be his position if he loses the election and wins the election dispute? Will his claim to the vacant seat, as the winner in the election dispute, be sustainable in law though he lost the poll? In our view, by electing to participate in the by-election, he cannot reject its result, only because he lost it and opt for the result in the election dispute. Because of his participation in the by-election he will be bound by the election result and abdicate his right, if any, in the election dispute. The petitioner's candidacy in the by-election will also imply his acceptance of the official results of the original election, since he cannot seek to be re-elected against a parliamentary seat which according to his own claim has already been won by him. 

38. We would like to mention here that the Writ Petition No.3046 of 1996, which involved identical facts and low points, and decided by another Bench of this court and referred to us by the petitioner; is not per in curiam with this writ petition. The constitutional issues decided in this case were not addressed there. 

39. Lastly, we would like to thank all the (our amici curiae for their able assistance. Without their help it would have, been difficult to decide the matter. We fail to understand why the Election Commission was not represented by anyone in this case though it involved constitutional issues of importance.  

40. In view of the above we do not find any reason to interfere with the impugned notification. In our opinion Election Commission is bound to hold election of constituency No.125, Barisal, 5 within ninety days from the date the seat has fallen vacant. 

41. The Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The stay order granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated. The Bangladesh Election Commission, the Deputy Commissioner and Returning Officer, Barisal are hereby directed to hold by-election in Constituency No.125, Barisal, 5 within ninety days from the date the seat has fallen vacant. However, counting of ninety days will not include the period during which the election schedule was stayed because of the writ petition and also the period between the disposal of the writ petition on 27-5-98 and the receipt of this order by the Election Commission. 

42. The Divisional Election Tribunal, Barisal is directed to proceed with the Election Case No.1 of 1997 and dispose of it in accordance with law.   

43. Let advance copies of the order portion be issued immediately to the respondent Nos.l-3 ie 1) The Bangladesh Election Commission, Shere Bangla Nagar, Dhaka, 2) Deputy Commissioner, Barisal and Returning Officer, Jatiya Sangsad constituency No.12S, Barisal, and the petitioners of this writ petition. 

Office is directed to send a copy of this Judgment and order to respondent No.1 Bangladesh Election Commission at once addressing it to the Chief Election Commissioner, Bangladesh Election Commission. 

End.

full_judgment:
AKM Sadeque, J. : At the instance of MM Enterprise Limited 224, Bara Maghbazar Dhaka represented by its Director, Syed Tazammul Hussain a Rule Nisi under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was issued upon the respondent General Certificate Officer, Collectorate Building Comilla and Bangladesh Krishi Bank, Monoharpur Branch Comilla calling upon them to show cause why the Certificate filed in Certificate Case No. 318/86-87, notice issued under section 10A of the Public Demands Recovery Act of 1913 and the order dated 11.12.88 passed there under should not be declared to have been issued-or made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. The petitioner is a Public Limited Company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. He has set up a Cold Storage and Ice Plant in the year 1980-81 at Barkamta under Debidwar Police Station in the District of Comilla. For preserving potatoes in the Cold Storage the petitioner applied to the Bangladesh Krishi Bank for loan in March, 1981 and the Bank sanctioned an amount of Tk. 42 Lac which was repaid with interest in full. In the year 1982 the petitioner again applied to the Bank for cash credit loan to purchase and preserve potatoes in the Cold Storage and an amount of Tk. 42 lac was sanctioned. The petitioner purchased and stored potatoes. This loan was also given against pledge of potatoes.

3. The petitioner has alleged that in 1981-82 a large number of newly established Cold Storages were also put into operation and there was also bumper crop of potatoes in 1982. Even after storage of potatoes by all the Cold Storages, unusually large quantities of potatoes remained with the growers. Consequently with the stock available with them growers continued to meet the market demand practically upto end of July and the Cold Storages could not start marketing the stored potatoes until the beginning of August although usually the selling season commences from middle of June. The Cold stored potatoes have to be marketed within a limited period before coming into market of winter vegetables which during these years come to market quite early (by November) on account of use of improved seeds and application of scientific methods.

4. The petitioner wanted to start sale from early August and approached the Bank for release of potatoes against deposit of amount paid as loan plus interest. But the Bank arbitrarily fixed an amount much higher which was far above the market price. On 4.8.82, the petitioner addressed a letter to the Manager of the Bank with request to release the potatoes against payment of loan advanced plus interest accrued thereon and to add another 5% on it to be on the safe side, but the Bank did not agree and wanted the petitioner to pay amount earlier fixed by it. The petitioner has annexed a copy of this letter which has been marked as Annexure-A to the writ petition. It has been further alleged by the petitioner that as all the Cold Storages started selling potatoes and supply became greater to demand and the price of potatoes started dropping in all the markets throughout the country, further buyers were not available on cash purchase basis. As the drop of price was continuing with further downward trend, on 16.9.82 the petitioner requested the bank to release potatoes upto 25% of the cash credit limit and offered second charges mortgage of the project as collateral security. But the Bank did not pay any heed. The petitioner could not make much headway in selling the potatoes due to the unreasonable and unrealistic attitude of the Bank. As the stock continued to remain unsold, on 17.10.82 the Bank addressed a letter to the petitioner noting that as on that date only 13,120 mds were sold as against the total stock of 88,440 maunds and expressed apprehension that it would not be possible to dispose of the pledged potatoes within the time schedule. The petitioner has annexed the true copies of the letters dated 19.9.82 and 17.10.82 in this regard to the Writ Petition which have been marked as Annexure-B and C respectively, Due to further fall in price and demand, the Bank agreed to release the potatoes either against payment of 75% of the cost of potatoes or 50% against trust receipt and this was communicated to the petitioner on 30.11.82. But by this time, the season of potatoes selling was almost over and fresh vegetable of all kinds were available in market in plenty. Consequently the belated decision of the Bank was of no avail and the petitioner suffered colossal loss. For this huge loss Bank was responsible to a very great extent because of not allowing release of potatoes even against payment of loan amount plus accrued interest per unit when the selling price was above cost. Consequently the petitioner could not adjust the cash credit loan in full.

5. Subsequently after a joint meeting of the Bankers and representatives of Bangladesh Cold Storage Association held under the Chairmanship of the Governor, Bangladesh Bank, it was recognized by all concerned that the colossal loss sustained by the Cold Storages were due to reasons beyond their control. Accordingly, in a subsequent meeting of the Bankers held under the Chairmanship of the Governor. Bangladesh Bank, held on 8.3.83 it was decided to re-schedule the repayment of outstanding loans but the Bank did not comply with the instructions and calculated both interest and penal interest on the outstanding amount. In 1983 the petitioner applied for renewal of the cash credit loan for Tk. 42 lac but the Bank allowed only a cash credit amount of Tk. 33 lac to the petitioner. The petitioner repaid the entire loan with interest and also paid substantial amounts to wards adjustment of the dues of 1982. The petitioner requested the Bank to waive the interest accrued in 1982 together with penal interest on the ground that the petitioner suffered the loss largely due to the unreasonable and unrealistic decision of the Bank. The Bank assured to consider the matter, but nothing was eventually done. If this was done there would remain no outstanding dues of 1982. The petitioner further alleged that in 1983 the bank arbitrarily decreased the loan amount by 9 lac compared to the previous year and this caused under-utilization of the storage capacity. In 1984 the petitioner applied for a loan of Tk. 60 lac but the Bank granted a loan Tk. 44 lac. During the selling season of 1984 the price of potatoes again dropped and consequently the petitioner could adjust the loan only to the extent of about 83% and the balance amount remained outstanding. In recognition of the loss sustained by the cold storage owners due to depressed market condition, Bangladesh Bank issued circular on February 20, 1985 and 23rd March, 1985 to allow cash credit facilities to those who had adjusted at least 80% of the past cash credit limits, but completely ignoring the directives, the Bank delayed sanctioning of the loan amount. The sanction was given on 8.5.85 for utilisation of the amount within 31.5.85 and added such conditions which rendered the smooth operation impossible thereby causing loss to the company. During 1985 also due to drop of potato price, Cold Storages could not adjust the full loan amount of cash credit and the Bangladesh Bank issued circular on 8th December, 1985 to renew cash credit facility for purchase and preservation of potatoes to those who repaid at least 80% of the amount availed of the past cash credit limit. Although the petitioner was eligible to get cash credit loan under this criteria, the Bank did not renew the cash credit loan to the petitioner. The petitioner has annexed photo copies of the circular issued by the Bangladesh Bank as aforesaid and marked as Annexure-'D' and 'E' respectively to the writ petition. The petitioner has further alleged that he had addressed a number of letters to the bank to settle the question of outstanding dues with the petitioner by deducting the interest and penal interest charged on the loan in 1982 and pointed out that upon such adjustment there would remain practically nothing outstanding but the Bank paid no heed to the repeated requests of the petitioner. On 14.11.88 the petitioner received a notice issued on 8th November, 1988 by General Certificate Officer, Comilla in Certificate Case No. 318/86-87 demanding payment of Tk. 45, 84, 646.00 being the claim of Bangladesh Krishi Bank and another sum of Tk. 15,016, 50 towards expenses within 30 days from the date of issue of the notice and directing not to transfer any movable or immovable property. After receipt of this notice on 14.11.88 the petitioner submitted a petition before the General Certificate Officer, Comilla on 3.12.88 stating that the claim of the Bank is not correct and the Bank by their unreasonable actions caused loss to the petitioner which needs determination in accordance with law. The petitioner further stated that without determining the amount of dues filing of certificate is against the principle of justice and violative of the fundamental rights of the petitioner and prayed that pending determination of the amount of dues the notice issued under section 10(ka) of the Public Demands Recovery Act of 1913 be rescinded. The petitioner has annexed the photo copy of the petition marked as Annexure-G to the Writ Petition. The General Certificate Officer recorded the order that "there was no specific objection in clear terms against the claim of the Bank. Therefore the parties should be present before him on 11.12.88 in a hearing". On 11.12.88 the petitioner submitted petition before the General Certificate Officer Comilla stating that for making statement regarding the amount claimed by the Bank it was necessary to examine the accounts of the Bank and prayed for directing the Bank to submit the statements of accounts in Court so that the petitioner could take copy, examine the same and submit objection and for this purpose prayed for 1 month's time. The learned Certificate Officer recorded an order; that as per order passed by him on 4.12.88, the petitioner did not submit any specific objection but instead applied for time to examine the correctness of the amount claimed by the Bank and that upon examination of record it appeared that by raising unnecessary objection the petitioner was delaying payment of Bank dues and speedy realisation of claimed amount, action under 14(Ga) be taken and towards that end notice under section 29 of the Public Demands Recovery Act be issued and the same be published in a national daily on 5.1.89. Immediately after receipt of the notice issued under section 10A of the Public Demands Recovery Act, the petitioner applied for certified copy of the requisition and certificate' filed in Certificate case No. 318/86-87 together with the order passed on the date of signing and filing the certificate but the learned certificate officer refused to allow certified copies of the requisition and certificate but agreed to allow copy of the order. It has been further stated by the petitioner that generally the Bank files civil suit for recovery of its dues; but in this case as they are aware that upon proper scrutiny and adjudication their claim will not stand, they have resorted to certificate proceeding. The Krishi Bank order does not stipulate any criteria as to which cases will be filed in civil Court for recovery of dues and which cases will be filed before the certificate officer under Public Demands Recovery Act and it leaves scope for arbitrary and discriminatory use of the provision of law. It has been further stated that the certificate proceeding can only be initiated for recovery of judicially determined amounts and in the instant case there was no such judicial determination and the claim has not become due.

6. We have stated the case of petitioner in extenso in order to bring out the grievances of the petitioner in clear cut line. The respondent No. 2 Bangladesh Krishi Bank opposed this writ application by filing affidavit-in opposition. So far the broad facts are concerned there is no serious denial of the same in the affidavit-in-opposition. The respondent No.2 has contended that the writ petition is not maintainable in view of Bangladesh Krishi Bank Order No. 27 of 1973 i.e. PO 27 of 1973 that the petitioner has made inordinate delay in making the writ application and that the petitioner has come before this court with unclear hands.

7. The respondent No.2 also asserted that the loan taken by the petitioner in the year 1981 was repayable within 31.11.81 but an amount of Tk. 25.65 lac which remained outstanding that year was adjusted by the petitioner from the loan amount sanctioned in 1982. After denying the allegations of various counts on petitioner's ability to repay the loan amount in time and his own contributory negligence as given in the petition, the respondent No. 2 stated that the petitioner defaulted to clear up its 1982 liabilities which stood at 20.99 lac, but the respondent in order to enable the petitioner to run the project sanctioned in 1983 an amount of 33 lac as cash credit loan which the petitioner avoided without any objection. The petitioner was also allowed time to repay the 1982 liability by November, 1984. The request of the petitioner for relief of the interest on loan amount of 1982 was rejected by the Bank authority after due consideration. The petitioner applied for Tk. 50 lac as cash credit loan in the year 1984. But assessing market of the potatoes the respondents Bank sanctioned Tk. 44 lac to the petitioner. In addition the respondent Bank also paid Tk. 2.33 lac towards payment of electricity bill. The respondent denied that the price of potates had fallen during the period concerned and the petitioner suffered loss on account of negligence of the respondent The respondent has further stated that the other cold storage owners dealing with potatoes fully cleared up their dues together with interest to the respondent Bank, in 1984, except the petitioner who also defaulted in 1984 to deposit its sale proceeds of that year. The respondent has clearly asserted that it is the petitioner and not the respondent Bank who was responsible for delay if at all in processing the sanction of the loan in the year 1985. The petitioner also defaulted to repay the Bank dues in 1985 on various pretexts when other cold storage owners of the region paid their dues with interest in full.
