It was not possible for the respondent Bank to sanction loan in favour of the petitioner in 1986 as in the meantime, the respondent had initiated the Certificate Case against the petitioner for recovery of loan money and interest. The petitioner finally adjusted its 1982 liabilities in 1984 after much persuasion by the respondent Bank. But in spite of repeated requests and reminders by the respondent Bank, petitioner defaulted to adjust its 1984 and 1985 loan liabilities. So the respondent Bank had no option but to file certificate case No. 318/86-87 as per provision of the PO No. 27 of 1973 against the petitioner for balance of Tk. 4466,238 upto 31.12.86 and interest of Tk. 1,15,508.60  upto 1.3.87 which would be supported by statement of accounts for the period from July 1981 to June 1985 now in possession of the respondent. The petitioner could contest the case before the General Certificate Officer stating his case, but instead he has chosen to bring the present writ application to avoid the repayment of huge loan money due from the petitioner to the respondent Bank. In these circumstances it is contended the writ application is liable to be rejected.

The averments in the writ petition and the affidavit-in-opposition which have been subsequently re-enforced by supplementary affidavits bringing out further facts before the court show that the loan transactions between the petitioner and the Bank were being continued during the years 1981 to 1985. The petitioner has not been able to repay the loan amounts in full except for the year 1982. The petitioner's case is that it is on account of the lack of action in time on behalf of the respondent Bank which made the petitioner to suffer huge loss in 1982. The respondent Bank also did not reschedule petitioner's loan in time and the petitioner has suffered huge financial loss also on that account. The factual case of the petitioner boils down to this that the petitioner would not be liable for the interest and penal interest which was imposed by the respondent Bank because of non payment of the loan amount in time; it is the respondent Bank who was actually to blame. On the other hand, the respondent's defence is that the petitioner willfully defaulted to repay the loan money, while the other Cold Storage concerned had all repaid the loan amounts during the period in question. So it turns out that there is dispute between the parties regarding the outstanding loan, particularly the interest and the penal interest. In other words, there is conflict between the parties as to the amount due.

8. Now in order to realise the outstanding dues from the petitioner the respondent Bank has recourse to section 21 of the Bangladesh Krishi Bank Order 1973. It is necessary to quote this section in full for the purpose of proper appreciation of the case.

"21. (1) Where any agriculturist who is liable to the Bank under any agreement makes default in repayment or otherwise fails to comply with the terms of this agreement with the Bank, such default or failure not being due to natural calamity, the Bank may, subject to any rules made in this behalf, take over the management of the concern of the agriculturist and sell or realise any property, pledged, mortgaged, hypothecated or assigned by the agriculturists to secure his liability to the Bank.

(2) All sums due to the Bank shall be recoverable as arrears of the land revenue.

(3) In the application of the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 (Bengal Act III of 1913 for the purpose of the recovery of the dues of the Bank, the provision of sections 7, 9, 10 and 13 of that Act shall not apply and the certificates issued under section 4 of the said Act shall be conclusive proof that the amount specified therein is due to the Bank

(4)

(5) Dues of the Bank may also be recovered by any other legal action without any ad valorem fee for the same.

(6) An officer (of the rank of Manager or above) of the Bank may exercise all the powers exercisable by a certificate officer under the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 (Bengal Act III of 1913) within the jurisdiction for the purpose of recovery of the dues of the Bank only".

There is a corresponding provision in the Public Demands Recovery Act namely section 10A(1) which is to the following effect:

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in section 7, when a certificate has been filed in the office of the Certificate-officer under section 4 or section 6 for the recovery of any dues under the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 or the Bangladesh Krishi Bank Order, 1973 or the Co-Operative Societies Act, 1940 or the Customs Act 1969 or for the recovery of any loan advanced by the Government or for the recovery of any money referred to in Article 15 of Schedule 1 the certificate officer shall, instead of causing a notice prescribed under section 7 to be served upon the certificate debtor, cause a demand-notice to be served upon the certificate debtor by registered post with acknowledgment due requiring the certificate debtor to deposit with the certificate-officer the amount of his debt within thirty days of the service of such notice.

(2) From and after the service of the demand-notice under sub-section (1) upon a certificate- debtor, the provisions of clauses (a) and (b) of section 8 shall apply.

(3) The provisions of section 9 or section 10 shall not apply in the case of a certificate for the recovery of any dues or loan specified in sub-section (1); and on the default of the certificate-debtor to deposit the amount of his debt as required by sub-section (1) the Certificate Officer shall proceed to execute the certificate in accordance with the provision of the Act"

In the instant case the respondent Bank has taken recourse to the above provisions and filed requisition under section 5 of the Public Demands Recovery Act against the petitioner. The petitioner has filed the certified copy of the requisition, under section 5 of the Public Demands Recovery Act which is Annexure-I to the supplementary affidavit. The respondent Bank has also filed the' photo copy of the same Requisition which is Annexure-3 to the supplementary affidavit- in-opposition on behalf of the respondent No. 2 Bangladesh Krishi Bank. We refer to Annexure-3 which is the' exact photo copy of the original. It is a printed form. The names of the loanees have been given on the left hand side and the amount of Public Demand has been given on the right hand side. It is endorsed on the reverse side of it.

উক্ত..........সালে.........উপলক্ষের উপরিল্লিখিত টাকা পাওনা আছে এ বিষয়ে অনুসন্ধান করিয়া প্রতীতি জন্মিয়াছে। আপনার নিকট অনুরোধ ঐ টাকা আদায় করিবেন।

১৯.........সালের.............মাসের............তারিখ

সত্যপাঠমুক্ত করা গেল।

স্বাঃ/ অস্পষ্ট

ম্যানেজার

বাংলাদেশ কৃষি ব্যাংক

This has initiated the proceeding against the petitioner. Now section 5 of the Public Demands Recovery Act is as follows:

"5. Requisition for Certificate in other cases:-

(1) When: any public demand payable to any person other than the Collector is due, such person may send to the certificate-officer, a written requisition in the prescribed form:

Provided that no action shall be taken under this Act, on a requisition made by a land mortgage bank registered or deemed to be registered under the Co-operative Societies Act 1940 (Act XXI of 1940) or an assignee of such bank, unless the requisition be countersigned by the Registrar of Co-operative Societies, Bangladesh.

(2) Every such requisition shall be signed and verified in the prescribed manner, and, except in such cases as may be prescribed, shall be chargeable with the fee of the amount which would be payable under the Court Fees Act 1870 (VII of 1870) in respect of a plaint for the recovery of a sum of money equal to that stated in the requisition as being due"

From the very language of this section it appears that requisition may be sent when a public demand becomes due. It must be ascertained that the amount is recoverable under Public Demands Recovery Act and has become due. Prior ascertainment of the demand due is necessary. The requisition is required to be signed and verified properly. In the instant case it is clear to see that there was no proper verification and there is no means to know how the amount due, was ascertained by the requisition authority, although, there are conflicting versions of it given by the petitioner and the respondent Bank. Now in pursuance of this Requisition the Certificate Officer himself had signed the certificate under section 6 of the Public Demands Recovery Act. We refer to Annexure-a, the photo copy of the original, to see what it was like. Here also we see that the Certificate Officer had actually copied the amount and names of the certificate debtors as in requisition, Annexure-3. On the reverse side of the Annexure-4 we again find a printed certification. Here also the reverse of this Annexure-4 is blank except for the signature of the certificate officer.

Now section 6 of the Public Demands Recovery Act is as follows:

6.	Filing of Certificate on Requisition:

On receipt of any such requisition, the Certificate-officer, if, he is satisfied that the demand is recoverable and that recovery by suit is not barred by law, may sign a certificate, in the prescribed form, stating that the demand is due; and shall include in the certificate the fee (if any) paid under section 5, sub-section (2); and shall cause the certificate to be filed in his office."

The very look of these annexure show that the certificate officer acted mechanically. There does not appear any material to show that the certificate officer could satisfy himself that the demand is due and recoverable.

<u>9. With regard to this aspect of the case, Mr. Abdul Wadud Khandaker the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has argued that the Public Demands Recovery Act 1913, was enacted for recovery of dues payable to the Public Exchequer.</u>

<u>Land Revenue, Income Tax, Customs Duty, Sales Tax, Excise Duty and other taxes payable to the Public Exchequer were within the purview of this Act. The amount of dues had to be determined by authorities prescribed under various statutes. Land Revenue, Income Tax, Customs Duty, Excise Duty, etc. are assessed and determined by Collectors of the Districts, Income Tax Officer, Collectors of Customs and Collectors of Land Customs respectively under several statutes. Every such statute provides for appeal and revision against the assessment The dues finally determined upon appeal and revision are recoverable under Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913. He has submitted that the mere signature of the respondent Bank in the Requisition under section 5 of the Public Demands Recovery Act (Annexure-3) does not indicate that the amount was finally determined by any competent authority. It was only a statement of the amount claimed on behalf of the respondent Bank by the Manager, Bangladesh Krishi Bank. There is also no provision in the Krishi Bank Order 1973 regarding any authority to determine the amounts due on behalf of the Bank. He has further submitted that a claim when admitted or determined by a competent authority under any statutory provision that can be realised as arrears of land revenue under PDR Act 1913. Dues cannot be recovered as arrears of land revenue unless these dues have been fixed, determined and established in accordance with law. In support of his submission, Mr. Khandker has cited the decision on the case of Miah Mohammad Latif Vs. Province of West Pakistan, through the Deputy Commissioner, Khairpur and another reported in 22 DLR (SC) 98, Mannaco Lab. Ltd. Vs. General Certificate Officer and Bangladesh Shilpa Bank reported in 42 DLR 159. Chittagong Engineering & Electric Supply Co. Ltd. Vs. Certificate Officer, Dacca and ors. reported in 17 DLR 404, Zakaria A Bawany Vs. Civy Deputy Collector Karachi and two others reported in PLD 1975 Karachi 1008. Relying on these decisions the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that in the instant case the amount claimed by the Bank has neither been admitted nor determined in accordance with law and as such it is not recoverable under the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913. With regard to the Certificate signed by the Certificate Officer under section 6 of the Public Demands Recovery Act Annexure-4 he has submitted that section 6 of the Public Demands Recovery Act provides that the Certificate Officer filing the certificate must be satisfied that the demand is due and this satisfaction means objective satisfaction based on adequate materials and not subjective or arbitrary satisfaction. In support of such view Mr. Khandaker has cited the decision reported in the case of Government of West Pakistan, through Secretary, Home Department and another Vs. Begum Agha Abdul Karim Shorish Kashmiri, 21 DLR (SC) 1; in the case of Abdul Latif Mina Vs. Government of' Bangladesh and others reported in 31 DLR (AD) 1 reported in AIR 1957 Punj 303. He has submitted that in the instant case there was no material before the certificate officer to be satisfied that the claim of the Bank was determined in accordance with law and the amount shown in the purported requisition had became due. He has submitted that there is nothing in the initial order of the certificate officer to show that he had really considered whether the amount due was recoverable under the law. The initial order reads as follows: সার্টিফিকেট মামলা গ্রহণ করা হইল। ১০ নং রেজিষ্ট্রিতে লিপিবদ্ধ করা ১০(ক) এবং গ ধারা নোটিশ জারী করা হউক। আগামী ৯/৪/৮৭ ইং তারিখ উপস্থাপন করুণ।</u>

<u>He has submitted that the certificate officer did not file the certificate and issue notice on being satisfied that the amount had become due. There was no material before him except the purported requisition signed by the Bank Manager to find that the amount was due and recoverable under law. He has further submitted that, the certificate Annexure-4 would show that he did not even properly verify or sign the same and there was non-application of mind on his part while signing the certificate. On this non-application of mind, the learned Advocate has cited the decision in the case of Gulam Mohiuddin Vs. Chief Settlement Commissioner, reported in 16 DLR (SC) 654 and submitted that the certificate officer had mechanically passed the order and signed the Certificate Annexure-4 without applying his mind. Therefore, this certificate is not a certificate in the eye of law. Again he has submitted that it is only the accounts maintained by the Bank upon which the Certificate Officer had proceeded to sign the certificate Annexure- 4. But the account maintained by the Bank is not sufficient without corroboration to fasten a person with liability. This view, he has submitted, has been supported by a decision in the case of M/s. Muhammad Siddik Muhammad Umar and another Vs. The Australasia Bank Ltd. reported in 18 DLR (SC) 430.</u>

10. We have carefully scrutinized the Requisition Annexure-3 and the Certificate Annexure-4 of the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition and also considered the submission made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. We are of the view that although the respondent Bank had filed the Requisition Annexure- 3 and the certificate officer had signed Annexure-4 both of them had done so only in mechanical manner without applying their mind as to whether the amount signed for was actually due. The amount was also not admitted or determined by a statutory authority. In view of the averments made in the Writ petition and also in the affidavit-in- opposition and the supplementary affidavits we are also of the view that the determination of the amount due is not possible without giving the petitioner a hearing. The facts admitted would show that the petitioner sought permission to be heard and lay his objection to the claim to the certificate officer although there was no provision for that. The impugned order dated 11.12.88 passed by the certificate officer shows that he considered the application of the petitioner as designed to delay payment. Section 10A of the Public Demands Recovery Act which has been quoted above dispensed with the service of notice under section 7 and reply thereto under section 9 and hearing by the Certificate Officer under section 10 of the Act.

<u>11. Generally when a Certificate is signed under section 6 of the PDR Act, a notice is served upon the certificate debtor under section 7 of the PDR Act and the certificate debtor is entitled to make a petition in the prescribed form signed and verified denying liability in whole or in part under section 9 of the Act within the period of 30 days from the service of any process for enforcing the certificate. Upon such denial of the liability under section 9 of the Act, the Certificate officer shall hear the petition, take evidence if necessary and determine whether the certificate debtor is liable for the whole or any part of the amount for which the certificate was signed and may vary, modify or set aside the certificate. So it is clear from these sections of the Public Demands Recovery Act that Certificate Officer has to determine whether the demand is due or not by sending notice of the demand to the certificate-debtor under section 7 upon which the certificate-debtor is entitled to put objection to the demand under section 9 and be heard under section 10 of the Act. These provisions ensure that no false or frivolous demand is made against the certificate debtor. The certificate issued under the PDR Act amounts to a decree which takes away or gives a valuable right. So ample provisions have been made in the PDR Act to safeguard the interest of the certificate-debtor; but by insertion of section 10A of the PDR Act by EP Ordinance XXV of 1961 certificate-debtor has been deprived of any opportunity of hearing to protect his right In the instant case it appears that there is sufficient dispute between the petitioner and the respondents as to the amount due. Had it been a case of admitted dues it should be a different case. Obviously the claim of the respondent Bank has not been admitted or determined by a statutory authority. We already found that a claim when admitted by borrower or fixed and determined in accordance with law becomes the dues recoverable under PDR Act, 1913, Recourse could not be had under PDR Act, 1913 to recover Bank's claim which has not been determined or admitted. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has drawn our attention to section 5(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and contended that disputes of civil nature cannot be adjudicated by certificate officer, although sections 7, 9, 10 and 13 of the PDR Act, 1913 were intended to avoid injustice arising out of error or omissions. This section however did not contemplate adjudication of civil nature because certificate proceedings are initiated only for amount due, that is, amount already fixed and determined by authority prescribed by statute or by a competent Court. In support of his contention he cited the case of Miah Md. Latif Vs. Province of WP reported in 22 DLR (SC) 98, 100(10). We find there is much force in this contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. He has further submitted that the insertion of section 10A, the provisions of sections 7, 9, 10 have been made inapplicable. Section 10A provides arbitrary power without provision for any hearing. So it is inconsistent with Article 31 of the Constitution and also with section 75 of the PDR Act, 1913.The learned counsel for the respondent could not refute this argument. Sections 7, and 10 are in consonance with natural justice also but they have been done away with by the insertion of section 10A of the PDR Act, 1913.</u>

<u>12. The arbitrariness of the order of the Certificate-Officer also appears from the relevant order passed by him on receipt of the Requisition Annexure-I which is a follows:</u>

<u>সার্টিফিকেট মামলা গ্রহণ করা হইল। ১০নং রেজ্রিষ্ট্রিতে লিপিবদ্ধ করুণ। ১০(ক) নং ধারায় নোটিশ জারী করা হউক। আগামী ৯.৪.৮৭ ইং তারিখ উপস্থাপন করুন।</u>

<u>This order is arbitrary, repressive and violative of Article 31 of the Constitution. In the instant case when the dues of the petitioner to the respondent Bank is in serious dispute, it was for the Bank to avail of civil Court for adjudication of the claim and not to resort to certificate proceeding under section 10A which has done away with the requirements under sections 7, 9 and 10 of the Act in derogation of the needs of natural justice. We have already noticed that insertion of section 10A of the PDR Act has shut the door to any hearing. It is not understandable how, when there is such a huge claim against the petitioner to which the petitioner has got tangible objection, there could be summary realisation of the claim without the same being determined by competent authority or settled up by the civil Court. As a matter of fact sub-section 5 of section 21 of the Bangladesh Krishi Bank Order 1973 has left such an alternative to the respondent Bank.</u>

13. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also urged upon us to strike down section 10A of the PDR Act being inconsistent under Article 31 of the Constitution. He has submitted that this Provision of section 10A of the PDR Act which was inserted during the Martial Law regime is violative of Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution. Further it is void as per Article 26(1) of the Constitution. But the learned counsel for the respondent has pointed out no such prayer was made for striking down this provision of law in the writ application nor any Rule was issued to that effect. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has, however, submitted that no specific prayer for striking down a provision of law which is inconsistent with the Articles of the Constitution need not be made and no specific Rule in this regard need be issued for striking down a law if it is found inconsistent with the fundamental rights embodied in the Constitution. He has cited the decision in the case of Dr. Nurul Islam Vs. Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Population Control and others, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201 in this regard.

<u>14. We hold that section 10A of the PDR Act is against the principle of natural justice and also of offends fends against the Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution, particularly in cases of claims or dues under genuine dispute. It is, however, not necessary for us to strike down section 10A in this case since we find that the petitioner is entitled to succeed even without that.</u>

15. Now before parting with the case few words about the jurisdiction is to be recorded. It was submitted by Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate for the respondent Bank that sections 34 and 51 of the PDR Act 1913 has provided remedy by way of suit and appeal. It was submitted on behalf of the respondent No. 2 that section 34 of the PDR Act provided remedy against the order of the certificate-officer and section 51 also provided appeal. Without availing of these provision the petitioner cannot invoke writ jurisdiction. In support of the contention he has relied on the decision reported in 29 DLR (AD) 231. But this submission cannot be sustained because section 34 provides for civil suit within 6 months from the service of notice upon the certificate-debtor under section 7, and if the debtor files petition in accordance with section 9 denying the liability. In the instant case there was no notice served under section 7 nor any petition under section 9 by the certificate-debtor nor any determination under section 10 of the PDR Act; no appeal filed in accordance with section 51 from the order passed under section 10A. Therefore section 34 of the PDR Act could not be availed of by the petitioner. Again so far an appeal under section 51 is concerned the order dated 11.12.88 passed by the certificate officer was not an order passed according to statutory provision because provision of section 10A of the Act rules out any proceeding before the certificate-officer regarding the dispute as to the dues. Therefore, it is highly doubtful whether this impugned order was appealable under section 51 of the PDR Act. Again, in this writ application the very vires of section 10A of the PDR Act in view of Article 31 of the Constitution has been challenged. Writ jurisdiction is the proper jurisdiction for deciding such constitutional point. In such view of the matter we find that the petitioner has rightly availed of the Constitutional Jurisdiction of this Court for remedy of his grievance and the writ petition is maintainable.

In view of the above discussion and observations we hold that the certificate filed in Certificate Case No. 318/86-87 and notice issued under section 10A of the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 as well as the impugned order dated 11.12.88 are without lawful authority and are of no legal effect. The Rule is

therefore made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
AR Yusuf with Korban Ali, SK Ansar Ali, Abdur Razzaque and Nawab Ali, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Aminul Huq, Attorney-General with AF Hasan Arif, Deputy Attorney-General and Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, Asstt. Attorney-General ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Professor Golam Azam   ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others  ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mohammad Ismail Uddin Sarker, J.: This rule Nisi was issued upon an application under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause why the Notification No. 403/Imn/lII dated 18.4.73, Annexure-B to the petition issued by the Respondent No. 1 in so far as it relates to the petitioner, Prof. Golam Azam, read with the show cause notice being No. Sha: Ma: (Bahi-1)/138 dated 23.3.1992 (Annexure-K) should not be declared to have been made and issued without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. It is stated in the petition that the petitioner, Prof. Golam Azam, is a Bangladeshi citizen by birth having been born at Dhaka on the 22nd November, 1922; that his father late Moulana Ghulam Kabir was born in village Birgram, Police Station Nabinagar, District Comilla now Brahmanbaria and from generations they are permanent residents in the terriories now comprised in Bangladesh; that the petitioner passed the Intermediate Examination from the Islamia Intermediate Government College, Dhaka and then obtained his Graduation and his Masters Degree in Political Science from the University of Dhaka; that the petitioner was General Secretary of the Student's Union of the then Fazlul Huq Muslim Hall and he was also General Secretary of the Dhaka University Students Union wherein he played a very vital role in the Bengali Language Movement and as the General Secretary of the Dhaka University Students Union; the petitioner read a memorandum before the then Prime Minister of Pakistan on the 27th of November, 1948 at the Gymnasium ground of the Dhaka University urging him to make Bengali as one of the State Languages, as one of the main demands; that the petitioner was a professor of Political Science for five years in the Carmichael College, Rangpur; that he fought for restoration of democracy during the Ayub regime and was General Secretary of the Eastern Wing of the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM); that because of his active role in various democratic movements the petitioner was arrested once in 1955, then in 1964 but he was released by the order of the Dhaka High Court on Habeas Corpus petition; that the petitioner dedicated his life for the establishment of Islamic Social Justice in all spheres of the society and he became the Ameer (President) of the Jamaat-e-Islami of the then East Pakistan in 1969; that in the General Election of 1970 Jamaat-e-Islami took part in the election and obtained the second highest votes, next to the Awami League in the then East Pakistan; that from the election of 1970 political rivalry and enmity developed between the Jamaat-e-Islami and the Awami League and the petitioner being the head of the Jamaat-e-Islami became the target of the Awami League, which later on, formed the first Government in the independent Bangladesh; that in spite of political differences with Awami League the petitioner advocated for transfer of power to the Awami League as it obtained the highest number of seats in the then National Assembly; that during the liberation struggle the petitioner was actively engaged in helping people and saving them from the military atrocities of Yahya regime, but even then the Awami League considered the petitioner their arch enemy; that the petitioner was a resident of Bangladesh on the 25th of March, 1971 and he continued to be so resident and on the 22nd of November, 1971 he went to Lahore for attending his party's central working committee meeting and on the 3rd of December, 1971 the petitioner was returning to Dhaka by plane but the plane could not land at Dhaka Airport because of the war and as such the plane at first landed at Colombo and as there was bombing at that time at Karachi Airport the plane went to Jeddah where the petitioner remained a few days wherefrom he was sent back to Karachi along with the other passengers; that the petitioner had to remain in Pakistan against his will for some months as the then Government of Pakistan did not allow any Bangladeshi citizen to leave Pakistan, that the petitioner tried to go to London in the month of March, 1972 for making contact with his family but failed to obtain any travel document in Pakistan and thereafter arranged a Pakistani passport to go to Hajj in the month of December, 1972; that the petitioner during the Hajj met friends & acquaintances from Bangladesh who went for Hajj who informed him about a political mis-propaganda against the petitioner in Bangladesh; that thereafter the petitioner went to London in the first week of April, 1973 where he came to learn from a news item published in the Bangladesh Observer to the effect that he along with 38 others were declared by a notification dated 18.4.73 of the Department of Home Affairs of Bangladesh to be disqualified to become citizen of Bangladesh.

3. It is also stated in the petition that the petitioner found it impossible to return to Bangladesh and he stayed in England against his will but 1ie never went to Pakistan nor he obtained nationality or citizenship of any other country; that after the publication of the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 the petitioner continued to reside in England since the first week of April, 1973; that in the meantime in 1975 there was a change of Government and the political situation in Bangladesh; and the new Government of Bangladesh by a notification dated 17.1.76 (Annexure-C) invited applications from those persons whose citizenship was cancelled by the previous Government for restoration of their citizenship and accordingly the petitioner sent an application on 20.5.76 to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Bangladesh praying for restoration of his citizenship but having received no reply the petitioner sent another application on 12.1.77 to the Chief Martial Law Administrator renewing his prayer for restoration of citizenship but the petitioner received a reply from the Ministry of Home Affairs dated 23.4.77 (Annexure-E) to the following effect:

"With reference to your application dated 12.1.77 addressed to the Chief Martial Law Administrator, Government of Bangladesh, I am directed to inform you that the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh regret their inability to accede to your request to restore Bangladesh Citizenship".

4. The petitioner also received a letter dated 29.9.77 from the office of the High Commissioner for Bangladesh in England (Annexure-E 1) to the same effect; that in the meantime the petitioner lost his father in 1973 and his old mother applied on 14.11.77 to the Government of Bangladesh praying for restoration of the citizenship to the petitioner which was refused but the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh by their letter dated 11.3.78 expressed their no objection for granting visa to the petitioner to see his ailing mother and accordingly the petitioner obtained visa from London and entered Bangladesh on 11.7.78 with a visa for three months; that after his arrival in Bangladesh on 11.7.78 the petitioner was registered by the concerned authority as a Foreigner; that the petitioner obtained extension of his visa twice and then in order to avoid possible ouster from the court he filed an application for registration as a citizen of Bangladesh to the Ministry of Home Affairs on 8.11.78 surrendering his Pakistani passport to the authority concerned, that thereafter the petitioner has been permanently residing in Bangladesh considering himself a citizen of Bangladesh by birth; that on 27.5.80 some members of the Parliament inquired from the Government about the stay of the petitioner in Bangladesh on which the then Minister for Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh made a statement in the Parliament to the effect that the petitioner had filed an application praying for registration as a citizen of Bangladesh by surrendering his Pakistani passport and that the matter is pending decision of the Government; that thereafter the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration Section vide letter dated 28.4.81 asked the petitioner to submit an affidavit with oath of allegiance to Bangladesh and the petitioner submitted the required affidavit on 30.4.81; that after a long silence the petitioner received a letter dated 3.12.86 from the Ministry of Home Affairs (Annexure H-1) requesting him to let the Ministry to know as to why he was staying in Bangladesh without visa since he had not approached the authority for extension of visa after he had registered his name with the Foreigners Registration Office on 12.7.78 to which the petitioner sent a reply on 22.12.86 (Annexure H-2) asserting himself as a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and informing that on 8.11.78 he made an application for restoration of his citizenship by surrendering his passport and that his application was under the active consideration of the authorities; that the petitioner also asserted himself as a citizen of Bangladesh in a Press Conference held on 30.5.88; that the name of the petitioner was also published in the voter list published on 5.8.83 (Annexure-M) as well as in the voter list published on 15.2.90 (Annexure-I); that the petitioner thought that the clouds about his citizenship was over and he was a citizen of Bangladesh; that the petitioner was elected as the Chief of his party, Jamaat-e-Islami of Bangladesh, and after the general election held in 1991 the Prime Minister personally met the petitioner for the support of his party before formation of the Government and during the election of the President both the candidates for the office of President of the country also requested him for the support of his party; that all an a sudden the petitioner received a notice dated 23.3.92 (Annexure-K) from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration Branch to show cause by 10 AM of 24th of March, 1992 why the petitioner should not be deported from Bangladesh and why other legal actions should not be taken against him as he had been disqualified to be the citizen of Bangladesh by a Notification dated 18.4.73 and he is a registered Foreigner and as he became the Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami, Bangladesh in contravention of Article 38 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, to which the petitioner gave a reply on 24.3.92 (Annexure K-1) asserting his right as a citizen of Bangladesh and denying the allegations made in the show cause notice and also soliciting for personal hearing in the matter; but the respondent No. 1 illegally arrested the petitioner and detained him at the Dhaka Central Jail by issuing an order of detention dated 24.3.92 under section 3 of the Foreigners Act, 1946; that the petitioner sent a demand for justice notice to the respondent No.1 (Annexure-L) and thereafter challenged the order of detention by filing Writ Petition No. 1148 of 1992 on which a Rule was issued on 30.3.92.

5. It is submitted by the petitioner in the petition that he was a Bangladeshi citizen by birth in accordance with the provision of Article 2 of Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 (PO 149 of 1972) that the impugned Notification (Annexure-B) was issued against the provisions of PO 149 of 1972 and the provision of the Citizenship Act 1951; that the petitioner having been born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh, having been continuously resident therein was a citizen of Bangladesh by the operation of law; that the impugned notification was malafide and issued for collateral purposes; that the impugned notification was ultra vires the Constitution and that the provision of Foreigners Act was not applicable to the petitioner.

6. The respondent No. 1 controverted the statements of the petitioner made in the petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition wherein it is stated that the petitioner and his fore-fathers were born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh but he is "now" not a citizen of Bangladesh as he has been staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh; that the petitioner had actively participated in the anti-Bangladeshi campaign both inside and outside the country during the war of liberation and he continued to be a citizen of Pakistan that Armed Cadre of Jamaat-e-Islami such as Rajaker, Al-Badr and Al-Shams were placed under the disposal of Pakistan Army in the then East Pakistan during the war of liberation; that as the petitioner had actively participated in the Anti-liberation Movement the Government of Bangladesh disqualified him from being a citizen of Bangladesh by the impugned Notification (Annexure-B); that the people of Bangladesh are well aware about the role of the petitioner during the war of liberation who actively collaborated with Pakistani Army in raising the Rajakers, Al-Badr and Al-Shams, that the conduct of the petitioner makes it clear that he placed the Jamaat-e-Islami at the disposal of Pakistan Army; that it was not true that the petitioner was staying in Pakistan against his will, that it was also not true that the petitioner went to Saudi Arabia in 1972 for the purpose of performing Hajj but his mission to Saudi Arabia was to orchestrate anti-Bangladesh sentiment and he lobbied actively to dissuade the Muslim countries from recognizing Bangladesh as an independent state; that in the year 1972 the petitioner had organized "East Pakistan Recovery Committee" in Lahore; that in the same year the petitioner attended the Islamic Youth Conference in Riadh wherein he appealed to all of them to join in liberation struggle for recapturing East Pakistan and he had also organized a committee for recapturing East Pakistan in London; that in 1973 the petitioner went to Bengali in Libya to attend the conference of the Foreign Ministers of the Islamic countries and there he made an appeal not to recognize Bangladesh as an independent State; that the petitioner met the Saudi Badsha for seven times from 1973 to 1976 for not giving recognition to Bangladesh; that the Government being satisfied about the conduct of the petitioner passed the impugned order (Annexure-B); that during his stay in the United Kingdom after the liberation of Bangladesh he did not endeavor to obtain citizenship of Bangladesh and for his conduct and continuous citizenship of Pakistan he was declared not to be citizen of Bangladesh by the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 22.6.73; that the petitioner went abroad before the liberation of Bangladesh and he did not submit his oath of allegiance to Bangladesh as he continued to be the citizen of Pakistan; that immediately after the liberation of Bangladesh as many as 14187 persons living in the United Kingdom obtained Bangladeshi Passport by surrendering their Pakistani Passport but the petitioner did not make any attempt to obtain Bangladeshi Passport and he remained as a Pakistani citizen in London; that the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 disqualifying the petitioner and 38 persons from being citizen of Bangladesh was issued in accordance with the provision of Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972; that the petitioner was permitted to travel to Bangladesh as a foreign national to see his ailing mother after his prayer for citizenship of Bangladesh was turned down twice by the Government; that the entry of the petitioner in Bangladesh was admittedly as a Pakistani citizen and he continued to stay in Bangladesh as a registered foreign national; that the petitioner came to Bangladesh with Pakistani Passport which was issued by Pakistan Embassy in London on 11.1.77, that the petitioner applied to the Government of Pakistan for his Passport affirming that he was a Pakistani National and he obtained extension of his visa twice in Bangladesh as a Pakistani national and thereby admitted himself to be a Pakistani national even in the year 1978, that the petitioner applied to the Ministry of Home Affairs for Bangladeshi citizenship and his application for Citizenship of Bangladesh was not supported by oath of allegiance as required by law; that the petitioner cannot be considered as a Bangladeshi Citizen as he had been staying in Bangladesh after registering himself as a Foreign national on his arrival with a Pakistani Passport; that the petitioner did not submit oath of allegiance voluntarily when he applied for restoration of citizenship of Bangladesh but on the asking of the Government he submitted his oath of allegiance on 30.4.81, that the petitioner was staying in Bangladesh illegally without extending his visa for which he was asked to show cause in 1986 and that non-consideration of his application for citizenship for a long time would not entitle the petitioner to be a citizen of Bangladesh.

7. It is also stated in the affidavit-in- opposition that the petitioner knew very well that he was residing in Bangladesh as a foreign national by registering himself as a foreign national and he had only applied for his citizenship and as such his enrollment as a voter was a bonafide mistake due to concealment of facts about his foreign nationality; that the selection of the petitioner as Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami of Bangladesh was illegal, he being a foreign national and he became the head of the political party to destabilise the sovereignty of Bangladesh; that the fact that the Presidential Candidate went to the petitioner for his support would not ipso facto entitle the petitioner to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that the petitioner by his conduct had renounced his citizenship of Bangladesh and thereby he is disqualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that the application challenging the impugned notification (Annexure-B) is not tenable in law, rather such a belated application is liable to be rejected; that the petitioner came to Bangladesh with Pakistani Passport and he was registered as a foreign national; that he was disqualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh due to anti-Bangladesh activities and unseeming conduct; that the petitioner's continued stay in Bangladesh as a foreign national without any visa was illegal and that is why he was asked by the Government to explain as to how he was staying in Bangladesh; and as the reasons shown in his reply were not tenable in law, the Government took action under the Foreigners Act 1946 and that the impugned notification Annexure-B was issued neither malafide nor with any political motive or for any collateral purpose.

8. In the affidavit-in-reply it is stated that on the 26th of March, 1971 the petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law and continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that he had genuine political difference with Awami League, the party which formed the Government in 1972 but he did not participate in the anti-Bangladeshi campaign inside or outside Bangladesh; that it was denied that the petitioner or the Jamaat-e-Islami had any organizational link with Razakar, AI-Shams or Al-Badr, that the domicile of origin of the petitioner being the territories comprised in Bangladesh his position as a citizen of Bangladesh is protected; that the petitioner's case falls in the same category as that of 38 other people who were also disqualified to be citizen of Bangladesh and anyone of them applied for citizenship was readily granted the same; that on the 30th of November, 1973 the then Awami League Government granted a clemency to the persons who were convicted or accused of offences under the Bangladesh Collaborators (Special Tribunal) Order 1972; that the petitioner reiterated the statements made in paragraph 2-12 of the petition and denied the allegation that he played any heinous role during the war of independence. It is also stated that the petitioner could not be held responsible for the alleged rape, arson, looting and genocide, committed by the Pakistan Army. He also denied that during the Hajj in 1972 the petitioner made any anti-Bangladeshi campaign to dissuade the Muslim countries from giving recognition to Bangladesh or that he organised "East Pakistan Recovery Committee" in Lahore in that year or went to Bengazi in Libya for making any appeal to the Foreign Ministers Conference of Islamic Countries not to recognise Bangladesh or the petitioner met the king of Saudi Arabia seven times as alleged. It is also stated therein that under compulsion the petitioner had to retain his Pakistani Passport as a travel document in a foreign country as England. It is also denied that the petitioner entered Bangladesh as a Pakistani citizen and he merely used Pakistani Passport as a travel document; on the other hand, at the earliest opportunity he surrendered his Pakistani Passport to the Bangladesh authority by making fresh application for citizenship; that the petitioner did not enclose his oath of allegiance with the application for citizenship because he was not asked to do so; that it was also denied that the petitioner could not reconcile with the existence of Bangladesh; that it was also denied that the petitioner is a foreign national or he concealed his status for which voter lists were prepared due to bonafide mistake; it is also stated therein that Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 was ultra vires of the Constitution inasmuch it did not provide any guideline to the executive for the exercise of the power under that Article.

9. It is contended by Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, that the petitioner, his father and his grand-father having been born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh, the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth from the date of coming of Bangladesh into existence on 26.3.71 according to the provisions of the Bangladesh Laws Continuance and Enforcement Order 1971, Bangladesh (Adaptation of Existing Laws) Order 1972 (PO 48 of 1972), the Citizenship Act 1951 and the PO 149 of 1972 and as such the impugned Notification dated 18.4.73 was illegal, malafide and motivated by political enmity. The learned Advocate has also contended that the impugned notification under Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 having been made without giving any opportunity to the petitioner to explain his position the same was bad in law being contrary to the principle of natural justice. The learned Advocate has further contended that Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 having conferred uncontrolled and unfettered discretion amounting to discrimination the said Article is violative of Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh inasmuch as it has not provided any principle or guideline for the exercise of the power given to the Government.

10. Mr. Aminul Huq, the learned Attorney-General, on the other hand, has contended that the petitioner was never a citizen of Bangladesh and the argument of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is based upon an erroneous assumption and supposition that the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law either under the Citizenship Act, 1951 or under the provisions of PO 149 of 1972. According to the learned Attorney-General, the petitioner was disqualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh because of his conduct during the war of liberation and immediately thereafter. The learned Attorney-General secondly has contended that the principle of natural justice is not applicable in the present case inasmuch as no vested right has been affected by the impugned notification. According to the learned Attorney-General. Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 is not ultra virese the Constitution inasmuch as Article 2 laid down the principle and policy for invoking the power under Article 3 of the said PO. The learned Attorney-General further submitted that because of the delay and laches on the part of the petitioner in invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court, the petitioner is not entitled to any relief and as such the application should be rejected.

11. Article 6 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh provides that Citizenship of Bangladesh shall be determined and regulated by law. Under Article 152 of the Constitution a "citizen" means a person who is a citizen of Bangladesh according to the law relating to citizenship.

12. The Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order 1972 (PO 149 of 1972) was made by the President and published in the Official Gazette on the 15th December. 1972 which is as follows:

1. (1) This Order may be called the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary provisions) Order. 1972.

(2) It shall come into force at once and shall be deemed to have taken effect on the 26th day of March, 1971

1A. In this order unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context "Prescribed" means prescribed by rules made under this Order.

2. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law on the commencement of this Order every person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh-

(i) who or whose father or grandfather was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and who was permanent resident of such territories on the 25th day of March 1971 and continues to be so resident; or

(ii) who was a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident and is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force;

Provided that if any person is a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh or his dependent is. in the course of his employment or for the pursuit of his studies residing in a country which was at war with or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh such person or his dependents shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh.

2A. A person to whom Article 2 would have ordinarily applied but for his residence in the United Kingdom shall be deemed to continue to be permanent resident in Bangladesh:

Provided that the Government may notify in the Official Gazette any person or categories of persons to whom this Article shall not apply-

2B. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in Article 2 or in any other law for the time being in force a person shall not except as provided in clause (2) qualify himself to be a citizen of Bangladesh if he-

(i) owes affirms or acknowledges expressly or by conduct allegiance to a foreign state or

(ii) is notified under the proviso to Article 2A:

Provided that citizen of Bangladesh shall not merely by reason of being a citizen or acquiring citizenship of a state specified in or under clause (2) cease to be a citizen of Bangladesh.

(2) The Government may grant citizenship of Bangladesh to any person who is a citizen of any state of Europe or North America or of any other state which the Government may by notification in the Official Gazette specify in this behalf.

3. In case of doubt as to whether a person is qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 of this Order the question shall be decided by the Government which decision shall be final.

4. The Government may, upon an application made to it in this behalf in the manner prescribed, grant citizenship to any/person.

4A. The Government may upon an application, made to it in this behalf in the manner prescribed, grant right of permanent residence to any person on such conditions as may be prescribed.

5. The Government may make rules for carrying out the purpose of this Order."

13. It may be noted that when PO 149 of 1972 was made on 15.12.72 there was only 5 Articles namely Articles 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, which are made effective from the 26th March, 1971. Articles 2A and 2B were inserted in the said Order firstly by Ordinance No. X of 1973 and thereafter by Act V of 1973, and that Article 2B was later on substituted by Ordinance No. VII of 1978. The new Articles 1 A and 4A were inserted by Act LVIII of 1990. It may also be noted that by section 1(2) of Act No. V of 1973, the Act shall be deemed to have taken effect on the 26th day of March, 1971; in other words, Articles 2A and 2B are effective retrospectively from the 26th March, 1971. The impugned notification dated 18.4.73 (Annexure-B) is to the following effect:—

"Whereas it appears that the persons specified below have been staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh and by their conduct cannot be deemed to be citizen of Bangladesh:

And whereas the said persons have continued to be citizen of Pakistan:

Now, therefore, the Government declares under Article 3 of the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order 1972 (PO 149 of 1972), that the persons specified below do not qualify themselves to be the citizens of Bangladesh:—

1. .....................

2.   ....................

3. Prof. Golam Azam, S/o. Golam Kabir of Birgaon, PS Nabinagar, Dist. Comilla and of Elephant Road, Magbazar, Dhaka.

4. ...............

by Order of the Government

Sd/- S. Ahmed,

Secretary."

14. Before entering into any discussion of the contention raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner as well by the learned Attorney-General it is to be mentioned that we are concerned with vires of Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 and the legality or otherwise of the impugned notification Annexure-B. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondents some books, periodicals and news items were mentioned and during the hearing the learned Attorney- General has produced before us a number of the books, periodicals and news items as reproduced either in some books or periodicals and some daily newspapers which quoted certain events and news as was published in the various dailies in 1971. The learned Attorney-General also produced a copy of Gazette Notification dated 15th February, 1972 wherein a proclamation was issued under the provision of the Bangladesh Collaborator (Special Tribunal) Order 1972 (PO 8 of 1972). Except the Gazette Notification dated 15th February, 1972 the other publications are of the dates subsequent to the issuance of the impugned Notification and some of the publications are of the year 1991 and 1992 though the news items and events relate to the period during the war of liberation. Further, the petitioner also challenged the authenticity of some of the events mentioned in the subsequent publications. Except some news items and one photograph showing that the petitioner met General Tikka Khan or General Yahya Khan, there is nothing to directly implicate the petitioner in any of the atrocities alleged to have been perpetrated by the Pakistani Army or their associates the Rajakars, Al-Badrs or the Al-Shams. Except that the petitioner was hobnobbing with the Military Junta during the war of liberation, we do not find anything that the petitioner was in any away directly involved in perpetuating the alleged atrocities during the war of independence. In my view, none of these reports is of any help for solving the legal question raised before us in this matter and, as such, I will refrain from mentioning any such reports or events in course of my discussion of the points raised in this matter.

15. The first contention raised by Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, is that the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law. The learned Advocate has contended that in view of the Proclamation of Independence issued on the 10th April, 1971 from Mujibnagar, the Laws Continuance and Enforcement Order 1971 dated the 10th April, 1971 also issued from Mujibnagar, the Provisional Constitution of Bangladesh Order 1972 and the Bangladesh (Adaptation of Existing Laws) Order 1972 (PO 48 of 1972) the petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by virtue of the provisions contained in the Pakistan Citizenship Act, 1951 as adopted in Bangladesh. According to the learned Advocate for the petitioner the Citizenship Act, 1951 is an existing law on and from the 26th March, 1971 and the petitioner, has acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by virtue of the provisions of the Citizenship Act, 1951. The learned Attorney-General, on the other hand, has contended that the Bangladesh. Citizenship (Temporary Provision) Order 1972 (PO 149 of 1972) although was made on 15.12.72 but it shall be deemed to have taken effect on the 26th day of March, 1971 as provided in clause (2) of Article 1 of PO 149 of 1972.

16. The question is whether provisions of the Citizenship Act of 1951 will be applicable in determining the citizenship of the petitioner or the provisions of PO 149 of 1972 will be applicable in his case. As PO 149 of 1972 is retrospective in operation from the 26th of March, 1971 it occupies the whole field relating to citizenship in Bangladesh. In these circumstances the former Act is to be deemed to be repealed by implication by the latter Act. The old order change the yielding place to the new. The provisions of the Citizenship Act 1951 must yield to the provisions of PO 49 of 1972. In other words, the provisions of PO 149 of 1972 will prevail upon the provisions of the Citizenship Act, 1951 in the field of determination of citizenship of every person in Bangladesh.

17. Moreover Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 begins with a non-obstantive clause which says that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law on the commencement of this Order every person shall be deemed to be citizen of Bangladesh. The clause "in any other law" includes the Citizenship Act, 1951. As such the provisions of PO 149 of 1972 will override the provisions of the Citizenship Act, 1951. Hence I hold that the provisions of the Citizenship Act, 1951 are not applicable in the case of petitioner in determining the question of his citizenship in Bangladesh.

18. In this connection it may be mentioned that the learned Advocate for the petitioner has drawn our attention to section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1951 and contended that the petitioner acquired the citizenship of Bangladesh by virtue of section 3 but if we go through the provisions of section 3 of the said Act it will appear that those provisions will be of no help in determining the question of citizenship in the present context. It may also be mentioned in this connection that in the petition it has been stated that the petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and the learned Advocate for the petitioner has also contended that by virtue of section 4 of the Citizenship Act, 1951 as adopted in Bangladesh by the provisions of PO 48 of 1972 the petitioner acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by birth. But section 4 provides that every person after the commencement of the Act shall be a citizen of Pakistan by birth and there are some exceptions mentioned therein. If we read "Bangladesh" in place of "Pakistan" in section 4 then every person born in Bangladesh after the commencement of this Act shall be citizen of Bangladesh by birth but this Act commenced on or from the 13th of April, 1951 long after the birth of the petitioner.

19. Now let us consider whether the petitioner acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by virtue of the provisions of PO 149 of 1972. As has been quoted above Article 2 of the said PO provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, on the commencement of this Order every person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh—(i) who or whose father or grand-father was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of such territories on the 25th March, 1971 and continued to be so resident; or (ii) who was a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident and not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force: provided that if any person is a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh or his dependent is, in the course of his employment or for the pursuit of his studies, residing in a country, which was at war with, or engaged in military operation against Bangladesh and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh, such person or his dependents, shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh.

20. This Article provides the qualification for acquisition of citizenship of Bangladesh on the commencement of the Order by only two categories of persons. In the first category the person must have the three qualifications namely-(i) who or whose father or grandfather was born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh; (ii) who was a permanent resident of such territory on the 25th day of March, 1971 and (iii) who continues to be so resident. For the second category of person the three qualifications are (i) who was a permanent resident of the territory now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971, (ii) who continues to be so resident and (iii) who is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force. The proviso made provision only for the person who or whose dependent in course of his employment or for the pursuit of his studies was residing in country at war with Bangladesh i.e. in Pakistan and who was prevented from returning to Bangladesh.

21. The petitioner comes to the first Category of persons. So far as the first qualification is concerned there is no dispute that not only the petitioner but his father and grand-father were born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh; so far as his permanent residence is concerned there is also no dispute that he was a permanent resident of the territory now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971 and so far as the 3rd qualification is concerned the question is whether the petitioner continued to be so resident in Bangladesh i.e. whether the petitioner continued to be the permanent resident of Bangladesh or whether the petitioner can be deemed to be continued to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh.

22. In support of his contention that the petitioner acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by operation of law i.e. PO 149 of 1972 the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Bishal Deo Tewari Vs. State reported in 27 DLR 622 in particular to the following observation:

"On the promulgation of this Order which came into force on the 26th March, 1971 the only point that is to be determined is the nationality of the petitioner on the 25th March, 1971. Article 2 makes it clear that who or whose father or grand-father was born in the territories of Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of such territory on the 25lh March, 1971 continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh. "

That case arose out of an order passed by the Deputy Inspector General of Police, Special Branch, Bangladesh and Civil Authority directing Bishal Deo Tewari to reside within the jurisdiction of Sutrapur Police Station under the provisions of Foreigners Order, 1951 and he moved the High Court Division against the order of his detention within the jurisdiction of Lalbagh Police Station by an application under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure stating, inter-alia that he was a national of Bangladesh having been born in Dhaka and after his studies he was managing and performing Puja of Dhakeswari Mondir as Sebayet. In that view on the facts the High Court Division made the observation quoted above. Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate, submitted that the High Court Division has laid down that a person who was born in Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh, and since the petitioner was born in Bangladesh and he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 he continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh. At first sight, it may appear so if we read the observation quoted above without considering the facts and circumstances under which that case arose. That decision is based on the fact that Bishal Deo Tewari "has been living in this country for generations being born at 23/1 Dhakeswari Road within the Police Station of Lalbagh in the District of Dhaka on 4.10.28. He passed Matriculation Examination from Nabakumar Institution, Dhaka in the year 1948 althrough but he did not prosecute further study and started managing and performing Puja as his parent was shebayet of Dhakeswari Deity. So in that case there was no dispute that being born on 4.10.28 he has been continuously living in this country. So the question of his being continuing permanent resident was not disputed in that case; that is why their Lordships determined his citizenship only on the point as to whether on the 25th March, 1971 he was a resident of Bangladesh. In other words since his birth and his continuous residence in Bangladesh was not questioned, the only point for determination was whether he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 and finding that he was so resident on the 25th of March, 1971 their Lordships held that he continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh as he was never absent from the territory now comprised in Bangladesh. In my view that decision is of no help in determining the question of acquisition of citizenship by the petitioner in the present case.

23. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Hamidul Huq Chowdhury and others-Vs. Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 381, in particular to the following observation made therein:

"The contention of the respondents that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was a citizen of Pakistan is based upon firstly, that he was away from Bangladesh and then by a notification dated 18.4.73 the Government declared that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury did not qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury claimed that he never became a citizen of any other state and his citizenship by statutory provision continued to be Bangladeshi. It appears to us on a perusal of the notification dated 18.4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury by statutory provisions was a citizen of Bangladesh. This notification, however, was subsequently declared void by another notification of the Government dated 19.7.1977. In this view we hold that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh though he was away from the country."

24. The learned Advocate for the petitioner laid much stress on the observation made by their Lordships as quoted above as the late Mr. Hamidul Haq Chowdhury was also one of the 39 persons to whom the impugned notification dated 1.8.4.73 (Annexure-B) was issued. That case related to the taking over of the newspapers, the Bangladesh Observer, Purbadesh and the Weekly Chitrali as abandoned property. In that case one of the contentions of the Government was that Mr. and Mrs. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury were the share- holders of the majority shares of those concerns and since late Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was living in Pakistan those properties were declared to be abandoned and at the hearing of that case it was mentioned that by the impugned order dated 18.4.73 late Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was deemed to be not a citizen of Bangladesh and he was continuing as a citizen of Pakistan. Against that contention the subsequent notification dated 19.7.77 was produced to show that the notification dated 18.4.73. So far as it related to Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was corrected by the subsequent notification cancelling the previous one. There was no determination of citizenship nor any issue was there before their Lordships as to whether late Chowdhury acquired citizenship of Bangladesh. Hence I am of the view that the observations made by their Lordships in that case is of no help to the learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention that the petitioner acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by the statutory provision of PO 149 of 1972 inasmuch as the notification dated 18.4.73 has not been cancelled or withdrawn by the Government so far as the petitioner is concerned nor the observations can be taken as an authority for the proposition that prior to the notification dated 18.4.73 the petitioner continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh.

25. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Muktar Ahmed Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 34 DLR 29. In that case Muktar Ahmed had migrated from India to the then East Pakistan on 28.2.51 and got himself along with the members of his family domiciled in the then East Pakistan by obtaining domicile certificates on 25.9.52. During liberation war he remained in Bangladesh althrough and on 29.4.72 he swore an affidavit affirming his allegiance to Bangladesh; but due to the prevailing situations he filed an application to the National Committee of Red Cross for going to Pakistan but he did not pursue that application which was rejected later on. He applied for formal citizenship certificate on 17.3.75 which was refused by the Government and he filed a Writ Petition challenging the order of the Government refusing to grant him citizenship certificate. In view of provision of Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 and in view of the admitted fact of that case their Lordships held that he became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law. Their Lordships further held that the mere fact that he filed an application for going over to Pakistan cannot take away his citizenship. Thus the question before their Lordships was whether Muktar Ahmed lost his citizenship of Bangladesh by merely filing an application for going" over to Pakistan and their Lordships answered the question in the negative because Muktar Ahmed has all the three qualifications to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh inasmuch as he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971, he continued to be so resident in Bangladesh and he was not otherwise declared to be disqualified for being a citizen of Bangladesh under any law. As such it has been held that his citizenship clings to him. But the case of the present petitioner is quite different from the case of Muktar Ahmed inasmuch as he did not continue to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh.

26. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Abdul Hoque Vs. Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 113 and the same case decided by the Appellate Division and reported as the People's Republic of Bangladesh Vs. Abdul Hoque reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 143. In that case Abdul Hoque was admittedly born in Satkhira within Bangladesh in 1932. He was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971; he resided in the then East Pakistan althrough upto November, 1971 when he had to go to the then West Pakistan and he came back to Bangladesh after the political change in August, 1975. He came to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and on his arrival he surrendered the passport and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh; but the Government refused to grant the same and he was asked to leave the country. So he moved this Court by a Writ Petition and their Lordships of the High Court Division on consideration of the facts and circumstances of that case held him to be a Stateless subject who had no nationality. It was held that he cannot be asked to leave the country. On appeal by the Government, their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that High Court Division was not correct in holding that Abdul Hoque was a Stateless person. Their Lordships noticed the factual position of the case. It was not disputed by the Government that Abdul Hoque was born in this country; that he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971, that he went to the then West Pakistan on a business tour; that he was an indoor patient in a hospital of Karachi for about 8 months and when he came out from hospital the repatriation process ceased. Thus he returned to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and surrendered the passport to the Bangladesh Authority; and he applied for citizenship certificate from the Bangladesh Government. The Government having denied the citizenship certificate he filed the writ petition. Their Lordships considered the proviso to Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 in particular the provision considering the facts of that case held that his temporary absence was covered by the proviso to Article 2 and in the eye of law he remained a resident of Bangladesh. As has been pointed out earlier, the proviso applies to only those categories of persons who in course of his employment or whose dependent for pursuit of his studies was residing in Pakistan and who was prevented from returning to Bangladesh. As a matter of fact Abdul Hoque was a Pan (betel leaf) dealer who used to supply Pan to different dealers in the then West Pakistan and he went to Karachi for collection of his dues. As such their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that his case was covered by the proviso to Article 2.

27. The learned Advocate for the petitioner laid much stress on this case because like Abdul Hoque the petitioner was born in Bangladesh and was a permanent resident in Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 and like him the petitioner also went to the then West Pakistan in November, 1971 and like him returned to Bangladesh with a Pakistani Passport. By taking the view that Abdul Hoque went to Pakistan on a business tour their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that the proviso to Article 2 covered his case and as such held that Abdul Hoque was deemed to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh although he was temporarily absent. The learned Advocate laid much stress on the observation of their Lordships that Abdul Hoque's temporary absence was covered by the proviso to Article 2 and contended that the absence of the present petitioner should also be regarded as temporary absence so as to be covered by the proviso to Article 2. It may be mentioned that the proviso to Article 2 does not say about the temporary absence of any person; what it says is that if any person in the course of his employment or for the pursuit of his study was residing in Pakistan and was prevented from returning to Bangladesh, then he should be deemed to be continued to be resident in Bangladesh. Moreover, in that case Abdul Hoque all along was in Pakistan and his case was that he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh; but admittedly the petitioner left Pakistan in the month of December 1972 and did not return to Bangladesh and he was staying outside Bangladesh till 1978 and as such by no stretch of imagination it can be said that the petitioner was prevented from returning to Bangladesh from Pakistan. Considering the facts and circumstances of the present case I am of the view that the proviso to Article 2 is not attracted in the present case. Further, as the learned Attorney- General has rightly pointed out that there is the notification dated 18.4.73 which will prevent to attract the proviso to Article 2. According to the learned Attorney-General, the petitioner was residing in Pakistan for a "Politico Military Mission" and his stay there was neither in course of his employment nor as a dependent for the pursuit of his studies and unless the expression "in the course of his employment" is expanded to include such a mission it cannot be said that the petitioner's case comes within the purview of the proviso to Article 2. In view of the fact that the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 was in force against him and in view of the fact that the petitioner was not residing in Pakistan in course of his employment or for the pursuit of his studies, I am of the view that the proviso to Article 2 is of no help to the petitioner.

28. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Mirza Shahab ispahani Vs. The Government of Bangladesh reported in 40 DLR 87 to the judgment of which one of us was party and the same case decided by the Appellate Division upholding the decision of the High Court Division reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116. The question of citizenship arose in that case incidentally because the property of Mirza Shahab Ispahani was declared as abandoned property. The fact of that case is that Mirza Shahab Ispahani is the son of late Mr. Justice MA Ispahani who retired as the Chief Justice of Dhaka High Court and died in Bangladesh in 1982. He was buried in Dhaka. His son was born in 1941 in Calcutta and while Mr. Justice Ispahani was a District Judge he opted for the then East Pakistan in 1947 and since then Mr. justice Ispahani lived in the then East Pakistan and died there. Mirza Shahab Ispahani while a student was sent to London for prosecuting his studies. He went to England on a passport issued to him from Dhaka which was his permanent address. After his studies he became a Chartered Accountant and had his own earnings in England. He got an allotment of a plot of land at the Gulshan Model Town and built a house thereon. He let out the house to the then Deputy High Commissioner for Britain in Dhaka on a monthly rent. His mother was living in Dhaka and he had a flat at the Ispahani Colony in Dhaka. Finding him absent his property was declared as abandoned 'property. Mirza Shahab Ispahani was holding a Pakistan passport till he surrendered the same on 28.2.72 when he applied for a British passport and he got a British passport on 14.4.1972 valid upto the 13th of May, 1992. The contention of the Government was that he was citizen of Pakistan after the 25th of March, 1971 and as such he was not a citizen of Bangladesh and his property was rightly declared as abandoned property. The High Court Division as well as their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that his case was covered by Article 2A of PO 149 of 1972 which provides that a person to whom Article 2 would have ordinarily applied but for his residence in the United Kingdom shall be deemed to continue to be permanent resident in Bangladesh within the meaning of Article 2.
