In at case there was no dispute regarding the other qualifications except that he did not continue to be permanent resident of Bangladesh as he had been living in UK since 1952; but Article 2A provides that such resident in United Kingdom shall be deemed to be permanent resident of Bangladesh; in other words, although in actual fact he was residing in UK and was not residing in Bangladesh but by fiction of law he shall be deemed to be permanent resident in Bangladesh. In that case their Lordships further considered the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General on behalf of the Government that since MS Ispahani was not permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 he cannot be deemed to be a citizen 'of Bangladesh. This contention, according to their Lordships, was misconceived inasmuch as Article 3 pointedly says that in case of doubt as to whether the person is qualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 the question shall be decided by the Government whose decision shall be final. Their Lordships further noticed that the Government at no stage was called upon to express its view under Article 3. It was further held that the nationality of Mirza Shahab Ispahani was not at issue. In 40 DLR (AD) at page 130 Shahabuddin Ahmed, J (as his Lordship then was) observed as follows:

"Respondent does not come under clause (i) of Article 2, but his case is that he comes under clause (ii) in view of the fact that he was a permanent resident" of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh" on the 25th March, 1971 and continued to be so. From before 25th March, 1971 he had been residing in UK, first for study then for the purpose of professional work. He did not physically continue to reside in Bangladesh but on the strength of Article 2A of PO 149 of 1972, in spite of his residence in the UK "he shall be deemed to be permanent resident of Bangladesh." If he is a Bangladeshi citizen he cannot be a citizen of Pakistan at the same time; he may, however, be a citizen of Bangladesh and UK at the same time."

I am of the view that the case of Mirza Shahab Ispahani is of no help to the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

29. In this connection it may be mentioned that citizenship is distinct from nationality and their Lordships of the Appellate Division held in the case of Mirza Shahab Ispahani that citizenship is a creature solely of domestic law. It refers to rights which a state confers upon its national. Mention may be made in this connection to the following observations made by the Supreme Court of India in the case of State Trading Corporation of India Vs. The Commercial Tax Officer reported in AIR 1963 (SC) JB.

"But the question still remains whether "nationality" and "citizenship" are interchangeable terms. "Nationality" has reference to the jural relationship which may arise for consideration under international law. On the other hand, "citizenship" has reference to the jural relationship under municipal law. In other words, nationality determines the civil rights of a person, natural or artificial, particularly with reference to international law, whereas citizenship is intimately connected with civil rights under municipal law. Hence all citizens are nationals of a particular State but all nationals may not be citizens of the State. In other words citizens are those persons who have full political rights as distinguished from nationals who may not enjoy full political rights and are still domiciled in that country."

30. The learned Advocate in this connection has referred to Chapter 7 of Dicey and Morris on the Conflict of Laws, Eleventh Edition, in particular to Rule 10 at page 128 wherein it is stated that every independent person can acquire domicile of choice by the combination of residence and intention of permanent or indefinite residence but not otherwise; and the learned Advocate has submitted that intention is one of the factors for determination of the citizenship of a person. It may be pointed out that the concepts of domicile or of nationality are matters relating to private international law by which personal rights such as marriage, divorce, majority or minority, the right of succession, etc. are determined and these are different from the rights of citizenship.

31. In this connection the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Advocate General, Government of East Pakistan, Dhaka Vs. Benoy Bhusan Majumder and others reported in 25 DLR (SC) 9. In that case the respondents after obtaining migration certificate went to India from the then East Pakistan on the 9th December, 1964 from their village home in the District of Bakergonj and they were found in their village in 1967. A case was started against them under section 14 of the Foreigners Act 1946. Their defence was that due to communal disturbances in the then East Pakistan in the year 1964 they temporarily took shelter in India but came back to Pakistan to their village home within a short time when the condition became normal. The trial Magistrate found them guilty of offence under section 14 of the Foreigners Act and on appeal the Sessions Judge, Bakergonj upheld the conviction. On revision to the High Court a learned Single Judge found on evidence that there were communal disturbances in the then East Pakistan in the year 1964 for which the respondents went to Calcutta on the strength of migration certificates, not with the intention of settling there permanently but to take shelter for a temporary period to protect their lives and within a month or two after their entry in India they returned to their house under a border slip. The learned Single Judge held that the respondents who were then admittedly Pakistani citizen before their entry in India did not lose their citizenship by merely crossing into India and staying there for a month or two on the strength of migration certificate. On appeal by the Advocate General of the then Government of East Pakistan, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that the respondents who were admittedly the citizens of Pakistan before their departure to India did not lose their Pakistani Citizenship by their entry in. India and their temporary stay in that country in the then abnormal situation obtaining in some areas of the then East Pakistan and held that the respondents were not foreigners within the meaning of section 2 (a) of the Foreigners Act. So this case is of no help for the petitioner to hold that temporary physical absence does not discontinue his continuing residence in Bangladesh.

32. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has contended that the impugned notification (Annexure-B) is a prospective order and it cannot affect the petitioner, since according to the learned Advocate till the 17th of April, 1973 the petitioner should be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. The learned Advocate has contended that the expression "do not qualify" is not retrospective in nature and as such it must be read prospectively. In this connection the learned Advocate has referred to Bindra's Interpretation of Statutes 5th Edition 1970 wherein the author expressed himself as follows:

"A legislature can certainly give retrospective effect to pieces of legislation passed by it but an executive Government exercising subordinate and delegated powers cannot make legislation retrospective in effect unless that power is expressly conferred. The rule-making authority does not possess plenary power to give the subordinate delegated legislation retrospective operation unless and until that power is expressly conferred by the parent enactment. Hence the rule is well established that even in a case where the executive Government acts as a delegate of legislative authority, it has no plenary power to provide for retrospective operation unless and until that power is expressly conferred by the parent enactment"

Relying on this passage the learned Advocate for the petitioner has contended that although Article 3 of the PO 149 of 1972 has been expressly made retrospective in operation from 26.3.1971 but the order contained in the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 cannot act retrospectively. In support of his contention Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate has referred to five cases of the Indian jurisdiction. The first of which is the case of Modi Food Products Ltd. Vs. The Commissioner of Sales Tax reported in AIR 1956 (All.) 35 wherein a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court held that a legislature can certainly give retrospective effect to a piece of legislation passed by it but an executive Government exercising subordinate and delegated legislative powers cannot make legislation retrospective in effect unless that power is expressly conferred by the statute. In that case the petitioner was a dealer in non-edible oils. The UP Sales Tax Act came into force with effect from 1.4.48. The petitioner submitted its return for the period from 6.1.1946 to 3.5.1947. There was an amendment of the UP Sales Tax Act by Act No. XXV of 1948 inserting Section 3A by which a higher rate of Sales Tax was authorised and in exercise of the power under the new section 3A the State Government issued notification on 8.6.48 declaring that with effect from 9.4.48 sales tax shall be at the higher rate. It was in that circumstances held that new amendment will not operate retrospectively. Needless to mention that as a general rule taxing statute does not operate retrospectively. The second case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of ML Bagga-Vs. C Murhar Rao reported in AIR 1956 Hyderabad 35 wherein it has been laid down by a Division Bench that parties were governed by the law in force on the date when a suit is instituted or a proceeding commenced and any subsequent amendment or alteration cannot affect pending proceedings, must always be read subject to the corollary that a legislature could always expressly provide that pending proceeding be affected by an amendment of the law. In that case the respondent moved the Rent Controller on 10.1.55 for an order of eviction of the tenant on the ground of his being a defaulter and an order for eviction was passed but the petitioner claimed protection under a new rule which came into force subsequently and it was held therein that the subsequent new rules have no retrospective effect to protect the tenant from eviction. A similar question came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Sayedur Rahman Vs. The Chief Election Commissioner, reported in 17 DLR. (SC) 23. In that case Mr. Sayedur Rahman was elected a Member to the Provincial Assembly but he was unseated by the Election Tribunal because of Section 116 of the Representation of People Act, 1957 (Act XXXI of 1957) which provided that a Government Contractor was disqualified to be elected as a Member of the Provincial Assembly. The Dhaka High Court on appeal affirmed the decision of the Election Tribunal. He thereafter filed an appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan and during the pendency of the appeal before the Supreme Court the Representation of People Act 1957 was repealed with retrospective effect stating that the Act to be deemed to be repealed on 23rd March, 1962; and as the election was held in May 1962 and the Election Tribunal passed its order on the 7th of February, 1963 the Supreme Court of Pakistan therefore held that there was no doubt that the amending Act was retrospective in operation and since the disqualification was removed by the amending Act, the membership of Mr. Sayedur Rahman was upheld by the Supreme Court. The 3rd case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Sarder and others Vs. The State reported in AIR 1961 Calcutta 181. In that case an FIR was lodged on 17.12.57 alleging abduction against the accused and charge sheet was submitted on 24.4.58. What happened in that case was that the investigation was started and major portion was completed under the Calcutta Police Act and then by an amendment section 156 of the Cr PC was made applicable by a notification dated 24.2.58. In those circumstances it was held that the subsequent amendment will be of no help for the prosecution. The 4th case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that of Callcuta Wynad Motor Service (Private) Ltd. Vs. The Stat, of Kera/(l and others reported in AIR 1959 (Kera) 347. In that case what happened is that the term of Regional Transport Authority expired before the order was made on 13.11.58 giving licence for plying of buses in a certain route and the Government by a subsequent notification dated 23.12.58 ordered the continuation of the old Regional Transport Authority and as such it was held that when the executive Government acts as a delegate of a legislative body it had no plenary power to provide for retrospective operation unless and until that power is expressly conferred by the parent enactment and this case was decided following the case report in AIR 1956 (Hyderabad) 35 as referred to above. The next case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of India Sugars and Refineries Ltd. Vs. State of Mysore and others reported in AIR 1960 (Mysore) 326 wherein it was held that the power conferred on the Government under the Madras Sugar Factory Control Act, 1949 to levy did not include a power to impose such retrospectively. In that case by certain notification enhanced rate of sales tax was levied. In that case it was held that unless expressly provided, the power to levy can be exercised only prospectively and not retrospectively.

33. These five decisions were referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner on the assumption that the petitioner was a citizen of Bangladesh from 26.3.71 till 18.4.73 when the impugned notification was made. In view of my discussion above, it cannot be said that the petitioner was a citizen of Bangladesh prior to the making of the impugned notification on 18.4.73 In my view these five cases referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner have no manner of application in the case before us.

34. Another contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner in this connection was that the action of the Government was out and out malafide and the impugned notification was made on account of political enmity and as such the impugned notification was bad in law. It is stated in the petition that Jamaat-e-Islami contested the general election held in 1970 against the Awami League and as such the Awami League Government which was formed after the liberation of Bangladesh was inimical towards the petitioner because of which the impugned notification was made for collateral purpose. But the impugned notification (Annexure-B) itself shows that there are as many as 38 other persons who have also been declared to be deemed not to be citizens of Bangladesh along with the petitioner by the same notification. There is nothing to show that the other 38 belonged to Jamaat-e-Islami. Apparently those persons belonged to different political party and some of them belonged to no political party. Furthermore, before the impugned notification the first general election was held in independent Bangladesh in the month of March, 1973. As such this cannot be treated as a ground for issuance of the impugned notification. I, therefore, hold that there was no malafide in issuing the impugned notification.

35. Another point has been raised in this connection by Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, as to how a doubt as to the citizenship is to be resolved and the learned Advocate has referred to section 19 of the Citizenship Act, 1951 and Rule 24 of the Citizenship Rule 1952. But the said section 19 provides that where a person with respect to whose citizenship a doubt exists, whether on question of law or of fact makes application in that behalf to the Central Government, the Central Government may grant him a certificate that at the date of the certificate he was a citizen of Pakistan. Thus section 19 refers to the granting of a citizenship certificate and Rule 24 provides that the Central Government may on application made to it in that behalf grant a certificate of citizenship in Form Q1 to any person with respect to whose citizenship a doubt exists whether on a question of law or of facts and it further provides that the Certificate of Citizenship granted in Form Q1 shall be withdrawn as soon as possible and not later than the issue of a certificate of citizenship under any of these rules. It shall be granted for one year in the first instance but may be extended from time to time. It appears, therefore, that section 19 and the Rule 24 provide for granting a provisional certificate of citizenship till the doubt is resolved. There is nothing in the said section 19 or the said Rule 24 providing any guideline for resolution of the question of citizenship of a doubtful nature. Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 laid down the principle for acquisition of citizenship of Bangladesh and when the three conditions laid down therein are fulfilled the person concerned automatically acquires the citizenship of Bangladesh and the doubt referred to in Article 3 relates to one of the three conditions only, either there should be a doubt as to the place of birth or as to whether the person was a permanent resident in Bangladesh on the 25th of March, 1971 or whether he continued to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh. The impugned notification (Annexure-B) relates only to the 3rd condition namely, "continued to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh" and the impugned notification has expressly stated that the persons mentioned therein including the petitioner have been staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh and as such by their conduct they cannot be deemed to be the citizen of Bangladesh. Moreover, those persons have been continued to be the citizens of Pakistan.

<u>36. Relying upon the word "conduct" the learned Attorney-General tried to argue pointing out to certain subsequent events as anti-state activities of the petitioner dis-entitling him to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. But the events and the alleged conduct of the petitioner referred to by the learned Attorney-General may be taken into consideration if any case is made out under Article 2B of the said Presidential Order. Mr. AR Yusuf has pointed out, and in my opinion rightly, that Article 2A and 2B were inserted in PO 149 of 1972 subsequent to the making of the impugned notification. It may be mentioned that although Article 2A and Article 2B were first inserted in PO 149 of 1972 by Ordinance No. X of 1973 on 23.5.73 and subsequently by Act. V of 1973 dated 25.6.73 and although by section 1 (2) of Act V of 1973 the newly inserted Article 2A and 2B were given retrospective effect from 26.3.71 the fact remains that the impugned notification was made before the passing of the amending Act or Ordinance. As such I am of the view that Article 2B is not applicable in the present case as the impugned notification was made prior to the insertion of Article 2B in the PO 149 of 1972.</u>

37. The learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to the voter list published on 5.8.83 (Annexure-M) and the voter list published on 15.2.90 (Annexure-I) and submitted that as the petitioner was duly enrolled as a voter in the voter list and as according to sub-Article(2) of Article 122 of the Constitution no one can be enlisted as a. voter unless he is citizen of Bangladesh and also in view of the provision of Article 8(1) of the Bangladesh Electoral Roll Order 1972 (PO 104 of 1972) providing that the Electoral Roll shall contain the names of every citizen, the petitioner should be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. The learned Attorney-General, however, has pointed out that the petitioner was described in the voter list of 1983 as a service-holder and in the voter list of 1990 as a businessman and because of this mis-description the petitioner might have been enrolled as voter by bonafide mistake. Be that as it may, simply because the petitioner was enlisted as a voter will not ipso-facto make him a citizen of Bangladesh because, as has been pointed out earlier, according to Article 6 of the Constitution the citizenship of Bangladesh shall be determined and regulated by law; and the citizenship of the petitioner is to be determined in accordance with the provisions of PO 149 of 1972. I have already held that the petitioner cannot be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 of the said PO.

38. The next ground urged by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the impugned notification (Annexure-B) is bad in law because before issuance of the said notification the petitioner was not given any opportunity to explain his position. In other words, the learned Advocate submitted that the impugned notification is bad for not complying with the principle of natural justice. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Shah Abdur Rahman Vs. The Collector and Deputy Commissioner, Bahawal Nagar and ors. reported in 16 DLR (SC)470. That is a case of removal of a Chairman of a Union Committee without giving any notice to him to show cause and as such the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that although there is no specific provision in the Basic Democracies Order entitling the member proceeded against for giving an opportunity to show cause, the member was entitled to such opportunity on the principle of natural justice. The learned Advocate then referred to the case of Saiyyid Abul Ala Maudoodi and others Vs. The Govt. of West Pakistan and others reported in PLD 1964(SC) 673 and 17 DLR (SC) 209 wherein their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan referred to the case of Shah Abdur Rahman reported in 16 DLR (SC) 470 as already referred. The learned Advocate has also referred to the case of Steamer Agent Association Vs. Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD) 272. In this case the Steamer agent's licence for carrying on LMD business was withdrawn by the authority without giving any prior notice and it was held that the principle of natural justice requiring prior hearing before withdrawal of the licence was required. This case also followed the decision in the case of Shah Abdur Rahman reported in 16 DLR (SC) 470. The learned Advocate has also referred to the case of M/s Hake Mohammad Ali & Sons Vs. Burmah Eastern Ltd. reported in 38 DLR (AD) 41 in support of his contention. In this case the licence for running a petrol pump was cancelled without giving any prior show cause notice and Their Lordships of the Appellate. Division held that -the principle of natural justice was violated in cancelling the licence without giving any notice. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also referred to the case of Commissioner of Income-Tax, East Pakistan Vs. Fazlur Rahman reported in 16 DLR (SC) 410. In this case the respondent filed four applications under Section 33A of the Income Tax Act against certain assessment order but the Commissioner without giving the respondent a hearing dismissed the application and it was held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan following the decision in the case of Chief Commissioner, Karachi and another Vs. Mrs. Dina Sohrab Katrak reported in 11 DLR (SC) 113, that mere absence of a provision as to notice cannot override the principle of natural justice. Reference was also made to the case of University of Dhaka Vs. Zakir Ahmed deported in 16 DLR (SC) 722. In this case Zakir Ahmed was expelled from the University for a period of two years without giving any prior notice and the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that the order of expulsion without serving any prior notice was bad for not complying with the principle of natural justice. The learned Advocate lastly referred to the case of Ridge Vs. Baldwin reported in 1963 (2) All England Reports 66. In this case the Chief Constable Ridge was dismissed from service without serving any prior notice to show cause and the House of Lords by a majority judgment held that the order of dismissal was bad for non-compliance of the principle of natural justice.

39. The learned Attorney-General, however, did not dispute the principle laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan or our Appellate Division or by the House of Lords but has contended that the principle of natural justice, audi alteram partem, is not of universal application and has further submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the present case the principle of natural justice is not applicable.

40. So far as the case reported in 16 DLR (SC) 470 is concerned, that was the case of removal of the Chairman of a Town Committee from his office. The case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 272 relates to withdrawal of licence from carrying on LMD business. The case reported in 38 DLR (AD) 42 is also related to cancellation of licence. It is well settled that if an order affects the vested right in property or status or has penal consequences there must be an opportunity to show cause before passing such order. This general proposition of law is not disputed by the learned Attorney-General but he has contended that the principle of natural justice is not of universal application. So far as the decisions of Pakistan Supreme Court are concerned the latest in point of time as has been referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Saiyyid Abul Ala Malldoodi reported in 17 DLR (SC) 209. In that case the then Governments of West Pakistan and East Pakistan simultaneously issued orders under section 16 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1908 declaring the Jamaat-e-Islami to be an unlawful association. These orders were struck down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan finding the said Section 16 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1908 ultra vires the Constitution being inconsistent with the fundamental right Article 7, freedom of association. But all the five learned judges expressed their opinion on the principle of natural justice. Cornelius, CJ agreed with the comment made in Willoughby's Commentary on the Constitution of United States, 1929 Vol. III page 1681 wherein the learned Author reproduced an observation of a learned judge of the New York Supreme Court to the effect that he was "opposed to the judiciary attempting to set bounds to legislative authority or declaring a statute invalid upon any fanciful theory of higher law or principles of natural right outside the Constitution." Cornelius CJ observed that it was a valid comment. SA Rahman, J referring to the cases of Chief Commissioner of Karachi Vs. Mrs. Dina Sohrab Katrak (11 DLR SC 113), M/s. Farid Sons Limited Vs. the Government of Pakistan (13 DLR SC 233) and the Province of East Pakistan Vs. Nur Ahmed (16 DLR SC 375) held that the principle of natural justice requiring a hearing to be granted to a person before being condemned, applies not only to judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings but also to administrative proceeding, provided that the relevant statute does not exclude its application and requires the administrative authority concerned to base its decision on an objective determination of facts. Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, laid much stress on the observation of his Lordship. In the same judgment Fazle Akbar J after referring to' the case of M/s. Farid Sons Ltd. held that the Court cannot question the subjective satisfaction of the Government and thereby held that the question of natural justice was not applicable in that case. Kaikaus, J made general observations without referring to any particular case about the applicability of principles of natural justice in an administrative or a judicial or quasi-judicial capacity but observed that there must be some exception to the general rule. Homoodur Rahman, J after making reference to the cases of Mrs. Dina Sohrab Katrak, M/s. Farid Sons Ltd. and the case of Ridge Vs. Baldwin reported in 1963(2) All England Report 66 observed as follows:

"No doubt, there are observations in the judgments relied upon by the learned counsel which tend, at first sight, to support this wide contention, but a more careful examination of these decisions will reveal that this proposition cannot be as wide or universal as is sought to be contended by learned counsel. In my view, the nature of the thing to be done, the manner in which it is to be done and the circumstances in which it is to be done are important considerations which must be taken into account in determining whether above-mentioned principle should be applied in a given case or not."

After considering the aforesaid three cases his Lordship pointed out that even in the case of Ridge Vs. Baldwin in the dissenting judgment it was observed by Lord Evershed that" it has been said many times that the exact requirements in any case of the so-called principle of natural justice cannot be precisely defined; that they depend in each case on the circumstances of that case and to point out that even the decisions on this point were not uniform nor was it possible to extract from them the means of propounding a precise statement of the circumstances of the cases in which the principles can be invoked before the Courts". His Lordship agreed with these observations, as they coincide with his own views in this matter; and his Lordship then held that the rule of principle of natural justice was not of universal application.

<u>41. It will appear from the cases referred to above that in case of removal of dismissal from service or cancellation of licence or removal from office the rule of audi alteram partem was made applicable. In other words, if anyone is deprived of his property or office or status he must be given a prior notice before being penalised by any order. In the case before us can it be said that the petitioner was deprived of any vested right? It is not a case of cancellation of one's citizenship. The impugned notification (Annexure-B) disqualified 39 persons including the petitioner from being deemed to be citizen of Bangladesh because there was doubt in their case. In the case of the petitioner although there was no dispute that he was born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh and he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971; there was doubt as to whether he continued to be permanent resident of Bangladesh. Admittedly on the date when the impugned notification was issued, that is on the 18th April, 1973, the petitioner was not residing in Bangladesh from the 16th December, 1971, nor he could be deemed to be permanent resident of Bangladesh under the proviso to Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972. By the impugned notification the Government in exercise of its power under Article 3 declared that the petitioner along with 38 others were not to be deemed to be citizen of Bangladesh. As the petitioner had no vested right there is no question of service of any prior notice to him.</u>

42. The learned Attorney-General, however, contended that it was not practicable for the service of any notice upon the petitioner as he was admittedly then residing outside the country.

The learned Attorney-General argued that the Gazette Notification published on the 15th February, 1972 under the provision of PO 8 of 1972 may be regarded as substantial compliance with the principle of natural justice. As has been observed by Hamoodur Rahman, J in the case of Moulana Moudoodi in my view the nature of the thing to be done, the manner in which it is to be done and the circumstances under which the notification was made do not call for the service of any prior notice to the petitioner in the facts and circumstances of the case. I, therefore, hold that in the facts and circumstances of the present case the principle of natural justice is not applicable.

43. Next comes the question of vires of Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has contended that Article 3 is violative of Article 27 and Article 31 of the Constitution inasmuch as it did not provide any principle or guideline for the exercise of the power by the Government. According to the learned Advocate, conferment of such unfettered and uncontrolled discretion amounts to discrimination and as such the impugned Article 3 is unconstitutional. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has relied upon the case of Dr. Nurul Islam Vs. Bangladesh reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 140. In that case Dr. Nurul Islam challenged the order of his compulsory retirement on the ground that section 9(2) of Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 was ultra vires the Constitution and also on the ground that the order of his compulsory retirement was bad in law being actuated by malice in law. Dr. Nurul Islam was then Professor of Medicine and Director of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. By an order dated 22nd November, 1978 Government made the post of Director of the IPGMR a non-practicing post and released him of his duty as Professor of Medicine. He challenged the legality of this order in Writ Petition No. 591 of 1979 and this Court by an order dated 6th December, 1979 declared that order to have been made without any lawful authority. Thereafter the order of compulsory retirement was passed. All the five Hon'ble judges of the Appellate Division held that the order of compulsory retirement was made only to circumvent the order passed by this Court in the earlier Writ Petition and, as such, the order of compulsory retirement was bad being malice in law. Three of the learned Judges considered the provision of sub-section (2) of section 9 under which the order of compulsory retirement was passed and held that section 9(2) of the said Act was ultra vires of the Constitution being inconsistent with Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Two of the learned Judges including the learned Chief Justice refrained from declaring the law as unconstitutional on the principle that the Court will not declare the law unconstitutional if the case can be disposed of on some other point. Fazle Munim, J (as his Lordship then was) after making elaborate discussion and referring to the various cases held, that section 9(2) of the said Act wall unconstitutional. Ruhul Islam, J also, after detailed discussion, declared the law as unconstitutional and BH Chowdhury, J (as his Lordship then was) without any discussion held that neither the Act or the Rules provided any principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion of the Government when it proposed to retire the Government servant under section 9(2) and as such held section 9(2) ultra vires of the Constitution.

44. To understand the case more fully section 9(2) of the Public Servants Retirement Act 1974 may be quoted which is as follows:

"The Government may, at any time, retire from service a public servant who has completed 25 years of service without assigning any reason".

Considering this provision their Lordships of the Appellate Division held this provision of law to be unconstitutional as it provided no principle or guideline for the exercise of this power by the Government. In that case there were as many as 34 Doctors who have at that time completed 25 years of service but only four out of 34 including Dr. Nurul Islam were compulsorily retired. There is nothing in the law to show how the four out of 34 were chosen and naturally it was discriminatory and as such it has been held that the impugned section 9(2) was unconstitutional. In the present case the impugned Article 3 reads as follows:

"In case of doubt as to whether a person is qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 of this Order, the question shall be decided by the Government, which decision shall be final."

It has been contended by the learned Attorney-General that principle or guideline is there in Article 2 which provided for the qualifications to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. In other words the "doubt" is confined to Article 2 of the Order, that is either there must be doubt as to whether a person was born within territory now comprised in Bangladesh or there must be doubt as to whether he was a permanent resident in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 or there must be doubt as to whether he continued to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh. Reading Article 2 and Article 3 together we find that the cases in which doubt may arise has been expressly mentioned in Article 2. The learned Attorney-General has referred to paragraph 87 of the report in Dr. Nunul Islam's case which is as follows:

"The minimum principle or guide-line as has been provided in service rules as appear from the cases cited in this judgment is that public interest or the interest of public service If either the impugned Act or the rules made thereunder provided such principle, the minimum requirement of law as showing the existence of some guide-line for the exercise of discretion in retiring a Government servant who has completed 25 years of service would, I think, be satisfied, thus making it immune from any challenge on the ground of discrimination violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. I am of the opinion, therefore, that in the absence of such a guide-line either in the Act or the rules framed thereunder, section 9 (2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act (XII of 1974) suffers from unconstitutionality and the impugned action based on it is open to the challenge of being discriminatory and in violation of the equality provisions of the Constitution. "

The learned Attorney General has submitted that in that case since there was no principle or guideline either in section 9(2) or the rules framed thereunder their Lordships declared that section as unconstitutional but In the present case it cannot be declared unconstitutional on that ground as the principle is provided there in Article 2.

45. Judicial decision must of necessity be dependent on the facts and circumstances of a particular case and what superciliously appears to be an unequal application of law, may not necessarily amount to denial of actual protection of law unless it is shown that there is an element of discrimination. Reference may be made in this connection to the case of Budhan Chowdhury and others Vs. State of Bihar reported in AIR 1955 (SC) 191. In that case section 30 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which empowered the Government to appoint Special Magistrate to try certain offences was challenged as being discriminatory. In that case the accused was convicted and sentenced to suffer RI for five years under section 366 of the Penal Code. The question of discrimination arose because the Magistrate on receipt of the charge-sheet may either send the case to the Court of Sessions or to the Court of a Magistrate specially empowered under section 30 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and since the procedure in the two courts are different, it was argued that section 30 was discriminatory and, as such, unconstitutional. The Supreme Court of India repelled the argument and held that it was not discriminatory. Reference may also he made to the case Matajog Dobey Vs. HC Dhari reported in AIR 1956 (SC) 44. In that case section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was challenged as unconstitutional being discriminatory inasmuch as a Government Servant without any sanction from the Government cannot be prosecuted like other persons. It was held by the Supreme Court of India that section 197 is not discriminatory. In that case it has been observed as follows:

"It has to be borne in mind that a discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory power and that abuse of power is not to be easily assumed where the discretion is vested in the Government and not in a minor official."

This case is relevant for the purpose of our case to show that the discretion under Article 3 was not left with any official but it was left with the Government itself. In the case of Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia and others Vs. Shri Justice SR Tendolkar and others reported in AIR 1958 (SC) 538, a Commission of Enquiry was appointed to enquire into the affairs of the Companies and the firms which were promoted or controlled by Ram" Krishna Dalmia, Jaidayal Dalmia, Shanti Prasad Jain. The appointment of Commission of Enquiry in that case was challenged on the ground of discrimination which the Supreme Court of India rejected. In that case the Supreme Court of India made the following observation:

"In the tempo of the prevailing conditions in modern society events occur which were never foreseen and it is impossible for Parliament or any legislature to foresee eventualities and therefore, it must leave the duty of taking the necessary action to appropriate Government."

In the case of Jibendra Kishore Achharyya Chowdhury Vs. The Province of East Pakistan reported in PLD 1957 (SC) 9X, section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was challenged us unconstitutional and repealing that contention Munir, CJ. observed as follows:

"The Act challenged in these cases is not discriminatory on the face of it because it does no more than empower the Provincial Government to acquire the interest of such rent-receivers as may be specified in the notification in any district, part of a district or local area and the Provincial Government could as it has actually done so far as the rent receivers throughout the Province at one and the same time, and if the law be as I think it is, that in cases where a statute is not ex facie discriminatory, but is capable of being administered in a discriminatory manner, the challenging the constitutionality of that statute must show that it has actually been administered to the detriment of a particular class and in a partial, unjust and oppressive manner; the appellant's case must fail because the acquisition challenged is not piecemeal but wholesale, and nobody can have any occasion to complain that he or the class to which he belongs has been singled out for a discriminatory treatment."

In the present case the petitioner also failed to establish that the impugned notification was issued in a discriminatory manners so far as he is concerned because ex facie Article 3 is not discriminatory. In the case of East West Steamship Vs. Pakistan reported in PLD 1958 (SC) 41 Munir, CJ made similar observations as quoted above. In the case of Waris Miah Vs. The State reported in PLD 1957 (SC) 157 Munir, CJ declared section 23 of Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 as unconstitutional being violative of the equality clause because the impugned provision gave power to the Government or the State. Bank of Pakistan to determine whether a person who offends any provision of the Act was to be tried under the ordinary law or by the Adjudication Officer or by a Tribunal. Since the Act as framed made provision for discrimination between the persons falling in the same class the relevant provision of law was declared unconstitutional. In the case of Province of East Pakistan Vs. Sirajul Huq Patwari reported in 19 DLR (SC) 281 a Full Bench of the Dhaka High Court by a majority decision declared section 57 of the Electoral College Act 1964 as invalid and as result thereof the Union Council, Town Committee and Union Committee constituted in the then Province of East Pakistan have been rendered illegal bodies. In reversing the decision of the Dhaka High Court, Hamoodur Rahman, J as his Lordship then was, made the following observations:

"One of the cardinal principles of interpretation is that a law should be interpreted in such a manner that it should rather be saved than destroyed. The Courts should lean in favour of upholding the constitutionality of legislation and it is, therefore, incumbent upon Courts to be extremely reluctant to strike down laws as unconstitutional. This power should be exercised only when absolutely necessary, for injudicious exercise of this power might well result in grave and serious consequence as had actually happened in this case."

I respectfully agree with the above observations made by his Lordship. The learned Attorney-General in this connection has referred to the case of Ch. Tika Ramji and others Vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh and others reported in AIR 1956 (SC) 676 in particular to the following observation of their Lordships of the Privy Council quoted from the case of Commonwealth of Australia and others Vs. Bank of New South Wales and others reported in 1950 AC 235:

"Every case must be judged on its own facts and in its own setting of time and circumstances, and it may be that in regard to some economic activities and at some stage of social development it might be maintained that prohibition with a view to State monopoly was the only practical and reasonable manner of regulation, and that inter-State trade, commerce and intercourse thus prohibited and thus monopolized remained absolutely free."

On the other hand, Mr. AR Yusuf has drawn our attention to paragraph 51 of the reports, and I think rightly, that in that case the discretion of Cane Commissioner under the relevant Act was not unfettered but it was conditioned that he should consult the Factory and the Co-operative Society and further that his order was subject to an appeal to the State Government and this was provided in the rule framed under the statute under challenge. So this case is of no help to the learned Attorney-General.

46. In the present case Article 3 is not ex-facie discriminatory. It is to be guided by the principle laid down in Article 2 and, as such, it cannot be said that Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 has given unfettered discretion to the Government to declare a person not to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh in case of doubt.

<u>47. I, therefore, hold that Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 is not ultra vires of the Constitution. The last point to be considered is, whether the petitioner is guilty of laches in moving this Court in the Writ Jurisdiction. The learned Attorney-General has submitted that the remedy by way of Writ being extraordinary one the aggrieved person must come to the Court expeditiously and unreasonable delay would disentitle him to such an extraordinary remedy. In support of his contention the learned Attorney-General referred to the case of Standard Vacuum Oil Co. Vs. the Trustees of the Port of Chittagong reported in 13 DLR 804 wherein Murshed, J presiding over the Division Bench observed as follows:</u>

<u>"There is no law of limitation, as such, with regard to Writ Petitions. But, it is well settled that this Court will refuse to exercise its discretion to issue writs of mandamus or orders of a like nature, if the petitioners do not come to Court with due diligence and expedition."</u>

<u>He has also referred to the case of Akhtaruddin Khan Vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in 15 DLR 1 wherein Murshed, J presiding over the Division Bench observed as follows:</u>

<u>"No period of limitation has been prescribed by law with regard to the seeking of any relief sought for under Article 98 of the Constitution just as there was no law of limitation applicable to the issuance of a prerogative Writ by this Court on an application of an aggrieved party. It has, however, been consistently held that an aggrieved patty, seeking a speedy relief such as the issuance of prerogative writ, given in summary proceedings, must show due diligence in asking for such relief."</u>

<u>The learned Attorney-General also referred to the case of M/s. Panna Lal Binji Vs. Union of India reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 397 wherein it has been held that it is well-settled that such conduct of the petitioners would disentitle them to any relief at the hand of the Court. The next case referred to is the case of Rabindra Nath Vs. Union of India reported in AIR 1970 (SC) 470 wherein it has been held that if the Government has turned down one representation, making of another representation on similar line would not enable the petitioner to explain the delay. In the case before us the petitioner took no step since the rejection of his prayer for restoration of citizenship since 1977. After long 15 years the petitioner woke up when steps were taken under the Foreigners Act; as such he is not entitled to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court. The learned Attorney-General also referred to the case of Durga Prosad Vs. Chief Controller of Imports and Exports reported in AIR. 1970 (SC) 769, the case of Tilak Chand Moti Chand Vs. HB Munshi reported in AIR 1970 (SC) 878 and also the case of M/s D. Cawasji and Co. Vs. State of Mysore reported in AIR 1975(SC) 813; in all these cases it was stressed that the petitioner should move the Writ jurisdiction with utmost expedition.</u>

<u>48. Mr. AR Yusuf has referred to the case of Shafiqur Rahman Vs. Certificate Officer, Dhaka reported in 29 DLR (SC) 233 and referred to the observations that in the particular case the petitioner may not rush to the Court on the initiation of the proceeding but when he was threatened with some actual danger he can approach the Court for appropriate relief. In this case the petitioner took lease of the premises of a cinema hall for 15 years for the purpose of exhibiting films. Under the Amusement Act 1923 he used to affix stamps with the cinema tickets issued to the customers and, according to him no amusement tax was due from him; but in spite of that several certificate proceedings for recovery of amusement tax were started against him. In pursuance of the certificate proceedings, distress warrant was issued and some properties were attached. But since the sale proceeds were insufficient, body warrant was issued against the petitioner and at this stage the petitioner filed a Writ Petition in the High Court and it was held that the petitioner was guilty of laches. So this decision is of no help to the petitioner, rather it goes against the petitioner. While disposing of that case their Lordships of the Appellate Division made the following observation:</u>

<u>"In view of the authorities which have been cited we have no manner of doubt that even in a proceeding for writ in the nature of certiorari the aggrieved person must show diligence and a sense of urgency for the purpose of invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction. In particular case he may not rush to the Court immediately on the initiation of a proceeding which, according to him, is a nullity but has not yet threatened him with any actual danger but when some positive steps have been taken in the said proceeding to his prejudice and he instead of resisting it, submits to it and carries out various orders made in the said proceeding, he has, 'in accordance with the authorities referred to above, distinctly disentitled himself to the said extraordinary remedy. In the instant case the appellant did not come to the Court for necessary relief after positive action had been taken by the holder of the certificates against him in execution of the disputed certificates. Rather, he submitted to the same and prayed for some installments for payment of the dues under the said certificates which were granted by the certificate officer but there having been defaults in the payment of the said installments an order of attachment of the cinema house was made and some of the movable properties were seized, leading to the institution of a claim case by one Mr. Abu Ahmed Sharifuddin. The said claim case was thereafter investigated and some of the attached movables were released in favour of the said claimant.</u>

<u>In the circumstances in our view, the High Court was correct in holding that because of the laches the appellant was not entitled to the extraordinary remedy."</u>

<u>In the instant case before us although the petitioner asserted in his petition that he was a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and it was admitted by all the three Governments namely, the Government of late Ziaur Rahman, the government of Mr. Hossain Mohammad Ershad as well as the present Government that was the reason for which the petitioner did not come to this Court for challenging the impugned notification; but the petitioner's case has similarity with the case reported in 29 DLR (SC) 232 inasmuch as the petitioner was aware of the impugned notification as far back in the month of April, and after the change of the Government the petitioner applied for restoration of his citizenship from London but his prayer was rejected as far back in April, 1977 (Annexure-E). Thereafter, the petitioner entered into Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport for a short visit after obtaining visa for three months. After coming over here the petitioner registered him as foreigner and he extended his visa two times and in the meantime he applied for citizenship and the matter is still pending. It is only when that the petitioner was taken into detention under the Foreigners Act that he came to this Court. The petitioner's case is similar to the case reported in 29 DLR (SC) 232 mentioned above inasmuch as in that case the petitioner rushed to the High Court when body-warrant was issued. Although the petitioner tried to explain the delay saying that he was under the impression that he was a citizen of Bangladesh but that cannot be regarded as an excuse for delay in moving the Court in Writ Jurisdiction because the petitioner knows very well that he was no longer a citizen. of Bangladesh, at least since the publication of the impugned notification Annexure- B which he came to learn in April, 1973 and his prayer for restoration of citizenship having been rejected by the Government as far back as in 1977. I, therefore, hold that the petitioner is guilty of laches in coming to the Court in moving the writ petition.</u>

49. In view of the above discussion the Rule is discharged.

Badrul Islam Choudhury J: I have the opportunity to hear my senior brother Judge, Mr. Justice Mohammad Ismail Uddin Sarker, pronouncing his laborious and extensive judgment in this case. I regret to say that I do not agree with him on some material points and as such I propose to deliver the following dissenting judgment.

51. The facts of the case as well as the claims and counter claims of the contending parties have been elaborately discussed by my brother Mr. Justice Mohammad Ismail Uddin Sarker. So I refrain from narrating the same again and like to enter into the merit of the case straight away.

52. Our Constitution does not contain elaborate provision on Citizenship as is the case with the Constitution of India. Article 6(1) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh simply provides that the citizenship of Bangladesh shall be determined and regulated by law. So the first and foremost question that is to be determined is what is the existing law on the subject of citizenship of Bangladesh. In view of the Proclamation of Independence issued on 10th April, 1971 read with the Laws Continuance Enforcement Order, 1971 and the Bangladesh (Adaptation of Existing Bangladesh Laws) Order, 1972) (PO 48 of 1972) there remains no doubt about the fact that laws which were in force in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh before the 26th day of March, 1971 remained so in force in independent Bangladesh with necessary adaptations. On 25th March, 1971 there was a law having the title "Pakistan Citizenship Act, 1951 (Act II of 1951)" in force in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh. Therefore, in view of the Proclamation of Independence, and the above quoted Presidential Orders, this Act No. II of 1951 became an existing law in Bangladesh and this law held sway till the 14th December, 1972 i.e. the day previous to the proclamation of the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 (PO No. 149 of 1972). At the very outset it may be pointed out that only Articles 2 and 2B of PO No. 149 of 1972 contain non-obstante clause i.e. the provisions of these two Articles override the provisions of all other laws on the subject. The Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 as a whole was not provided with overriding force. Article 2 enumerates the qualifications for the purpose of deeming person to be a citizen of Bangladesh and Article 2B enumerates disqualification, with some exceptions. Therefore, the provisions of the Citizenship Act of 1951 so far as they relate to the qualifications and disqualification for the purpose of acquisition of citizenship of Bangladesh, were eclipsed, or rather, kept in suspension by the provisions of Articles 2 and 2B of PO 149 of 1972. The other provisions of Act II of 1951 so far as they are not inconsistent with any provision of PO 149 of 1972 remained operative to side with the provisions of PO 149 of 1972. Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has contended that PO 149 of 1972 which was promulgated on the 15th December 1972 cannot take away the vested right of citizenship of Bangladesh acquired by the petitioner under the provision of the Citizenship Act of 1951 in spite of the fact that PO No. 149 of 1972 was given retrospective effect on and from 26th day of March, 1971. In other words, his contention is that a right which accrued to the petitioner by operation of the provision of the then existing law i.e. Act II of 1951, cannot be taken away by a subsequent legislation even with retrospective effect On the other hand, Mr. Aminul Haque, the learned Attorney-General, contended that retrospective law is one which interferes with the right of a person already vested in him before the enactment of such law and this is well within the competence of the law making authority. In this connection, it is worthy to mention the comments of Craies on 'Statute Law' which runs:

"A statute is to be deemed to be retrospective, which takes away or impairs any vested right acquired under existing laws, or creates a new obligation, or imposes a new duty, or attaches a new disability in respect to transactions or considerations already past (7th Edition, page 387).

It has also been held in different cases that by giving retrospective effect to a particular legislation rights already vested can be impaired for public interest. In the instant case, in unequivocal language contained in clause (2) of Article 1 of the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 it has been provided that the Order shall come into force at once and shall be deemed to have taken effect on the 26th day of March, 1971. So there remains no doubt about the fact that for the purpose of determining whether a person qualifies to be a citizen of Bangladesh or not the law that has to be looked into is the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 (PO No. 149 of 1972) in spite of the fact that this Order was issued on 15th December, 1972. The order has retrospective effect and holds the field with effect from 26th day of March, 1971. In view of the matter, the question whether the petitioner Prof. Golam Azam is deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh or not is to be considered and decided with reference to the provisions of PO No. 149 of 1972 and not the Citizenship Act, 1951.

53. In this case, Notification No. 403 dated Dhaka the 18th April, 1973 has been challenged. This Notification is on the face of it issued in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972. It reads as follows:

"Whereas, it appears that the persons specified below have been staying abroad since before liberation of Bangladesh and by their conduct cannot be deemed to be citizen of Bangladesh; And whereas the said persons have continued to be citizen of Pakistan;

Now, therefore, the Government declares under Article 3 of the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 (PO 149 of 1972), that the persons specified below do not qualify themselves to be the citizens of Bangladesh."

The Notification contains the names of 39 persons and the name of late Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury a veteran lawyer of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, appears at the top and that of the present petitioner Prof. Golam Azam, in serial No. 3 As the impugned Notification quoted above was issued under Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972, in order to adjudicate whether this Notification comes within the purview of Article 3, it is necessary to keep in our view the provisions of Article 3 as well as that of Article 2. Articles 2 and 3 of PO 149 of 1972 provide:

"2. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, on the commencement of this Order, every person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh.

(i) who or whose father or grand-father was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of such territories on the 25th day of March, 1971, and continues to be so resident; or

(ii) who was a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971, and continues to be so resident and is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force:

Provided that if any person is a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh or his dependent is, in the course of his employment or for the pursuit of his studies, residing in a country which was at war with or engaged in military operations against, Bangladesh, and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh, such person, or his dependents, shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh.

3. In case of doubt as to whether a person is qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 of this Order the question shall be decided by the Government, which decision shall be final."

54. It will not be out of place to mention here that initially the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 contained only five Articles of which Article 1 relates to the title and commencement of the Order, Article 2 as quoted above, contains the qualifications required for a person to be deemed to be citizen of Bangladesh, Article 3 vests the Government with power to give decision in case of doubt as to whether a person qualifies to be a citizen as per provision of Article 2. Article 4 confers power upon the Government to grant citizenship to any person on an application made to that effect and the last Article 5 relates to rule making power of the Government. Subsequently on 23.5.73 by promulgating Ordinance No. X of 1973 two new Articles namely, 2A and 2B have been added to the Order. This Ordinance was not given retrospective effect. However, on 22.6.73 Act No. V of 1973 was passed incorporating the amendments introduced by Ordinance No. X of 1973, to meet the requirement of Article 93(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Thereafter, by Ordinance No. 7 of 1978 added Article 2B was substituted by a new Article 2B, as it now stands, with some textual changes, and lastly, by Act 58 of 1990 Article 1A and 4A were added to PO 149 of 1972. The newly added Article 1A defines the term "prescribed" and 4A empowers the government to grant right of permanent resident to any person on such terms and conditions as may be prescribed on an application made by such person in that regard. Since Article 2A and 2B contain some more provisions relating to qualification and disqualification for acquisition of citizenship of Bangladesh, I think it expedient to quote these two Articles as well:

"2A. A person to whom Article 2 would have ordinarily applied but for his residence in the United Kingdom shall be deemed to continue to be permanent resident in Bangladesh within the meaning of that Article;

Provided that the Government may notify, in the Official Gazette, any person or categories of persons to whom this Article shall not apply.

2B(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in Article 2 or in any other law for the time being in force, a person shall not, except as provided in clause (2), qualify himself to be a citizen of Bangladesh if he-

(i) Owes, affirms or acknowledges, expressly or by conduct, allegiance to a foreign state, or

(ii) is notified under the proviso to Article 2A:

Provided that a citizen of Bangladesh shall not, merely by reason of being a citizen or acquiring citizenship of a state specified in or under clause (2), cease to be a citizen of Bangladesh.

(2) The Government may grant citizenship of Bangladesh to any person who is a citizen of any state of Europe or North America or of any other state which the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, specify in this behalf."

55. These Articles 2A and 2B were added to the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 "after" the issuance of the impugned Notification dated 18.4.73 disqualifying the present petitioner and 38 others from being deemed to be citizens of Bangladesh.

56. PO No. 149 of 1972 came into effect on and from 26th day of March, 1971. There is no dispute about the fact that petitioner Prof. Golam Azam and his father and grand-father were born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh. Article 3 of the Order, as quoted above, empowers the government to give a decision in case of doubt as to whether a person qualifies himself to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh in accordance with the provisions of Article 2 of the Order. So Article 2 is the main provision of law on which the question whether petitioner Prof. Golam Azam is deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh or disqualifies to be such a citizen, has to be decided. Article 2 has, at the outset it should be mentioned, made two categories of persons who are to be deemed to be citizens of Bangladesh. The provision relating to the first category is contained in clause (i). This clause provides that in order to be qualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh a person, his father or his grand-father must have been born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh that he was a permanent resident of such territories on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident. Under clause (ii) of Article 2 in order to qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh a person must have been a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on 25th March, 1971, continues to be so resident and is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law in force. So clause (i) deals with the cases of citizenship by birth or by descent and clause (ii) with citizenship by domicile i.e. who or whose fore-fathers were not born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh but who were permanent resident of such territory on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident. It also needs be mentioned that the special condition "is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force" appearing in clause (ii), is applicable only in the case of persons who were not born or whose father or grand-father were not born within the territories now comprised in Bangladesh. Apparently, this disqualification is applicable to the persons who migrated to the territories now comprised in Bangladesh at any time before the 25th day of March, 1971.

<u>57. PO No. 149 of 1972 though promulgated on 15th December 1972, came into force on the 26th day of March, 1971, as has been provided in sub-article (2) of Article 1. So 26th day of March, 1971 is the commencing day of this Order. Article 2(i) of the Order provides that a person who or whose father or grand-father was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of such territories on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. There is no doubt about the fact that petitioner Prof. Golam Azam, his father and grand-father were born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh. It is also not challenged that on the 25th day of March 1971, the day mentioned in Article 2, he was permanently residing in the territories comprised in Bangladesh. It is also not challenged by the respondents that on the 26th day of March, 1971, the day on which PO No. 149 of 1972 came into force, he was permanently residing in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh with his parents and family members. In the present case the words "and continues to be so resident" appearing in Article 2 is of utmost importance for the purpose of deciding the case. For this purpose, the first question that crops up is which shall be the material date for the purpose of deciding as to whether the petitioner Prof. Golam Azam continued to be permanent resident of Bangladesh. Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, contends that since PO 149 of 1972 was given retrospective effect and in view of the fact that it came into force on the 26th day of March, 1971 the material or the relevant date for the purpose of determining whether the petitioner was continuing to be a resident of Bangladesh is 26th day of March, 1971. Since PO No. 149 of 1972 came into force with effect from 26th day of March, 1971 the state of things, so far as it relates to the petitioner, as it prevailed on the 26th day of March, 1971 has to be taken into consideration and therefore, I hold that the contention of Mr. AR Yusuf carries weight. I am also constrained to say that I am unable to agree with the contention of the learned Attorney-General to the effect that in view of the Notification issued on 18th April, 1973, Annexure-B, disqualifying the petitioner along with others from being deemed to be citizens of Bangladesh it sha" be deemed to have taken effect on and from 26th day of March, 1971. At the same time, I am unable to agree with the contention of Mr. AR Yusuf that once citizenship of Bangladesh is acquired by a person he cannot be divested of the same at any time after 26th day of March 1971. The words "continues to be so resident" indicates a continuous phenomenon and a person who became citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law i.e. as per provisions of Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972, can divest himself of such citizenship if he abandons his residence in Bangladesh permanently and becomes permanent resident of some other countries. In that view of the matter, we are now called upon to determine whether the petitioner Prof. Golam Azam by going to Pakistan on the 22nd day of November, 1971 ceased to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh and thereby became disqualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. It is also necessary to determine whether his stay in Pakistan is covered by the proviso to Article 2 of PO No. 149 of 1972.</u>

58. At the very outset, I would like to point out that as per the case of the petitioner he was not residing in Pakistan on the date of issuance of the impugned Notification, Annexure-B dated 18.4.73. His case that he went to perform Haj in December, 1972 and from Saudi Arabia went to London in the first week of April, 1973, has not been seriously challenged in the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent. Only a general denial has been made therein. So it becomes clear that on the date of issuance of the impugned Notification petitioner Prof. Golam Azam was not residing in Pakistan but in the United Kingdom and therefore, his case can be said to be covered by Article 2A of the Order which provides that a person to whom Article 2 would have ordinarily applied but for his residence in the UK shall be deemed to continue to be permanent resident of Bangladesh within the meaning of Article 2. The learned Attorney-General has pointed out that the impugned Notification was issued taking into consideration that since 22nd November, 1971 the petitioner was residing in Pakistan and it was not known to the Government of Bangladesh about his claimed visit to Saudi Arabia for Hajj or going to UK. His further contention is that the Notification in question has retrospective effect from the date of the coming into force of the PO itself and as such the petitioner's subsequent arrival in UK would in no way affect the legality of the impugned Notification. Mr. AR Yusuf, on the other hand, contends that it is well within the competence of the legislature to give retrospective effect to a particular legislation and thereby affect the right of a person already vested in him. But, according to him, the executive government while exercising power delegated by such legislation, cannot give any retrospective effect to its order unless such a power is specifically conferred by the law itself. According to him, Article 3 or any provision of PO 149 of 1972 does not empower the Government to pass any order giving retrospective effect and as such the impugned Notification, Annexure-B, must be taken to have come into force and taken effect from the date of its issuance i.e. 18th day of April 1973.

59. The most vital question is whether the petitioner because of his absence from Bangladesh from 22.11.71 till his return on 11.7.78, ceased to continue to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh and thereby rendered himself disqualified to be citizen of Bangladesh. On this point Mr. Yusuf has referred the cases of Bishal Deo Tewati Vs. The State, reported in 27 DLR 622. The Advocate General, Government of East Pakistan, Dacca Vs. Benoy Bhusan Majumder and others reported in 25 DLR (SC) 9; Mukhtar Ahmed Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 34 DLR page 29, Mirza Slrahab Ispahani Vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in 40 DLR 87 and appeal arising out of it reported in 40 DLR (AD) 117, Hamidul Hoq Chowdhury and others Vs. Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 381; Abdul Huq Vs. Government of Bangladesh and another reported in 33 DLR 113 and the appeal arising out of that decision reported in 1882 BLD (AD) 143.

60. The facts of the case of Bishal Deo Tewari, 27 DLR 622, are completely different from the facts of the present case and, as such, I may safely refrain from discussing that case. The case of Mokhtar Ahmed, 34 DLR 29, also is quite distinguishable. In that case the petitioner Mokhtar Ahmed migrated from India to the then East Pakistan and obtained domicile certificate in 1952 and had been living here even after the war of liberation of 1971. He also by an affidavit, expressed his allegiance to Bangladesh on 29.4.72, but due to the situation prevailing in the country at that time he filed an application to the International Committee of Red Cross for going to Pakistan but did not pursue the same and as a result it was rejected. His name was entered in the voters list prepared after the war of liberation and he cast his vote in the referendum held in 1977. Under an impression that a formal citizenship certificate would help him rehabilitate in the society, he applied for the same on 17.3.75. It was rejected by order dated 5.10.77 which he challenged in a writ petition and in that circumstances it was held by a Division Bench of this Court consisting of Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed (as he was then) and Mr. Justice Rafiqur Rahman, that:

"Judging the admitted facts in the light of the provisions of President's Order 149 of 1972 it is clear that the petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law.

The next question is whether he abandoned that right by any positive act or has otherwise disqualified himself so as to be deprived of his citizenship. The impugned memo does not refer to any positive act. It merely refers to his filing an application to the International Committee of Red Cross with a view to go over to Pakistan. The mere fact that he filed an application for going over to Pakistan cannot take away his citizenship. The Bangladesh Citizenship Order, PO 149 of 1972 has enumerated different situations in which a person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh, but has not discriminated among its citizens no matter in which way they have become citizens of this country. So the petitioner is on the same footing as any other citizen. His citizenship, therefore, clings to him. He could voluntarily renounce it or he could be deprived of it if he had incurred any disqualification. Though he filed the application, he did not even pursue it. He filed an affidavit affirming allegiance to Bangladesh in 1972. The petitioner having not acquired the citizenship of any other country his citizenship of Bangladesh which he acquired long before cannot evaporate and he continues to be a citizen of this country."

61. So what we find from the case of Mukhter Ahmed is that because of his domicile in the then East Pakistan and his continuous residence in Bangladesh on and after 25th day of March, 1971 he became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law long before the impugned order dated 5.10.77 disqualifying him to be citizen of Bangladesh. In spite of the fact that he once applied to the ICRC for going over to Pakistan the Court held that his citizenship clings to him so long he does not voluntarily renounce it or he could be deprived of it if he had incurred any disqualification. It may be mentioned here once again, that a person falling under clause (ii) of Art 2 of PO No. 149 of 1972 only can be "otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law." Mukhter Ahmed comes under this category. But Prof. Golam Azam falls under the category of persons enumerated in clause (i) of Art 2, being born in the territories comprising in Bangladesh. The special disqualification mentioned in clause (ii) is not applicable in his case.

62. In Advocate General; Government of East Pakistan Vs. Benoy Bhusan Majumder and others. 25 DLR (SC) 9, the respondents who were residents of the then East Pakistan having their home within the district of Barisal, in November, 1964 went to India on obtaining migration certificate from the Deputy High Commission of India in Dhaka. It may be mentioned here that there was a communal disturbance of some magnitude in that year. Thereafter in 1967 the respondents were found in their village home in the district of Barisal and were prosecuted under section 14 of the Foreigners Act for entering East Pakistan without valid travel documents being citizens of India. The Magistrate found them guilty and accordingly convicted them, which, on appeal, was upheld by the Sessions Judge. On revision a Single Judge of the then High Court Dhaka set aside the sentence. Against that order the Advocate General of East Pakistan moved the Supreme Court of Pakistan and leave was granted to consider if the respondents having gone to India on the strength of Migration Certificate lost their Pakistani citizenship. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan after taking into consideration the provisions of sections 3, 4, 6, 7, 13 and 16 of the Pakistan Citizenship Act, 1951 (which with necessary adaptation has become an existing law of Bangladesh) held:

The expression "migration" envisages two conceptions, namely, going away from the territory of one country to the territory of another and the intention to abandon the domicile of the country of departure and to acquire the domicile of the court by of arrival in order to make that country a place of his permanent abode and residence. The meaning "migration" to the effect is indicated in section 3(d) of the Pakistan Citizenship Act. This, in its context, has the notion of change of allegiance from the country of arrival."
