After enunciating the above quoted principle of law which is general in its applicability, their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan took into consideration the evidence recorded by the Magistrate at the time of trial of the respondents and further held:

"The Migration Certificate on the strength of which they crossed into the Indian territory at the most, contained an admission of the respondents that they had intended to settle in India, but this admission was capable of being explained away. In the exigencies of circumstances created by the disturbances in East Pakistan in 1964, it was perhaps not unnatural on the part of the respondents to cross into India under a Migration Certificate for their personal safety. The normal travel documents, such as passport and visa, were not likely to be available to them in those circumstanced and, therefore, they were circumstances to avail of the Migration Certificate in order to facilitate their entry into India. The mere grant of the Migration Certificate did not confer Indian citizenship on the respondents under the Indian Citizenship Act, 1955, nor was there any evidence to show if the respondents applied for securing Indian citizenship under the applicable provisions of the said Indian Act. On the contrary, the evidence was that they, in accordance with their promise to the Chairman of the Union Council returned home to East Pakistan within 1 or-1-1/2. months of their departure. In the facts of this case as stated above, the respondents, who were admittedly the citizens of Pakistan before their departure for India, did not lose their Pakistan citizenship by their entry into India and their temporary stay in that country in the then abnormal situation obtaining in some areas in East Pakistan."

63. So what we find in this case is that the Supreme Court of Pakistan in spite of holding that migration envisages going away from the territory of one country to the territory of another with the intention to abandon the domicile of the country of departure and to acquire the domicile of the country of arrival in order to make that country as a place of permanent abode and residence, was liberal enough to take into consideration the exigencies of the situation, that is, the communal disturbance prevailing at that time, and held that respondents went to India on the strength of migration certificate for a temporary period in order to secure their personal safety. In the present case the contention of the petitioner that due to difference of political ideology and his contesting the general election of 1970 he incurred the displeasure and enmity of the Awami League which formed the first government in liberated Bangladesh after independence and apprehending political victimisation he did not return to Bangladesh till the change of the government in 1975 but never abandoned his citizenship of Bangladesh nor acquired citizenship of any other country including Pakistan.

64. Mirza Shahab Ispahani, son of a former Chief Justice of the erstwhile High Court of East Pakistan, migrated to the then East Pakistan along with his parents after the partition of the sub-continent in 1947. He stayed with his parents in the then East Pakistan upto 1952 when he was sent to England for higher studies. He went there with Pakistan passport and renewed it from time to time. After becoming a Chartered Accountant he secured employment in England and had been staying there for the purpose of earning. With his own income he procured a plot and house in Gulshan Model Town and also hired a flat in Ispahani Colony, Maghbazar, which is the exclusive property of the Ispahani family. During the war of liberation he was staying in London and on 14.4.72 obtained a British Passport which was subsequently renewed. He visited Bangladesh in October, 1972 on the strength of that British Passport and made arrangements for the looking after of his properties here. After his return to England his Gulshan property was treated as abandoned on the plea that he was a citizen of a country which was at war against Bangladesh in 1971 i.e. Pakistan. His repeated representations were turned down by the government whereupon he moved the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 120 of 1985 and a Division Bench, of which one of us was a member Judge, (40 DLR 87) held-

"As the disputed property has been claimed to be an abandoned property solely on the basis that the petitioner was a citizen of Pakistan after the 25th day of March, 1971, there 'cannot be any escape from the consequences that follow from the citizenship laws of Bangladesh. If by the citizenship laws of Bangladesh the petitioner is deemed to be a resident in Bangladesh on and after 25th day of March, 1971, then his Bangladeshi citizenship was not lost at any time, even, though he may not have applied for Bangladeshi Passport, for citizenship and acquisition of passport are not synonymous".

65. Against the decision of the High Court Division, the Government of Bangladesh preferred an appeal and their Lordships of the Appellate Division in that case 40 DLR(AD)117 held:

"Residence" or 'permanent residence' both expressions have been used in PO 149 of 1972. In Art. 2 (ii) it is the permanent resident that was contemplated in contra-distinction of persons whose residence was in UK. The respondent's mother 'and family are residing in Dhaka. Apart from the house in question he has rented a flat in the Ispahani Colony. He works in the United Kingdom as a Chartered Accountant, Even in proviso added in Article 2 those persons .residing in Pakistan but had been stranded' shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh."

66. It will be worthwhile to mention here that even after liberation of Bangladesh Mirza Shahab Ispahani, the petitioner of that case, did not obtain Bangladeshi passport, rather he preferred to obtain a British passport and on that strength he visited Bangladesh in 1972. Taking that fact into consideration the High Court Division held that citizenship and passport are not synonymous: The Appellate Division taking into consideration that Mirza Shahab Ispahani was owning, managing and possessing properties in Bangladesh in spite of the fact that he was rather habitually residing in UK held that even in the proviso added to Article 2 those persons residing in Pakistan but had been stranded would be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh. It cannot be said that while making this observation their Lordships of the Appellate Division ignored the words in course of employment or in pursuit of studies" appearing in the proviso to Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972. The present petitioner Prof. Golam Azam has asserted that he went to Lahore on 22nd November, 1971 in order to attend a meeting of the Central Committee of the' Jamaat-e-Islami of which he was the Amir of the then East Pakistan wing and because of breaking out of war on the 3rd of December, 1971 his plane could not land at Dhaka Airport and had to return to Pakistan via Colombo and Jeddah after the ceasefire, that thereafter because of the absence of diplomatic relations and disruption of communication between Pakistan and Bangladesh it was not possible for him to return home. The above mentioned averments of the petitioner so far as they relate to the breaking out of war between India and Pakistan, disruption of all sorts of communication and non-recognition of Bangladesh by Pakistan till 1974 are hard facts and because of these the Bangladeshis who were residing in Pakistan including the government servants, were not allowed to return to their homeland i.e. Bangladesh until a pact was signed between Mrs. Indira Gandhi, the then Prime Minister of India and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, the then Prime Minister of Pakistan and repatriation of stranded Bangladeshis started sometime in the middle of 1973. So the contention of the petitioner that he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh from Pakistan due to circumstances beyond his control, cannot be brushed aside lightly.

67. In the case of Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury and others Vs. Bangladesh, 33 DLR 381, the properties of Mr. Chowdhury i.e. two daily newspapers and a weekly magazine as well as the press, in which he and his wife held lion's share, were enlisted as abandoned properties and taken over by the government on the ground that the same vested in the government because of the fact that their owners were citizens of Pakistan. Challenging that order of taking over Mr. Chowdhury moved the High Court Division in Writ Petition' Nos. 482 and 483 of 1980. Since the properties in question were taken over as abandoned property treating their owners Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury and his wife as citizens of Pakistan, the question whether they were citizens of Pakistan or of Bangladesh inevitably came up for consideration of the Court. A Division Bench consisting of Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury and Mr. Justice Sultan Hossain Khan, held:

"The contention of the respondents that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was a citizen of Pakistan is based upon firstly, that he was away from Bangladesh, that by a notification dated 18.4.73 the government declared that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, did not qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury claimed that he never became citizen of any other State and his, citizenship by statutory provision continued to be Bangladeshi. It appears to us on perusal of the Notification dated 18.4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury by statutory provision was a citizen of Bangladesh. This notification, however, was subsequently declared void by another notification of the government date 19.7.77. In this view we hold that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh ever since the emergence of Bangladesh 'though he was away from the country."

68. I have already stated that the name of Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury topped the list of the 39 persons who were disqualified to be citizens of Bangladesh by the impugned notification dated 18.4.73, Annexure-B. In his writ petition Mr. Chowdhury took the plea that the newspapers published by his company were critical about the activities of the leaders of the Awami League and the petitioner had played active role in politics and had political difference with the leaders of Awami League as a result of which bitter enmity developed between the petitioner No. 1 and the papers controlled by his company from one side and the Awarni League on the other, that Awami League came into power in Bangladesh in the 3rd week of December, 1971 and Mr. Chowdhury was in London since October, 1971 in connection 'with an arbitration case along with some other lawyers of Dhaka. His further contention was that in view of the hostility of the party in power against the petitioner No. 1 and the then law and order situation in Bangladesh he could not return to Dhaka as his personal safety was threatened. The facts of these of Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury have many similarities with those of the present case. In both the cases the petitioners alleged that due to political difference, ill feeling and enmity existed between the leaders of the party in power on one side and the petitioner on the other for which they did not dare to return to Bangladesh before the political change that took place in August, 1975. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury went to London in connection with an arbitration case as claimed by him, and the present petitioner Golam Azam went to Lahore, according to him, to attend a conference of the political party of which he was the Provincial leader. Both of them were declared not qualified to be citizen of Bangladesh by the same notification and in that view of the matter, in the reported case Hamidul Huq Chowdhury asserted and in the present case Prof. Golam Azam asserts that they never became citizen of any other State and their citizenship by statutory provisions continued to be Bangladeshi and in that perspective it was held:

"It appears to us on a perusal of the notification dated 18.4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury by statutory provisions was a citizen of Bangladesh."

This observation of the Court lends support to the contention of Mr. AR Yusuf that prior to the issuance of the notification dated 18.4.73 Prof. Golam Azam was a citizen of Bangladesh by statutory provision i.e. under the provision of PO 149 of 1972.

69. The last case on which the learned Advocate for the petitioner has relied upon is that of Abdul Huq. Vs. The Government of Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 113 and the appeal arising out of it reported in 1982 BW (AD) 143. That petitioner, Abdul. Huq, who happened to be a dealer of ration commodities in Dhaka and trader of betel leaf (pan), was born in Satkhira in 1972 and subsequently lived in Calcutta. However, since partition in 1947 he and his parents were living in erstwhile East Pakistan and continued to live there upto November, 1971 when he went to the then West Pakistan and did not come back from there till the political change took place in August, 1975. Sometime after his return to Bangladesh with Pakistani passport he surrendered the same and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh. His prayer being rejected, he moved the High Court Division of the Supreme Court in its Extraordinary Original Jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. A Division Bench of this Court held that so far the petitioner's right to obtain citizenship of Bangladesh was concerned it was no doubt the discretion of the executive government to be exercised in accordance with law. The Court further held that the petitioner was away from the country for about 5 years without obtaining citizenship of Bangladesh. His domicile is within the territory of Bangladesh and he could not be held to have permanently acquired the status of the citizen of Pakistan, he became a stateless subject and therefore, in his case the Foreigners Act was not applicable and he cannot be deported or asked to leave the country under the provisions of the said Act. On appeal against the said judgment by the Government their Lordships of the Appellate Division (1982 BW (AD) 143) after quoting the whole of PO 149 of 1972 held:

"The respondent was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh but his temporary absence is covered by the proviso quoted above and the law says "he shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh" notwithstanding his temporary residence "in a country which was at war or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh.  His assertion that he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh by the circumstances which had not been challenged. In the eye or law, therefore, he remains a resident of Bangladesh. In that view of the matter, the impugned order of deportation must be declared as not lawfully made, and has no force of law."

The Court further held that the question of respondent's statelessness did not at all arise. In his writ petition Abdul Haque took the plea that he went to Pakistan on business purposes in November, 1971, that immediately after liberation he fell ill and was hospitalized for about eight months there and came out of the hospital when repatriation of Bangladeshis had stopped and so he could not come back earlier. It may be pointed out, by the way, that this contention was not apparently correct, because if Abdul Haque was in hospital for eight months immediately after liberation then he came out of the hospital before the repatriation started. Be that as it may, their Lordships of the Appellate Division had accepted his plea that he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh due to circumstances which were beyond his control. Like Abdul Huq the present petitioner went to Pakistan in November, 1971 when the war of liberation was going on. Abdul Huq went on business purpose while the present petitioner went to attend a political meeting. After five years Abdul Haque came to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport. The petitioner Golam Azam came to this country with a Pakistani passport in 1978 i.e. after 7 years. No doubt going to Pakistan to attend a political meeting is not covered by the words "in course of his employment or for the pursuit of his studies" in strict sense of the term. But if these two conditions are interpreted in their strictest sense then business tour, as was the case with Abdul Huq, also does not come within the purview of the proviso to Article 2, because, employment inevitably connotes employer and employee which means service in some organization or under some body and a businessman is not an employee of anybody unless he is in service under some other businessman. In spite of that their Lordships of the Appellate Division have brought the case of Abdul Haque within the generally accepted principle of beneficial construction of statute. In this regard it will be worthwhile to quote Maxwell's 'Interpretation of Statutes', (12th Edition, pages 92 and 93) The author states:

"Previous editions of this work have referred to this relaxation of strictly literal principles of interpretation as beneficial construction: and the modem cases provide many instances of the judge's reluctance to stand upon the letter of the statute. They will not, of course, supply omissions, but where they are faced with a choice between a wide meaning which carries out what appears to have been the object of the legislature more fully, and a narrow meaning which carries it out less fully or not at all they will often choose the former. Beneficial construction is a tendency, rather than a rule."

One well-known example of beneficial construction is that which has been placed upon the words "soldier being in actual military service" and "mariner or seaman being at sea" in Section II of the Wills Act, 1837. They have been held, for instance, to include a Territorial Officer who has received orders to join his unit, and a female typist employed on an ocean going liner."

70. Lastly, in the case of Abdul Qayum Vs. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, 44 DLR 340, a Division Bench of this Court has held that "unless a Bangladeshi citizen acquired citizenship of any other country, he continues to be the citizen of Bangladesh."

<u>71. It is not expected that two cases will agree in their facts and circumstances in all details. There must be some differences in the facts and circumstances between one case and another. Keeping this in view, the law enunciated by superior Courts are to be applied in subsequent cases if there are some similarities between them and if such application is not' against good reasoning’s and common sense.</u>

<u>72. Prom the decisions and rulings of the High Court Division and the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as well as of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, discussed above, we find that in the case of Mirza Shahab Ispahani the principle laid down which has general applicability is that passport and citizenship are not synonymous. In view of this settled principle of law the fact that petitioner Golam Azam was holding a Pakistani Passport at the time of his arrival in Bangladesh cannot be ground for holding that he has acquired citizenship of Pakistan. In the case of Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, 33 DLR 381, the principle enunciated that prior to the notification dated 18.4.73 Mr. Chowdhury by statutory provision was a citizen of Bangladesh is equally applicable in the case of the present petitioner Golam Azam, because he like Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and like Mr. Chowdhury he was permanently residing in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971 and thereafter, until 'he went to Pakistan in November, 1971. The law enunciated by the highest Court of the country in the case of Abdul Haque 1982 BLD (AD) 143, is more applicable in the present case because the facts of the two cases are almost same and in that case their Lordships of the Appellate Division has held that in spite of his temporary absence the petitioner shall be deemed to continue to be the resident of Bangladesh. Prof. Golam Azam, the present petitioner, in his writ petition has stated that on 3rd December, 1971 he started from Karachi but due to the declaration of war his plane could not land at Dhaka and went back to Colombo and then Jeddah where he had to stay for some days and thereafter all the passengers were taken back to Karachi, that he stayed in Pakistan till December, 1972 as because the government of Pakistan was not allowing Bangladeshis to leave the country and so he took a Pakistani passport for performing Hajj and after performing Hajj he instead of returning to Pakistan, went to London so as to find a way to return to his home country but on reaching there he learnt that he had been declared disqualified to be the citizen of Bangladesh in April, 1973 and so it was not possible for him to approach the Bangladesh Mission in London for granting him Bangladeshi passport. These averments cannot be taken lightly because after the impugned Notification Bangladesh High Commission in London could not issue a passport in his favour. It is evident from Annexure-D attached to the writ petition, that on 20.5.76 he sent a petition addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh for restoration of his Bangladesh citizenship and getting no reply he again sent a petition to the Chief Martial Law Administrator on 12.1.77, Annexure-Dl. There is no allegation from the side of the government that Prof. Golam Azam, the petitioner, applied for or has been granted citizenship of Pakistan. The only allegation against him is that he obtained a Pakistani passport. The prayers of the petitioner were turned down by Annexures-P and P(1), once directly by the Ministry of Home Affairs and again through the High Commission of Bangladesh in UK. Thereafter on his prayer he was granted visa by Bangladesh High Commission in London on receiving clearance from the government of Bangladesh. On the strength of the Pakistani passport and visa granted by the Bangladesh High Commission he reached Dhaka on 11.7.78. He made a fresh application for granting him citizenship on 8.11.78. It may be mentioned here that the learned Attorney-General has laid much stress on the fact that the petitioner on arriving Bangladesh got himself registered as a foreigner and argued that this clearly indicated that he did not treat himself as a citizen of Bangladesh. It may be pointed out that anybody entering into a country with a passport not issued by that country is required to be registered as a foreigner and this is a matter of course only. This in no way could be termed as renunciation of Bangladesh Citizenship. It is not disputed that the petition filed on 8.11.78 for restoration of citizenship of the petitioner has not yet been finally disposed of by the government, or at least, he has not been informed anything in this regard. On the other hand, there are documents attached to the writ petition showing that none else but the Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Home Affairs in reply to the questions of members, stated in the House of the Nation, that is, the Parliament that the petition of Prof. Golam Azam was under consideration of the government. The last statement in this regard was made on 12.1.92 while the previous statement was made as early as in 1980. From all these facts and circumstance it becomes crystal clear that Prof. Golam Azam never renounced his citizenship of Bangladesh which he acquired by birth and by operation of law. A person cannot be deprived of the citizenship of his country of birth unless be himself renounces it by taking up citizenship of another country in contravention of the law of his country of origin.</u>

73. The learned Attorney-General has taken us through some news items and booklets describing anti-Bangladesh activities of the petitioner and his collaboration with Pakistan Army during and after the war of liberation and has contended that by such anti-Bangladesh activities during and after liberation the petitioner by his conduct affirmed his allegiance to Pakistan and thereby disqualified himself to be a citizen of Bangladesh as has been provided in Article 2B(1) of PO 149 of 1972.

74. A special law, namely, the Bangladesh Collaborators (Special Tribunal) Order, 1972 (PO No. 8 of 1972) was made for trial and punishment of persons who, during the war of liberation, collaborated with Pakistan Army and in doing so committed other criminal offences. Under that law some were tried and punished. But subsequently clemency was granted to the convicts and persons wanted for trial except those convicted or wanted for heinous crimes like murder, rape, arson, etc. The law itself has ultimately been repealed. But in spite of the repeal of PO No. 8 of 1972 any person can be tried and punished under the ordinary law of the land if it, is proved by sufficient evidence that he committed or abetted the commission of offences like murder, rape, arson, etc. during the war of liberation or engaged himself in anti-Bangladesh activities after liberation of Bangladesh. But neither PO No. 8 of 1972 contained nor PO No. 149 of 1972 contains any provision disqualifying a person from being a citizen of Bangladesh for collaboration with the occupation army during the war of liberation and committing or abetting murder, rape or arson in course of such collaboration or for indulging in anti-Bangladesh activities after independence. Moreover, commission of any such offence is yet not reported against the petitioner in a competent Court of law. Till now nobody has come forward to set the criminal law in motion against the petitioner by lodging an FIR with the police or by filing a petition of complaint before any Magistrate.

75. Taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of the present case as well as the law as enunciated by the highest Court of the country i.e. the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, particularly in the case of Abdul Huque, I hold that the temporary absence of Prof. Golam Azam, the petitioner, from Bangladesh does not disqualify him from being a citizen of Bangladesh and as such the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 is not in accordance with law and therefore is of no legal effect.

76. The next question that has been raised is the principle of audi alteram partem i.e. the principle of natural justice that no one should be condemned unheard. On this point Mr. AR Yusuf has referred to the cases of the Government of East Pakistan Vs. Nur Mohammad reported in PLD 1964 (SC) 451, Abdur Rahman, Advocate Vs. The Collector and Deputy Commissioner, Bahawalnagar, PLD 1964 (SC) 461, Bangladesh Steamer Agencies Association Vs. Bangladesh, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 271 and Sayiid Abul Ala Moududi Vs. the Government of Pakistan reported in 17 DLR (SC) 209. In the first three cases mentioned above the law that has been laid down is that the principle of natural justice that no one should be condemned unheard should be read in every legislation in the absence of any provision to the contrary contained in the law itself. However, in the case of Sayed Abul Aliz Moududi, 17 DLR (SC) 209 his Lordship Mr. Justice Fazle-Akbar of the Supreme C of Pakistan held:

"This rule expressed in the maxim audi alteram partem was fully considered by this Court in Messrs. Farid Sons Ltd., Karachi and another Vs. Government of Pakistan and another and therefore, needs no elaboration.

In a variety of situations the Court has enforced this doctrine by checking attempts of executive to disregard this deep-rooted demand of fair-play.

No doubt as far as possible it must be respected in period of calm and even in times of trouble. But certainly it cannot be said that it is merely a technical conception with a fixed content unrelated to time place and circumstances. It is really a matter of procedure and its application must depend on the particular facts and circumstances of the case. What is unfair in one situation may be fair in another. Furthermore, there may be conceivable circumstances in time of emergency in which it might be necessary for the authorities to take immediate action, for example, the activities of an association may be subversive to government and a serious menace to the country. In such circumstances it will be unrealistic to impeach the action of the Government on the ground that the association was not heard. It must be remembered that sometimes because of abnormal conditions, abnormal means are required to cope with them and this justifies the authorities to take immediate action under the law enabling them to do so. Hence taking action in an emergency without observing the maxim audi alteram partem would be a valid exercise of plenary administrative discretion."

In the same case Mr. Justice Hamoodur Rahman observed:

"No doubt, there are observations in the judgments relied upon by the learned counsel which tend, at first sight, to support this wide contention, but a more careful examination of these decisions will reveal that this proposition cannot be as wide or as universal as is sought to be contended by learned counsel. In my view, the nature of the thing to be done, the manner in which it is to be done and the circumstances in which it is to be done arc important considerations which must be taken into account in determining whether the above mentioned principle should be applied in a given case or not."

I am in respectful agreement with the above quoted observations of their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan and hold that the principle of audi alteram partem is not of universal applicability and the question whether this principle should be applied or not depends upon the nature of the thing to be done, the manner in which it is to be done and the circumstances in which it is to be done. The learned Attorney-General has conceded that the principle of natural justice should be followed as far as practicable whenever any person's right is going to be adversely affected by any action whether by a Court of law or a Tribunal or an Administrative Authority. At the same time, he contended that in the present case this doctrine is not at all applicable in view of the fact that the government by the impugned order did not cancel the citizenship of the petitioner nor deprive him of his citizenship. The government in exercise of the power conferred by Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 has given a decision only to remove a doubt as to whether the petitioner fulfilled the requirements of Article 2 so as to be treated as a citizen of Bangladesh or not. His second contention is that since the petitioner was not available in the country and his whereabouts were not known to the Government it was impracticable to serve a show cause notice upon him so as to give him an opportunity of being heard. Whatever may be the language of Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 there is no doubt about the fact that an order passed under this Article declaring a person not qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh in actual effect interferes with his political status which entails some fundamental rights enumerated in the Constitution which are available to a citizen only. Therefore, it is not worthy to say that by the impugned order no right vested in the petitioner was taken away. Next comes the question whether it was practicable to serve a show cause notice upon the petitioner and the other thirty-eight persons to give them chance to defend themselves as against the proposed action. There is no doubt of the fact that the present petitioner at the relevant time was not available in Bangladesh and therefore, it was not physically possible to serve any notice upon him in person. But our laws provide different modes of service, such as service at the last known residence of the person concerned or by publication in official gazette or in some newspapers and these are treated to be valid and legal service of notice. The government could easily publish a show cause notice either in the gazette or in any newspaper or serve the same at the last known residence in Bangladesh of the petitioner. But this has not been done. This is not a case of emergency as it was in the case of Sayed Abul Ala Moududi. A delay of a month or two in taking a decision regarding the political status of the petitioner and the others mentioned in the notification and to cause service of notice in the meantime would not harm anybody or the public interest or the State of Bangladesh. I am, therefore, of opinion that this is not an exceptional case as has been stated by their Lordships Mr. Fazle Akbar and Mr. Hamoodur Rahman JJ and this being an ordinary case without demanding urgent action, a notice should have been issued asking the person concerned to show cause as to why they should not be declared to be not qualified to be citizens of Bangladesh. Failure to do so has rendered the impugned notification repugnant to the principle of natural justice that no one should be condemned unheard.

Mr. AR Yusuf has lastly taken the stand that the powers conferred upon the executive government in Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 is unfettered and unrestricted and therefore, it may be used in a discriminatory way as there is no guide-line laid down either in the Order itself or in the Rules framed thereunder as to how and in what circumstances this power should be exercised. On this point he referred to the case of Dr. Nurul Islam Vs. The Government, 1981 BLD (AD) 140. I do not think it necessary to discuss the facts of that case and the law enunciated (Appellate Division in view of the fact that, in Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 is not devoid of Iv principle or guide-line. This Article 3 is closely connected and dependent on Article 2 of the said Order and Article 2 lays down the guide-line or the principles or the qualifications which are required for a person in order to be deemed to be qualified as citizen of Bangladesh in case of doubt as to whether a particular the qualifications or is lacking in anyone mentioned in Article 2 then and then only the government can invoke Article 3 and give decision on the point. Therefore, I hold that this Article is not without any principle or guide-line for the exercise of power conferred by it upon the executive government. Therefore, Article 3 is not ultra-vires to Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

<u>77. It has been argued by the learned Attorney- General that due to laches on the part of the petitioner in moving this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution the petitioner is not entitled to get any relief. He has contended that in order to invoke the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court the party aggrieved must come to the Court without any delay and laches in this respect would frustrate his purpose. On this point he has referred to the decision reported in 13 DLR 804, 15 DLR page I, AIR 1957 (SC) 397, AIR 1970 (SC) 117 and AIR 1975 (SC) 13. On the other hand, Mr. AR Yusuf has referred to the case of Shafiqur Rahman Vs. Local Certificate Officer, Dhaka reported in 29 DLR (SC) 232. In the last mentioned case it has been held:</u>

<u>"Even in a proceeding for writ in the nature of certiorari, the aggrieved person must show diligence and a sense of urgency for the purpose of invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction. In a particular case he may not rush to the Court immediately on the initiation of a proceeding which, according to him, is a nullity but has not yet threatened him with any actual danger but when some positive steps have been taken in the said proceeding to his prejudice and he, instead of resisting it, submits to it and carried out various orders made in the said proceeding, he has, in accordance with the authorities referred to above, distinctly disentitled himself to the said extraordinary remedy."</u>

<u>In the instant case no doubt the impugned order disqualifying the petitioner from being deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh was passed as early as in 1973 and the present writ petition has been filed in March, 1992. So there is a gap of about 19 years. However, the contention of Mr. AR Yusuf is that though the order was issued as early as in 1973 yet no right was threatened till the show cause notice dated 23.3.92 was served upon the petitioner. It is apparent from the writ petition and the other papers that the impugned order, Annexure-B was passed when the petitioner was outside the country. He, after learning about it, had been submitting representation after representation to the executive government for redress of his grievance. Two of his petitions were rejected in 1978 but he was granted visa to visit Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and immediately after his arrival he surrendered his passport and applied for citizenship on 7.11.78. After lapse of his renewed visa he was not disturbed so far as his stay in Bangladesh was concerned. Rather on 28.1.81 he was asked by the appropriate authority to furnish an affidavit of allegiance which he did the following day. Then there was no reply to his petition. But the Minister-in-charge of the Ministry concerned i.e. the Ministry of Home Affairs, once on 27th May, 1980 and again on 12th January, 1992 made statement in the Parliament to the effect that Prof. Golam Azam's petition for restoration of citizenship was under active consideration of the government. In the meantime, the petitioner was enrolled as voter in the electoral rolls finally published once in 1983 and again in 1990. No doubt the inclusion of the name of the petitioner in the voter list cannot be deemed to have rescinded the Government's Order contained in the impugned notification, Annexure-B dated 18.4.73. But all these facts and circumstances including the inclusion of his name as a voter, Minister's statements in Parliament and top political leaders meeting the petitioner and discussing matters of national importance with him, were sufficient to make the petitioner believe that his petition for restoration of his citizenship was not only under active consideration but under favourable consideration of the Government. Therefore his right to stay in Bangladesh and to exercise the right of franchise an exclusive right of citizens only was not threatened till the notice dated 23.3.92 asking him to show cause why he should not be deported from Bangladesh being a foreigner. Immediately on receipt of this notice the petitioner gave his reply and he being taken into detention moved this Court in its extraordinary original jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. It should be kept in mind that the Supreme Court has always deprecated the tendency to rush to Court before exhausting available administrative remedies. Under the facts and circumstances of this case I am of the opinion that the present writ petition does not suffer from inordinate delay and that the delay that has occurred has been satisfactorily explained.</u>

78. From what has been discussed above I hold that the impugned Notification dated 18.4.73. Annexure- B. and the notice to show cause dated 23.3.92. Annexure-K, are not in accordance with law and have no legal effect and therefore liable to be struck down.

The Rule is fit to be made absolute. Mohammad Ismail Uddin Sarker, J and Badrul Islam Chowdhury. J.

In view of our difference of opinion let this matter be placed before the learned Chief Justice for favour of necessary orders.

High Court Division

(Special Original Jurisdiction)

Anwarul Hoque Choudhury, J.

Writ Petition No. 1316 of 1992.

Professor Golam Azam ----- Petitioner

Vs.

Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and others ----- Respondents.

Judgment April 22nd, 1993.

AR Yusuf with Abdur Razzak, SK Ansar Ali and Md. Nowab Ali, Advocates-For the Petitioner.

Aminul Huq, Attorney-General with AF Hasan Arif, Deputy Attorney-General, Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, specially appointed Advocate and Mir Hashmat Ali, Assistant Attorney General ----- For the Respondents.

Judgment

This Rule arises out of an application under Article 102(2)(a)(i) (ii) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and IS directed against notification dated 18.4.73 (Annexure 'B') issued by respondent No. 1 namely. the Government of Bangladesh so far as it relates to the petitioner Golam Azam as the notification included the name of many others and by the notification it was communicated that the petitioner is disqualified to be citizen of Bangladesh and is also directed against the show cause notice dated 23.3.92 (Annexure 'K') as to why he should not be deported from Bangladesh being a foreign citizen. This Rule originally heard by a Division Bench of this court consisting of Mr. Justice Mohammad Ismail Uddin Sarker and Mr. Justice Badrul Islam Chowdhury for a number of days from 19th July till 5th August, 1992 and the judgment was delivered on 6th, 9th , 10th, 11th and 12th August. 1992. But the Division Bench delivered a split judgment and consequently this matter was referred to the learned Chief Justice for necessary order and the learned Chief Justice referred this matter to me for hearing.

82. This matter was heard by this Bench also for a number of days during the Ramazan and there after it was argued by the learned lawyers for both the parties in extension for nearly 17 days and the judgment is delivered today on 21.4.93. It would be necessary to state in some detail the facts which are somewhat complicated. It is the case of petitioner that he is a Bangladeshi citizen by birth having been born in Dhaka on 22nd November, 1922. His late father Moulana Golam Kabir was born in village Birgram, Police Station Nabinagar, District Comilla, now Brahmanbaria and from generations he, his father and grandfather both paternal and maternal had been living permanently in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh. The petitioner Prof. Golam Azam had his education in this country and he was always a meritorious student. He passed Junior Madrasha Examination in 1937 and was placed in the 1st. Division. He got his SSC Examination also from here and was placed at the 13th position. In 1944 he got his Intermediate Examination from the Islamia Intermediate Government College Dhaka and was placed in the 1st. Division securing 10th position. Mr. Golam Azam obtained his Master’s Degree in Political Science from Dhaka University in 1950. From his student days he was involved in political activities. He participated in all the Student Movements including the Language Movement in 1951-52. He was elected General Secretary of DUCSU in 1946-47 and also the next year 1948-49. He was the student who read the memorandum before the then Prime Minister of Pakistan on the 27th of November, 1948 at the Gymnasium ground of the Dhaka University urging him to make Bengali as one of the State Languages. The petitioner after his MA joined as a Professor of Political Science in Carmichael College, Rangpur and worked there for 5 years. He fought for the restoration of democracy during the Ayub regime and was the General Secretary of the Eastern Wing of the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM) Because of his political activity, the petitioner was arrested once in 1955 and then in 1964 but he was released by the order of the Hon'ble High Court in Habeas Corpus petition. It is the case of the petitioner before this Court that he dedicated his life for the establishment of Islamic Social Justice in all spheres of the society and he became the Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami of the then East Pakistan in 1969. In the General Election held in 1970 Jamaat-e-Islami took part and according to the petitioner Jamaat-e-Islami obtained the second highest votes next to the Awami League though not securing any seats in the Parliament. It is the further case of the petitioner that he being the head of Jamaat-e-Islami became the target of the Awami League which subsequently fought for the independence of Bangladesh but in spite of the political differences with Awami League the petitioner advocated for transfer of power to the Awami League as it obtained the highest number of seats in the then National Assembly in the 1970 Election. During the liberation struggle the petitioner was actively engaged in helping people and saving them from the military atrocities of Yahya regime but even then the Awami League considered the petitioner to be their enemy. In this background the petitioner averts before this Court that he was a resident of Bangladesh on the 25th of March, 1971 and continued to be so resident thereafter. It is the further case of the petitioner that nearly 8 months after March, 71 during which the petitioner continued to be a resident of this country in Bangladesh living at his house at Maghbazar he went to Lahore on 22nd November, 1971 for attending his party's central working committee meeting. He stayed there for some time, attended the said meeting and thereafter on 3rd December, 1971 the petitioner was returning to Dhaka as usual by aero plane but could not land at Dhaka Airport because at that time war had started between India and Pakistan and his plane had to turn back to Karachi instead of landing at Dhaka. It was diverted to Colombo as there was bombing at Karachi Airport also and thereafter the plane went again to Jeddah where the petitioner had to remain. Thereafter he was sent back to Karachi along with other passengers.

83. The petitioner had to remain in Pakistan against his will and against his wishes and he remained there in Pakistan for 11 months because at that time the then Government of Pakistan did not allow the Bangalees to go out of Pakistan. The petitioner tried to go to London immediately and in the month of March, 1972 made contact with his family in Bangladesh but the petitioner failed to obtain any travel document in Pakistan and thereafter he had to apply for a Pakistani passport to go to Saudi Arabia to perform Hajj in the month of December, 1972. The petitioner during the Hajj met his friends and acquaintances from Bangladesh and the petitioner was informed about the political propaganda against him in Bangladesh. The petitioner was afraid and thought that his life will be at stake. He then without coming to Bangladesh after the Hajj went to London in the 1st week of April 1973 where he came to learn from a news item published in the Bangladesh Observer to the effect that he along with 38 others were declared by the said notification dated 18.4.73 to be disqualified to become a citizen of Bangladesh.

84. It is the averment in the petition before this court that he found it impossible to return to Bangladesh and therefore, he stayed in England against his will and he never went to Pakistan and never obtained Pakistani passport in order to obtain Pakistani nationality or citizenship nor he obtained citizenship of any other country. After the notification dated 18.4.73 disqualifying him to be a Bangladeshi along with 38 others the petitioner continued to reside in England. In the meantime in 1975 there was a change of Government in Bangladesh and also a change in political situation when the new Government headed by Major-General Ziaur Rahman by a notification dated 17.1.76 (Annexure 'e') invited applications from those persons whose citizenship was previously "cancelled" by the previous Government. The petitioner immediately applied for the same by an application dated 20.5.76 addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Bangladesh. The petitioner did not get any reply and therefore, on 12.1.77 almost a year thereafter he again wrote to the Chief Martial Law Administrator praying for renewing or restoration of citizenship. This time, the petitioner received a reply from the Ministry of Home Affairs on 23.4.77 (Annexure 'E') where it was stated that the Government of Bangladesh regrets their inability to accede to his request to restore Bangladesh citizenship. The petitioner also received a letter from the High Commissioner for Bangladesh in England to the same effect. In the meantime the petitioner's father died and his mother became seriously ill and his old mother applied on 14.11.77. When the Government of Bangladesh by their letter dated 11.3.78 expressed their no objection for granting visa to the petitioner to see his ailing mother and accordingly the petitioner obtained visa from London and entered Bangladesh on 11.7.78 with a visa for 3 months and he was registered as a foreigner. He got extension of his visa twice. He again filed an application for registration as a citizen of Bangladesh to the Home Ministry on 8.11.78 after surrendering his Pakistani passport. Thereafter the petitioner resided at his Maghbazar house and considered himself to be a citizen of Bangladesh. On 27.5.80 some members of the Parliament inquired from the Government of Bangladesh during the Parliament session about the stay of the petitioner in Bangladesh and it was mentioned by the Minister that the petitioner had filed an application praying for registration as a citizen of Bangladesh by surrendering his Pakistani passport and the matter is pending for the decision of the Government. On 28.4.81 the Ministry of Home Affairs asked the petitioner to submit oath of allegiance to Bangladesh and the petitioner submitted the required affidavit 2 days thereafter on 30.4.81. Thereafter, there was a long silence on the part of the Government. On 3.12.86 almost after 5 years he received a letter from the Ministry of Home Affairs (when General HM Ershad was in power) requesting him to let the Ministry know as to how he was staying in Bangladesh without visa and had stayed under what authority to which the petitioner sent a reply on 22.12.86 (Annexure 'H'-2) asserting himself as a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and informed that on 8.11.78 he made an application for restoration of the citizenship by surrendering his Pakistani passport and that his application is under active consideration of the authority. There was again a silence. It is the further case of the petitioner that in the meantime his name has been published in the voters list published on 5.8.83 (Annexure M) and the voter list published on 15.2.90 (Annexure '1') which prompted the petitioner to think that the doubt about the citizenship of the petitioner has been-removed, the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh where after the petitioner was elected as Chief of the Jamaat-e- Islami. It is his further case that after he was elected as Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami, Presidential candidates namely, both the candidates for the office of President in the election held in 1991, met the petitioner personally seeking his support in the Parliament where his party by this time had obtained a number of seats. When that is the matter all on a sudden the petitioner received a notice dated 23.3.92 (Annexure 'K') asking him to show cause by 10-00 AM on 24th of March, 1992 why the petitioner should not be deported from Bangladesh, he being a foreigner and other legal action should not be taken against him as he has been disqualified to be citizen of Bangladesh vide notification dated 18.4.73 and that he became the Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami in contravention of Article 38 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. The petitioner gave a reply on 24.3.92 (Annexure-I) stating that he is a citizen of Bangladesh, denying all the allegations made in the show cause notice and soliciting a personal hearing in the matter but the authority illegally arrested the petitioner and detained him at Dhaka Central Jail by issuing an order of detention dated 24.3.92 under section 3 of the Foreigners Act, 1946. The petitioner sent a demand of justice notice (Annexure L) but finding no response he moved this court in Writ Jurisdiction and obtained this Rule on 30.3.92.

85. These statements of the petitioner have been challenged by the respondent Government by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. It has been stated by the respondent Government that the petitioner and also his fore-fathers were born in the territory now comprising in Bangladesh but now he is not a citizen of Bangladesh because he was staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh. It is in the affidavit of the Government that the petitioner had actively participated in the anti-Bangladesh campaign both inside and outside the country during the war of liberation and continued to remain a citizen of Pakistan all along and never submitted oath of allegiance to Bangladesh. It is the further case of the Government that in 1971, 'Razakars' were raised to augment the strength of West Pakistani troops. Razakars rose to about 50,000 in strength and the armed cadre of Jamaat-e-Islami joined the Razakars and were placed at the disposal of. Pakistan Army. For the activities of the petitioner and his party namely, Jamaat-e-Islam during the liberation war of 1971 and for his anti-Bangladesh Movement, the government of Bangladesh vide notification dated 18.4.73 disqualified him and this has been stated in the affidavit-in-opposition in Paragraph (3). It has been further stated that during the liberation war, the petitioner actively collaborated with the Pakistan Army in raising notorious force of Razakars, Al-Badr and Al-Shams, in preparing and waging war against Bangladesh. It has been further stated that nearly 65,000 women were raped in Bangladesh by Pakistani forces and this was evident from a report submitted by a prominent Journalist namely 'David Lushak' and referring to the report published in Sunday Times on 20th January, 1971 it is stated that the Razakars have now extended their operation.to prostitution. At Agrabad in Chittagong they ran a camp of young girls who were allocated to 19 senior Officers. Golam Azam associated with Pakistani Army Officers and it was evident from a photocopy as published in Dainik Purba Desh of April 6,1971 and also the photograph where he was seen sitting with Tikka Khan. The conduct of the petitioner from the above made it clear that the petitioner placed the Jamaat-e-Islami at the disposal of Pakistan Army. As to the averments that Golam Azam was staying there at his own will and not against his will as claimed it is evident from his own conduct. It has been further stated that the petitioner took advantage of the huge congregation in Saudi Arabia to orchestrate his anti-Bangladesh sentiment and lobbied actively to dissuade the Muslim countries from giving recognition to sovereign Bangladesh. It has been further alleged that he organised an organization with the name and style "East Pakistan Recovery Committee". He attended an Islamic Youth Conference in Riyadh and he made an appeal to all of them to join in the liberation struggle for recapturing East Pakistan and in the same year Golam Azam had organised a committee for recapturing East Pakistan in Lahore and he without being invited went to Bengazi in Libya to attend the Conference of the Foreign Ministers of the Islamic countries and he made an appeal to them not to recognize Bangladesh as an independent State. According to the respondent, these facts were reported in various journals and books and particularly the book written by Prof. Abu Sayed which was shown to the court. It is the case of the respondents that Golam Azam was declared not to be a citizen of Bangladesh for his continuous stay abroad since before liberation of Bangladesh, his conduct and his citizenship of Pakistan was the basis of the notification dated 18.4.73 issued from the Ministry of Home Affairs. It was legal and was passed with lawful authority. The question of serving a show cause notice upon Golam Azam as claimed does not arise because his 'whereabouts" were not known and it was not mandatory on the part of the Government to serve the notice upon the petitioner (para 9).

It is the further case that the petitioner went out of the country before liberation and he did not submit any oath of allegiance to sovereign Bangladesh before or after liberation and he did not do so deliberately and as such his claim that he did not renounce his Bangladesh citizenship is not tenable. He never was a citizen of Bangladesh but continued with the citizenship of Pakistan. The petitioner .entered into Bangladesh as a Pakistani citizen registering himself as a foreigner and remained in Bangladesh as a Pakistani citizen and became the Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami in violation of the Constitution and he being a foreigner he was asked to leave the country immediately and as to political rivalry with Awami League in power the petitioner was put to strict proof thereof as it is not known to the deponent so also the claim of leaders meeting him for vote.

86. To this affidavit-in-opposition there was an affidavit-in-reply by the petitioner. It has been stated' therein that on 26th March, 1971 the petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law and continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh thereafter. He had genuine political difference with the Awami League, the political party which formed the Government in 1972 and therefore, he did not come then to Bangladesh and again when he eventually came back he never participated in any anti-Bangladesh campaign either inside or outside Bangladesh. He denied that Jamaat-e-Islami had anything to do with Razakars, Al-Badr or Al-Shams. The other persons who had also been declared to be not qualified for citizenship of Bangladesh stand on the same footing as the petitioner, but all of them out of 38 who applied had received citizenship but the petitioner has been disqualified. It has been further stated that in the month of November, 1973 the then Government granted amnesty to all persons and even to all accused for offences under the Bangladesh Collaborators Order, 1972. The affidavit-in-reply denied the allegations that the petitioner played any heinous role during the war of independence and it has been stated that the petitioner could not be held responsible for the looting, raping, arson and genocide committed by the Pakistani soldiers because he was not in Pakistani Army, nor collaborated with them in any manner in killing or looting or raping. He denied that during the Hajj in 1972 he made any anti-Bangladeshi campaign against Bangladesh to dissuade the Muslim countries from giving recognition to Bangladesh and he denied that he organized any organization like the East Pakistan Recovery Committee in Lahore in that year of 1972 or he went to Libya for making an appeal to Muslim Foreign Ministers not to recognize Bangladesh, nor he met the King of Saudi Arabia several times as alleged. It is his case that he obtained a Pakistani passport as a travel document He did not enter into Bangladesh as a Pakistani citizen stating that he merely used Pakistani passport as a travel document and at the earliest opportunity thereafter he gave up the Pakistani passport by surrendering and affirmed his allegiance to Bangladesh by an affidavit.

87. Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, took great pains in taking me through the long and elaborate judgment of both the judges running almost to 130 pages in total and by reference to various decisions of the Supreme Court of India, Pakistan and Supreme Court of Bangladesh and also of the House of Lords and of the Privy Council, submitted his first point to the effect that the existence or non-existence of petitioner's citizenship is referable to Article 2 of the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 (PO 149 of 1972) hereinafter referred to as the Citizenship Order, 1972.

88. The petitioner, according to the learned counsel, admittedly was a permanent resident of the territories now comprised Bangladesh' on the 25th day of March, 1971 which means one day before Bangladesh was born and he continued to be so resident on and from 26th day of March, 1971 the day Bangladesh came into existence. It is the contention of the learned Counsel that in the law 26th of March, 1971 has not been mentioned. Yet the relevant dates in Article 2 would be 25th and 26th and if a person is found to be present on 25th and permanently residing and continues to so reside thereafter from 26th he would continue to be a Bangladeshi citizen by birth. The petitioner's citizenship having been acquired on birth on the basis of Bangladeshi origin; it would not even be subject to disqualification as may be in the case of only naturalized citizen as under section 16 of the Pakistan Citizenship Act, 1951 subsequently adopted by Bangladesh as existing law which also even a naturalized citizen for acting against the State may be disqualified but only after a due hearing as provided in section 16.

89. It is the further contention of the learned Counsel that conduct as under 2B(I)(i) having not been relevant under Article 2 of the Citizenship Order, 1972 at the time when the impugned notification was issued, the notification suffers from an inherent infirmity, in view of the fact that the Government in exercising the power under Article 2 for removing doubts under Article 2 had considered conduct and other matters which are irrelevant to Article 2 of the Order as it stood on that day and the Government having acted upon irrelevant consideration, has acted by travelling beyond Article 2 and as such acted without jurisdiction.

90. Mr. AR Yusuf further submitted that Golam Azam being a citizen by birth would not lose his citizenship by mere, temporary absence abroad and his 11 months residence in Pakistan would not make him a Pakistani National nor it would prove any allegiance either to the Government of Pakistan or to the Constitution of Pakistan for his citizenship to evaporate and in fact citizenship of origin clings to a person. His citizenship is relatable to his domicile of origin. According to Mr. Yusuf, the domicile of origin of any person is never lost but remains in suspension under a superior pressure of a new domicile if he acquires subsequently, and the moment the new acquired domicile is surrendered, the original domicile would be revived. It has been further argued that a person's right, even if appears to be doubtful to an executive authority, the said authority cannot finally decider the matter ex parte. He should have been heard. And this non-hearing in the decision making process would make the whole proceeding coram non judice and without jurisdiction rendering the notification void ab initio. He has referred to a number of decisions on this point. (11 DLR (SC) 113, 13 DLR (SC) 233, 16 DLR (SC) 417, 375, 566, 722, 1964 (A C) 40 Ridge Vs. Baldwin).

91. He further submitted that the petitioner stayed in Pakistan under compulsion and against his will when residence must be voluntary. He could not come out and was prevented from coming out taking his matter also under the proviso to Art. 2 of the Order.

92. He further submits that every person has a right to be treated in accordance with law and that law would be referable, in the instant case, to the law that was existing when the impugned notification was passed and Art 2B(I) which was not in existence when the impugned order was passed, allegiance to a foreign country or conduct of an individual as a disqualification would not be available to pass the impugned notification of dis- qualification.

93. Mr. AR Yusuf lastly submits that the petitioner came to this court in time. He was not delayed but rather he acted promptly and at the earliest opportunity he came before this court to which point I shall also advert at the relevant portion of the judgment.

94. Mr. Aminul Haq, the learned Attorney- General appearing for the State, who argued the matter also for a number of days and took me through a large number of local and foreign newspaper reports, local books and periodicals, submitted to the effect that the petitioner by his conduct and behavior remained right from the liberation war days of April, 1971 till the creation of Bangladesh an enemy of Bangladesh. Before the liberation war he was in favour of six points but turned round after the Army crackdown, in favour of Pakistan Army. He never believed in Bangladesh. Bangladesh is a non-existent identity to him and he had allegiance to Pakistan. He was rightly disqualified as he is a Pakistani and an anti-Bangladeshi, collaborated with Pakistan army during the war of liberation.

95. The learned Attorney-General then submitted that this "conduct" of the petitioner would disqualify him from being a citizen of Bangladesh.

96. It is the submission Of the learned Attorney- General that the legislature by giving the amended law namely Article 2B(I), a retrospective operation from 26th day of March, 1971 the said would be regarded as validating any order, correcting and or certifying any order passed during those days after 26th March, 1971 till the amendment was made by addition and his citizenship having been refused by the Government in the central level the said notification should not be lightly interfered with because that will be an act of interference with a necessity which can be called a public necessity for public good. The learned Attorney-General submitted that the petitioner had been too late in coming to this court to ventilate his grievance in which he ought to have been very prompt and therefore, according to the learned Attorney-General, this petition filed by the petitioner ought to have been dismissed in the very outset without issuance of any Rule, being delayed and thus, not maintainable.

97. Before adverting to the rival contentions it would be convenient to narrate the law which would be relevant in the instant case remembering that in a writ jurisdiction which is for review of administrative action as under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh this court does not decide between the parties but examine the exercises of power by an administrative or executive authority performing functions in the affairs of the republic on the touchstone of the doctrine of ultra vires and also would examine the decision making process keeping in mind the law that when a thing is to be done by following a procedure and the mandates of the law, it need be done by following that law and the procedure, and no other.

This matter arises out of a notification (Annexure 'B') issued by the Government in exercise of the power under Article 3 of the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provision) Order, 1972 hereinafter referred to as Citizenship Order, 1972. The notification recites that the decision has been taken under Article 3 of the Order on the ground that these persons have stayed abroad since before liberation of Bangladesh and by their conduct cannot be deemed to be a resident of Bangladesh and that they continued to be a citizen of Pakistan. Those persons were declared disqualified to be the citizens of Bangladesh and those persons included Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, Mr. AS Saadi, Advocate, Prof. Golam Azam, Mr: Korban Ali, Bar-at-Law, Mr. Nurul Amin, Mr. Mohammad Ali, Mr. Humayun Khan Panni and a numbers of others, in total 38 persons.

98. The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was enacted and adopted in November, 1972. The Preamble of the Constitution recites that the people of Bangladesh, proclaimed Independence on the 26th of March, 1971 and through a historic war of national independence, established the independent, sovereign People's Republic of Bangladesh. Article 2 of the Constitution provided that the territories of the Republic of Bangladesh shall comprise the territories which immediately before the proclamation of independence of 26th March, 1971 "constituted East Pakistan". These two dates therefore are important to remember namely, 25th day of March, 1971 and 26th day of March, 1971.

99. Article 2 of the Citizenship Order 1972 as it originally stood provided thus: Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, on the commencement of this Order, every person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh.

(i) Who or whose father or grandfather was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of such territories on the 25th day of March, 1971, and continues to be so resident;

(ii) Who was a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on 25th day of March 1971 and continues to be so resident and is not otherwise disqualified from being citizen by or under any law for the time being in force. Provided that if any person who is a permanent resident of Bangladesh is in the course of his employment or for the pursuit of his studies, residing in a country which was at war or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh such person or his dependents shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh."

100. This provision qualifying a person to be deemed to be a citizen or not should be understood and explained within this qualifying clause as in Article 2. Art 3 is not a qualifying clause, rather an enabling clause authorizing the Government of Bangladesh to decide and to decide finally in case of doubt as to whether a person is qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh as under Article 2 of this Order or not.

101. Looking at Article 2 of the Order as it stood originally, it will be seen that in the qualifying clause as in Article 2(i) and Art. 2(ii) minus the proviso to Article 2 which made an exception to this the points for consideration for a decision under Article 3 for resolving a doubt as under Article 2(i) in case of citizen by birth but not citizen by virtue of permanent resident as in Article 2(ii) would be three in number namely (a) whether a person or his father or his grandfather was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh, and (b) whether he is found to be a permanent resident of the territory now comprising Bangladesh on the 25th day March, 1971 which means the last night of the existence of East Pakistan and (c) the said person continues to be so resident.

102. In the Indian Constitution Articles 5 to 11 govern this field of Indian Citizenship. In Article 5 of the said Indian Constitution there exists a similar provision as in Article 2 of Bangladesh Citizenship Order, 1972. Article 5 of the Indian Constitution provides that "at the commencement of this Constitution every person who has his domicile in the territory of India and-

(a) who was born in the territory of India; or

(b) either of whose parents was born in the territory of India; or

(c) who has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India for not less then five years immediately preceding such commencement, shall be a citizen of India."

<u>103. It is to be noted that Article 5 of the Indian Constitution refers to an expression namely" domicile of a person domiciled in India which domicile is considered in India to be an essential requirement for acquiring the status of the Indian citizenship. The term 'domicile' is not defined in the Indian Constitution but it means a permanent home or a place where he resides with the intention of remaining there for an indefinite period. Domicile is not the same thing as residence (AIR 1965 Patna 371). Residence implies a purely physical fact, the fact of just being present and living in a particular place, but domicile is not only residence; it is residence coupled with intention to live indefinitely in the place. (Dicey-Conflict of Laws, 6th Ed. 78). Domicile means permanent home and in the language of Lord Cranworth as expressed in the case of Whicker Vs. Hume, reported in 28 LJ Chancery:</u>

<u>"By domicile we mean home, the permanent home and if you do not understand your permanent home I am afraid that no illustration drawn from foreign writers or foreign language will very much help you to it. "</u>

<u>Therefore, domicile means a permanent home and not mere residence. No person can be without a domicile or a permanent home and since the object of determining a person's domicile is to connect him with some system or rule of law it is obvious that for the purpose of any given inquiry, a person cannot have more than one domicile (1911 "KB 516, 527) and the Rule to this effect is now well established. Hence if a person has two homes in different countries, he in the absence of a contrary intention is domiciled in that country in which he has his principal home.</u>

<u>104. In our citizenship laws as referable to Citizenship Order, 1972 the legislature without using the word domicile has used the expression "permanent residence" which more or less bears the same meaning as meant by the expression domicile of origin which means permanent home.</u>

<u>105. If any person wishes to claim citizenship he must prove that he had a permanent home or domicile of origin in Bangladesh and that he had permanently so domiciled in the territory once called East Pakistan on 25th day of March 1971 and he continues to be so resident of that territory thereafter on and from 26th. If these are found then he would be citizen of Bangladesh on the commencement day of the Order, 1972.</u>

106. The expression "continue to be so resident" as appears in Article 2 obviously means by the application of ejusdem generis rules to mean "so permanently resident" thereafter in Bangladesh as distinguished from the proviso to Article 2 which proviso is added to explain the legislative intention to meet the situation prevailing at that historical moment of this nation's birth along with its ten (10) crores of people, clearly providing for the absentee Bangladeshis resident in Pakistan. This is also in conformity with the generally accepted view of the courts that residence anywhere must be a voluntary residence and not residence out of compulsion which compulsory residence shall bear no consequences. For example, a British soldier who resided out of compulsion in a Nazi Prison Camp in Germany cannot be called an enemy in England for residing on an enemy territory for his property to vest in the Government as enemy property. Now back to the proviso it is seen that the proviso provided that a person who is permanent resident of the territory now Bangladesh but resident in the territory at war with or in military operation against Bangladesh, in connection with studies or service and is prevented from returning to Bangladesh "shall be deemed to be resident in Bangladesh" as in condition number 3 in Article 2(i). The definition relating to student or service holders as in proviso do not appear to be exhaustive but inclusive of hundreds of other Bangladeshis stranded in Pakistan and in fact those hundreds of others were subsequently repatriated officially to Bangladesh long after 16th of December, 1971 as is evident by the tripartite agreement in 1974 among Bangladesh, Pakistan and India which also repatriated 194 war prisoners.

<u>107. It is further seen that the very proviso to Article 2 used the expression permanent resident to denote those who had domicile of origin in Bangladesh and then used the expressions "residence" to ,denote those temporarily resident or habitual resident in Pakistan and prevented from returning. Further, the expression "prevented" would mean and include both actual physical prevention and also mental prevention arising out of fear of life or personal safety or other difficult circumstances which would prevent them from returning to Bangladesh. The petitioner pleaded fear and risk of life while Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was also disqualified on the same grounds as the petitioner under the same notification.</u>

108. In the case of Bishal Deo Tewari Vs. The State, reported in 27 DLR 622 a very similar matter came for decision. In that case the petitioner Bishal Deo Tewari was the pujari of Dhakeshwari Mandie at Dhaka. His parent was the sebayet of that Dhakeshwari Deity. It is claimed that the petitioner besides being the owner of a house at 7, Orphanage Road has got other landed properties in Dhaka and a sweetmeat shop and Municipal licence for business at Dhaka. He was arrested under the Foreigners Act as Indian National and detained for an unauthorised entry into Bangladesh' from India. The impugned order issued under the Foreigners Order 1951 by the Civil Authority on 1.7.75 and thereafter detained in Dhaka Central Jail. It has been argued in that case on behalf of Bishal Deo Tewari that he is a national of this country, and also of the then East Pakistan and as such cannot be served with the order under the Foreigners Order, 1951. The Government opposed the Rule by the Government that the petitioner is an Indian National and this impression of the Government was founded upon some correspondence between the Government of Bangladesh and the Indian High Commissioner in Bangladesh. The Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court who heard the matter consisting of Mr. Justice KM Sobhan and Mr. Justice SM Hussain quoted Article 2 of the Presidential Order 149 of 1972 namely the Citizenship Order of 1972, which was the relevant provision in that case and after quoting the provision the Court observed thus:

"On the promulgation of this Order namely PO 149 of 1972 which came into force on the 26th day of March, 1971 the only point that is to be determined is the nationality of the petitioner on the 25th day of March, 1971. Article 2 makes it clear that who or whose father or grandfather was born in the territories of Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of such territory on the 25th day of March, 1971 continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh."

109. In that case under report it was held that when one was permanent resident on 25th of March he continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh thereafter. The order under the Foreigner Order, 1951 was set aside when in fact Bishal Deo Tewari was in India for a considerable period. He entered into Bangladesh from India after the War of Liberation.

<u>110. Article 2(i), 2(ii) and the proviso thus, covers all, whether physically present or not, but Bangladeshi by birth or permanently domiciled and also persons of Bangladeshi origin who are in temporary residence in Pakistan for service or studies and otherwise and prevented from returning to Bangladesh. Temporary residence in Pakistan would thus, come under the proviso to Article 2 and in the tripartite agreement between Bangladesh, Pakistan and India it was further extended to all "stranded" Bangladeshis in Pakistan, as a Government policy.</u>

111. A similar point came for consideration before a Division Bench of this court in the case of Abdul Hoque Vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 33 DLR 113 which was subsequently taken to Appellate Division, reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 143. In that case under report, Abdul Hoque admittedly was born in Satkhira within the territory of Bangladesh in 1932. He was a permanent resident admittedly on the territory now comprised in Bangladesh on 25th day of March, 1971. He went to Karachi in November, 1971 which is also the date when Golam Azam left for Lahore to attend a Conference in November, 1971, which is much after the commencing day of Citizenship Ordinance of 1971 on 26th day of March, 1971. Abdul Hoque went to Karachi in November, 1971 to collect dues from Karachi trader dealing in pan business and became ill and was in hospital for 8 months.
