When he came out of hospital the repatriation of Bangladeshis was over and thus could not come back. He eventually came back to Bangladesh in 1975 with a Pakistani passport as a travel document. He surrendered his Pakistani passport to the Government of Bangladesh and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh which was refused and he was asked to leave the country immediately under the Foreigners Act, 1946. Abdul Hoque challenged this order. The High Court Division observed that he was a stateless person and thus cannot be deported.

112. The Government made an appeal before the Appellate Division and their Lordships of the Appellate Division dismissed the appeal filed by the State. It is to be noted that the stand of the Government in that case was that the Government had refused to grant the citizenship of the petitioner as he left this country in November, 1971 as a Collaborator and he came back after 5 years and asked for citizenship which was refused and Government asked him to leave the country. The Appellate Division after quoting Art. 2 of the Citizenship Order of 1972 including the proviso to Art. 2 found that the respondent was born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh but his temporary absence is covered by the proviso and the proviso provided that he shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh notwithstanding his temporary residence in a country which was at war or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh if he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh. The court considered that A. Hoque asserted that he was "prevented" from returning to Bangladesh but the circumstances as mentioned by him in the petition namely that he was in hospital for some time and he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh had not been challenged, The' finding of the Appellate Division is that Abdul Hoque remained a resident of Bangladesh and therefore, the court held that the order of deportation must be declared as not lawfully made and the Government appeal was dismissed.

113. In this case under report one thing is important to note and it is that the time of residence to qualify or to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh has been defined to be residence on the mid-night of 25th/26th March, 1971 he being a permanent resident of East Pakistan was entitled to be a lawful citizen of Bangladesh which supports the contention of the learned Counsel Mr. AR Yusuf that 25th /26th mid-night is the terminal point. If one touches both the points he is a citizen by birth.

114. A point of similar nature again came up for decision in the case of Mira Shahab Ispahani Vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 40 DLR 87. The said case was decided by the Appellate Division upholding the decision of the High Court Division, reported in 40 DLR (AD)

116. The question of citizenship and the qualification clause as in Article 2 of Citizenship Order 1971 came up for discussion in that case Mirza Shahab was born not in Bangladesh or in East Pakistan but in Calcutta in the year 1941. Justice Ispahani was also not born in East Pakistan now Bangladesh. He opted for East Pakistan in 1947, later he became the Chief Justice of East Pakistan. Mirza Shahab Ispahani was all along a student in England. He went to England with International passport issued to him from, Dhaka which was his permanent address. He became a Chartered Accountant and later on got a land at Gulshan Model Town and built a house and it was declared thereafter an abandoned property. The question that had to be decided in that case was whether he is a Pakistani citizen on and from 25th March, 1971 and hence not a citizen of Bangladesh. In that case Mirza Shahab Ispahani travelled to Bangladesh with a. Pakistani passport. He had no Bangladeshi passport though he has a house of his own at Gulshan where his mother had been living. That case however was covered by Article 2A of the Presidential Order which provided that a person to whom Article 2 would have ordinarily applied but for his residence in the United Kingdom shall be deemed to continue to be perman~l1t resident in Bangladesh within the meaning Of Article 2 but certain observation of that case has been referred to by the learned Counsel Mr. AR Yusuf before this court and 1 would like to refer to those which are thus:

"He is a qualified Chartered Accountant making a living in UK and it is by his own earning he obtained a plot from DIT and built his house and rented it to a Foreign Mission. He himself visits Dhaka occasionally which is his permanent residence. His ordinary residence as understood in Europe is in UK. If his habitual residence is UK then his permanent residence is bound to be Dhaka, Bangladesh. Again if his ordinary residence is taken as UK then again it is Bangladesh which is to be taken as his permanent residence because he owns a house and rented a flat and his mother lives here and the father is buried here. It is not by naked assertion but by deeds and acts that a domicile is established. "

In his dissenting judgment Habibur Rahman J, however came to the view that Mirza Sahab Ispahani was never born in the territory now comprised Bangladesh and does not come under Article 2(ii) of the Order as he had no permanent residence here and had also not been found here on 25th of March 1971 and his Lordship allowed the appeal.

115. It is thus, seen that the Appellate Division in Ispahani case explained the expression permanent residence, ordinary residence and habitual residence and considered that as Mirza Shahab Ispahani has been living in London and having obtained a DIT plot at Dhaka, built a house at Dhaka where his mother is living, his permanent residence is at Dhaka and not in UK. He is not residing in United Kingdom but' only has his habitual residence and not permanent residence there in UK. Permanent residence therefore, according to their Lordships of the Appellate Division, is the permanent home of a person where he has a house and his family would be residing.

116. On an examination of the above 3 decided cases on this qualification clause as under Article Z of the Order including the proviso to Art. 2 it thus, appears that the expression permanent resident as occurred in Article 2 has been distinguished from the expression ordinary resident giving permanent resident the status of domicile as it is understood in International Law when it concerns sovereign State. Their Lordships had also, while examining the proviso to Art. 2 which speaks of a prevention clause, in Abdul Hoque's case extended' the sway of the proviso to all that were resident in Pakistan irrespective of being a student or employed as service holder and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh and this extension of entry to all Bangalees that were "stranded" in Pakistan is found in the Tripartite Agreement signed on 9th of April, 1971 by the Foreign Ministers of India., Pakistan and Bangladesh which agreement was shown to me by the Attorney-General. It acknowledges the fact that for harmony and reconciliation all the "three governments agreed to complete repatriation of Bangalees from Pakistan, Pakistanis in Bangladesh and the Pakistani prisoners of war in India" and it declared that such civilian repatriation had started in September, 1973 and 3,00,000 had been repatriated and it hoped that the repatriation of prisoners of war would be completed by the end of April, 1974 and because of the progress of this, three-way repatriation started under the Delhi Agreement on 29th August, 1973. Governments of these three countries were gratified that such a large number of persons (in their language) "detained and stranded" in these three countries reached their destination which expression 'stranded" is much wider in term and goes beyond persons prevented.

117. From a reading of this Tripartite Agreement signed by Dr. Kamal Hossain for Bangladesh, Swaran Singh for India and Mr. Aziz Ahmed for Pakistan as respective Foreign Ministers it is seen that there it has been stated that as Prime Minister Bhutto had asked the people of Bangladesh to forgive and forget the past crimes and as the Prime Minister of Bangladesh said that he also wanted the people to forget the past and to make a fresh start stating that the people of Bangladesh know how to forgive and having regard to the appeal of the Prime Minister of Pakistan to the people of Bangladesh to forgive and forget the mistakes of the past and the foreign minister of Bangladesh having Slated that the Government of Bangladesh had decided not to proceed with the trial as an act of clemency it was agreed that 195 prisoners of war may be repatriated to Pakistan along with the other prisoners of war now in the process of repatriation under the Delhi Agreement.

118.  This agreement also brings home the point as I have stated hereinbefore that residence in Pakistan for all the Bangalees by a deeming clause as in Article 2 was considered to be residence in Bangladesh and if one considers 25th March, 1971 to be the starting point then till repatriation started in September, 1973 residence in Pakistan for the period of 30 months till repatriation, would be residence in Bangladesh but in the instant case after 11 months of residence in Pakistan the petitioner was disqualified.

<u>119.  The scheme of the whole legislation as it stood originally and as it stood when the impugned disqualification order was passed, was to grant citizenship to all on the basis of permanent residence in Bangladesh as on 25th March 1971 and on the commencing day on 26th March, 1971 and it was extended under Article 2(ii) to persons not born in the territory now Bangladesh but found to be a permanent resident on 25th March, 1971 and also to persons who were resident in Pakistan on the commencing day of this Order and thereafter "stranded" and "prevented" from returning.</u>

120.  In the instant case the petitioner was been here and thus, comes under Article 2(i). He stayed in Bangladesh as permanent resident on 25th of March, 1971 and was present here physically on 25th of March and 26th March, 1971 and he continued to be so permanently resident after the commencing day of the Order and the petitioner is not proved to have gone to Pakistan any time after November, 1972 when he left to reside there permanently. He stayed in Pakistan for 11 months and he stated that his stay in Pakistan was against his will. He went to Lahore" on 22.11.71 temporarily to attend his party meeting while his wife, seven children, father and mother all were living at Dhaka (para-14). After 10 days war broke out on 3.12.71 and he started for Dhaka on the same day by aeroplane but the aeroplane carrying him, after reaching near Dhaka could not land at Dhaka Airport because of war. He was taken back to land at Colombo. Thereafter as there was bombing at Karachi Airport, his plane took him along with others to Jeddah, where after they were taken to Karachi. He had to remain in Karachi against his will for 11 months as the then Government of Pakistan did not allow any Bangladeshi to leave Pakistan and while he was unwillingly staying in Pakistan he in the month of March, 1972 tried to go to London but could not get any passport for that but only for Hajj. He obtained a Pakistani passport as travel document and this was done before repatriation had started for Bangladeshi nationals in September, 1973 and when in Mecca he heard that political mispropaganda is high in Bangladesh against him and he was informed that is his life will be at stake if he went back to Bangladesh. (paras 16, 17, 18). There was no Bangladeshi Embassy in Saudi Arabia also then so he went to London in 1st week of April, 1973 when some days thereafter he was disqualified (Para-19).

121.  To all these except a general denial by the State and asserting that he was staying there willingly there is nothing to make those statements improbable. He could have fear of life which fear is rather personal to him as all fears are. He wanted to come back to Bangladesh but he failed. He lived there unwillingly. He was prevented out of fear to return at that time as the political position of the petitioner was then debated and is still been debated. All these do not appear to be unfounded. It was possible for him in that situation to react as he did. I thus, agree with BI Choudhury, J in finding that the petitioner also came under the proviso to Article 2 for his temporary unwilling residence in Pakistan and on the day the impugned notification was issued he was a citizen of Bangladesh by and under the statutory provision as in Article 2.

<u>122.  One conduct of the petitioner seems to be clear and it is that after he went out of Pakistan in November, 1972 where he was for some time, he never went back to Pakistan thereafter to seek its nationality or establish a permanent home there. Even in a moment of crisis when he was without the citizenship of Bangladesh and almost a stateless person he did not go to Pakistan or opted for Pakistan which he could do, as many other disqualified persons did. This conduct and this intention to be identified as a Bangladeshi is relevant for the purpose of distinguishing mere residence from domicile of origin.</u>

<u>123.  Abdul Hoque's case as referred to hereinbefore covers the point of being prevented from returning but a similar point of being prevented out of political difference of opinion with the then party in power and fear of safety which is also the petitioner's -case is covered by the decision of this court in Hamidul Huq Choudhury's case reported in 33 DLR. In that case Hamidul Huq Choudhury's press at Dhaka was declared abandoned and he was disqualified to be citizen on the same ground as the petitioner. It was stated in his writ petition that the then party in power had political hostility and bias against the petitioner, He was a permanent resident but did not return to Bangladesh because of law and order situation and "threat to his life". The Division Bench, in the relevant portion of the judgment (para-15) observed-thus:</u>

<u>"The contention of the respondent that Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury was a citizen of Pakistan was based upon firstly, that he was away from Bangladesh and that by notification dated 18A.1973 the Government declared that Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury did not qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh, Mr. Chowdhury claimed that he never became a citizen of any other state and his citizenship by statutory provision continued to be Bangladeshi. It appears to us on a perusal of notification dated 18.4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury by statutory provision was a citizen of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>This notification was subsequently declared void by another notification of the Government dated 19.7.77. In this view we hold that Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh though he was away from the country"</u>

<u>The contention of the Attorney-General that Article 2B(I)(ii) would act as a validation of the impugned notification to correct its error has no basis, as there cannot be any validation by implication but by law itself and more so of a past and closed transaction (Corpus Juris Vol. 59. Pages 1181-1184 & 434-439). Moreover, this added Article 2B(I)(i) would not also be available to the Government to remove a doubt whether a person is qualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Art. 2 of the Order, as on the day the notification was issued and made effective on 18.4.73 the amendment made on 19.5.73 was not even born or added to Art. 2.</u>

<u>Except this disqualification clause as in Art. 2B (I) added subsequently to the 'Citizenship Order of 1972 as it originally stood, the said Order does not anywhere make any other "conduct" such as treason, sedition, waging war against Government established by law, which are in Penal Code, a disqualification for citizenship. This appears to be a clear and deliberate omission made by the legislature in Citizenship Order 1972 (PO 149 of 1972) at that time the law of Citizenship Order, 1972 was first promulgated on 15th December, 1972 with a retrospective effect from 26th March, 1971.</u>

124. In this regard Ismail Uddin Sarker, J in his judgment in this case at page 60 observed thus:

"Relying upon the word "conduct" the learned Attorney-General tried to argue pointing out to certain subsequent events as anti-state activities of the petitioner disentitling him to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. But the events and the alleged conduct of the petitioner referred to by the learned Attorney-General may be taken into consideration if any case is made out under Article 2B of the said Presidential Order. Mr. AR Yusuf has pointed out, and in my opinion rightly, that Article 2A and 2B were inserted in PO 149 of 1972 subsequent to the making of the impugned notification the fact remains that the impugned notification was made before the passing of the amending Act or Ordinance. As such, I am of the view that Article 2B 'is not applicable in the present case as the impugned notification was made prior to the insertion of Article 2B in the PO 149 of 1972."

125. I am in agreement with the above which supports the view I have taken hereinbefore to the effect that "conduct" and Article 2B(l)(1) is not attracted and thus, irrelevant for this case of citizenship.

126. This part of the political conduct of the petitioner appears to have been argued at length as the Government affidavit-in-opposition shows before the Division Bench, but Sarker, J on this, at the relevant part of his judgment at pages 24-25, observed as follows:

"Further the petitioner also challenged the authenticity of some of the events mentioned in the subsequent publications. Except some news items and one photograph showing that the petitioner met General Tikka Khan or General Yahya Khan, there is nothing to directly implicate the petitioner in any of the atrocities alleged to have been perpetuated by the Pakistani Army or their associates-the Rajakars, A1- Badars or the At-Shams. Except that the petitioner was hobnobbing with the Military Junta during the war of liberation, we do not find anything that the petitioner was in any way directly involved in perpetuating the alleged atrocities during the war of independence. In my view, none of these reports is of any help for solving the legal question raised before us in this matter and as such I will refrain from mentioning any such reports or events in course of my discussion of the points raised in this matter."

127. In this regard BI Chowdhury, J in his judgment at pages 124-125 observed thus:

"But neither PO No. 8 of 1972 contained nor PO No. 149 of 1972 contains any provision disqualifying a person from being a citizen of Bangladesh during the war of liberation and committing or abetting murder, rape or arson in course of such collaboration or for indulging in anti-Bangladesh activities after independence. Moreover, commission of any such offence is yet to be proved against the petitioner in a competent court of law. Till now nobody has come forward to set the criminal law in motion against the petitioner by lodging an FIR with the police or by filing a petition of complaint before any Magistrate."

<u>128. I, on my part, would put an end to this by holding as I did before that if Golam Azam is charged for abetting murder, rape or arson in collaboration with Pakistan army or charged for sedition or for treason or for waging war against the Bangladesh Government, he will answer those, but for this citizenship matter those would be irrelevant and being irrelevant I would make no comment further on those allegations, keeping in mind that this Citizenship case centered round Article 2 only and no further. Justice is to be done in accordance with law and any attempt to be wiser than the law is by good law forbidden.</u>

129. The learned Attorney-General before me however again laid much emphasis on this "conduct" of the petitioner urging that much papers could not be shown before the Division Bench and with the leave of the court he showed some other writing from the book written by Professor Abu Syeed on the activities of the petitioner subsequent to the independence of Bangladesh in foreign countries. By referring to the book of Prof. Abu Syeed the learned Attorney-General submitted that the petitioner had been in Saudi Arabia after Hajj in a "Politico Military Mission" urging the Muslim countries such as Saudi Arabia and Libya not to recognise Bangladesh and the learned Attorney-General also showed a book published by the petitioner's own party, namely Jamaat-e-Islami, showing that the said Jamat book also corroborated the fact that he was in other Muslim countries like Libya. But while reading the Jamaat book it shows that the petitioner went to those and urged the Muslim countries to help the new State of Bangladesh and that he even obtained money from them through Rabita-e-al- Islami to help the new State of Bangladesh. Which of these versions are true cannot be decided in this writ jurisdiction without knowing the sources of their respective information which source, according to the Attorney-General, are hearsay and they thus being not relevant also, need not be gone into.

130. The petitioner's case had again been that he used a Pakistani passport only as a travel document He never went back to Pakistan thereafter at any point of time to reside there showing allegiance to Pakistan as many others did and if there was. any doubt as to that he ought to have been given a chance to explain his position and thus, there would exist at least a "legitimate expectation" that the government would hear him before they took away that vested right ex parte and, according to Mr. AR Yusuf, even God did not punish or condemn Adam without giving him a hearing.

131. There comes in the question of show cause and a hearing in observance of the principle of natural justice.

132. It has been argued at the bar that the petitioner has no vested right, being not a citizen, to be heard and there was no violation of the natural justice clause.

133. The law in this regard is otherwise. For the purpose of natural justice the question which would matter is not whether the applicant has some right but whether any power has been exercised over him to his disadvantage ex parte. It is not a question of right but a matter of exercise of government power in a manner which is just fair, reasonable and considerate.

<u>134. Natural justice is nothing but a procedural justice. Being procedural it cannot however be said that it is not vested. This procedural matter speaks of some substantive right, as part of the procedure to be followed in every case where the executive authority decides a matter to the detriment and prejudice of any person. In none of those situations where the natural justice clause is invoked there existed any legal right for such an asking but the matter involves what the court often calls a legitimate expectation of procedural justice'. When that is not specifically ousted by the law itself, the court would read in to the law such a clause. The justice of the common law in such a case will supply the omission of the legislature. This was first expressed in Coopers' case decided in 1863 reported in (1863) 14 CBNS 180 where the Biblical precedent of the Garden of Eden cited in Dr. Bentley's case decided in 1723, was reiterated.</u>

135. Byles, J. delivering the judgment of the court of Common Pleas, in Coopers case, observed thus: "That being so a long course of decision beginning with Dr. Bentley's case, ending with some more recent cases established that although there are no positive words in statute requiring that the party should be heard, yet the justice of the common law, will supply the omission of the legislature. The judgment of Mr. Justice Forts, as in Dr. Bentley's case, is somewhat quaint but it is very applicable and had been applied from that time to the present day. He says the objection for want of notice can never be got over. The law of God and the man both gave the party an opportunity to make his defence if he has any. I remember to have heard it observed by a very learned man upon such an occasion that even God himself did not pass sentence upon Adam before he was called upon to make his defence "Adam (says God),where art thou, Hast thou not eaten of the tree whereof I commanded thee that thou shoud'nt not eat" ? And the same question was put to Eve also. If therefore, the Board acted judicially, although there are no words in the statute to that effect, it is plain they acted wrongly.

136. There is some ambiguity in the dicta about legitimate expectation which may apparently mean either expectation of fair hearing only or expectation of the licence or other benefit or expectation of the benefit itself which is being sought for. But the result in all these cases are the same. No matter what the legitimate expectations are, it would not absolve the public authority from affording a hearing. Natural justice in procedure thus means" fair play in action". This duty to act fairly by following the procedure of natural justice even in administrative proceeding or orders is an integral part of the law itself and it need not be super added. This is the law in this regard followed by the superior court of this sub-continent including our courts till today.

<u>137. In the instant case therefore the question would be whether in view of the assertion of the petitioner that he would come within the qualifying clause as in Article 2 fairly and squarely a reasonable expectation of being heard would exist in him and that would create a right and if the authority chooses not to hear him before his right has been negatived by an ex parte order, could the authority be allowed to say that they acted legally, rightly and fairly. The answer is in the negative and this will thus make the proceeding leading to the notification dated 18.4.73 coram non judice and without jurisdiction.</u>

138. One of the judges of the Division Bench in this case held that natural justice is not a must in all cases and it would depend upon the circumstances of each case and reference was made to the decision in Abul Ala Maudoodi's case reported in PLD 1964 (SC) 673 to the effect that it depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The said narration as in Maudoodi's case is a good law but it is seen that there his Lordship Hamodoor Rahman J, in fact, observed thus: "The nature of the thing to be done and the manner in which it is to be done and the circumstances in which it is to be done are important considerations which must be taken into account in determining whether the above mentioned principle should be applied in a given case or not."

139. But when this observation of Hamoodur Rahman, J is read by reference to the context (which ought to have been so) it would read:

"It is not difficult to conceive of cases where from the very question of the action to be taken this principle cannot possibly have any application. Thus, can it be said, that when a breach of the peace is taking place in the view, of the officer or the authority empowered to prevent breaches of peace by restricting movement of persons he must give them an opportunity 'of showing cause before taking action? To hold so would, in my view, amount to justifying the action itself and therefore I cannot agree that this Rule is of universal application. In this view of the matter I am also inclined to agree with the High Court, that in the cause of action properly coming within the scope of the Criminal. Law Amendment Act 1908 the rule of audi alteram partem would not be applicable for, the circumstances in which it would become necessary to take action under the said Act are such that they can brook no delay nor the statute imposes upon the Govt. a duty to adjudicate or to decide controversies. The power conferred is in the nature of a police power designed to take preventive action in an emergent situation. "

140. I respectfully agree with the above and it needs be mentioned that in Maudoodi's case Government action against Jamaat-e-Islami was taken under the Criminal Law Amendment Act which was enacted for the purpose of prohibiting formation of association dangerous to public peace and section 16 of that Act empowered the Provincial Government to declare any association unlawful if in the opinion of the said government the association constitutes a danger to public peace or had the object of interfering with the maintenance of law and order.

141. Thus Kaikaus, J. in his own judgment in that very case, observed thus:

"The next contention of Mr. Brohi is that the impugned orders having been passed without hearing the respondents are void on the principle of audi alteram partem, that is, no man shall be condemned unheard. It is not necessary now in view of a number of judgments of this court to go into the question whether impugned orders were passed in an administrative or judicial or quasi judicial capacity. If an order affects rights in property or status' or has penal consequences, there must be an opportunity to show cause even if the order is passed in an administrative capacity. Although the manner in which the opportunity is afforded will vary' with' different class of cases. Mr. Manzur Qadir contends that the present is a case of interference with law and order when urgent action was made and grant of hearing before the order is not possible. I am prepared to concede that when an emergency requires the passing of an order without hearing the party an order may be passed and to this extent there has to be a proviso to the maxim audi alteram partem but action can be taken ex parte to the extent to which it is absolutely necessary, ex parte order is in such cases to be regarded only as an interim order or a provisional order which will remain in force till a final order is passed after hearing the party but it would be essential that there is an opportunity to show cause after the order was passed. In the present case there is in the first place no proof at all of any emergency which would call for immediate action."

In the instant case of Golam Azam the Government while exercising the power under Article 3 of the Citizenship Order of 1972 had not been exercising a "police power" in-an emergency to prevent an immediate unlawful dangerous act threatening public safety or law and order in the country or in a part of the country. But in fact the Government did exercise a power in peace time and exercised the power in disqualifying the petitioner along with 38 others in which Hamidul. Huq Chowdhury topped the list when there was no proved emergency. Government was not acting in an emergency but long after the liberation of Bangladesh and in peace time and in fact no such immediate danger or emergency had even been pleaded in this case by the government nor they made out a case of emergency nor we find any proved emergency. Before this court it was the case of the government that he could not be heard as his" whereabouts were not known" and by giving notice in his collaboration case it had been complied with. Mr. AR Yusuf argued that this is not the correct position as his whereabouts were known to Government and they sent notice at his Maghbazar address in the collaboration case that time to appear and reply.

142. It is seen that the Citizenship Order, 1972 had also made no provision for any appeal or for any representation or for any review before any committee and made the decision of the Government [mal. This is finally deciding the matter ex parte, in which case the necessity of hearing him before the final order was passed, closing the door for ever was more urgent. He ought to have been heard in his defence.

<u>143. It is true that Article 3 of the Citizenship Order 1972 in case of doubt makes the decision of the government final. It is argued that as the decision in this matter would be regarded to be final this court would not reopen the said finality arrived at by the Government' in issuing the notification.</u>

<u>144. In modem legislation this sort of finality clause is every common but this finality clause would only mean that the order which is legal is only final and that there is no appeal. The often quoted expression of Lord Denning MR in the case of Regina Vs. Medical Appeal Tribunal, Ex parte Gilmore reported in 1957 1 QB 574 is to the effect that the expression that the decision shall be final would mean" final only as to the question of fact and not to the question of law" and therefore if there is an error or if the decision had been arrived at not in accordance with law then in spite of the finality clause it would be a nullity. In fact the finality clause in matters like this will not automatically render the decision final because an order which is a nullity is no decision in the eye of law at all for it to be final. There must be a final decision which is good in law.</u>

<u>145. There remains the question of delay in filing of this application as pleaded by the respondent Government. Under the law for an aggrieved person to come before this court under Article 102 of the Constitution, no statutory limitation is provided for as in a suit. The jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution is a jurisdiction in law and also in equity. A court thus, entertains a petition if the delay is explained to the satisfaction of the court and it would be explained and examined in the light of the attending facts and circumstances of each case.</u>

146. In the case of Sajique Rahman Vs. Certificate Officer, Dhaka, reported in 29 DLR (SC) at page 232 it was held thus:

"Even in a proceeding for writ in the nature of certiorari the aggrieved person must show diligence and a sense of urgency for the purpose of invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction. In a particular case he must not rush to the court immediately on the initiation of a proceeding which according to him is a nullity but has not threatened him with any actual danger but when some positive steps have been taken in the said proceeding to his prejudice and he instead of resisting it, submits to it and carries out various orders made in the said proceeding, he has in accordance with the authorities referred to above, disentitled himself to the said extraordinary remedy,"

In the case of Ram Chandra Sankar Deodhar Vs. The State of Maharashtra, a similar point came for consideration before the Supreme Court of India, reported in 1974 SCC at page 317. In that case under report the petitioner challenged the legality of splitting up of the State cadre of Mamlatdars to the Divisional Cadre but moved the writ petition after 12 years of delay. Bhagawati, J who delivered the judgment for the Supreme Court, in meeting this preliminary point of delay, raised by the State, observed thus:

"We do not think that this contention should prevail with us. In the first place it must, be remembered that the Rule which says that the court may not enquire into belated and stale claims is not a rule of law, but a rule of practice based on the sound and proper exercise of discretion and there is no inviolable rule that wherever there is delay the court must necessarily refuse to entertain the petition. Every case must depend on its own facts,"

147. In that case under report 12 years delay was condoned. In Tilal Chand's case reported in 1969 SCR (India) at page 824 Hidayatullah CJ observed thus:

"This is one of discretion of the case to follow from case to case. There is no lower limit and there is no upper limit. It will depend on the remedy claimed and how the delay arose............ the action of the court cannot harm innocent parties, if their right emerges by reason of delay on the part of the person moving the court."

148. In the instant case the question is whether the petitioner had explained the delay and moved the court in time when his position was actually threatened in the light of decisions as above. It had been stated by the learned Counsel that when Golam Azam left this country in November, 1971 there was no requirement of a passport to travel between East and West. He went to Lahore in November, 1971 when few days thereafter war broke out between India and Pakistan. Pakistan Army thereafter surrendered. Pakistan did not recognize Bangladesh for some time and the petitioner could not get a travel document from Pakistan to come out of that country or to travel to Bangladesh and then repatriation had not started. So out of necessity he had to obtain a Pakistani passport and with that document he went to Saudi Arabia in November, 1972 only for Hajj and thereafter he went to London in April, 1973 when few days thereafter he was disqualified from being a citizen of Bangladesh. He was not able to come back to Bangladesh because of this political rivalry with the party in power. He had fear of his life and therefore was prevented from coming to Bangladesh. During those days, according to him, he would not get any redress even if he would apply. Thereafter there was change of government in 1975 and in the year 1976 he was again faced with a Notification dated 17.l.76 (Annexure-D) issued by the then Government of Bangladesh asking those persons whose citizenship have been previously" cancelled" to apply for it. He applied for it. There was no reply. A reminder (Annexure-D 1) dated 12.l.77 was sent by him from London and he got a reply (Annexure-E) dated 23.4.77 in which his application was not accepted which he received in London. During those days there was Martial Law in the country and also a state of Emergency proclaimed much earlier on 28th of December, 1974 and because of which emergency fundamental rights as in Arts. 27, 31, 32, 33, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39,40 and 42 were suspended by that emergency, proclaimed by President Mohammadullah and this proclamation of emergency continued throughout the successive governments till it was withdrawn by another proclamation on 27th November, 1979.

149. Mr. AR Yusuf also referred to some deliberation made in the Parliament in 1980 where the Foreign Minister told the House that Golam Azam's application had been received and it is under consideration and if he would be refused he would be intimated. In the meantime nobody disturbed him. His name came out in the voters list and he exercised his right of franchise. He was visited by leaders of the country both in power and in opposition and there was no immediate threat or danger to his position and he was hoping that his case will be considered when suddenly he received the impugned notice to show cause as to why he should not be deported and should not be arrested for his illegal stay in this country. Immediately thereafter the petitioner came before this court only when the matter was finally decided against him. Therefore he was not delayed.

150. I have given my anxious consideration to the submissions made by the petitioner's lawyer before this court and find that the petitioner's application did not suffer from any sheer negligence to assert a right no' he was indolent or callous. He was hoping to get it and his right was re-offered by Government again in 1974 after he was disqualified in 1973 when things in Bangladesh was against him and fundamental rights suspended. He applied twice, his matter was in the process of being considered on either way as stated in Parliament Leaders in power met him for his party's support, his name appeared in voters list. He was here for long hoping to get registration when he was served with the deportation notice and immediately he came to the Court. In the process no right had accrued to a third party and if his application is heard no prejudice would be caused to the right of any innocent third party. I agree with BJ Chowdhury J when he held that this petition is not so delayed as to be not maintainable.

151. On the premises above I thus, find the writ to be maintainable and having found on merits that the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth within Article 2 of the Order and also prevented from returning to Bangladesh for some time as under the Proviso to Article 2 of the Citizenship Order, he cannot be treated as a foreigner, he being a citizen of Bangladesh and cannot, therefore, be ordered to show cause as to why he should not be deported from Bangladesh (Annexure-K) and this notice having been issued without lawful authority to a citizen of Bangladesh, is therefore, declared to be illegal and without lawful authority. Consequently, the disqualification notification as issued by the previous Government on 18.4.73 (Annexure-B) is also declared to be bad in law because initially it was ordered in violation of the principle of natural justice against a person who by statutory provision was then a citizen and acting in excess of jurisdiction by travelling beyond Article 2 as it stood on the notification day, thereby rendering the proceeding in passing the notification dated 18.4.73 coram non judice rendering the whole order void ab initio being without jurisdiction.

152. There is a second order (Annexure-K-2).

This matter had not been argued before this court because it is a matter pending in another writ being Writ Petition No. 1148 of 1992 and that being the case this court does not pass any order as to the legality or illegality of the detention of the petitioner under the Foreigners Act

153. I, therefore, having agreed with the judgment delivered by BI Chowdhury, J make the Rule absolute.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and decree dated 5th March, 1989 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Appeal From Original Decree No. 24 of 1985).
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman J: The point involved in this appeal by special leave is, whether the provision of rule 4 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be applied when the non-appealing defendant has not been impleaded in the appeal at all and is not before the Appellate Court.

2. The short fact that will be necessary for disposal of this appeal, is that, plaintiff-respondent No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 491 of 1981 in the Court of 4th Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the defendants-appellants and one Afroza Begum (Defendant No. 2) for specific performance of contract. The suit was ultimately decreed ex parte against all the defendants namely, defendant Nos. 1-7 and defendant Nos. 1-6 were directed to execute and register the sale deed within 60 days in favour of the plaintiff failing which plaintiff will get the same through court.

3. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid ex parte decree, defendant Nos. 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 filed First Appeal No. 24 of 1985 before the High Court Division, Dhaka. Defendant No. 2 Afroza Begum did not file any appeal nor was she impleaded in the appeal as a party respondent by the appealing defendants. Plaintiff took a preliminary objection as to the maintainability of the appeal in the absence of defendant No. 2, when she was not impleaded as a party respondent in the appeal though she was a necessary party in the appeal.

4. The learned Judges of the High Court Division by the impugned order upheld the contention of the plaintiff and held that the appeal was incompetent and not maintainable and in that view rule 4 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure had no application in the First Appeal before the High Court Division.

5. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate appearing for the defendants-appellants, submits that in view of rule 4 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure, one of several defendants may obtain reversal of the whole decree where it proceeds on ground common to all and as such the learned Judges of the High Court Division wrongly held that the appeal was not maintainable without making defendant No. 2 a party-respondent in the appeal. He next contends that Order 41 rule 20 of the Code authorises the appellate Court to add a respondent who was a party in the suit, but who has not been made a party in the appeal and learned Judges ought to have exercised their discretion in this regard.

6. Mr. TH Khan, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, submits that Order 41 rule 4 of the Code has no application in the appeal before the High Court Division as the appeal was incompetent and not maintainable due to non-impleading of a necessary party.

<u>7. Mr. Moinul Huq, learned Advocate appearing as Amicus Curiae submits that the observation of the learned Judges of the High Court Division that rule 4 of Order 41 of the Code, "applies only when the non-appealing plaintiff or defendant is impleaded in the appeal", is not correct. He further submits that what is true for a suit is not true for an appeal and thereby he submits that the impugned order is not a lawful one. In support of his contentions he has cited the case of Joy Kumar Datta and others Vs. Sitanath Dat a reported in 4 DLR 400.</u>

8. From the tenor of arguments of the learned Advocate for the appellants and from the submissions of the learned Amicus Curiae, it appears that they wanted to argue that rule 4 of Order 41 of the Code is an enabling provision by which one of several plaintiffs or defendants to a decree proceeding on a common ground can prefer an appeal and this rule nowhere speaks of adding the non- appealing plaintiffs or defendants as a party respondent in the appeal. According to them, some of the appealing defendants can take the benefit of this enabling provision without bringing the non-appealing defendant on record.

9. On the other hand, Mr. TH Khan, learned Advocate, broadly contends that this provision of Order 41 rule 4 of the Code can be called in aid only when the necessary parties are before the appellate Court and non-impleading of the remaining defendants or any of them when the decree appealed from by some of the defendants is joint and indivisible is fatal to the appeal.

<u>10. At the outset it is to be stated that in the present case the plaintiff got an ex parte decree against defendants 1-6 and the decree was joint and indivisible against all the defendants. Consequently, if any of the non-appealing defendant is not brought on record and not before the appellate Court then there is. a possibility of inconsistent and contradictory decrees regarding the same subject matter under litigation. An appeal can be filed by some of the defendants when it proceeds from a ground common to all the defendants under Order 41 rule 4 of the Code. The language of rule 4 of Order 41 of the Code creates a legal fiction in the sense that the appeal filed by some of the defendants will be treated to be an appeal on behalf of all the defendants and the benefit of the appeal may be extended in favour of the non-appealing defendants by the appellate Court. This legal fiction has been created for the benefit of those who preferred the appeal as well as for those who are not preferring appeal, as because the ground of the decree against all of them is common. Thus the provision of rule 4 of Order 41 only authorises one of the several plaintiffs or defendants to prefer appeal. But the appeal which was incompetent at its inception for omission to implead a necessary party would remain incompetent till the end of it, unless otherwise during the pendency of the appeal necessary parties are brought on record.</u>

<u>11. There is a long line of decisions of this sub-continent that rule 4 of Order 41 of the Code will apply provided the appeal is properly constituted. In the case of Shah Muhammad and others Vs. Muhammad Bakhsh reported in PLD 1972 (SC) 321, Hamoodur Rahman, CJ delivering the judgment observed as follows:</u>

<u>"This is merely an enabling provision which confers a privilege on one of the plaintiffs or defendants to prefer an appeal from a decree which proceeds on any ground common to all the plaintiffs or to all the defendants. It nowhere lays down that any person, who is a necessary party to the appeal, can be excluded and still the appeal will be properly constituted. The provisions of this rule do not also exclude the operation of the provisions of Order XXII of the Code. They would apply only where the provisions of Order XXII pose no difficultly in the prosecution of the appeal. In order to exercise the powers given by this rule, all persons to be affected by the order must be before a Court. It would be totally wrong to hold that an Appellate Court can proceed to hear an appeal, even if the necessary parties are not before it. The provisions of this rule do not, therefore, indicate that any abatement that occurs on the death of one of the appellants can be ignored or overlooked or even set aside. It would be wholly wrong to think that the provisions of rule 4 of Order XLI of the Civil Procedure Code nullify the provisions of rules 3 and 4 of Order XXII, or that they prevent an appeal from abatement if it otherwise stands abated. If we were to read the provisions of rule 4 of Order XLI in the manner in which the learned counsel appearing for the appellants wants us to do, then it would render completely nugatory the other provisions of. the Code relating to abatement of appeals. This could not have been the intention of the framers of the above-mentioned rule. As was rightly pointed out by a Full Bench of the Lahore High Court in the case of Nanak Vs. Ahmad AIi, the provisions of rule 4 of Order XLI of the Code cannot be applied where the non-appealing plaintiff or defendant, as the case may be, has not been impleaded in the appeal at all and is not before the appellate Court."</u>

<u>12. As on fact we have already found that the plaintiffs suit was a suit for specific performance of contract against all the defendants wherein the decree appealed from was joint and indivisible. In the case of Mst. Murad Begum etc. Vs. Muhammad Rafiq etc. reported in PLD 1974 (SC) 322, which was a case of specific performance of contract, the plaintiffs got ex parte decree against 16 defendants and the regular First Appeal before the High Court was filed only by 7 defendants out of 16 defendants, impleading 5 defendants as respondents and leaving out 4 defendants altogether and the Supreme Court held that the appeal being not properly constituted must be dismissed on that score. In that decision the Supreme Court held as follows:</u>

<u>"Once it is found that the decree appealed from by some of the defendants was joint and indivisible against all the defendants, then it follows that their failure to implead the remaining defendants, or any of them, would render the appeal incompetent. The principle underlying this rule is that otherwise inconsistent and contradictory decrees would come into existence regarding the same subject-matter and as a result of the same litigation. This principle has been reiterated by the superior Courts on several occasions."</u>

<u>13. In the case of Nanak Vs. Ahmad Ali reported in AIR 1946 Lahore 399 (Full Bench), while interpreting Order 41 rule 4, the learned Judges observed as follows:</u>

<u>"Mr. Asa Ram Aggarwal, the learned counsel for the appellant, had to concede that according to the view consistently taken in this Court rule 4 of Order 41 cannot be applied where the non-appealing plaintiff or defendant, as the case may be, has not been impleaded in the appeal at all and is not before the appellate Court."</u>

14. Thus, the learned Judges of the High Court Division were perfectly correct in holding that the appeal before the High Court Division was incompetent and not maintainable in law. From the judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the preliminary objection was taken by the plaintiff as to the maintainability of the appeal and the learned Advocate for the appellant failed to furnish any substantial argument against this objection and referred to Order 41 rule 4 of the Code in support of the maintainability of the appeal.

<u>15. In disposing of this appeal, we may point out that admittedly defendant No. 2 was a necessary party in the appeal before the High Court Division and his addition as a party after the period of limitation could have been cured provided the appellants would have prayed for the same. It is found from the record that the appeal was filed on 6.2.1985 and the matter was taken up for final hearing on 5.3.89 and even at this stage no application was filed for adding defendant No. 2 as party respondent by the appellants. Necessary party having been omitted, the appellate Court could have exercised its discretion vested in it under Order 41 rule 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but the same cannot be done suo motu by the Court itself without any application by the appealing defendants themselves. In the case of Muhammad Jamil Vs.The Chairman, Industrial Court, West Pakistan and another reported in PLD 1964 (SC) 559, Fazle Akbar J observed as follows :</u>

<u>"Mr. Zairian has prayed for condonation of delay. No doubt under Order XLI, rule 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court has power in a proper case to allow a necessary party to be added as respondent, but the power to take the action is discretionary and should not be exercised in case of extreme neglect. On 13th February, 1963, the Court enquired suo motu why the employer was not added as a party in this case and the appellant thereafter on 19th February, 1963, filed a petition for adding the employer as a respondent in the appeal. He, however, even then did not file any petition for condonation of the delay. In the petition he merely stated that through inadvertence he did not implead the employer as a party. The employer has acquired a valuable right which we do not think should be taken away from him in the circumstances of the present case. The preliminary objection therefore ought to prevail."</u>

16. Thus, the second point of Mr. Fazlul Karim cannot be accepted when there is nothing on record to show that at any point of time any application was filed before the High Court Division during the pendency of the appeal for four years for addition of defendant No. 2 as a party respondent.

<u>17. Before parting with the case it may be mentioned that the point involved in this appeal being so elementary and fundamental, the assistance which was expected from Mr. Moinul Huq appearing as Amicus Curiae was not sufficient. Since Mr. Moinul Huq has cited 4 DLR case, we need to speak a word in this regard. The 4 DLR case was primarily a case relating to adoption under Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law. From the concluding portion of the reported decision it appears that an argument was made by the appellants that the appeals were not maintainable inasmuch as all the defendants were not made parties. In reply, the learned Advocate for the respondents contended that rule 4 Order 41 of the Code speaks of filing of appeal by defendants on behalf of all the defendants. In the context of that case, the reference of rule 4 Order 41 of the Code in that case by the learned Judges is nothing but an orbiter Further, this decision was placed before Mr. Fazle Akbar, J. himself in a subsequent case of Iman Ali Halsana and others Vs. Furkun Ali Mondal and others reported in PLD 1960 (Dacca) 3 = 11 DLR 347. In that case a preliminary objection was taken that appellant No. I having died during the pendency of the second appeal, and no steps having been taken for substitution of his legal representative the appeal abated. In that case the learned Advocate for the appellant tried to overcome this difficulty by seeking aid of Order 41 rule 4 of the Code, wherein Fazle Akbar, J. observed keeping in view of the 4 DLR case as follows:</u>

<u>"If, at this stage, by exercising power under Order XLI, rule 4, we reverse the entire decree, we shall be trenching upon other provisions of the Code. We think that Order XLI rule 4, should not be applied to enable the litigants to ignore the other provisions of the Code. We, therefore, respectfully agree with the observations of the Full Bench of the Patna and Lahore High Courts that Order XLI rule 4, cannot override or create exceptions to Order XXII rules 3 and 11. Furthermore, in our opinion, sub-rule (4) of rule 4 of Order XXII does not help the appellants in this case. In these circumstances, we hold that the provisions of Order XLI rule 4 cannot be applied to this case."</u>

18. Thus, we have no hesitation to hold that the observation of the 4 DLR case on which Mr. Moinul Huq relied is just an obiter and not a judicial dictum. Mr. Moinul Huq's submission that what is true for a suit is not true of an appeal is difficult to understand, simply because if a suit or appeal is imperfectly constituted, it is obvious that it must be dismissed.

19. For the reasons stated above, the application filed by defendant No. 2, Afroza Begum before this Court for addition as party is rejected. Consequently, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

A TM Afzal J: I have ultimately decided to fall in line with the majority opinion that the appeal be dismissed but that is not to say that I have found the judgment of the High Court Division to be wholly satisfactory. I shall explain why.

21. Facts of the case, briefly, arc that respondent No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 491 of 1981 in the 4th Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the appellants, who are defendant Nos. 1 and 3-6, Afroza Begum (defendant No. 2) and the Government (defendant No. 7) for specific performance of contract for sale of the Suitland. The plaintiff alleged that defendant Nos. 1-6 as heirs of late Md. Hossain Bhuiyan inherited lands at Savar and they executed a bainapatra on 8.12.79 for sale of some lands out of 5 bighas situated at Nayabarimouza at Savar. It was, however, found that the said Md. Hossain had no interest in the said land but he had some other land at Mohammadpur for which two sale deeds were executed on 7.5.80. The appellants arc executants of the said sale deeds but defendant No. 2, Afroza Begum did not execute the same. However, the defendants subsequently changed their mind and the plaintiff preferred appeal before the District Registrar for registering of the said two sale deeds. The District Registrar having found that the sale deeds had not been proved refused to register the same under the Registration Act on 27.2.81 whereupon the plaintiff filed the present suit.

22. The suit was decreed ex parte on 1.10.84 and defendant Nos. 1-6 were directed to execute and register a deed of sale in favour of the plaintiff.

23. The appellants being aggrieved by the said ex parte decree preferred First Appeal No. 24 of 1985 in the High Court Division, Dhaka.

24. It has been stated by the appellants in the leave petition that through inadvertence defendant No. 2 Afroza Begum was not made a party in the said First Appeal. At the hearing of the appeal a preliminary objection was raised on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent that the appeal was incompetent and as such not maintainable inasmuch as defendant No. 2 Afroza Begum neither filed any appeal nor she was impleaded as respondent by the appellants. The learned Judges of the High Court Division upon considering the provisions of Order XLI rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure found that "the defendant No. 2, Afroza Begum having not been impleaded in the appeal the rule does not apply in the present appeal. That being the position the appeal is incompetent and as such not maintainable". Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed.

25. It will be seen that the High Court Division found the appeal to be not maintainable merely because the provisions of Order XLI rule 4 CPC was inapplicable in the absence of defendant No. 2 Afroza Begum. Was it a sufficient finding for dismissing the appeal ? That is the question at issue.

26. Order XLI rule 4 CPC reads as follows:

4. "Where there are more plaintiffs or more defendants than one in a suit, and the decree appealed from proceeds on any ground common to all the plaintiffs or to all the defendants, any one of the plaintiffs or of the defendants may appeal from the whole decree, and thereupon the Appellate Court may reverse or vary the decree in favour of all the plaintiffs or defendants, as the case may be.

27. This rule does not say anything about maintainability or non-maintainability of an appeal. It has really two parts. The first part says that where there are more plaintiffs or more defendants than one in a suit, and the decree appealed from proceeds on any ground common to all the plaintiffs or to all the defendants, anyone of the plaintiffs or of the defendants may appeal from the whole decree. This is an enabling provision so far as the parties are concerned. The other part which is also an enabling provision is in respect of the Appellate Court. It says that in the case of an appeal as aforesaid the appellate Court may reverse or vary the decree in favour of all the plaintiffs or defendants, as the case may be. It is, therefore, clear that it cannot be said only with reference to the provision of rule 4, as the High Court Division has done in the present case, that an appeal in the absence of a non-appealing plaintiff or defendant has become non-maintainable. In order to reach the conclusion that the appeal has become non-maintainable it was necessary to find something further, such as, that the party which was left out was a necessary party or that the decree was indivisible for which the appeal could not be proceeded with, over and above finding that rule 4 does not apply when the non-appealing plaintiff or defendant is not impleaded in the appeal. It is one thing to say that rule 4 does not apply and it is quite different to hold that the appeal has become non-maintainable. To illustrate the point the Full Bench case of the Lahore High Court, Nanak Vs. Ahmed Ali AIR (33) 1946 Lahore 399 which has been followed in many subsequent cases and referred to by my learned brother Latifur Rahman, J may be noticed. In that case one Ahmed Ali brought a suit for the cancellation of a sale deed executed by one Gumani, defendant No. 1, in favour of Nanak and Khair-ud-Dm, defendants 2 and 3. The suit was decreed by the First Appellate Court and against the said decree both defendants 2 and 3 filed a second appeal in the High Court. During the pendency of the appeal Nanak died but his legal representatives were not brought on record in time. It was contended by the plaintiff-respondent that the appeal had abated not only against Nanak but it would be deemed to have abated as a whole inasmuch as there was a joint decree against Nanak and Khair-ud-Din, The question was whether the abatement of the appeal in respect of Nanak would result in the total dismissal of the appeal or whether the appeal of Khair-uddin could still be-prcceeded with. On behalf of the appellant Khair-ud-Din the enabling provision of rule 4 of Order XLI CPC was invoked for the contention that the appellant should still be permitted to continue the appeal against the decree in its entirety inasmuch as the appeal proceeded on a ground common to himself and Nanak. It was found that there was a wide divergence of judicial opinion on the question as to whether rule 4 should apply in such a case. This gave rise to the reference to the Full Bench.

28. The Full Bench after hearing the learned counsel for the parties came to the conclusion that even apart from Order XLI rule 4 CPC the abatement of Nanak's appeal does not make Khair-ud-Din's appeal incompetent and that the latter's appeal can still proceed. It was, however, observed that the learned counsel for the appellant conceded in keeping with the consistent view of that court that rule 4 of Order XLI could not be applied where the non-appealing plaintiff or defendant, as the case may be, had not been impleaded in the appeal at all and is not before the Appellate Court.

29. This legal position is now well-settled and it is also well-established that the provision of this rule does not exclude the operation of the provision of Order XXII of the Code. Hamoodur Rahman CJ in the case of Shah Mohammad Vs. Mohammad Baksh PLD 1972 (SC) 321 (also referred to in the judgment of Latifur Rahman J) in interpreting rule 4, inter alia, observed that it nowhere lays down that any person, who is a necessary party to the appeal, can be excluded and still the appeal will be properly constituted. In order to exercise the powers given by this rule all persons to be affected by the order must be before the Court, it was observed. It would be totally wrong to hold, the learned Chief Justice further said, that the appellate Court can proceed to hear an appeal even if the necessary parties are not before it.

30. In that case one of the defendant appellants died during the pendency of the first appeal and another during the pendency of the second appeal in the High Court and the legal representatives of the deceased appellants were not brought on record. The appeal was declared to have abated as a whole at both the stages because it was found that the 25 defendants (appellants) in the suit were in joint possession of the house, each one of them was a necessary party, and the death of one of them would result in the appeal being not properly constituted.

31. Leave was granted in that case to consider whether the provisions of rule 4 of Order XLI CPC should have been applied in the case and the right to prosecute the appeal held to have survived to the remaining appellants after the death of anyone of them. The Supreme Court found that the provisions of rule 4 of order XLI do not nullify the provisions of rules 3 and 4 of Order XXII and they do not prevent an appeal from abatement if it otherwise stands abated. Rule 4 was found to be inapplicable in the facts of that case but then in order to determine the question of the abatement of the appeal as a whole it was considered further whether the decree was indivisible or not. Upon examining the pleadings in the case it was found that the decree was indivisible and each one of the appellants was a necessary party to the appeal and in the absence of anyone of them the decree could not be varied or altered. The death of one such party without substitution of his heirs was, therefore, the Supreme Court found "rightly held to have resulted in the total abatement of the appeal."

<u>32. The facts of the case reported in PLD 1974 (SC) 322 also cited in the judgment of my learned brother Latifur Rahman J, are that Qazi Mehr Din, the predecessor-in-interest of the respondents entered into a contract with Sh. Mehr Din., the predecessor-in-interest .of the appellants, for selling his agricultural land measuring 893 bighas on 15th March 1926 and possession of the land was delivered to Sh. Mehr Din on the same date. On 14th March 1938 Qazi Mehr Din filed a suit for possession of the disputed land against the vendee Sh. Mehr Din and fifteen others alleging that the vendee had failed to pay the balance of the sale price as stipulated. This suit was decreed on 30th December, 1943 by the District Judge of Rahim Yar Khan, the decree was ex parte against defendant Nos. 5 to 16. Then there is a chequered history which is not necessary and ultimately the appeal by some of the defendants against the said decree fell to be considered by the High Court Division of West Pakistan (Baghdadul Jadid). The High Court dismissed the appeal for the reason that the legal representatives of certain defendants who were necessary parties had not been brought on the record by the appellants with the result that the appeal against them had abated and that it could' not proceed in respect of the other defendants as the interests of all the defendants in the suit were joint and indivisible and inconsistent decrees in respect of the same subject matter were likely to come into existence if the appeal was to be allowed in part. The Supreme Court upheld this view taken by the High Court and observed that once it is found that the decree appealed from by some of the defendants was joint and indivisible against all the defendants, then it follows that their failure to implead the remaining defendants, or any of them would render the appeal incompetent. The principle underlying this rule is that otherwise inconsistent and contradictory decrees would come into existence regarding the same subject matter and as a result of the same litigation.</u>

<u>33. From the decisions referred to above it follows that in order to hold that an appeal has become non-maintainable in the absence of a non-appealing plaintiff or defendant, as the case may be, it is necessary to give further reason than merely saying that rule 4 does not apply. This the High Court Division has not done in the present case. Mr. Moinul Huq, learned advocate, appearing as amicus curiae in this appeal, has, therefore, submitted, I think rightly, that the High Court Division was not justified in holding that the appeal was incompetent and not maintainable merely upon finding that defendant No. 2, Afroza Begum, having not been impleaded in the appeal, rule 4 does not apply without saying anything further as to why the appeal cannot proceed even in spite of rule 4.</u>

<u>34. Mr. TH Khan, learned Advocate for respondent No. 1, has submitted that having regard to the frame of the suit, nature of the reliefs claimed and nature of the relief awarded by the decree appealed from, defendant No. 2 was a necessary and essential party in the appeal and without her the appeal was imperfectly constituted and as such not maintainable. He further submitted that the plaintiff obtained a joint decree for specific performance of contract against all the defendant Nos. 1-6, and defendant No. 2 having not been brought on record and she having not filed any appeal there was possibility of two inconsistent and conflicting decrees if the appeal was to proceed in her absence and as such the appeal became non-maintainable. Undoubtedly these are cogent grounds for which the appeal may be held to be not maintainable. But none of these grounds and their validity is found to have been considered by the High Court Division in its cryptic judgment. It is possible to argue in both ways in the facts of a given case (and why not in this case also) that in the absence of a non-appealing plaintiff or defendant an appeal has or has not abated or become non-maintainable as a whole and it is for the Court to decide one way or the other. The High Court Division has not done this exercise at all before finding that the appeal was not maintainable.</u>

<u>35. That an appeal does not become necessarily incompetent in the absence of a non-appealing plaintiff or defendant will be clear from the decision of this Court in the case of Hupen Majhi Vs. Munshi A Khair 32 DLR (AD) 96 in which it has been observed "it is to be remembered that on the death of a non-substituted appellant, the appeal against him abates and it is to be taken that he has not appealed. But under rule 4 the other defendant-appellants are entitled to make an appeal and carry it to conclusion. Therefore, the defendant-appellants who were not dead could carry the appeal to its conclusion, and since no question of two conflicting decrees coming into existence arises, this is a fit case where provisions of rules 4 and 33 of Order 41 of the Code will apply."</u>

36. Further, even if it was found that defendant No. 2 was a necessary party who was not impleaded as respondent, the court could yet consider, Mr. Moinul Huq, I think again rightly submitted, whether it would exercise its power under rule 20 of Order XLI. Rule 20 is in the following terms;

"20. where it appears to the Court at the hearing that any person who was a party to the suit in the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, but who has not been made a party to the appeal, is interested in the result of the appeal the Court may adjourn the hearing to a future day to be fixed by the Court and direct that such person be made a respondent."

<u>37. In this connection Mr. Moinul Huq has particularly referred to the decision reported in 17 DLR, Dhaka 643 in the case of Mohendra Nath Vs. Susila and submitted that the High Court Division should or, at any rate, could have followed the course taken in that case. It is interesting to note that in that case which was also a first appeal, two of the defendants were not impleaded as respondents in the said appeal and the objection was taken by no one else than Mr. Moinul Huq himself that the appeal became incompetent for not impleading the necessary parties to it. In that case the appeal was filed in 1959 and the objection was raised at the hearing of the appeal in 1965. The question of limitation was therefore involved in adding the two defendants against whom the appeal would be directed (unlike in the present case). The Division Bench upon considering the provisions of Order 1 rule 10 and Order XLI rule 20 CPC and various decisions directed that the said defendants be impleaded as respondents in the appeal. Murshed, CJ observed in that decision "that the provisions of Order XLI rule 20 are directed to serve the interest of justice. The primary requirement is that of dispensation of justice. It enables the Court, in appropriate circumstances, to add parties to a proceeding so that full justice may be done. We ourselves feel no difficulty in construing the language of Order 41 rule 20, to mean that if a Court considers it to be necessary it has ample powers to add to an appeal persons who were originally parties to the suit if such a course is the requirement of justice."</u>

<u>38. Mr. Moinul Huq has cited some other decisions 12 DLR 745 and 16 DLR (SC) 386 in support of his submission that under rule 20, the Court has power in a proper case to allow a necessary party to be added as a respondent. As to the power of the Court to add a necessary party whether at the stage of the suit or at the stage of the appeal subject to law there can hardly be any doubt and the power can be exercised suo mote. The matter is, however, in the discretion of the Court. In the present case it does not appear that the High Court Division gave any attention to rule 20 before dismissing the appeal. It may be observed that the special facts in the case as could be considered were that the appeal was against an ex parte decree, that under Order IX rule 13 CPC the decree could be set aside against all the defendants even though only one defendant had applied under the said rule and that defendant No.2 Afroza Begum was admittedly not an executant of the two sale deeds which having been refused registration by the District Registrar, the plaintiff brought the suit.</u>

It has been stated in the leave petition that an application for addition of Afroza Begum (defendant No. 2) as a party respondent was filed in the Court on the day, the appeal was dismissed i.e. the 5th March, 1989 but the said application was refused by the High Court Division. This has been reiterated in the concise statement of the appellants. Respondent No.1 has, however, denied that any such application was filed till the dismissal order was passed on 5.3.89. We have been shown a sworn petition for addition of Afroza Begum in the first appeal bearing the date 5th March 1989. However, I am not prepared to believe that the said application was filed in the Court before the dismissal order was passed and even then the Court did not take notice of the same; rather it will appear that wisdom dawned on the appellants after the damage was done. Even so, one feels in retrospect that had the attention of the High Court Division been drawn to Order XLI rule 20 the matter perhaps would not have come to such a pass and the appeal could be spared a technical knockout.

End.

Dhunat Degree College &ors ----- Petitioners
