full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J: This Rule arises out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against the judgment and decree dated 23-3-95 passed by the District Judge, Bogra allowing the appeal in part by reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-6-94 passed by the Subordinate Judge Court No.1, Bogra in Other Class Suit No. 155 of 1990 dismissing the suit.

2. The plaintiff opposite party No.1 was the Principal of Dhunat Degree College. On 10-7-90 the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 155 of 1990 against the petitioner and others in the court of Subordinate Judge, Bogra praying for a decree for declaration to the effect that the resolutions adopted by the Governing Body of Dhunat Degree College on 1-7-1990 and the memo No. 17-1-90-536(6) dated 1-7-90 issued by defendant No. 2 be declared unlawful, fraudulent, without jurisdiction, null and viod, violative of principle of natural justice and not binding upon the plaintiff with a further prayer that the post of the plaintiff as principal of the college be declared in order and valid and has in no way been ineffective nor jeopardised.

3. The short facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 joined at Dhunat College as a Principal on 14-7-1984. In course of time enmity ensued between the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 10 and 13. The defendant No. 13 is the lecturer of the said college. In the discharge of official duty the plaintiff as principal had to take steps against the defendant No. 13 who was one of the invigilators during the period of SSC examination in 1986 and as such the defendant No. 13 developed an enmity with the plaintiff. There was conspiracy for assaulting and insulting the plaintiff and defendant No. 13 took active role in that conspiracy and to get rid of him the defendant No. 13 along with others filed an application leveling certain allegations against the plaintiff to the Deputy Commissioner, Bogra who got it enquired by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (General) Bogra and the said report was considered by the Governing Body of the College in a meeting held on 1-7-90 and after considering that report they adopted a resolution in pursuance of which the impugned Memo dated 1-7-90 was issued against the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 suspending him from the post of principal without initiating any departmental proceeding against him and as such, the plaintiff had no other alternative but to file instant suit for above mentioned declarations on the ground that the impugned memo communicated to him is violative of law inasmuch as the plaintiff was not given any opportunity of being heard before passing the said impugned memo.

4. The defendant Nos. 1-3 and 7-14 entered their appearance and contested the suit by filing a written statement. They denied the material allegations of the plaint and also contended that the past performance of the plaintiff was not good. He resorted to some unfair means in appointing lecturers of the college. There were other specific allegations too against him. He misappropriated huge amount of money from the college fund. In view of series of allegations against the plaintiff an inquiry was held by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (General) Bogra. The inquiry report was placed before the Governing Body for consideration and taking necessary decision and in a meeting the Governing Body of the college held on 1-7-90, the Governing Body considered the said report submitted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (General), Bogra and resolved that a criminal case be started against the principal and he be placed on suspension immediately and a committee be constituted for taking disciplinary action against the principal and part of that decision was communicated to the plaintiff vide impugned memo dated 1-7-90. They further contended that the instant suit suffers from want of cause of action and as such, the suit is not maintainable.

5. At the trial plaintiff examined 3 witnesses in support of his case and defendant examined 2 witnesses in support of their case. The trial Court after considering the materials and evidence on record before it dismissed the suit holding that the suit is premature one inasmuch as the suspension order is a temporary order. The plaintiff opposite party No. 1 being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree of the trial Court preferred an appeal before the District. Judge, Bogra which was registered as Other Class Appeal No. 164 of 1993 and the District Judge after hearing both the parties allowed the appeal in part after setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and decreed the suit in part and declared the impugned memo dated 1-7-90 issued under the signature of defendant No. 2 as illegal. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree of the appellate Court the defendant petitioners preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr. Mozaffar Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioners, submits that the trial Court dismissed the suit as not maintainable on the ground of pre-maturity and absence of cause of action as no penal action was taken by the Governing Body in suspending the plaintiff opposite party but the learned District Judge without discarding such a plea set aside the judgment and decree without reasons and as such, the judgment of reversal passed by the learned District. Judge cannot be sustained in law. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned District. Judge also committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the decree in part declaring the impugad memo as to be illegal while observing that the Governing Body committed no illegality in taking the resolution dated 1-7-90. He also submits that the impugned order of suspension pending enquiry cannot be challenged as it does not give rise to any cause of action and the suit being hit by provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as no consequential prayer was made and the court below failed to give any finding although issues on these points were framed. The learned Advocate finally submits that the impugned resolution and the memo are free from procedural defect as it provides provision for formation of enquiry committee for enquiry and taking action.

7. Mr. MA Aziz, the learned Advocate, appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 submits that a teacher can only be placed under suspension pending enquiry but in the instant case no disciplinary action has been initiated and as such the impugned memo is violative of rule 16 (1) (a) of the College Teachers (University of Rajshahi) Terms and Conditions of Service, 1980. When Mr. Aziz was confronted with Ext. Cha (8) he found it difficult to support the impugned judgment.

8. On perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the learned District Judge allowed the appeal and decreed the suit in part on the ground that the impugned memo dated 1-7-90 is violative of rule 16 (1) (a) of the College Teachers (University of Rajshahi) Terms and Conditions of Service, 1980. It further appears from the impugned Judgment that the learned appellate Court below found that the enquiry held by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (General) Bogra in connection with the allegations leveled against the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is administrative inquiry and as such, it was not necessary that he should be given an opportunity of being heard and that inquiry held by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (General) is valid and legal. It further appears that the learned appellate Court below also found that the resolution dated 1-7-90 adopted by the Governing Body of the defendant No. 1 college is valid and legal. The learned appellate Court below further found that the impugned memo is defective on the ground of procedural defects but he struck down the order of suspension which was communicated to the plaintiff opposite party No.1 vide Ext. 4 the impugned memo dated 1-7-90, on the ground that it contravenes the provision of section 16(1)(a) of the rule.

9. On perusal of the plaint it appears that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 filed the aforesaid suit challenging the validity and legality of the resolution dated 1-7-90 passed by the Governing Body in their meeting held on the aforesaid date as well as the memo dated 1-7-90 communicated to him under the signature of the President of the Governing Body. It appears that the learned District Judge, in our opinion, rightly found that the resolution adopted by the Governing Body in their meeting held on 1-7-90 is legal and valid and if that be so the subsequent observations made by the learned District Judge that the impugned memo Exhibit 4 dated 1-7-90 is violative of the rule 16(1) (a) is self contradictory. But the impugned memo Exhibit 4 simply a part of the decision of the resolution dated 1-7-90 was communicated to the plaintiff opposite party No.1 by the President of the Governing Body of the college. It is found by the appellate Court that the resolution adopted by the Governing Body in their meeting held on 1-7-90 is within their jurisdiction and the same is legal and valid. If that be so then the impugned memo dated. 1-7-90 cannot be struck down on any ground whatsoever and here the appellate Court below fell into an error. The appellate Court struck down the impugned memo dated 1-7-90 on the ground that it does not indicate that any charges have been framed against the appellant nor does it indicate that the Governing Body is going to frame any charges. The said observation of the appellate Court below is not tenable in law in view of the fact that in making such an observation the appellate Court below completely lost sight of Exhibit cha (8) the resolution dated 1-7-90, adopted by the Governing Body in their meeting held on that date whereas it has been resolved by the Governing Body that the plaintiff be placed on suspension immediately and a criminal case be instituted against him. It was also resolved by the Governing Body that a disciplinary action may be started against him by setting up an appropriate committee under section 16(1)(a) of the rule. It is submitted by Mr. Mozaffar Hossain, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioner, that they could not complete the departmental proceeding in the matter because of an order of injunction granted by the trial Court, Be that as it may, it is crystal clear from the resolution dated 1-7-90 that it does not suffer from any illegality whatsoever inasmuch as it complied with the requirements of rule 16(1)(a) of "The College Teachers (University of Rajshahi) Terms and Condition of Service, 1980. The relevant portion of the resolution runs as follows:

গভর্নিং বডির অন্যতম সদস্য জনাব আলতাব হোসেন বলেন অধ্যক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে উল্লেখিত প্রতিবেদনের বিষয়বস্তু ছাড়া আরও বহু সুনির্দিষ্ট প্রমাণাদি থাকার কারণে এ ধরণের অযোগ্য দুর্নীতিপরায়ন, স্বেচ্ছাচারি অধ্যক্ষকে কলেজের প্রধান হিসাবে রাখার কোন যৌক্তিকতা নাই। তিনি অধ্যক্ষকে কলেজের প্রধান হিসাবে রাখার কোন যৌক্তিকতা নাই। তিনি অধ্যক্ষকে সাময়িকভাবে বরখাস্তকরণ সহ তার অধ্যক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে অতিরিক্ত জেলা প্রশাসক (সার্বিক) সাহেবের তদন্ত প্রতিবেদনের উপর ভিত্তি করে একটি ফৌজদারী মামলা দায়েরও বিভাগীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণের প্রস্তাব করেন। জনাব শাহজাহান আলী তালুকদার মাননীয় সংসদ সদস্য ছাড়া উপস্থিত সকল সদস্য বৃন্দ প্রস্তাবটি সর্ব সম্মতি ক্রমে গৃহীত হয়। তদানুসারে অবিলম্বে, একটি তদন্ত কমিটি গঠন সহ প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণের জন্য গভর্নিং বডির সভাপতি ও উপজেলা নির্বাহী অফিসারকে অনুরোধ করা হয়।”

In that view of the matter it appears to us that non-consideration of Exhibit cha (8) by the appellate Court below vitiated the impugned judgment which cannot be sustained in law.

<u>10. Here it may be mentioned that suspension as a prelude to disciplinary action is not a punishment and such kind of suspension does not give rise to a cause of action. There are various judicial decisions of this sub-continent on the question as to whether an interim order for temporary suspension of a person in any office is a penal action by itself and it has been consistently held in the negative. No judicial decision is available in support of the proposition that an interim administrative order for temporary suspension in any office required any prior show cause notice, particularly when such order is followed by a quasi judicial proceeding when the aggrieved person is unable to defend oneself before any final penal action is taken. So far the instant case is concerned we are of the view that vide impugned memo the plaintiff has been placed on suspension pending disciplinary action and the action taken is covered by Rule 16(1) (a) and (c) of the College Teachers (University of Rajshahi) Terms and Conditions of Service, 1980 and the same is only an interim order for a temporary period and the same is also in the nature of an administrative action for urgent preventive purpose to be followed by a regular proceeding by a three-member committee acting in a quasi-judicial manner under rule 16(1)(a) of the College Teachers (University of Rajshahi) Terms and Conditions of Service, 1980. It is, therefore, crystal clear that in the instant case the principle of natural justice is not attracted and the finding of the appellate Court below that the order is violative of rule 16(1)(a) of the Rules is absolutely erroneous and contrary to materials on record.</u>

<u>In that view of the matter also the instant suit suffers for want of cause of action but this vital legal aspect of the case was sorely missed by both the courts below though the trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground of prematurity but failed to notice this aspect of the case.</u>

<u>11. Mr. Mozaffar Hossain, the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioner, also submitted that the instant suit was not maintainable inasmuch as it was a suit for simple declaration that the resolution adopted by the Governing Body as well as the impugned memo dated 1-7-90 were unlawful, inoperative, fraudulent, without jurisdiction, violative of the principle of natural justice and not binding upon the plaintiff without any consequential prayer and in support of his contention he relied on the decision reported in 35 DLR 224 and 15 BLD 249. Mr. Abdul Aziz the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 did not dispute this proposition of law. Nevertheless, we would like to discuss this point as there are conflicting decisions in the High Court Division on this point. After the 35 DLR case there is another decision reported in 8 BLD 403, wherein another Single Bench following the decision of 35 DLR 224, held that in service matter a suit for simple declaration without asking for consequential relief for enforcing the declaratory decree is not maintainable. Similarly, in another case reported in 15 BLD 249, another Single Bench of this court held that a suit for declaration simpliciter without a prayer for consequential relief is not maintainable. But in the case of Fuzlul Karim vs. Agrani Bank reported in 11 BLD 528, a Division Bench of this court dissented from 35 DLR 224 and held that a suit for mere declaration without any prayer for consequential relief is maintainable. In arriving at such a finding the Division Bench considered the following cases namely, the case of High Commissioner for India and another vs. IM Lall, AIR 1948 (PC) 121=52 CWN (PC) 761=PLD 1948 (PC) 150, Yousuf Ali Khan vs. The Province of the Punjab PLD 1948 Lahore, 219, Habib Khan vs. Federation of Pakistan, PLD 1954 Sind, 199, Province of East Pakistan vs. Zaharul Huq 7 DLR 446, Province of East Pakistan vs. Mr. Golam Sarwar, 13 DLR 341 and Province of East Pakistan vs. Abdul Latif Talukder and another, 22 DLR 889. It appears that the aforesaid cases were not cited from the Bar in the 35 DLR Case. In the 8 BLD Case the Single Bench considered the 13 DLR and 22 DLR cases but did not follow them and followed the 35 DLR case as the said decision was affirmed by the Appellate Division in the CPSLA No. 229 of 1983 wherein their Lordships dismissed the Leave petition observing as follows:</u>

<u>"Since the plaintiffs' prayer for declaration was not followed by any consequential relief the learned Judge committed no illegality in holding that the omission to pray for any consequential relief for the purpose of enforcing declaratory decree was hit by the proviso to section 12 of the Specific Relief Act."</u>

12. The legal position is that law declared by the Appellate Division is binding on all courts including the High Court Division. The Division Bench failed to notice the fact that the 35 DLR case was affirmed by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in CPSLA No. 229 of 1983.

13. It thus appears that in differing with the decision of the Single Bench the Division Bench lost sight of the fact that 35 DLR 8 case was taken before the Appellate Division and their Lordships have upheld that decision observing that in the facts and circumstances of the case it was hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. So, the law has been settled once and for all by the Appellate Division that in service matter a suit for simple declaration without any prayer for consequential relief is not maintainable as it is hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and in that view of the matter we are of the opinion that the decision reported in 11 BLD 528 so far it relates to the proposition of law that a simple declaratory suit in a service matter is maintainable without any prayer for consequential relief is decided in per curium and as such, that decision cannot be considered as a binding precedent nor could it be treated as good law inasmuch as the view taken by the Division Bench in 11 BLD conflicts with the proposition of law as laid down by the Appellate Division in CPSLA No. 299 of 1983.

14. On a perusal of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial Court we notice that both the courts below sorely missed the point that the instant suit suffers from gross illegality in as much as it was hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In that view of the matter we find sufficient force in the submission of Mr. Mozaffar Hossain that the suit is not maintainable as framed and is hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

15. It is now well settled that suspension as a prelude to the disciplinary action is not a punishment and as such, it does not give rise to any cause of action and in the instant suit from Exhibit cha (8) it is crystal clear that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been placed under suspension in pursuance of resolution dated 1-7-90 wherein it has been resolved by the Governing Body that they would constitute an appropriate committee for taking disciplinary action against the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in view of the allegations leveled against him and in that view of the matter we hold that the instant suit suffers from want of cause of action but unfortunately, both the courts below sorely missed this point.

16. In view of the aforesaid discussions, we find substance in this revisional application. In the result the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 23-3-95 passed by the District Judge, Bogra in Other Class Appeal No. 167 of 1994 are set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge Court, No.1, Bogra in Other Class Suit No. 155 of 1990 are hereby restored on the grounds stated above and the suit is accordingly dismissed.

In view of the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 1.4.84 passed by the High Court Division. Chittagong Bench, in Civil Revision No. 332 (R) of 1982).
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ: In this appeal by special leave the question is whether the "doctrine" barring partial pre-emption stands in the way of the respondent-pre-emptor's way of getting pre-emption of four out of five holdings, transferred under the same kabala although he is a co-sharer in all the five holdings and as such is entitled to pre-empt them all.

2. This arises from Misc. Case No. 159 of 1965 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Satkania. It was filed by the pre-emptor-respondent claiming pre-emption of 4 out of 5 schedules of land transferred to the appellants under a registered kabala dated 30 September 1965 by his co-sharer, respondent No. 2. Objection was raised by the pre-emptees (appellants) on the ground that one of the lands, namely schedule III, was not sought to be pre-empted and as such the application for pre-emption was hit by the rule as to bar of partial pre-emption. Pre-emptor first claimed that 'Schedule-III' land was entirely his own and the Vendor had no title and interest therein, and as such, he was not required to pre-empt his own land. This claim of the pre-emptor was accepted by the Trial Court and the pre-emption prayed for in respect of the 4 schedules of land was allowed. The appellate Court, however, disagreed with the finding that the pre-emptee's vendor had no title in the schedule-III land but found that both the Vendor and the Pre-emptor were co-sharers in Schedule-III land and as this land was omitted in the application for pre-emption, the pre-emptor's application for pre-emption was hit by the rule as to bar of partial pre-emption; on this finding the appellate Court reversed the trial Court's decision and dismissed the application for pre-emption.

3. Pre-emptor challenged this decision in revision-CR No. 339 of 1983. In revision the pre-emptor did not challenge the appellate Court's finding that both he and the vendor were co-sharers in Schedule-III land, but accepted this finding as correct. He, however, took a new ground to justify the claim of pre-emption, and the learned Single Judge accepted the new ground. The learned Single Judge found that the land of each Schedules comprised a separate khatian and that each khatian constituted a separate holding, and that consideration for each of these holdings was separately shown in the kabala by which all of them were transferred. The consideration for schedule-III land was stated to be Tk. 400.00 and that of the other 4 Schedule lands was stated to be Tk. 200.00 each; the pre-emptor had deposited Tk. 800.00 representing the consideration for these four holdings he sought to pre-empt. On this finding the learned Single Judge, by an order dated 1 April 1984, read with the previous order dated 4 May 1981, reversed the appellate Court's decision and restored that of the Trial Court allowing pre-emption of four of the holdings. The learned Single Judge while giving this decision observed that pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is to be allowed holding-wise and that so long no holding is disturbed or split-up by pre-emption, it will not be a case of partial pre-emption.

4. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, learned Advocate for- the appellants, has seriously assailed the view taken by the learned Single Judge and has contended that when five holdings were transferred under a single kabala and when in each of the holdings the pre-emptor was a co-sharer, he must pre-empt all the holdings or none at all, for he cannot be permitted to pick and choose the holdings according to his own convenience. Learned Advocate further contends that the pre-emptor is also required to deposit the entire amount of the consideration money, as stated in the kabala, at the time of filing the application for pre-emption. Learned Advocate has sought reliance for this contention from "Salimuddln Mondal Vs. Mohitosh Biswas, 14 DLR 796, Babu Huq Vs. Laljan, 8 DLR 362 (same case as reported in 10 DLR, 54) and Makhan Lal Vs. Reazuddin Sepai 13 DLR 323. Mr. SS Halder, learned Advocate for the respondent has, on the other hand, relied upon a number of decisions including the decision in the case of Diam Hosain Vs. Haran Das, 13 DLR, 283, to substantiate his contention that pre-emption is to be sought "holding-wise" and not transaction-wise or kabala-wise and that so long no holding transferred is disturbed or split up by pre-emption, the question of partial pre-emption does not arise. He has contended that a holding may consist of several plots and a person seeking pre-emption is not permitted to pick and choose one or some of the plots of a holding and leave out other plots of the same holding, and this is what is prevented by the "rule as to bar of partial pre-emption". In this case, learned Advocate has pointed out, pre-emption of 4 holdings out of 5 will not result in spliuing up any of the holdings including the holding left out.

5. The 'doctrine' as to partial pre-emption or 'rule' barring pre-emption in part has not been laid down in any statute. In particular, section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act under which pre-emption has been sought in this case, does not speak of any such term. This section provides for pre-emption of "a portion or a share of a holding" on deposit of the entire consideration or value of the land transferred. The 'doctrine' of partial pre-emption has been evolved through interpretation, by courts, of the law relating to pre-emption keeping in view the object of pre-emption, i.e., convenience or inconvenience of parties involved. Section 96 has given right to pre-emption and also has laid down the procedure for seeking pre-emption. Right to pre-emption has been given to co-sharers in a holding and also to a person having land contiguous to the land transferred. Priority of the right, among persons seeking pre-emption, has also been laid down therein. In the case of Salimuddin (14 DLR 796), which was decided by a Single Bench, several holdings were sold by one sale deed as a single transaction; a co-sharer in the holdings transferred sought to pre-empt some of the holdings leaving out others. It was disallowed by the learned Single Bench on two grounds; one was that the consideration money which was paid in a lump for all the holdings together cannot be split up for the purpose of deposit at the time of filing of the application; and the other was that the "single transaction" covering all the holdings cannot be split up by pick and choose to suit the pre-emptor's purpose causing inconvenience to the purchaser. It appears that the learned Single Judge referred to section 14(2) of the Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899 and observed that the word 'holding' appearing in the statute, namely section 26 (F) BT Act, though singular, includes its plural also i.e. a 'holding' may be read as "holdings" as well. Emphasis is found to have been given on the fact that all the holdings sold together under a kabala constituted a 'single transaction' But the section did not speak of any 'transaction' or of "any single portion" or "instrument"; the section speaks of "a portion or a share of a holding". In Diam Hossain's case (13 DLR 283), decided under the same 'statute, 26(F) BT Act, another Single Bench took a different view and held that though a holding cannot be split up for the purpose of pre-emption, such as, by allowing pre-emption of one plot out of several plots comprising the same holding, but when two or more holdings are involved, a co-sharer is at liberty to seek pre-emption of one of the holding leaving out others. In that case two holdings were sold under a kabala, one for a consideration of Tk. 600.00 and the other for a consideration of Tk. 400.00 and pre-emption for one of the two holdings was sought for upon deposit of the consideration for that holding only. That pre-emption was allowed in view of the provision in section 26(F) BT Act that "a portion or a share of a holding" if transferred, could be pre-empted.

6. In Mosammat Asimon Nessa Vs. Md. Akbar Ali Sheikh and others, 19 DLR 659, a Division Bench of the High Court considered this very question in view of the conflicting decisions in the cases of Diam Hossain (13 DLR) and Solimuddin (14 DLR). The learned Judges held that the "right of pre-emption given to a co-sharer under section 26(F) BT Act, as well as section 96, State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, "is with reference to a holding", that is so say, the right accrues "holding-wise". In that case three holdings were transferred under one kabala but a co-sharer tenant prayed for pre-emption of two of the three holdings leaving out the 3rd one; plea of bar as to partial pre-emption was raised but it was rejected on the ground that none of the holdings transferred would be split up or disturbed by the pre-emption sought. The view taken in the 14 DLR case was dissented from and that taken in 13 DLR case was relied upon.

7. Mr. Gafur has tried to make out some distinction between the facts of this case (19 DLR) and those of the instant one. In the 19 DLR case the pre-emptor was found to be a co-sharer of two of the three holdings transferred and he wanted to pre-empt those two holdings leaving out the 3rd one; it was not stated any where whether he was co-sharer in that holdings also. If he were not a co-sharer in the left-out holding, the question of its pre-emption would not arise and the pre-emptor's prayer for pre-emption of the two holdings, in which he was a co-sharer, would not come under the doctrine of partial pre-emption. It is true that it was not clear whether the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the left-out holding; nevertheless, the interpretation of section 26(F) corresponding to section 96 as given by the Division Bench is of crucial importance; and according to this interpretation pre-emption is "holding wise" i.e. by pre-emption a holding cannot be split up; it is to be kept in tact and pre-empted; no part of it is to be left-out. This however does not mean that if several holdings are transferred by a kabala all of them are to be pre-empted. The expression 'holding' in singular according to the General Clauses Act need not include its plural 'holdings' for the purpose of pre-emption in the absence of any specific. provision to that effect. This view as to holding wise pre-emption was followed in a number of subsequent cases including Tamizuddin Vs. Guljan Bibi, 26 DLR P 93 and one unreported case, Birendra Nath Vs. Subal Chandra—Civil Revision No. 72 of 1978.

8. Mr. Abdul Gafur contends that a person seeking pre-emption must deposit the entire consideration money and if the consideration for several holdings sold by a single kabala was paid in lamp, the entire consideration money must be deposited; otherwise pre-emption for some of the holdings out of several holdings would fail. He sought reliance on this point from the case of Babu Huq Vs. Laljan Babi 8 DLR 362. In that case the pre-emptor had 7/15 share in a holding and the remaining share, 8/15, belonged to her brother; but her brother, who was possessing the entire holding, sold it to a stranger under a kabala for a consideration of Tk. 600/-. She sought pre-emption of the share of her brother and deposited the proportionate share of the consideration plus compensation i,e. she deposited Tk. 320/- in all, contending that she was not required to pre-empt her own portion, that is, 7/15 share. Her application for pre-emption was finally disallowed by a Single Bench on the ground that the consideration money could not be split up. The question of hardship on the part of the pre-emptor was raised but it was ruled out relying upon a decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Nurul Hossain Vs. Mihi Lal Sheikh (AIR 1948 Cal. 144) In that case it was observed that "a well settled rule of law should not be unsettled on the ground of hardship in one or two individual cases" but that "the certainty of the law should not be disturbed by artificial constructions". It appears that too much importance was given on the likely inconvenience or difficulty in apportioning the consideration money leaving out of consideration the all important question as to what was meant by the expression "a portion or a share of a holding transferred". This "expression" means that the co-sharer, by pre-empting the portion/share transferred to a stranger, he will keep in tact the original holding excluding the stranger-purchaser therefrom; and if he does not intend to pre-empt the other holdings transferred it is presumed that he has waived his right to pre-empt them.

9. Mr. Gafur has referred to an observation of his Court in the case of Haji Tozzamol Ali Vs. Abdus Satter, 34 DLR (AD) 217, in which the "doctrine" of partial pre-emption with its scope and limitation was discussed when the question raised there related to pre-emption by a contiguous land holder. It is to be noted that under section 26(F) BT Act right of pre-emption was given only to co-sharer-tenants; but under Section 96, State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, this right has been extended to a person who is not a co-sharer but who has got a land contiguous to the land transferred. Of course, right of pre-emption to such a person has been given the last priority i.e. he can claim pre-emption only when a co-sharer by inheritance or a co-sharer by purchase does not come to claim pre-emption. In the 34 DLR case, as well as in two other similar cases, Akhterunnessa Vs. Habibullah, 31 DLR (AD) 88 and Ahmed Hossain Vs. Basharat Ali, 32 DLR (AD) 54, only contiguous land holders claimed pre-emption on the ground of contiguity of their lands to the lands transferred. It was held that their right to pre-emption was limited to the extent to which their own lands were. contiguous to the lands transferred. "Rule" of bar of partial pre-emption was discussed in all its aspects in those cases and in the last mentioned case, where the land transferred consisted of several plots and holdings which were themselves contiguous to each other and formed a single compact block, but the pre-emptor got contiguity with one of those several plots or holdings, then it was held, he was to claim pre-emption of all the lands constituting the single block and he was not permitted to leave out any part therefrom. In 32 DLR case it was held that 'contiguity' was snapped and right to pre-emption was barred when the "contiguity" was broken by a public path lying in between the pre-emptor's land and that sought to be pre-empted on the ground of contiguity. In an earlier case—Makhan Lal Vs. Reazuddin (13 DLR 323), already referred to by Mr. Gafur, the High Court touched upon this question as to extent of contiguity and held that the contiguous land holder must pre-empt all the lands transferred if these lands are contiguous to his own land. In the instant case, the question of pre-emption by a contiguous land holder is not involved, and as such those decisions are not relevant except, of course, for the purpose of keeping in mind the general principle as to pre-emption, that is, convenience of the parties involved.

<u>10. Here in this case, five holdings we transferred by a single kabala and consideration money of each of the holdings was shown separately in the kabala. The petitioner deposited the consideration money for the four holdings he prayed for by way of pre-emption; there was no difficulty in allowing his prayer for pre-emption of the four holdings as pre-emption is preferable holding-wise. This pre-emption is not hit by the doctrine of partial pre-emption. Section 96 gives right to a co-sharer-tenant, like the respondent-pre-emptor to purchase the "portion or share of a holding transferred" By the pre-emption in question he is entitled to get those portions or shares so that he could keep in tact the original holding or holdings.</u>

In the result the pre-emption, as allowed by the High Court Division, is found to have been rightly allowed. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the purchaser- pre-emptee petitioner calls in question the judgment and order dated 28-11-92 passed by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Sylhet dismissing Miscellaneous Appeal No. 161 of 1985 and affirming the judgment and order dated 25-11-85 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 97 of 1980 (pre-emption case) by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sylhet.

2. The short fact leading to the issuance of the Rule is that, the pre-emptor opposite parties filed the aforesaid pre-emption case in the court of the Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet seeking pre-emption of the suit land measuring 0.05 decimal against the pre-emptee opposite parties claiming themselves as the co-sharer tenants of the holding by way of inheritance. The pre-emptee opposite party Nos. 3 and 4 sold the suitland to the preemptee-petitioners Nos. 1 and 2, who were strangers, by registered kabala dated 29-4-80 without giving any notice of the sale. The preemptee-petitioners contested the said preemption case by filing written objection denying all the material allegations in the petition contending, inter alia, that the preemptor-opposite parties were aware of the sale as they were requested to purchase the suitland before the sale in question but on their refusal to purchase the suitland was sold to the preemptee-petitioners Nos. 1 and 2. It was also contended by the preemptee-petitioners Nos. 1 and 2 in their written statement that the preemption case was bad for defect of parties as the preemptor opposite parties omitted to implead other co-sharer tenants of the disputed holding, namely, Khatian No. 339.

3. Preemptor-opposite parties examined only preemptor petitioner No. 3 as PW 1 and the preemptee petitioners examined 1 OPW in support of their respective case. The learned trial Court after due consideration of the evidence on record allowed the miscellaneous case by granting preemption in favour of the preemptor-opposite parties by the judgment and order dated 25-11-85.

4. Preemptee-petitioners being aggrieved by the said judgment and order preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 161 of 1985 in the Court of the District Judge, Sylhet. The learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Sylhet on transfer heard and dismissed the appeal by the impugned judgment and order dated 28-11-92 affirming the judgment and order of the trial Court. The preemptee petitioners again being dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order of the appellate Court below preferred civil revision and obtained the present Rule.

5. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the preemptee-petitioners submits that the pre- emptor opposite parties' application for preemption is liable to be dismissed for their failure to implead necessary parties on two counts namely, (1) failure of the pre-emptor opposite parties to implead some co-sharer tenants in the disputed holding till today and (ii) impleading of some parties after the statutory period of 4 (four) months is no impleading as required under section 96(2) read with section 96(1) of the Act. The trial Court as well as the appellate Court below, it is contended, having allowed the pre-emption case of the preemptor-petitioners in spite of the aforesaid defects committed an error of law justifying interference with the impugned judgment and order by this Court.

6. Learned Advocate for the preemptee-petitioners while elaborating his arguments placed reliance on 1 BCR (AD) 59 in support of his contention that necessary parties are required to be added as parties to the preemption application within the statatnry period of 4 months in view of section 96(2) read with section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951. It is urged by the learned Advocate that when the preemptee-petitioners raised objection as to non-impleading of necessary parties in their written objection the onus was on the preemptor-opposite parties to rectify defect of parties by impleading all the necessary parties before the trial for effective and complete adjudication of the claim of pre-emption. Learned Advocate referred to the case of Abdus Samad & others vs Md. Sohrab Ali &others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 113 and Md Abdul Jalil vs. Durjan Ali @ Siddique Hossain and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 269 in support of this contention. Learned Advocate referred to paragraph-4 of the written objection, cross-examination of PWI and Exts. '1' and A submitting that in spite of the objection taken by the preemptee-petitioners with regard to the defect of parties at the earliest point of time the preemptor opposite parties impleaded only 3 persons, although they were not necessary parties, leaving out the necessary parties who are palpably co-sharers in the disputed holding being Khatian No. 339, namely, one Martaza Bibi and another Julekha Bibi. The failure of the preemptor-opposite parties to implead the aforesaid Martaza Bibi and Julekha Bibi in violation of the mandatory provision of section 96(2) of the said Act has deprived them of their right of preemption in the present case.

7. The learned Advocate for the preemptor-opposite parties, on the other hand, vehemently contends that the pre-emptee petitioners were required in law to raise specific objection with regard to defect of parties by giving necessary particulars of the remaining co-sharer tenants in the disputed khatian at the earliest opportunity which they failed to do. It is further contended that the preemptor opposite parties none-the-less rectified this defect of parties by impleading 3 co-sharer tenants of the disputed holding as soon as they came to know about them during cross-examination of PW 1 vide order dated 21-7-85 of the trial Court. Since the rectification of this defect of parties was made before the trial was over their application for pre-emption no longer suffered from any defect of parties.

8. It is farther contended by the learned Advocate that the impleading of necessary parties is not mandatory but directory and, as such, non-impleading of Julekha and Martuza Bibi will not deprive the pre-emptor petitioners of their right of pre-emption in the present case. The learned Advocate, however, relied on the case of Motilal Sikder reported in 28 DLR (AD) 5 in this connection.

9. It is also contended by the learned Advocate that impleading of necessary parties is not required to be done within the statutory period of 4 months as envisaged under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but this may be done at any time before the trial.

10. The case of Abdus Samad & others vs. Md Sohrab Ali &others is reported both in 1 BCR (AD) 59 and 33 DLR (AD) 113. In this case Appellate Division has held that if the preemptor is a co-sharer tenant he is required to implead all the remaining co-sharer tenants in the holding in the interest of proper and complete adjudication in accordance with law. It is also held that if the pre-emptee or any of the parties disclose the existence of necessary parties before trial and the pre-emptor fails to implead him or them his application for pre-emption shall fail. Because presence of necessary parties is necessary for an effective and complete adjudication.

11. In the case of Md Abdul Jalil vs. Durjan Ali @ Siddique Hossain reported in 33 DLR (AD) 259 it is held that once the pre-emptee raises objection as to non-impleading of necessary parties before trial with some particulars the pre-emptor is under a legal obligation to lead evidence to show that the left-out co-sharers do not have any subsisting interest in the holding to justify non-impleading of those co-sharers.

12. The pre-emptor-opposite parties in this case sought pre-emption of the suitland of the disputed Khatian No. 339 by filing MiscellaneousCase No. 97/80 on 9-7-80. Preemptee petitioners in paragraph-4 of their written objection filed On 6-11-80 raised objection for non-impleading necessary parties in the pre-emption proceeding by the pre-emptor- opposite parties stating that the pre-emptor opposite parties did not implead the remaining co-sharers tenants in the disputed khatian No. 339. During the cross-examination of PW 1, the pre-emptee petitioners succeeded in bringing it on record that Julekha Bibiie the sister of the father of the pre- emptors and one Martuza Bibi were co-sharer tenants in the disputed holding and they were not made parties although they were alive. Exhibit-"I" and "A" are the attested Khatian of the disputed khatian No. 339. From these 2 Exhibits it is also seen that Martuza Bibi is a co-sharer tenant in the disputed holding.

13. The right of pre-emption is conferred by section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and according to section 96(5) there are three categories of pre-emptors namely, (a) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by way of inheritance, (b) a co-sharer tenant whose interest is created by purchase and (c) tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. In the instant case the pre-emptor opposite parties have claimed pre-emption of the suit land as a co-sharer tenant to the disputed khatian No. 339 through inheritance.

14. In terms of section 96(1) of the said Act the pre-emptor-opposite parties are required to file an application claiming pre-emption within 4 months of the registration of the sale deed which they have done. In terms of section 96(2) of the said Act the pre-emptor opposite parties were required to file their application claiming pre-emption by impleading the remaining co-sharer tenants in the disputed holding.

<u>15. From the language employed under section 96(1) and 96(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is clear that once the pre-emptor files pre-emption application within the statutory period of 4 months such application is not liable to fail for non-impleading of necessary parties within the period of said 4 months provided such necessary parties are impleaded at any stage of the proceedings. The head-note in 1 BCR (AD) 59 is wrongly written indicating that necessary parties are to be added within 4 months although it is not so said in the body of the judgment.</u>

16. Order 1 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure is applicable in case of non-joinder of necessary parties in the application for pre-emption in view of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 96(2) of the said Act creates obligation on the part of the pre-emptor to make co-sharer tenants in the disputed holding as parties to the pre-emption application. But such addition of parties in the pre-emption application is controlled by the provision of this section. This aspect is by now well settled in the case of Abdus Samad and others vs. Md Sobhan and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 113. Non-joinder of a co-sharer tenant will not itself defeat pre-emption proceeding in all cases although provision of section 96(2) of the Act with regard to the impleading of necessary parties to a preemption application is mandatory. Because such a co-sharer tenant may not have subsisting interest in the disputed holding or he may not have immediate contiguity in relation to other contiguous land holders.

17. In the case of Matilal Shikder reported in 28 DLR (AD) 5. Appellate Division has held in the context of the fact of that particular case that nori-joinder of necessary party will not be fatal to a pre-emption proceeding and the pre-emptor is only under obligation to implead necessary party provided the pre-emptee furnishes necessary particulars of the necessary party. In the aforesaid case the left-out contiguous land owner lost the contiguity between his land and the land transferred after amicable partition with his brother. In the context of that fact it was observed by the Appellate Division that the provision asto impleading of necessary parties in an application of pre-emption under section 96(2) of the Act is merely directory and not mandatory.

18. In the case of Abdus Samad vs. Sohrab Ali reported in 33 DLR (AD) 113 it is held that if the pre-emptee or for that matter any of the parties disclose existence of necessary parties and furnishes necessary particulars but the pre-emptor still omits to implead them the pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties.

19. In the case of Abdul Jalil vs. Durjan Ali reported in 33 DLR (AD) 269 it is also held that when the pre-emptee raises objection with regard to the defect of parties with some particulars at the earliest opportunity the onus is not on the pre-emptee but on the pre-emptor to lead evidence that the left-out co-sharers have no subsisting interest in the disputed holding. The relevant paragraph of the judgment is reproduced below:

"11. Mr. Anil Chandra Sarker, learned Advocate for the appellant, has contended that it was for the pre-emptor to lead evidence showing that the left-out co-sharers had lost their interest in the land in question by transfer or otherwise and that the High Court Division illegally shifted the burden of proof upon the pre-emptee in this respect. It is not disputed that the left-out persons are co-sharers by inheritance. But there is no evidence whatever to show that they got no subsisting interest in the land under pre-emption, Mr. Yeasin, the learned Advocate for the respondent, has failed to show us how it could be held that the left-out co-sharers lost or transferred their interest in the land under pre-emption. The onus of proof in this respect is upon the preemptor but his onus has not been discharged. The observation of the High Court Division as quoted above shows that it was for the preemptee to lead evidence to the effect that the 'left-out co-sharers still got interest in the land sought to be pre-empted. The High Court Division in this connection relied upon the decision of Motilal Sikder's case in which it was observed that the positive injunction as to parties under section 96(2) is directory. The facts of this case as set out above are not attracted by the decision in Motilal's case. On the contrary, these facts are attracted by the decision in the case of Abdus Samad vs. Sohrab Ali in which it has been held that non-joinder of parties who got right of pre-emption is fatal to the proceeding."

20. It appears from paragraph-4 of the written objection filed by the pre-emptee petitioners that the objection with regard to the non-joinder of necessary parties is not vague and wide. Moreover, cross-examination of PW 1 and Ext.'I' and 'A' in the instant case also disclosed necessary particulars of the left-out co-sharers. Because the disputed Khatian (Ext.'I' and 'A') disclose the names of the remaining co-sharer tenants pre-emptor-opposite party had therefore no difficulty in getting the names and particulars of the remaining co-sharer tenants of the disputed holding from the said Exts. I and A and cross-examination of PW 1 and could implead them before the trial, which they did not do. Hence, the present pre-emption case still suffers from defect of parties.

21. It is, however, urged by the learned Advocate of the pre-emptor opposite parties that although objection with regard to defect of parties was taken by the pre-emptee petitioners in rather vague and unspecified manner during the trial and appeal but this was abandoned at the stage of revision by failing to take any ground in this regard. Hence, the pre-emptee petitioners are debarred from agitating this ground at this stage and this Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction cannot act on this point.

<u>22. The learned Advocate for the pre-emptee petitioners have argued in reply with reference to two decisions reported in the case of Ashwini Kumar Karmaker being dead his heirs; Sree Radha Raman Karmaker and others vs. Hari Mohan and others and Derasatullah and others vs. Manik Mondal and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 1 and 88 respectively submitting that this Court can rectify any illegality in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction at the instance of the parties or even suomotu. I am inclined to accept this view as it appears to me to have substance. This Court in revisional jurisdiction is not powerless and can for the ends of justice rectify any illegality committed by the inferior court even if such defect is not pointed out by either party.</u>

23. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the impugned judgment and order dated 28-11-92 passed by the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 161 of 1985 and the judgment and the order dated 25-11-85 passed in Misc. Case No. 97 of 1980 are set aside without any order as to cost.

However, I feel that justice will be met if the case is sent back on remand to the trial Court for fresh trial by taking fresh evidence by giving the pre-emptor opposite parties a chance to amend their application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by adding left-out necessary parties.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptor petitioners calls in question the orders dated 9-6-85 and 30-11-85 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 1981 refusing to interfere with the order restoring the aforesaid Miscellaneous case which was dismissed for default on 25-2-85.

2. Fact relevant for the purpose of disposal of the present Rule is stated as follows:

Pre-emptor-petitioners filed preemption Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1981 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the Court of Munsif, Gazipur seeking pre-emption of the case land. The aforesaid preemption Miscellaneous case was decreed ex parte by order dated 28-11-81. The pre-emptee-opposite parties Nos. 1 to 3, therefore, filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure being Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 1981 for setting aside the ex-parte decree. But the said Miscellaneous case was dismissed for default by order dated 25-2-85.

3. The pre-emptee opposite parties, thereafter, filed an application for review under Order 47, rule 1 read with sections 114 and 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in terms of Order 47 rule 2 for restoration of the said Miscellaneous case on review of the dismissal order dated 25-2-85. But the trial Court by order dated 21-5-85 rejected the same as not maintainable. Subsequently, pre-emptee-opposite parties Nos. 1-3 filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 9-6-85 for restoration of the Miscellaneous case on reconsideration of the said order dated 21-5-85. Trial Court, thereupon, by order dated 9-6-85 restored the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 1981 by allowing the said application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

4. The pre-emptor petitioner being aggrieved by the said order dated 9-6-85 filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for correcting the aforesaid order dated 9-6-85 but the same was rejected by order dated 30-11-85 on the ground that the same court could not interfere with its earlier order. The pre-emptor petitioners having been aggrieved filed the instant revision and obtained the present Rule.

5. Learned Advocate Mr. Kazi Shahadat Hossain, appearing on behalf of the pre-emptor-petitioners, submits that the pre-emptee-opposite parties 1 to 3 wrongly filed the application for review of the order dated 25-2-85 dismissing the said Miscellaneous Case for default inasmuch as such dismissal order was liable to be challenged by filing appeal only under Order 43 rule 1(d). Hence, the court below was justified in rejecting the application for review by order dated 21-5-85 as not maintainable. It is urged by Mr Hossain that since the order dated 21-5-85 rejecting the application for review was rightly made, the pre-emptee opposite parties could challenge the said order dated 21-5-85 by filling a revision and not by filing an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for reconsideration of the said order dated 21-5-85. The court below, in the circumstances, having restored the said Miscellaneous case by allowing the aforesaid application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice.

<u>6. Learned Advocate Kazi Shahadat Hossain cited a decision in the case of Pujari Chatur Bhuj vs. Saiyeda Jobeda Begum reported in 22 DLR 383 in support of his contention that the order dated 21-5-85 being an order of rejection the application for review under Order 47, rule 1 or an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not competent except a civil revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is contended by the learned Advocate that section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be resorted to when there is a specific forum provided by law inasmuch as the same cannot be treated as an alternative mode for seeking redress. Learned Advocate for the preemptor-petitioners also relied on a decision reported in the case of Md Hossain Mollah & others vs. Assistant Deputy Custodian reported in 37 DLR 287 to strenghen his point already advanced that provision under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is only available to rectify any wrong when there is no remedy under the law and that the same cannot be pressed into service to further injustice or to condone gross negligence.</u>

7. In the case of Pujari Chatur Bhuj Das vs. Saiyeda Jobeda Begum reported in 22 DLR 383, the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 10 of 1960 and the same was decreed ex parte as the defendants failed to take any step. Hence, the defendant filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree contending that the said Title Suit was to be taken and heard analogously with Title Suit No. 106 of 1959 as per order of the District Judge. But it was not done. Hence, the defendants were not aware of the date of hearing. The trial Court refused to entertain such application on the ground that the defendants ought to have taken appropriate steps for setting aside the ex parte decree either by instituting a Miscellaneous case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure or by filing an appeal. A Single Bench of the then High Court at Dhaka presided over by Mr Justice Maksum-ul-Hakim in his revisional jurisdiction affirmed the above decision of the court as under:

"In my opinion, the stand taken by the learned Subordinate Judge in this case is clearly legal and valid. A proceeding under section 151, Civil Procedure Code cannot be taken when there are other remedies available for securing the redress. The inherent power conferred on the Court under section 151, Civil Procedure Code should only be resorted to in a case where there is no other provision or procedure for providing redress or rectifying a clear injustice. It is never an alternative mode for securing relief."

8. In the case of Md Hossain Mollah & ors vs. Assistant Deputy Custodian reported in 37 DLR 287 a similar view was taken by a Single Bench of this Division which is evident from the passage quoted below:

"From the decisions quoted above it is clear that when a party had got a right of appeal against the order he should go for an appeal, he cannot maintain an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for reversal of the ex parte order. In the instant case, the learned Munsif did exercise his jurisdiction with material irregularity in allowing the said application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was just and proper for restoration of a case under Order 9 r. 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure but it is not just and proper to entertain the application for restoration under Order 9, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure and under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Order 9, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for the plaintiff to bring a fresh suit which is dismissed either for non-service of summons in consequence of plaintiffs failure to pay cost or for non-appearance of both the plaintiff and defendants. In this connection, an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is also not maintainable, because inherent power of the court exists only where there is no express provision of law applicable to the case. The provisions of this section cannot be invoked to defeat the provisions of the Code nor can be invoked to further injustice or to condone gross negligence. The court cannot interfere under section 151 of the Code with appealable order."

<u>9. Mr Md Ashfaqul Islam, learned Advocate for the preemptee opposite parties, in reply submits that the order dated 25-2-85 dismissing the Miscellaneous case was an appealable order in terms of Order 43, rule l(d). But without filing any appeal an application for review was made for setting aside the said dismissal order in terms of order 47, rule 1 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the prayer for review was competent. Hence, the court below was not justified in rejecting the application for review as not maintainable vide order dated 21-5-85. Accordingly, it is submitted, an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by the pre-emptee opposite parties for restoration of the said Miscellaneous case on reconsideration of the said order dated 21-5-85. Learned Advocate for the preemptee opposite parties submits, without disputing the principle of law that, ordinarily provision under section 151 of the Code cannot be resorted to where there is specific forum provided for in law, but in a case where the court has passed a mistaken order affecting rights of a party in the proceeding redress can be had by resorting to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure without availing of other remedies or forum namely, revision or appeal which is inconvenient or otherwise time consuming or even expensive. The learned Advocate for the preemptee-opposite parties further submits that in a case where a wrong or mistaken order of the court has caused prejudice to the party in the proceeding the same court can rectify the situation by acting exdebito justitiae. In support of his aforesaid submissions the learned Advocate placed reliance on two decisions in the case of Atash Ali and others vs. Rebati Mohan Sarker and 3 others reported in 43 DLR 539 and the case of Mohan Bashi Saha vs. United Bank of India Ltd. &others reported in 15 DLR 383.</u>

10. In the aforesaid case of Atash Ali and others vs. Rebati Mohan Sarker and 3 others a Single Bench of this Division held as under:

"Where the Court itself passed a wrong order the court is competent to rectify the said order upon an application filed under section 151 CPC by either party to the proceeding or suomotu by invoking the inherent power under section 151 of the Code and exercise of such power is no error of law, rather by such exercise of power the Court does real and substantial justice for the administration of which the Court exists. Such exercise of power is in consonance with the principle actus curiae nomine gravabitan act of court shall prejudice none. In that view of the matter I do not find any error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice in making the impugned order."

In the aforesaid case of Mohan Bashi Saha vs. United Bank of India Ltd. and others Mr Justice Idris, while delivering a judgment of a Division Bench sitting with Mr Justice Hasan held as under:

"The jurisdiction of the Court to act ex debito justitiae cannot be ousted simply because another inconvenient remedy is also available."

11. In the present case the preemptee opposite parties instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 1981 under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree passed in the pre-emption case filed by the preemptor petitioner. The said Miscellaneous case was dismissed for default by the trial Court on 25-2-85 for non-appearance of the preemptee opposite parties. The said order dated 25-2-85 was an appealable order in terms of Order 43, rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. But in terms of the Order 47, rule 1(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure the preemptee-opposite parties were competent to file an application for review under Order 47 as he did not file any appeal, which was precisely done in this case by the preemptee-opposite parties.

12. Order 47, rule 1 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides as under:

"A party who is not appealing from a decree or order may apply for a review of judgment notwithstanding the pendency of an appeal by some other party except where the ground of such appeal is common to the applicant and the appellant, or when, being respondent, he can present to the Appellate Court the case on which he applies for the review."

<u>13. In spite of the fact that review application in the present case was competent the trial Court by order dated 21-5-85 rejected such application filed by the preemptee opposite parties as not maintainable, which, in fact, affected their right and interest. It is not, however, denying the fact that the preemptee-opposite parties could file a civil revisional application challenging the aforesaid order of dismissal dated 21-5-85 for unduly rejecting the application for review. But instead of doing that they filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was less expensive and convenient and speedier in the facts and circumstances of the case. I respectfully agree with the law laid down in the case of Atash Ali &others vs. Rebati Mohan Sarker and 3 others reported in 43 DLR 539 and Mohan Bashi Saha vs. United Bank of India Ltd &others reported in 15 DLR 383, that when a mistaken order has caused injustice to a party, such order can be set aside by invoking inherent jurisdiction of the Court or in acting exdebito justitiae for remedying such injustice.</u>

14. Our Appellate Division also agreed with the aforesaid position in the case of Punjab Ali vs. Mohd Mokarram Hossain reported in 29 DLR (SC) 185. The relevant paragraph of the judgment thereof is reproduced below:

"The court should not presume the existence of inherent power to do that for which specific provision has been made by a statute and should not invest itself with such jurisdiction for the purpose of getting round the express provisions of the law. Unintentional or inadvertent mistake of a Court causing injustice to a party, however, stands on a different footing and in the case of such a mistake the exercise of inherent power of a Court is not subject to those limitations on its exercise which have been set down by the judicial authorities noticed above."

<u>15. Since the court below through inadvertence or mistake disallowed the review application for restoration of Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 1981 although such application was competent in law the court below subsequently having restored the same by allowing the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure committed no error of law occasioning failure of justice.</u>

16. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

17. The trial Court is directed to proceed with Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 1981 in accordance with law.

18. The order of stay earlier passed by this Court staying all further proceedings of Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 1981 at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Let the lower court records be sent down expeditiously.

End.
