case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 25 November, 1986 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 71 of 1981).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman J: Respondent, Md. Fazlul Huq, was appointed as a clerk in the postal department of the Government in November, 1965. Subsequently by an order dated 3.5.1972 he was asked to act as Inspector of Post Offices, (hereinafter in brief IPO), at Netrokona Subdivision.

2. The order dated 3.5.1972 by which the plaintiff was asked to act as IPO was "issued in the interest of service to have immediate effect and until further orders." The order reads as follows:

"Mr. Fazlul Huq., Clerk Divisional Office Mymensingh is hereby ordered to act as Inspector of Post Offices, Netrokona Sub-Dn. vice Mr. Saifuddin Ahmed transferred on promotion as Assistant Supdt. of Post Offices, Mymensingh. Mr. Fazlul will make over charge of his branch on the fore-noon of 1-5-72. He is clearly given to understand that his appointment is purely temporary and may be terminated at any time without any previous notice and showing any reason".

3. 'By order dated 26th June, 1976 the respondent was reverted to his substantive post. and was asked to join in Mymensingh Office.

4. Respondent instituted OC Suit No. 253 of 1976 in the Court of Munsif, Netrokona for a declaration that the aforesaid order dated 26th June, 1976 was illegal and void.

5. The appellant contested that suit asserting, inter alia, that the plaintiff was ordered to act as an IPO, Netrokona in the vacancy caused by Mr. Saifuddin Ahmed on temporary basis due to non-availability of qualified hand; that every IPO is required to qualify through competitive examination; and that the plaintiff appeared in the competitive examination, but failed.

6. The trial Court dismissed the suit. It held that no clerk could be promoted to the cadre of IPO without passing a competitive examination as provided in Rules 297/1 of Post and Telegraphs Manual Volume IV. The trial Court considered the gradation list of Postal Officers corrected upto 1.7.1959 that showed that ten unqualified IPOs were declared to be absorbed in the cadre, but as no evidence was led how the ten IPOs were absorbed it held that the plaintiff could not claim to be absorbed as an IPO without having the requisite qualifications.

<u>7. On appeal the plaintiffs prayer for declaring the order of transfer as bad was rejected, but his other prayer with regard to the reversion to this post of clerk was allowed. After considering rule 50 of the Posts and Telegraphs Manual Volume IV which provides that vacancies from non-gazetted officers of more than one month but not more than four months' duration can be filled up temporarily, and rule 59 which provides that an IPO should not ordinarily remain in charge of the same division or at the same post for more than four years at a time, the appellate Court observed that the plaintiff held the post of IPO for more than four years and he was under the impression that he would be ultimately absorbed in the cadre of IPO. As the impugned order was passed without any notice the appellate Court after relying on Anwarul Huq Khan Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others 31 DLR 21 and the Government of Bangladesh Vs. Md. Ismail Hossain, 31 DLR (AD) 127 declared that the order of reversion amounted to reduction in rank and it was void and illegal. The High Court Division upheld the order of the appellate court.</u>

<u>8. In 31 DLR 21 it was held that an incumbent holding a post for considerable long time is entitled to protection under Article 135 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>9. In the Government of Bangladesh Vs. Md. Ismail Hossain reported in 31 DLR (AD) 127 the respondent, holding substantively the post of District Kanungo, was "appointed temporarily to the East Pakistan Civil Service (Executive) Class II", a temporary cadre dependent on early sanction. After seven years of service in that cadre he was reverted to his substantive post of District Kanungo without any notice. It was held that as the respondent was not appointed for a limited period within the tenure of cadre itself or any specified period and that as the word "temporarily" used in the order of appointment would mean the cadre itself and not relate to the appointment, his reversion to his substantive post was treated as a reduction in rank. With this reasoning the court distinguished the ratio in Hartwell Prescott Singh Vs. The Uttar Pradesh Government and others AIR 1953 (SC) 886, Parshotam Lai Dhingra Vs. Union of India PLD 1958 SC (India) 217, Abdul Majid Sheikh Vs. Mushaffe Ahmed and another 17 DLR 1965 (SC) 63, and Chairman Railway Board Vs. Abdul Majid 18 DLR (SC) 532.</u>

10. In the case reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 886 it was held "Reversion from a temporary post held by a person does not per se amount to reduction in rank because the temporary post held by him is not his substantive rank."

11. In the case reported in PLD 1958 (SC) India 217 the Indian Supreme Court held" [If] the servant has no right to the post, as where he is appointed to a post, permanent or temporary either on probation or on an officiating basis and whose temporary service has not ripened into a quasi-permanent service as defined in the Temporary Service Rules, the termination of his employment does not deprive him of any right and cannot, therefore, by itself be a punishment. One test for determining whether the termination of the service of a Government servant is by way of punishment is to ascertain whether the servant, but for such termination, had the right to hold the post. If he had a right to the post as in the three cases hereinbefore mentioned, the termination of his service will by itself be a punishment and he will be entitled to the protection of Art. 311. ... To put it in another way, if the Government has, by contract, express or implied, or under the rules, the right to terminate the employment at any time, then such termination in the manner provided by the contract or the rules is prima facie and per se, not a punishment and does not attract the provisions of Art. 311."

<u>12. In State of Bombay Vs. FA Abraham AIR 1962 (SC) 794 the Indian Supreme Court held that "a person officiating in a post has no right to hold it for all times. He may have been given the officiating post because the permanent incumbent was not available, having gone on leave or being away for some other reasons. When the permanent incumbent comes back, the person officiating is naturally reverted to his original post. This is no reduction in rank for it was the very term on which he had been given the officiating post. Again, sometimes a person is given an officiating post to test his suitability to be made permanent in it later. Here again, it is an implied term of the officiating appointment that if he is found unsuitable; he would have to go back. If, therefore, the appropriate authorities find him unsuitable for the higher rank and then revert him back to his original lower rank; the action taken is in accordance with the terms on which the officiating post had been given. It is in no way a punishment and is not, therefore, a reduction in rank."</u>

<u>13. The Pakistan Supreme Court consistently held in a number of decisions that reversion of an incumbent to his substantive post from the higher post to which he was temporarily promoted is not a reduction in rank: Pakistan Vs. Fazal Rahman Khundkar and another PLD 1959 (SC) 82, Province of West Pakistan Vs. Bashir Ahmed, PLD 1959 (SC) 93 and Pakistan and another Vs. Quazi Syed Hikmat Hussain PLD 1959 (SC) 107.</u>

<u>14. In the case reported in 18 DLR 1966 (SC) 532, Chairman, East Pakistan Railway Board, Chittagong and another Vs. Abdul Majid Sardar, Ticket Collector, PE Railway, the Pakistan Supreme upheld the reversion of the respondent to his substantive post of Tally Clerk from that of a Ticket Collector to which he was temporarily promoted.</u>

<u>15. The respondent however relied on 17 DLR (SC) 63 and 22 DLR (SC) 331 and submitted that his case is not a case of reversion simpliciter.</u>

<u>16. In Khushi Muhammad & others Vs. General Manager (now Vice-Chairman), Pakistan Western Railway 22 DLR (SC) 331 as no rule was shown to the court that an incumbent holding a post in the grade in a temporary or officiating capacity should rank lower in point of seniority to one who was appointed later in the service in the same capacity against a reserved post in the same category it was held that all the incumbents were to be treated at par in the matter of seniority in the grade after they entered it. This case has no relevance in the case.</u>

17. For the meaning of the term "until further order" our attention has been drawn to the following observation of Cornelius, CJ in Abdul Majid Vs. Mushafee Ahmed, Section Officer, Government of Pakistan and others 17 DLR SC 63 (68) .

"It is clearly impossible to construe the expression "until further orders" as conferring absolute power of retention or dismissal upon the competent authority. The matter of public employment is governed by a complex of laws, commencing with constitutional instruments and ending with statutory rules, which have been authoritatively construed, by the Superior Courts, in relevant respects. Therefore, these words can only mean that the appointee was subject to lawful orders made by competent authority."

18. Our attention is also drawn to the following observation of Kaikaus J made in 17 DLR (SC) 63 (74):

"To repeat, the Government could not as an ordinary and permanent arrangement fill permanent posts by employees subject to a condition of termination of employment by notice. The Government could fill the post in this manner if the Government was unable to get a person with proper qualifications and was filling the post as interim measure till it secured a person with proper qualifications, and conceivably in some other special circumstances, for some time but it cannot adopt it as a rule that the post will be filed in this manner. When I ask myself the question as to why the Government is filling a permanent post in this manner I find no answer except that the Government wants to retain a power of arbitrary termination of service so as to defeat the constitutional guarantee. No condition of service that is intended to defeat a constitutional guarantee can be permitted to be operative."

19. In this case we find no reason to ascribe any bad motive to the appointing authority.

20. The above observations of Cornelius, CJ and Kaikaus, J., made in a case of termination of service with fourteen days' notice are hardly relevant in this case where there is no question of termination of service.

21. The only question which calls for determination in this case whether the impugned reversion to the respondent's substantive post after his acting in a higher post can be termed as reduction in rank.

<u>22. The case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 127, relied on by the appellate Court as well as by the High Court Division, come up for consideration in Saleh Ahmed Joardar Vs. People's Republic of Bangladesh 36 DLR (AD) 26. After finding that the case of Saleh Ahmed and that of Ismail Hossain of 31 DLR (AD) 127, being both a case of reversion to substantive post, "substantially the same", Fazle Munim, CJ in delivering the majority opinion held "Yet, a different conclusion must be reached by us inthe case at hand".</u>

<u>23. After considering an unreported case of the Pakistan Supreme Court where a petition for special leave to appeal by one Kudrutullah challenging an order of reversion from a temporary, appointment to a higher post to the incumbent's substantive post was dismissed in limine, Fazle Munim CJ observed at para 17 of the report:</u>

<u>"We have, therefore, before us two sets of views by two of the highest tribunals of the two countries which are opposed to each other in respect of an interpretation relating to the expression "temporarily" used in the same order of appointment covering those cases and the present one for consideration before us. In Kudratulla's case the Supreme Court of Pakistan appears to prefer the plain meaning of the expression "temporarily" and therefore, refused to hold the appointment as permanent. Whereas this Court seems to have studied in depth and therefore, arrived at a contrary finding, that is, the expression "temporarily" would, in the opinion of the learned Judges of this Court, make the appointment temporary if the service itself was temporary, not otherwise. Instead of qualifying the word "appointed", the expression "temporarily" has been interpreted to qualify "the East Pakistan Civil Service (Executive) Class II." In the particular facts of Ismail Hossain's case the interpretation so given may appear to be just and correct, but at the same time it may seem to be contrary to the general principle of interpretation of such expression, the expression 'temporarily', being an adverb qualifies the verbs "is appointed," it cannot qualify the word (East Pakistan Civil) "Service" which is a noun. When an officer is selected from one service to another service by such expression as "appointed temporarily" the idea of temporariness attaches to the appointment, but the temporary nature of appointment may be 'whittled down by any subsequent event or development. 'For example, if an officer is appointed temporarily from one service to another service and continues in the latter service for a very long period, it may become difficult to hold that he was still a temporary officer in the latter service. On the other hand, if after such appointment he is reverted back to his parent service soon thereafter, it would be equally difficult to hold that this could not be done as the expression 'temporarily' did not mean that the appointment was temporary."</u>

<u>24. In distinguishing the case of Saleh Ahmed from that of Ismail Hossain, Fazle Munim CJ observed at para 16 of the report:</u>

<u>"Apart from any possible change of meaning of the expression "temporarily" that may occur due to different intentions of the appointing authority or its subsequent conduct or development showing the temporary nature of the appointment, it may be mentioned that the basis upon which Court arrived at conclusion in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Md. Ismail, Hossain, does no longer exist in the instant case as the cadre itself in which the appellant was appointed temporarily now stands abolished. In such background, Ismail Hossain's case cannot cover the instant case. In Ismail Hossain's case though the respondent was appointed temporarily, as the cadre itself continued to exist, the appointment though temporary was held to be permanent. Had it been otherwise, that is, if the cadre stood abolished at the date of the judgment, the decision of the Court would have, in all probability, been different. If the implications of Ismail Hossain's case are remembered, that is to say, if the cadre is temporary the appointment would also be temporary but not so if the cadre continues to exist then the abolition of the cadre itself renders that decision inapplicable to the case before us. We were told that the service was abolished in 1977."</u>

<u>25. Shahabuddin Ahmed, J. as he was then, in his dissent however observed in para 26 "that the East Pakistan Civil Service and in which both this appellant and Md. Ismail Hossain wee e "temporarily" appointed was never abolished at any time; but this cadre was in existence both in 1967 when this appellant was reverted and also in 1973 when Ismail Hossain was reverted".</u>

26. We have quoted at length some observations made in Saleh Ahmed's case as both the appellant and the respondent relied on them adding their own emphasis, but they will be of little help in the facts of this case. The instant case is nota case of abolition of cadre. Again, there is nothing in the conduct of the appointing authority to show that the respondent's temporary appointment to the post of IPO was intended to be permanent.

27. In the first few months after liberation of the country there was a shortage of qualified hands. Where strict adherence to rule 50 as to transfer for filling temporary vacancy was not practicable, the sanctioning authority under that very rule is authorised to make acting arrangement according to administrative requirements. In the departmental instructions it has been emphasised that such temporary appointment to the post of IPOs when qualified officials are not available will not give a claim for permanent appointment or for relaxation of conditions of recruitment to the Inspectors' cadre.

28. The post of an IPO is a promotion post. PW1 asserted that there could not be any promotion to the post of IPO without appearing successfully in the competitive examination of the Department. The respondent, deposing as PW 1, conceded' that he did not know any instance of promotion without passing the competitive examination. He appeared in the competitive examination of the Department during the period when he was officiating as an IPO, but failed to pass that examination.

29. Our attention is drawn to Mominul Huq Vs. Bangladesh 38 DLR 391 where one of us, Mustafa Kamal, J. observed that where in the rules of service promotion is an act of volition, a matter of positive action to be taken by the appropriate authority, one cannot import a legal fiction. The learned Munsif in a very straightforward manner held that the plaintiff cannot be retained in the post for which he is not qualified with the help of the court.

<u>30. Any order of reversion after an incumbent's appointment' to a higher post and continuing there for some duration will surely cause a disappointment as he would no longer draw the benefits of that higher post, but that cannot be called a reduction in rank per se.</u>

<u>31. The uninterrupted service rendered by the respondent for about five years, if considered as "one non-temporary or quasi-permanent", as suggested by the learned counsel for the respondent, even then the impugned order of reversion cannot be termed as an instance of reduction in rank for attracting the protection under Art. 135 of the Constitution. The language of the impugned order indicates in unmistaken manner that it was never meant to be an order of promotion. In the facts of the case the respondent was not entitled to any show-cause notice nor there was any violation of any principle of natural justice.</u>

<u>32. Therefore, the respondent's contention that he acquired a vested right to the post of IPO by virtue of his acting in that capacity for about five years and enjoying all the emoluments and other benefits must fail. The appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree of the trial Court are restored. No costs.</u>

<u>Before we part with the case, we like to point out and disapprove the manner in which the paperbook was prepared by the appellant. Permission was sought and given to the appellant to prepare the paperbook out of court. The paper book is prepared in a most clumsy manner. Not only papers of different sizes, and photocopies, not easily readable, were used, the orders mentioned in the judgments of the courts below were not included. The very impugned order of reversion is not there. Subsequently, additional paper book has been filed containing a number of departmental circulars without mentioning whether those were exhibited or not in the trial Court. The Attorney-General's Office, which looks after the litigations of the Republic, the single biggest litigant in the country, in the Supreme Court, is expected to follow the rules as to preparation of paper book meticulously so that it sets up a model other litigants may emulate. Prayer for dispensation of paper book or preparation of paper book out of court if facilely prayed for and readily allowed then it would not only whittle down the Rules framed for the convenience of both the court and the counsel, it will cause further trouble if at the hearing of the appeal additional supplemental paper books are filed as an after-thought. The 'main object of the Rules for preparation of paper book is to avoid a clutter which cannot be used as a sorting device for ascertaining facts at the last court of the country.</u>

End.

Abdul Hafiz (Md) and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Director General, Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Government of Bangladesh ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: By this application under Article 102 of the Constitution an order contained in Memo No. 485/DAB (Dhaka) dated 8 April, 1996 has been called in question whereupon a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order contained in Memo No. 485/DAB(Dhaka) dated 8-4-96 (Annexure-A) issued by respondent No.2 should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule may be summarised as follows: The petitioners are full brothers, petitioner No.1 is the Director of Madina Metal Industries, a private Limited Company having been incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act. 1913. The petitioner No.2 is the Managing Director and petitioner Nos.3 and 4 are the Directors of the said Company. The added respondent No.4 AI-Haj Md Faroque is also a full brother of the petitioners and was one of the Directors of the Company. The added respondent No.4 managed the affairs of the Company for about fourteen (14) years as the Managing Director. During 14 years as the Managing Director, he did neither call any meeting of the Board of Directors nor general meeting of the Company. He controlled all the affairs of the company without participation of any other Director. Through a resolution in a meeting of the Board of Directors, the respondent No.4 was removed from the office of the Managing Director and in his place the petitioner No. 2 was appointed as the Managing Director of the Company. In the meeting of the Directors, the new Managing Director, was authorized by the Board to take legal action against the former Managing Director, respondent No.4. The respondent No.4 filed a suit being Title suit No.212 of 1995 in the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for a declaration that he is the Managing Director of the company along with an application for injunction restraining the petitioners from interfering in the affairs of the Company. The learned Subordinate Judge granted an order of injunction. On appeal, the order of injunction was set aside. The respondent No.4 thereafter moved a Civil Revisional Application before the High Court Division and from the statements of the said Revisional application, the petitioner for the first time, came to know that the respondent No.4 made an arrangement for the investigation of the affairs of the Company by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. The petitioners thereafter received the impugned letter issued by the respondent No.2 District Anti-Corruption Officer, Bureau of Anti-Corruption demanding of them for their examination and also producing documents in the interest of proper enquiry. 3. The petitioners challenged the said letter of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption before this Court in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present Rule. 4. The respondent No.4 opposed the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. In the affidavit in-opposition it is stated that instead of appearing before the Bureau of Anti-Corruption, the petitioners approached this court and invoked Special Original Jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution and the writ petition, as such, is not maintainable. It is further stated that the writ petition was solely directed to make delay of the enquiry process. 5. Mr. Moudud Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule, contended, first, that there must be a proceeding before any court of law and unless there is a proceeding before any court of law against the petitioners, they cannot be compelled to appear before the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to face any sort of inquiry. 6. The second branch of contention raised is that the impugned notice issued under the provisions of sections 94/160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is ex facie illegal and the Bureau of Anti-Corruption got no lawful authority to summon the petitioners to have their statement recorded. 7. Finally, Mr. Moudud Ahmed contended that the impugned notice is violative of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 35(4) of the Constitution in the sense that asking the petitioners to be present for examination and recording statements amounts to compelling them to be witnesses against themselves. 8. Mr. Md Farid, learned Advocate, on the other hand, submitted that the notice dated 8-4-96 issued by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption is given on the basis of an order passed by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka sending the petition of complaint to the District Anti-Corruption Officer to take lawful steps on holding proper enquiry and the District Anti-Corruption Officer has got the lawful authority to issue notice upon the petitioner to appear before him in the interest of proper enquiry. 9. For answering the first and second branch of contention raised from the side of the petitioners, it will be appropriate to extract the relevant provisions of sections 94 and 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and also section 3 of the Anti- Corruption Act of 1957 Sections 94 and 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are as follows: Section 94 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, "94 (1) Whenever any Court or any officer in charge of a police-station considers that the production of any document or other thing is necessary or desirable for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code by or before such Court or officer, such Court may issue a summons, or such officer a written order, to the person in whose possession or power such document or, thing is believed to be, requiring him to attend and produce it, or to produce it, at the time and place stated in the summons or order. Provided that no such officer shall" issue any such order requiring the production of any document or other thing which is in the custody of a bank or banker as defined in the Banker's Books Evidence Act (XVIII of 1891), and relates, or might disclose any information which relates, to the bank account of any person except...." (a) for the purpose of investigating an offence under sections 403, 406, 408 and 409 and sections 421 to 424 both inclusive and sections 465 to 477A (both inclusive) of the Penal Code, with the prior permission in writing of a Sessions Judge, and (b) in other cases, with the prior permission in writing of the High Court Division. (2) Any person required under this section merely to produce a document or other thing shall be deemed to have complied with the requisition if he causes such document or thing to be produced instead of attending personally to product the same. (3) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to affect the Evidence Act, 1872, sections 123 and 124, or to apply to a letter, postcard, telegram or other document or any parcel or thing in the custody of the Postal or Telegraph authorities." Section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: "160. Any Police officer making an investigation under this Chapter may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself of any person being within the limits of his own or any adjoining station who, from the information given or otherwise, appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the cases; and such person, shall attend as so required." Section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act of 1957: "3. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Police Act, 1861, the Government may constitute a Bureau to be called the Bureau of Anti-Corruption for enquiry into and investigation in Bangladesh of the offences specified in the Schedule and offences notified by the Government. (2) Subject to any orders which the Government may make in this behalf, officers of the Bureau shall have throughout the state in relation to the enquiry into, and investigation of, such offences all powers of seizure, search and arrest of persons concerned in such offences and all other powers, duties, privileges and liabilities which the police officers of the state have in connection with the investigation of such offences. (3) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 any officer of the Bureau may subject to any orders which the Government may make in this behalf, exercise any of the powers of an officer-in-charge of a police station in the area in which he is for the time being and when so exercising such powers shall, subject to any such orders as aforesaid, be deemed to be an officer-in-charge of a police station discharging the functions of such an office within the limits of his station." 10. Section 94 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that any officer-in-charge of the police station may, for the purpose of any enquiry, issue a summon to a person in whose possession or power any document is believed to be requiring him to attend and produce the document at the time and place stated in the summon. 11. Section 160 of the Code lays down that any police officer making an investigation under Chapter XIV may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself or any person being within the limits of his own or any adjoining station who, from the information given or otherwise, appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case; and such person shall attend as so required. 12. A reading of section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act reveals that any officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption shall be deemed to be an officer-in-charge of a Police Station discharging the functions of a police officer. 13. From the above provision it is manifestly clear that the officer of a Bureau of Anti-Corruption is officer-in-charge of a police station and in discharging the functions of a police officer as enjoined under section 94 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can summon witnesses to attend before him with the documents and to give statements before him. The notice dated 8-4-96 is nothing but a summon requiring the petitioners to appear before the District Anti-Corruption Officer who is deemed to be officer-in-charge of a police station. From the materials on record, it appears, that the District Anti-Corruption Officer did not issue notices to the petitioners out of his own accord but he issued the same in obedience to the order of the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. It is true that under section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the District Anti-Corruption officer is not authorized by law to require the attendance of the petitioners in an inquiry but the authority of the respondent No.2, the District Anti-Corruption Officer requiring the petitioners to attend and give statements before him in the interest of an inquiry under the provisions of section 94 of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be questioned. 14. The order passed by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka is quoted as hereunder:

মুখ্য মহানগর হাকিমের আদালত, ঢাকা

 

সূত্রঃ সিং আর, মামলা নং-৬০২/৯৬

ধারা- ৪৬৫/৪৬৭/৪৬৮/৪৭১ দঃ বিঃ

 

আদেশপত্র

মোঃ ফারুক-----বনাম-----আবদুল হাফিজ গং তারিখ আদেশ স্বাক্ষর ১৬-৩-৯৬ দরখাস্তকারীর নালিশি আরজি দেখিলাম। বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবির বক্তব্য শুনিলাম। তদন্ত পূর্বক আইনানুগ ব্যবস্থা নেওয়ার জন্য জেলা দুর্নীতি দমন অফিসারের নিকট পাঠানো হউক। স্বা-আহাম্মেদ উল্লাহ এম এম ঢাকা 15. From the order dated 16-3-96 passed by the Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, it appears that the learned Metropolitan Magistrate sent the petition of complaint to the District Anti-Corruption Officer for taking necessary step on holding enquiry. The learned Metropolitan Magistrate did not direct the District Anti-Corruption Officer to submit any report in obedience to the said order. The District Anti-Corruption Officer only issued notices to the petitioners in obedience to the order of the learned Metropolitan Magistrate in the interest of a proper inquiry. 16. It appears further from the materials on record that respondent No.4 filed a petition of complaint before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka alleging commission of offences by the petitioners under sections 465, 467 and 471 of Penal Code. The offences under the above sections are specified in the schedule (C) appended to the Anti-Corruption Act. Under the provision of section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act, the Anti- Corruption Officer is authorized to make any enquiry, investigation of offences of the aforesaid sections along with other sections of the Penal Code. The District Anti-Corruption officer issued notice to the petitioners only is the complaint made against them. The first and second branches of contention raised on behalf of the petitioners do not appear to have any merit and the same, thus, fail. 17. It remains now to consider the last and final branch of contention from the side of the petitioners that the impugned notice is violative of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 35(4) of the Constitution. The contention though apparently attractive does not seem to have much substance. 18. To appreciate the contention raised it will be profitable to quote Article 35(4) of the Constitution which runs as follows: "35(1) ........... (2).................. (3).................. (4) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself' 19. Article 35(4) of our Constitution corresponds to Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India and the language of Article 20(3) is exactly the same as of Article 35(4) of our Constitution. Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India reads as follows: "20(1) ............... (2).................. (3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself." 20. Article 35(4) of our Constitution and Article 20(3) of Indian Constitution use the words "accused of an offence". From the language of the said Article it appears that the same will be attracted only, if the proceedings start with an accusation and the person who seeks its protection is already an accused person when he is compelled to give evidence and make statement. It has already been noticed that the learned Metropolitan Magistrate by the order dated 16-3-96 sent the petition of complaint to the District Anti-Corruption Officer for taking step on holding enquiry and the District Anti-Corruption Officer simply issued the impugned notices to the petitioners for recording statements in the interest of a proper enquiry. The enquiry to be carried on by Anti-Corruption Officer appears to be no more than the work of a fact finding commission. The commission of offence may be or may not be discovered as a result of enquiry and the commission of offence, if discovered, then only criminal proceedings may be started against the petitioners. The learned Magistrate did not take cognizance against the petitioners and they had not been made accused. The petitioners, thus, cannot be said to be persons "accused of an offence" as required by Article 35(4) of the Constitution. The Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Article 35(4) does not appear to have been violated in the instant case. 21. The Indian Supreme Court had occasion to deal with similar questions on the alleged violation of Article 20(3) of Indian Constitution in the case of State of Bombay vs Kathi Kaluoghad, AIR 1961 (SC) 1808. Raja Narayanlal Bansilal vs Maneek, AIR 1961 (SC) 29 and Smt Nandini Satpathy vs Kathi Kaluoghad AIR 1961 (SC) 1808 Sinha, CJ, speaking for the majority of the Court, states thus: "To bring the statement in question within the prohibition of Article 20(3), the person accused must have stood in the character of an accused person at the time he made the statement. It is not enough that he should become an accused at any time after the statement has been made." The essence of the decisions in Raja Narayanlal Bansilal vs Maneek, AIR 1961 (SC) 29 and Smt, Nandini Satpathy vs PL Dani AIR 1978 (SC) 1025 is that to bring a person within the meaning of 'accused of an offence' that person must assimilate the character of an 'accused person' in the sense that he must be accused of any offence. 22. It need be stated further that in the impugned notice, no compulsion is mandated upon the petitioners to give evidence against themselves. In the enquiry before the District Anti-Corruption Officer, the petitioners can very well controvert the allegations made against them in the petition of complaint. It cannot, thus, be suggested that by mere issuance of notices, the petitioners, as accused persons, are compelled to give evidence or to be witnesses against themselves. Article 35(4), therefore, is of no avail to the petitioners. 23. It will be worthy to consider one legal aspect of the matter. The petitioners invoked extraordinary original jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution for declaring the impugned order to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The petitioners could very well invoke criminal jurisdiction under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure to ventilate their grievances. But without availing of the remedy, available to them, under the Criminal jurisdiction, they invoked the writ jurisdiction. The petitioners cannot be allowed to thwart a jurisdiction under which they could ventilate their grievances. We are of this view that the extraordinary writ jurisdiction had been invoked by the petitioners under a total misconception of law. The writ petition does not appear to be at all maintainable. 24. In view of the discussion made hereinbefore, we are of the view that this Rule is devoid of any substance and the same must be discharged. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to cost. End.

(From the judgment and order dated 10.5.1988 passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench, Chittagong in Civil Revision No. 131 of 1985). 
This decision is dissented from the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 171.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed C.J.: In this appeal by special leave the question is whether, on the death of a monthly tenant judgment-debtor, his heirs can be substituted for the purpose of execution of the decree for ejectment. In order words, whether a monthly tenancy is heritable. In an earlier decision of this Court in the case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Suresh Chandra Das, 32 DLR (171, which was followed in the case of Abdul Latif Vs. Abdul Mannan 1982 BCR, AD, 428, it was held by this Court that a monthly tenancy was not heritable and that the right of a monthly tenant in respect of a premises was his personal right which ceased on his death. Facts leading to this question are given below.

2. Respondents-landlords filed Other Suit No.172 of 1976 in the First Court of Munsif, Chittagong for ejectment of their monthly tenant, Sukhendu Bikash Das, on the ground of default in the payment of rent and also of bonafide requirement of the premises by them. The suit was decreed and the decree was upheld upto the High Court Division and thereafter the decree was put into execution by filing Execution Case No. 23 of 1984 against the tenant-judgment-debtor. During the pendency of the Execution Proceeding, the tenant, Sukhendu Das, died whereupon his heirs, who are appellants before us, were substituted. But they challenged the continuation of the Execution Proceeding by an application under section 151 of the Civil PC alleging that the tenancy created in favour of their predecessor, Sukhendu Das, ceased to exist on his death as it was his personal right and, as such, the decree against him became infructuous. Their contention was upheld by the learned Munsif who further held that for ejectment of the appellants a fresh suit was to be filed. But in revision, CR No.131 of 1985, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, held that the decree passed against the original tenant during his life time was perfectly valid and did not become infructuous and further that his heirs, though they did not inherit the tenancy right, were not trespassers either, but they became "tenants by sufferance". The Execution Proceeding was therefore held maintainable. Both the learned Single Judge and the learned Munsif sought support for their respective views from the decision of this Court in the earlier case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Suresh Chandra Das, 32 DLR (AD) 171 as referred to above.

3. Mr. SR Pal, learned Counsel, has appeared for the appellants in this case. He has submitted, though half-heartedly, that in view of the decision in the 32 DLR (AD) 171, the relationship of landlord and tenant in this case snapped on the death of the original tenant, Sukhendu Das, that his heirs did not inherit the tenancy and as such they could not have been substituted in the execution proceeding as the tenancy in favour of Sukhendu Das was a personal right which "is not heritable". The learned Counsel has, however, expressed serious doubt about the correctness of the decision in the 32 DLR (AD) 171 case and has submitted that if contention of the appellants in this case is rejected and decision of the learned Single Judge is upheld, the decision of this Court in 32 DLR (AD) 171 that the right of a monthly tenant is not heritable cannot but be reviewed and reconsidered.

4. In the earlier case, Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel had appeared for the appellant-landlord, and submitted that a monthly tenancy was heritable. To assist the Court Mr. SR Pal was engaged as amicus curiae in that ease. After hearing both Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed and Mr. SR Pal in that case, this Court rejected Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed's contention and held as stated above. In the instant case, Mr. SR Pal his appeared for the appellants-tenants; he has relied upon 32 DLR (AD) 171 decision in the different context. We engaged Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed as amicus curiae in this case. On behalf of the respondents-landlords Mr. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record has appeared to defend the decision of the High Court Division that the Execution Proceeding is quite maintainable.

5. As appears, the question before us in this appeal is a question of great public importance. Both Mr. SR Pal and Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed cited before us a great number of decisions including some decisions from the Indian jurisdiction. Mr. Pal, though he defends the High Court Division's decision in this case, has expressed the view that the earlier decision of this Court is not correct and that it has created serious complications in the landlord-tenant relation in respect of monthly tenants. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed has reiterated his earlier stand that the right of a monthly tenant is heritable and that the earlier decision of this Court was not based on correct interpretation of Sections 105 and 106 of the Transfer of Property Act governing "lease of immovable property". Both the learned Counsels have contended that the earlier decision of this Court had resulted from an erroneous view that a lease under section 105, TP Act is quite different from a lease under section 106 of that Act. They contend that a tenancy, whatever may be its duration, is a "lease" and that the right of the tenant is not a personal right but it is survived by, and passes on, to his "legal representatives", as defined in the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 and also within the meaning of section 2(11) of the CP Code. In a nutshell, the decision in the previous case, in their opinion, needs to be reconsidered.

<u>6. Section 105 of the TP Act says that lease of an immovable property "is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property". This section is quoted below.</u>

<u>"105. A lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property, made for a certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised, or of money, a share of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically or on specified occasions to the transferor by the transferee, who accepts the transfer on such terms". (relevant portion only).</u>

<u>It appears clearly that "lease" in this section is a right only of occupation of an immovable property for a certain time and that this right is created by transfer from one person to another. The transferor is called 'lessor' and the transferee is called 'lessee'. The period of the right of enjoyment of the property, under this section, is for a "certain time" or" in perpetuity".</u>

<u>7. Section 106 TP Act speaks of duration of certain leases "in the absence of contract, or local law or usage to the contrary"; it also provides for termination of certain leases by notice, again, in the absence of any contract, local law or usage to the contrary. This section is quoted below:</u>

<u>"106. In the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six months' notice expiring with the end of a year of the tenancy; and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen days' notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy " (relevant portion only)</u>

<u>This section provides that in the absence of a contract (or local law or usage), a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes "shall be deemed to be" a lease from year to year; and a lease for any other purpose, say for residential purpose, "shall be deemed to be" a lease from "month to month". It is here from which the term 'monthly tenancy' is derived. At to termination of these two kinds of leases, one from "year to year" and the other "from month to month", it has been provided in this section that in the case of the former, it is terminable by six months' notice expiring with the end of the year of the tenancy, and in the case of the latter, it is terminable by fifteen days' notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. On careful consideration of these sections, we find that a 'lease', whatever may be its purpose or duration, is created only under section 105. This section does not say that a lease for an agricultural or manufacturing purpose shall always be a lease from year to year, or a lease for any other purpose shall always be a lease from month to month. In this section a legal fiction has been introduced in the words, "shall be deemed to be", just to fill up the vacuum left in the contract if any, or when there is no contract creating the lease, as to duration of the lease and the manner of its termination. As to a tenancy from month to month, it is provided, it shall be deemed to be terminable by fifteen days notice. This does not necessarily mean that its duration is only one month and that on the expiry of one month it shall cease to exist. A monthly tenancy, if provided in the contract, may continue for months or years together unless it is determined by a notice to quit under this section. In the case of monthly tenancy, the period of which has been fixed in the contract, it shall continue till the expiration of that period which may be one month or one year or several years. Similarly, the period of notice to quit may also vary in terms of the contract, such as, if the contract fixes the period of notice, say, two months, then notice of fifteen days will not be valid.</u>

<u>8. Section 111, TP Act, shows different ways and grounds for determination of a lease. One of the grounds for determination of a lease is "efflux of time limited thereby". That is, the period of the lease stated in the lease-agreement has expired. This means that if the period of a lease is fixed by the contract, written or creating the lease, then the lease shall stand terminated on the expiry of this period. Another way of determination of a lease is by serving a notice to quit upon the lessee by the lessor. This provision comes into play when no definite period has been fixed in the contract creating the lease. A lease may also be determined by voluntary surrender of the property to the lessor by the lessee. It may be noted that "death" of the lessee has not been mentioned in this section as a ground for determination of a lease.</u>

<u>9. In the previous decision of this Court 132 DLR (AD) 171], a clear distinction was made between a lease under section 105 and a lease under section 106 of the TP Act; whereas, these two sections do not appear to say so. In that decision a lease under section 105 was held to be a right in an immovable property but not so a lease under section 106. Upon consideration of section 105 it was observed in para 11 of that decision : "The lease, as defined, no doubt creates an interest in immovable property and the Act also says that it is transferable" We are to see the true character of the lease created under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act." It was further observed in para 13; "Analysing in this way, we find that a relationship is created under this section between the landlord and the tenant which is of a personal nature. The right of occupation of the premises has been given, and this right of occupation from month to month, from its very nature, cannot but be personal and so cannot create an interest in the land as a lease under section 105 does. The right of occupation remains personal with the tenant. The right being personal it ceases with the death of either party and so on the death of the tenant, the tenancy ceases and hence it is not heritable".</u>

<u>10. The Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963, in section 2(8), defines "tenant" which expression includes his "legal representative" "as defined in the Civil Procedure Code". A tenant under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance means "any person by whom, or on whose account, rent is payable for any premises and includes a legal representative as defined in the Civil Procedure Code". Furthermore, a person continuing in possession after the termination of a tenancy is also a tenant under this definition. A "legal representative" within the meaning of section 2(11) of the Civil PC means "a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, and includes any person who intermeddles with the estate of the deceased and where a party sues or is sued in a representative character the person on whom the estate devolves on the death of the party so suing or sued". A tenant under the Ordinance is same as a lessee under the TP Act and the monthly tenancy is also a lease within the meaning of section 105 TP Act. 'Tenancy' has not been defined in the Ordinance, but it clearly falls within "lease" as described in section 105 TP Act. "Tenancy" relates to "premises" which has been defined in the Ordinance". "Premises" means any building/hut or its part to be left for residential or non-residential purpose and includes garden, out-house and also furniture supplied by landlord. Whereas, lease 'covers all immovable property including a premises'. A legal representative of a person is one who represents his estate on his death. The lease under section 105 TP Act is transfer of a right to enjoy an immovable property. This right to enjoy, by occupation of a premises, which is no doubt an immovable property, is a limited right. Premises Rent Control Ordinance is intended to govern some specific aspects of a monthly tenancy, such as, the procedure for determination of a tenancy, for protecting tenant against unjust or improper eviction and prohibition of increase in the rent by undue means. Section 18 of the Ordinance is relevant for this purpose. Provision of this section shall prevail "notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 or the Contract Act, 1872". The provision is that no order or decree for recovery of possession of a premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent in full and regularly and performs all other conditions of the tenancy. In the previous decision the definition of "legal representative" of a tenant was of course looked into, but it was observed in para 8 that "the definition was inserted in the Ordinance only to emphasize the tenant's liability to pay rent and nothing more and this meaning becomes clear when we advert to the second half of the definition of 'tenant' which says that it also includes a person continuing in possession after the termination of the tenancy". We find it rather difficult to accept this view as correct that 'legal representative' of a deceased tenant will be brought to the scene only to pay rent and not to inherit the deceased tenant's right to hold the tenancy for the purpose of enjoying or occupying the premises.</u>

<u>11. A monthly tenancy being a lease within the meaning of section 105, TP Act, it is an interest in an immovable property. It is transfer of an interest in the property as shown in this section. The TP Act does not specifically say that a lease is heritable also, because this Act is not intended to govern the matter of succession to immovable property. But the incidence of heritability is easily discernible from the tenancy being an interest in the property. It is also easily gathered from the fact that a contract, which creates a tenancy is binding upon the parties to the contract as well as upon their heirs, and that, a contract is legally enforceable against parties thereto and their heirs. A tenancy may be created under a statute also; such as, on legal termination of a tenancy, a person continuing in possession and paying rent to the landlord, who accepts it, becomes a statutory tenant. In the instant case, we are not dealing with any statutory tenant. The tenancy in this case is a contractual tenancy. Right in such a tenancy is ordinarily heritable, though this right is limited "to enjoy" and occupy the property only, and the tenant is liable to be ejected either on the expiration of the fixed period, if any, or by notice to quit.</u>

12. A number of cases from Indian jurisdiction have been cited before us in order to support the view that a monthly tenancy is heritable though right in the tenancy is limited or partial and the tenant inherits only that right which the original tenant held and nothing more. Among others, the following cases have been considered by us: Rajib Hossain and another Vs. Nowab Unus Khan, AIR 1937 Nagpur, 321; Anwar Ali Bepari Vs. Janakilal Roy Chowdhury, 43 CWN, 797; Smt. Vishnawati Vs. BV Chowdhury, AIR 1970, All. 389; Sau Nakabai Vs. Mahadu Sakharam Adsule and others, AIR 1980 Bom. 208. The then Dhaka High Court also held this view in the case of Gouribala Pal Vs. Kunjalal Saha, 12 DLR 37. The Indian Supreme Court, in the case of Damadilal and others Vs. Parashram and others, AIR 1976 (SC) 2229 considered the question as to heritability of a in contract. There is no dispute that a contractual tenant has an estate or property in the subject-matter of the tenancy and heritability is an incident of the tenancy. It cannot be assumed, however, that with the determination of the tenancy the estate must necessarily disappear and the statute can only preserve his status of irremovability and not the estate he had in the premises in his occupation".

<u>13. That a tenancy is an interest in an immovable property was considered from another angle in a Letters-Patent appeal in the case of Ramchandra Annappa Vs. Subraya Timmaya, AIR 1951 Boni. 127. The question there was whether "tenancy right is protected under section 53A of the TP Act." It was contended that the tenancy being merely a transfer of a "partial right in property" viz a right to enjoy the property, it could not be said to be a transfer of property within the meaning of the expression used in section 53A of TP Act. The contention was rejected and it was held that though the right is only to enjoy the property still it is a right and the tenancy is a transfer of immovable property within the meaning of section 53A of the TP Act.</u>

<u>14. This Court in the previous decision (32 DLR (AD) 171) took into consideration two concepts of English law of tenancy to support the view that a monthly tenancy creates only "personal right" of the tenant which vanishes with his death. One of the concepts is "tenancy-at-will". Such a tenancy under the English law is created and continues at the mere will of the landlord; it is terminable at any time, without any notice, at the mere will of the landlord; it is also terminable at any time, without any notice at the wish of the tenant. The relation between landlord and tenant under this concept of tenancy is a personal relation between the two and is terminable by the death of either of them. From this point of view, this Court came to the conclusion that a tenancy from month to month is in the nature of the English tenancy of "tenancy-at-will". In our law governing tenancy there is no such concept as "tenancy-at-will" to be terminable at any time and without any notice at the mere wish of either party. Under our law a person may get possessory right in an immovable property by a licence granted by the owner of such property. Such a right is terminable, at any time, at the mere will of the person granting the licence. The person who is granted this right is Galled a "licensee". A licensee is not a tenant; but a tenant from month to month under TP Act is different from a licensee. Taking them at par is found to have led to the erroneous view that a monthly tenant is same as a "tenant-at-will". A tenancy from month to month, as we have already found, dots not mean that it is meant for only one month, at the end of which it ceases to exist, and thereupon, a fresh tenancy is to start. Similar view was taken in the case of Usha Rani Devi Vs. The Research Industries Ltd., 50 CWN, 461. There it has been held that a monthly tenancy is not a tenancy which commences or begins in one month, and on the expiry, a fresh tenancy is created in the following month or months, but is a tenancy for an unstated period, which is, however, determinable by either party by a notice to quit.</u>

<u>15. The other English concept, as considered by this Court in the earlier case, is "tenant by sufferance". A tenancy created by sufferance comes into being when, on the lawful termination of a tenancy, the landlord by his own act of negligence, does not take steps to enforce his right of evicting the tenant who therefore continues in possession by landlord's negative permission. Such a tenant by "sufferance" acquires no right in the property which can be transferred or inherited. Nevertheless, such a tenant is not a trespasser either, for neither he nor his predecessor-tenant entered upon the property by wrongful means. In the previous decision a tenant from month to month was thus taken as a synonym of the English "tenant by sufferance". In our law there is no such concept as "tenant by sufferance", who is liable to be evicted at any time and who does not inherit any right in the property. Under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, a tenant may continue in possession even after lawful termination of his tenancy. A lessee may continue in possession of a lease property on its lawful termination if the landlord either expressly or impliedly recognises him as lessee taking rent from him; he is called a tenant by holding over under section 116 of the TP Act. He is not a tenant by sufferance. Death of the original tenant is not a ground for determining the tenancy, nor a person continuing in possession of the tenancy on the death of the original tenant, as found in that decision, is a trespasser either. In such a circumstance, the only basis of his possession is the right of in her now ever limited in scope that right may be.</u>

16. In the instant case, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division accepted the contention of the appellants-tenants that they had not inherited the tenancy from their father, the original tenant, but nevertheless, held them to be "tenants by sufferance" as they were not trespassers. This view is erroneous.

17. If a monthly tenancy is found to be heritable a question may arise, whether any difficulty will be faced by landlord if a notice to quit is to be served on several persons who may inherit a tenancy right on the death of their predecessor-tenant. We do not think that any such difficulty will arise. For, on the death of the original tenant several heirs may inherit his right, and all of them become co-tenants or joint tenants. All of them may not be in actual occupation of the premises. A notice under section 106 TP Act must be addressed to all the co-tenants, or joint tenants, but service of the notice upon any one of them must be treated as prima facie service upon them all. If none of them is found in the premises the notice may be served upon "one of his family or servants at the premises". If none of them is found at the premises, the notice may be served by affixing it to any conspicuous part of the premises, as specifically laid down in the second paragraph of section 106. We get support to this view from a number of decisions including the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Harihar Banerji Vs. Ramshasi Roy, AIR 1918 (PC) 102. This decision was followed by us in SM Bindubashini Chanda Vs. Al-haj Jahanara Begum, 1982 BCR (AD) 181.

<u>18. In conclusion, we find that a tenancy from month to month is a lease which, like any other lease, is contemplated only in section 105 TP Act and that the right therein is heritable and not personal to vanish with the tenant's death. The right on inheritance is same as that of the original tenant and not in any way better or higher than his right. On re-consideration of the previous decision in 32 DLR (AD) 171 case in the light of the materials now placed before us, we find that that decision is not correct. The Execution Proceeding against the appellants in this case is maintainable. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is upheld, though on different grounds as given above. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed without, however, any order as to cost.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is directed at the instance of the defendant Government, represented by the ADC Revenue, Dinajpur and Assistant Commissioner (Land & Revenue), Dinajpur as to why delay of 1302 days in filing the connected revision shall not be condoned under section 5 of the Limitation Act.

2. The opposite party's Other Suit 193 of 1981 was dismissed on 12-9-83 against which the Govt. took Other Appeal 51 of 1985 which has been allowed on 11-8-85, decreeing the said suit declaring that the order dated 6-12-1979 passed by the defendant 2 in Misc. Case 413-6/77-78 leasing out a portion of the suit land to the defendant 3 as vested property, is illegal and void and the said order is not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. Against the same, the present proposed revision is being preferred by the Government. But there is delay of 1302 days in filing the revision.

4. Case of the defendant-petitioner for condonation of delay has been made out as follows:

5. The impugned judgment and decree in appeal was passed on 11-8-85. The Deputy Commissioner, Thakurgaon on 16-11-1985 sent a letter to the Deputy Attorney-General, deputed to the Rangpur Bench of the then concerned High Court Division for filing the revision. It was received on 17-11-1985. The Assistant Attorney-General in charge Me SA Hasan after necessary scrutiny found that some papers were not available in the records. He then wrote a letter to the Deputy Commissioner, Thakurgaon on 17-11-85 to send the necessary papers including vokalatnama, cost etc, on 20-11-85. A letter was sent along with vokalatnama and a cheque for necessary costs to the Deputy Attorney-General at Rangpur. It was received by the Assistant Attorney-General Mr SA Hasan. Mr Hasan then wrote another letter on 18-2-86 to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) who is also the Assistant Custodian of Vested and Non-resident Property (Land & Building), Thakurgaon who was the concerned Officer to send the necessary papers along with the certified copy of the judgments and decree of the said appeal and those of the suit. Because previously although the money as to the costs of the revision and vokalatnama, etc, was sent, papers like judgment and decree, etc. were not sent On 5-3-1986 certified copy of the judgment were sent to Mr Hasan, for filing the revision. But last date for filing the revision expired on 31-1-1986. It is alleged that thereafter entire file and records of the said case were misplaced and could not be traced out from the office of said Assistant Attorney-General Mr Hasan and he could not file the revision. After wards several letters were written from the office of the Deputy Commissioner Thasurgaon, such as memo No. 6(ছয়) 2/88-89 VP dated 23-5-89, memo No. 6(ছয়)2/88-89/59 VP dated 22-6-89 and memo No. 6(ছয়)-2/88-89" -170(2)NP dated 4-7-89 to the Deputy Attorney-General, Rangpur, mentioning name of the said Assistant Attorney-General, to know about the fate of the case. But no reply was communicated by Mr Hasan. In the meantime there was a change in the appointment of the Assistant Attorney-General and Mr Sajjad Ali Chowdhury was appointed as Assistant Attorney-General on 19-2-1989 in place of Mr Hasan. Mr Sajjad Ali Chowdhury having been entrusted with the charge of the Rangpur Bench tried to find out the said misplaced file and lastly on 4-7 -89 he could find out the file and record of the case. Thereafter he wrote a letter vide memo No. 33 VP dated 5-7-89 to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Thasurga on informing that since the previous Assistant Attorney-General Mr Hasan was transferred to the Jessore High Court Bench, so Mr Sajjad Ali Chowdhury needed fresh Vokalatnama and necessary costs to file the revisional application and accordingly, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Thakurgaon sent the Vokalatnama along with some amount to meet the cost, on 11-7-89 and it was received on 12-7-89 by Mr Sajjad Ali Chowdhury and then this revisional application was filed on 26-7-89 but there is delay of 1302 days.

6. Plaintiff opposite party is resisting the application for condonation of delay on the ground that it is utter negligence on the part of the Government in filing this revisional application and the delay is not bonafide, so it should not be condoned.

7. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that Government as a litigant should not suffer, even if negligence is found on the part of the Assistant Attorney-General, as in the instant case, because the Government's interest is the public interest and collective interest. The Government as litigant cannot take a quick decision regarding a case, as a private litigant can. Many persons and authorities are involved in case of the government and, as a result, sometimes, it may happen that Government cannot arrange everything such as Vokalatnama, filing cost and certified copy of the concerned case, etc. quickly and in time, as a private litigant can. So, it is not unlikely on the part of the Government to invite some delay, which may become sometimes unusual as it has happened in this case.

8. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also submits that although the delay is inordinate and unusual, in this case, it should be condoned considering the helpless position of the Government who is to depend upon many officers and agencies to work out a decision.

<u>9. Our Appellate Division in the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) & Assistant Custodian, Vested Property, Serajgonj vs. Md Abdul Majid and others, 17 BLD (AD) 57 has held that although there is no specific limitation provided for filing of a revision, it should be filed within 90 days which is prescribed by law for an appeal. In that case, their Lordships also held that in an appropriate case, the High Court Division can condone the reasonable delay.</u>

<u>10. Law of Limitation does not provide any period for filing a revision (See the decision in the case of Mohammad Eshaque vs. Ruhul Amin and others, 34 DLR 342). Therefore, it can be said that if the petitioner can satisfy the court as to the causes of delay and can furnish explanation as to the same the court can condone delay in appropriate case. It is also settled principle of law that delay of every day is to be explained and no discrimination can be made between a private party and the Government. Admitting all the aforesaid positions of law and fact the learned Deputy Attorney-General relied on the decision in the case of Collector, Land Acquisition Anantnag and another vs. Mst Katiji and others, reported in 1987 AIR (SC) 1353. In that decision their Lordships have held as under:</u>

<u>"Ordinarily a litigant does not stand to benefit by lodging an appeal late. Refusing to condone delay can result in a meritorious matter being thrown out at the very threshold and cause of justice being defeated. As against this when delay is condoned the highest that can happen is that a case would be decided on merit after hearing the parties.</u>

<u>Every day's delay must be explained does not mean that a pedantic approach should be made. Why not every hour's delay, every second's delay? The doctrine must be applied in a rational common sense pragmatic manner. When substantial justice and technical consideration are pitted against each other, cause of substantial justice deserves to be preferred for the other side cannot claim to have vested right in injustice being done because of a non-deliberate delay. There is no presumption that delay is occasioned deliberately, or on account of culpable negligence, or on account of malafides. A litigant does not stand to benefit by resorting to delay. In fact, he runs a serious risk.</u>

<u>It must be granted that judiciary is respected not on account of its power to legalise injustice on technical grounds but because it is capable of removing injustice and is expected to do so."</u>

<u>In the case of G Ramagowda, Major, etc. vs. Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bangalore, reported in 1988 AIR 897 it has been held as follows:</u>

<u>"The law of limitation is, no doubt, the same for a private citizen as for Government authorities. Government, like any other litigant, must take responsibility for the acts or commission of its officers. But a somewhat different complexion is imparted to the matter where Government makes out a case where public interest was shown to have suffered owing to acts of fraud or bad faith on the part of the officers or agents and where the officers were clearly at cross purposes with it. Thereafter, in assessing what, in a particular case, constitutes sufficient cause, for purposes of section 5, it might perhaps be somewhat unrealistic to exclude from the considerations that go into the judicial verdict, those factors which are peculiar to and characteristic of the functioning of the Government. Government decisions are proverbially slow, encumbered as they are, by a considerable degree of procedural red-tape in the process of their making. A certain amount of latitude is, therefore, not impermissible."</u>

<u>In the case of Bangladesh vs. Jaharuddin, reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 180 it has been held as under:</u>

<u>"In matters of condonation of delay Government does not enjoy any special privilege, but the fact remains that due to the necessity to obtain opinions on various authorities concerned before filing an appeal, some time may reasonably be expected to elapse which in the case of an individual does not happen. Some consideration in appropriate circumstances may, therefore, be extended to Government appearing as a litigant. In saying so, no rule is being laid down for not observing strictness of the proof of substantial and reasonable cause in making such delay. Standard of acceptance must, however, remain the same in case of both citizens and State."</u>

<u>In the case of Imanuddin Sheikh and others.vs. Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Bagerhat, reported in 14 BLD 198 wherein it has been held as follows:</u>

<u>"There is no doubt about the legal position that the law of limitation operates equally for or against the private party and also on the Government. But it is a fact, which must be accepted, that a private litigant is normally presumed to be aware of all the factors and aspects of his case and he has only to make up his own mind as to pursue further of his litigation, whereas in the case of Government, a longer time is required for enquiry and consideration vis-a-vis public interest by not only one agency, but several ones before taking final decision, and thereafter, acting thereon. Thus period of time which may be sufficient for a private litigant may not be so for the Government."</u>

<u>Mr Zahedul Bari, the learned Counsel for the opposite party, opposes the condonation of delay by citing the decision in the case of The Principal Secretary, President's Secretariat, and others vs. Mohammad Abdul Baten reported in 1994 BLT (SC) 90 where in their Lordships have held in the similar circumstances as in the present case, that the Assistant Attorney-General who was found negligent resulting in causing the delay in filing of the related application and that was dismissed. The learned Counsel also cites the decision in the case of Bangladesh vs. Abdul Wahed and others, reported in 12 BLD (HCD) 368. That decision, at first, was a dissenting one and it was resolved by a 3rd Judge, Mr Justice BB Roy Chowdhury, the then Judge of the High Court Division who has subscribed his view as under:</u>

<u>"The expression 'sufficient cause' being incapable of any precise definition, no hard and fast rule is there for determination what facts would constitute sufficient cause. It depends on the facts and circumstances of a particular case, but one rule is firmly established that once the normal period of limitation is allowed to run out the appellant has to explain every day's delay beyond the period of limitation and the Government cannot have a preferential treatment in this regard:'</u>

<u>In that case, the 3rd Judge, Mr Justice Syed Fuzle Ahmed has held as under:</u>

<u>"A party wishing to take advantage of section 5 of the Limitation Act must satisfy the court that it had not been negligent and had been prosecuting the case with due diligence and care. Petitioner is under strict legal duty to furnish cause for condonation of delay. The question of excusing delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act, has to be approached from' the point of view of the petitioner's conduct. The Court has no jurisdiction to extend the time where petitioner has been negligent and inactive."</u>

<u>In deciding the question of limitation and condoning the delay, I do not feel it necessary todiscuss the facts or merits of the case of the parties in this litigation.</u>

11. From my meticulous consideration of the aforesaid decisions and hearing the learned Counsels at a reasonable length, I am convinced that in this case, the delay has occurred for the negligence or for any connivance of the then Assistant Attorney- General Mr Hasan, with some interested hand, which is of course unseen. The explanation for delay, as made out in the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act, is clear and bonafide. No doubt the delay has been explained with cogent reasons as far as possible. Now only question remains, whether the litigant namely, Government in this case, which admittedly has to depend upon its officers and agencies to take final decision, shall suffer for delay which has been caused because of the conduct of the law officer, or the delay should be condoned giving chance to the losing party to fight the litigation, finally and effectively, on merits or the government shall be thrown out like a dumb driven cattle, on the point of limitation. Here, in the present case, from the activities of the Assistant Attorney-General it is apparent that he was very much negligent in conducting the Government briefs to file the connected Revision.

12. It is the settled principle of law that a litigant should not suffer for negligence of the Counselor of a lawyer as on him the litigant has to depend. Therefore, we cannot make a difference between the government and a private party in giving effect to the said principle of law.

13. A cheque and the Vokalatnama were already sent by the Deputy Commissioner, Thakurgaon to the Assistant Attorney-General Mr Hasan. Again the same emerged and the present Assistant Attorney-General had to bring it for the second time. The petitioner thus was totally dependent upon the Assistant Attorney-General Mr Hasan who was in charge of the matter to file its revision. Although the last date for filing of the revision expired on 30-1-1986, the same could not be filed on the ground that whole records of the case were misplaced from the office of the Assistant Attorney-General and were not traceable. So, the question poses whether the Government as a litigant should be saddled with the liability and be taxed and thrown out on point of limitation only or be considered with a lenient view giving a chance to the government, who admittedly has to depend on various authorities and agencies in taking necessary action to follow up a particular litigation involving public and collective interest. Examining the majority decisions including those of the Indian Supreme Court as quoted above, I am of the opinion that the Government's difficulty should be decided more closely and carefully as to condonation of delay to give relief to the Government which is a mere concept and it has to depend on others in making decision or taking action. Government's interest is nobody's interest and it is also everybody's interest In the present case also there was as Assistant Attorney-General in charge for filing the revision, but he could not file it because the case records were misplaced or may be for some unseen reason, so it was beyond the control of the Government as a litigant, like other litigants, to file the revision within time.

<u>14. The condonation of delay always depends upon the discretion of the court concerned. If the court is satisfied as to the reason and explanation of delay, it can be condoned.</u>

15. It is on record that in the last leg of the matter new appointments were made to the law officers. In this case also former Assistant Attorney-General Mr SA Hasan was replaced by Mr Sajjad Ali Chowdhury who very diligently tried to salvage the case from further ruination as to limitation which already ran away long before and he has made out the case in the present form for condonation of delay. It is clear that the Government as a litigant had been very active and it had no negligence in pursuing the matter. The question is not the days of delayit is the manner and bonafide how the delay has been explained. In this case the explanation of delay is found satisfactory and bonafide.

For the reason and discussions above the Rule is made absolute. The delay is condoned. The connected decision shall be listed for hearing as application for hearing on merits, for the purpose of issuance of Rule if any.

End.
