full_judgment:
By this application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the concurrent decisions of the courts below has been called in question by the defendant petitioners whereupon a Rule was issued calling upon the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 8-8-1990 passed by the learned District Judge, Cox's Bazar in Title Appeal No. 66 of 1988 shall not be set aside.

2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule may be summarised as follows:

The opposite party No.1 as plaintiff filed a suit being Other Suit No. 370 in the Court of Munsif, Cox's Bazar for a declaration that the registered sale deeds dated 31-8-77 executed by the proforma-defendant No. 7 (predecessor of opposite party Nos. 3-10 in favour of the defendant petitioners are forged, fraudulent, without consideration, collusive, void ab-initio; inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff. Subsequently, the suit, on transfer to the court of Assistant Judge, Chakaria, Cox's Bazar was renumbered as Other Suit No. 203.

3. Moulana Naimuddin Ahmed, being the owner of the suit land measuring .60 acres of land, gifted the same along with other properties in favour of defendant No. 7 by way of registered deed of gift who, thereafter, transferred the same in favour of the plaintiff by way of kabala deed dated 15 June, 1977 in the benami of his wife Ayesa Begum, defendant No. 2. Since purchase, the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land. Defendant Nos. 1-5 obtained two kabala deeds in respect of the suit land along with other lands in collusion with the defendant No. 7 on 8 August, 1977. The said two deeds are forged, fabricated and ante-dated.

4. During pendency of the suit, the plaintiff having been dispossessed by the defendants from the suit property on 30-4-1986, filed an application for amendment of the plaint inserting prayer for recovery of possession and for mesneprofit. The prayer for amendment was allowed by the Court. The suit, after amendment, stood as a suit for declaration that the defendant kabala deeds are forged, fraudulent, collusive, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff and also for recovery of khas possession over the suit land and mesneprofit.

5. The defendant Nos. 1-5 contested the suit by filing written statement traversing all the material allegations made in the plaint and stated that the defendant No. 7 entered into an agreement to sell with the defendant Nos. 3-5 for an area of .40 acres of land for a consideration of Taka 7,000.00 out of which Taka 5,000.00 had been paid as advance on 10 October, 1971 and the defendants were inducted into possession of the said land. It was further stated that the defendant Nos.l and 2 entered into a separate agreement to sell with the defendant No. 7 with respect to .30 acres of land for a consideration of Taka 5,000.00 out of which Taka 3,000.00 had been paid as advance on 30 December, 1971 and they were inducted into possession on the said land. The defendant Nos. 1-5 got kabala deed executed and registered on 31 August, 1977 on payment of rest consideration money to defendant No.7. It was pleaded that the plaintiff acquired no right, title and possession over the suit land.

6. The trial Judge held that the defendant No. 7 got No legal authority to transfer the disputed land by way of any legal instrument to the defendant Nos. 1-5 and the Bainapatra deeds in favour of the defendants were collusive and fraudulent The trial Judge, further, recorded finding that the plaintiff acquired right and title over the suit land before the execution and registration of the kabala deeds in favour of the defendant Nos. 1-5 by the defendant No. 7.

7. With the above findings, the trial Judge decreed the suit. The kabala deeds dated 8 August, 1977 in favour of the defendant Nos. 1-5 had been declared illegal, collusive, inoperative and fraudulent. Decree of recovery of Khas possession over the suit land had been also granted in favour of the plaintiff. The trial Judge rejected the relief of mesneprofit.

8. The defendant Nos. 1-5, being aggrieved by the said decree, carried an appeal being Title Appeal No. 66 of 1988 in the Court of District Judge, Cox's Bazar. The plaintiff took a cross objection before the District Judge in respect of mesneprofit not granted by trial Judge in his favour.

9. Learned District Judge concurred with the decisions arrived at by trial Judge that the Bainapatra deeds are false, collusive and ante-dated and those have been created to deprive the plaintiff. The learned District Judge held in agreement with the decision of the trial Judge that since the plaintiffs Kabala was prior to that of the defendant's kabala in respect of the same land, section 48 of Transfer of Property Act gives the plaintiff right to enjoy such property on priority basis. Learned District Judge, thus, dismissed the appeal and also the cross objection by the judgment and decree dated August, 8, 1990.

10. Feeling aggrieved by the aforesaid' judgment and decree, the defendant Nos. 1-5 approached this court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

11. Mr AQM Shafiullah, learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule, submitted that the plaint as has been couched is a suit within the purview of section 39 of the Specific Relief Act and the same does not fall within the frame work of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the suit framed under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is not at all maintainable and both the courts below failed to consider the legal aspect of the matter and committed a substantial error of law in awarding decree in favour of the plaintiff.

12. Mr SC Das, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff, on the other hand, contended that it is the substance and not form of the plaint which is to be looked and on perusal of the plaint as a whole it appears that the suit falls within the purview of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

13. In order to appreciate the rival contentions raised from both the sides, it will be appropriate to quote both section 39 and 42 of the Specific Relief Act which are extracted below:

"39. Any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such.instrument if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable; and the Court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.

If the instrument has been registered under the Registration Act, 1908, the Court shall also send a copy of its decree to the officer in whose office the instrument has been so registered; and such officer shall note on the copy of the instrument contained in his books the fact of its cancellation.

42. Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the Court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief:

Provided that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so".

14.From the above provisions it appears that relief by cancellation of instrument have been specifically provided for in section 39 of the Specific Relief Act. This section appears in Chapter-V which opens with the words "Of Cancellation Of Instruments. " Section 42 appears in Chapter-VI which opens with the words "Of Declaratory Decrees." Section 42 contemplates that any person is entitled to any legal character or to any property and the other person denies or interested in denying his title to such character or right. If by an instrument a person's right and title is clouded and threatened, he may seek a declaration under this section that by the instrument his right and title has not been affected. More so, if a prayer is couched in the terms that a person acquired no right and interest over any property, it is also covered by section 42. In the plaint the plaintiff made a categorical averment that kabala deeds in pursuance of the Bainapatras are absolutely collusive, illegal, inoperative and void ab-initio and by the kabala deeds, the defendants did not acquire any title and possession over the suit land. It is pointed out that the plaintiff is not a party in the disputed instrument. The relief sought for is to the following effect:

বাদীর প্রার্থনাঃ-

ক) ৭ নং মোকাবিলা বিবাদী কর্তৃক ১-৫ নং মূল বিবাদীগণের বরাবরে ফেরত ভাবে ও যোগ সাজস ক্রমে সুজিত ও সংঘটিত গত ৩১-৮-১৯৭৭ ইংরেজী ২৭৫৪ নং কবলা এবং ২৭৫৫ নং কবলা দলিলাদী সম্পূর্ণ বে-আইনী অকর্মন্য অবলবৎ যোগসাজসে ফেরবী শমধঢ টঠ-ধভর্ধধম-দলিল হওয়া উচ্চারণে বাদীর বরাবরে বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রি দেওয়ার।

খ) মোকদ্দমার তাবৎ ব্যয় বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রি দেওয়ার।

গ) মোকদ্দমার অবস্থাগতিকে বাদী অন্য যে যে প্রতিকার পাইতে পারেন তাহা ও বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রী দেওয়ার পক্ষে বিহীত আদেশ হয়।”

15. Keeping in view of the substance of the plaint and the relief sought it is manifestly clear that the suit falls under section 42 and not under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act and the plaintiff is entitled to a relief under section 42 of Specific Relief Act.

<u>16. Here, I feel inclined to observe that the pleading is not happy but the party must not suffer for confused and bad pleading. Law is settled that it is the substance and not the form of the plaint which at is to be looked and considered and Mufussil Court's pleadings are to be construed liberally. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Mohammad Zahoor Ali Khan vs. Mussaamat Thakoor Ranee, Moore's Indian Appeal volume II, 1866-7 page 468, observed that this Committee is always disposed to give a liberal construction to pleadings in Indian courts, so as to allow every question fairly arising on the case made by the pleadings to be raised and discussed in the suit. Reference may also be made in this connection to a decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Manmatha Nath Kuri vs. Muhammad Mokhlesur Rahman PLD 1969 (SC) 565. Hamoodur Rahman, CJ expressed views in the following terms:</u>

<u>"The plaint, which has been drafted by a Mofassil lawyer, is no doubt, very inartistically worded and it does not set out the cause of action with any degree of precision. But reading the plaint as a whole liberally, according to the accepted principle of construction of Mofassil pleadings, there can be no manner of doubt that the cause of action pleaded was in substance for damages under the Fatal Accidents Act, even though the draftsman had erroneously included therein averments of general damages by way of solatium for the grief and suffering caused to the parents by the loss of their child and other irrelevant matters."</u>

17. The interpretation of sections 39 and 42 of Specific Relief Act had been exhaustively dealt with in a Full Bench decision in the case of Daibakilal Basak vs. Iqbal Ahmed Quarishi and another 17 DLR 119. Sayem J, one of the three learned Judges constituting the Full Bench observed:

"Section 39, in my view, primarily provides a relief by way of a declaration. It does not expressly provide, as is done by the proviso to section 42 that an omission to pray for a further relief that might be asked for in the suit would entail its dismissal. If cancellation is not prayed in such a suit or having been prayed for has been refused, in a subsequent suit for cancellation the plaintiff may be confronted with the bar under Order 2, rule 2, of the Code of Civil Procedure, or by a bar of limitation, or by some other bars. But that cannot be a reason for the Court to assume that every suit brought under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act is to contain a prayer for cancellation, and so to insist on payment of an enhanced court-fee. It is only after the trial, as has already been noticed, that the Court is called upon to consider the question as to if, in exercise of its discretionary power under the section, a bare declaration should be granted. If the plaintiff is a party to the instrument the court refuses, as a rule, to grant such a declaratory relief, on the ground that the instrument, in such a case, need be avoided by cancellation. The plaintiff in such a case is required to pray for cancellation, by way of a consequential relief, where, however, the plaintiff is not a party to the instrument no such difficulty arises".

18. Learned Advocate for the petitioner relied upon the case of Sufia Khanam Chowdhury vs. Faizun Nessa Chowdhury, 39 DLR (AD), 46, in support of his contention that the suit falls under the purview of section 39 of the Specific Relief Act. In the said case Faizun Nessa Chowdhury, an old widow put her L TI on the blank paper believing' that she was executing a Bainapatra in favour of Sufia Khanam but from the Sub-Registrar, she came to know that in place of Bainapatra, she was asked to admit the execution of Sale Deed and, as such, she denied to execute the sale deed. The Sub-Registrar having refused to execute the deed, Sufia Khanam got the sale deed registered under section 77 of the Registration Act by filing a title suit in the court. Faizun Nessa Chowdhury also filed another suit for a declaration that the sale deed was void being brought about by fraud, collusiveness and misrepresentation. In that suit Faizun Nessa Chowdhury was a party to the instrument. But in the instant Suit plaintiff was not a party to the two kabala deeds in question. In the case of Sufia Khanam vs. Paizun Nesa Chowdhury 39 DLR (AD) 46, the case of Daibukilal vs. Iqbal Ahmed 17 DLR 119 had been considered along with a good number of decisions of our jurisdiction as well as Indian Jurisdiction. The Full Bench decision in Daibukilal's case was held to have given correct exposition of law by the Appellate Division in the cited case of Sufia Khanarn.The cited case, thus, cannot be of any assistance to the defendant petitioners.

19. Both the courts below concurrently found that the suit as framed comes within the purview of section 42 of Specific Relief Act and the suit cannot be thrown out as not maintainable. On a reading of the provisions of section 39 and 42 of the Specific Relief Act and also looking to the substance of the plaint, I am of this considered view that the suit as framed comes within the purview of section 42 of Specific Relief Act and the courts' below correctly decided this question in favour of the plaintiff. The decision, therefore, does not call for any interference by me.

20. Mr AQM Safiullah, learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners, next submitted that in pursuance of two Bainapatra deeds executed by defendant No. 7 (predecessor of opposite party Nos. 3-10) in favour of the defendant Nos. 1-5, the defendant No. 7, on receipt of rest consideration money executed and registered two kabala deeds dated 31-8-77 and the Kabala deed of the plaintiff having been executed and registered on 15-6-77, the right and title of the defendants over the suit land related back to the date of execution of the Bainapatra deeds and sale deeds of the defendants would prevail over the kabala deed of the plaintiff.

21. Mr SC Das, learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party, on the other hand, submitted that a sale deed executed earlier but registered later on will relate back to the date of its execution and not of any prior Bainapatra and the plaintiff's sale deed having been executed and registered prior to the execution and registration of the sale deed of the defendants, plaintiff's sale deed would prevail over the sale deed of the defendants.

22. Two questions are involved in answering the contentions raised by the learned Advocates of both the sides. The first one is whether the Bainapatra deeds which are marked as Exhibits-F and F1 are genuine or created documents through acts of forgery and if the Bainapatra deeds are seen to be genuine documents, then only the point raised by the learned Advocate for defendants deserves consideration.

23. The Bainapatra deeds were alleged to have been executed on 22-10-71 and 13-12-71. On a close scrutiny of the Bainapatra deeds it appears that one Bainapatra deed has been written on a stamp paper and another written on a cartridge paper purchased in the year 1969. Exhibit-8 is a kabala deed dated 4-8-71 which was executed by defendant No. 7 in favour of the father of defendant Nos. 1-5. It is recited in the said kabala deed that following the alleged agreement, defendant No.7 transferred the suit land in favour of the father of the defendant Nos. 1-5. Exhibit-4 is a deed of reconveyance executed by the father of defendant Nos. 1-5 in favour of defendant No. 7. From the above, it reveals that at the time of the alleged execution of the Bainapatra deeds, the defendant No.7 was not the owner of land, and, as such, the Bainapatra deeds by a person who was not the owner of the land got no legal force and also legal existence in the eye of law. In the written statement filed on 27-9-1996 by the defendant Nos. 1-5, defendant Nos. 4 and 5 had been shown as minors but in the Bainapatra deed Exhibit-F, it was not at all recited that the defendant No. 5 had been minor at that time. Exhibit-1, a school certificate duly proved by the Head Master of the concerned school is an evidence to show that the defendant No.5 was born only on 24-6-1974. The matter, thus, became manifestly clear that the defendant No. 5 was not at all born on the date of the alleged execution of Bainapatraie.in the year 1971, Both the courts below on a proper consideration and discussion of the legal evidence and other materials on record came to the positive finding that the Bainapatra Deeds Exhibits-F and F1 are totally false and are acts of forgery. On consideration of the materials on record I do not find any reason to disagree with the above findings arrived at by the courts below.

24. It remains now to answer to the other question whether the title of the defendants related back to the date of execution of the Bainapatra.

25. It has already been noticed that the Bainapatra deeds are false, created and product of forgery. Even if the Bainapatra deeds are taken to be genuine documents, then also the title of the defendants cannot relate back to the date of execution of the said Bainapatra deeds. Sale deed executed earlier but registered later in point of time will have precedence over sale deed executed later but registered earlier by operation of section 47 of the Registration Act. But a sale deed executed and registered later in point of time than a sale deed executed and registered earlier in point of time cannot have precedence over the sale deed executed and registered earlier on the plea of earlier execution of Bainapatra deed and title of the subsequent transferee cannot relate back to the date of execution of the Bainapatra and section 47 of the Registration Act got no manner of application in such a case. In the instant case the Bainapatra deeds are alleged to have been executed on 22-10-1971 and 13-12-1971. The kabala deed of the plaintiff was executed and registered on 15-6-1977 and the kabala deed of the defendants were executed and registered on 13-8-1977. The execution and registration of the kabala deed of the plaintiff was earlier in point of time than the execution and registration of the kabalas of the defendants and the right and title of the defendants over the land is dispute will not relateback to the execution of the alleged Bainapatra. In this context a decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Rafiqul Islam (Md) vs. Mir Abdul All 44 DLR (AD) 176 may be referred to. His Lordship Mustafa Kamal J, made the following observations:

"We have no manner of doubt whatsoever that an apparent error has crept in the judgment while applying section 47 of the Registration Act in the facts and circumstances of the case. When the same vendor executes and registers two sale deeds in respect of the same suit land in favour of two different purchasers on two different dates, section 47 of the Registration Act settles which one will prevail over the other. The sale-deed which was executed earlier but registered later in point of time will prevail over the sale deed executed later but registered earlier in point of time and the criterion in such cases for the purpose of determining when the sale takes effect is not the date of registration but the date of execution of the sale-deed itself. This court has committed an apparent error in relating back the defendant's sale deed to the date of his bainapatra dated 30-12-72. A sale deed which is registered will relate back to its own date of execution, not of any prior bainapatra. The plaintiff's sale-deed was executed and registered on 8-7-74 and the defendant's sale-deed was registered on 11-7-75. On a patent application of the principle of section 47, the plaintiffs sale-deed will clearly prevail over the defendants if the plaintiffs sale deed otherwise qualifies for comparison under section 47. There can be no liberal or extended application of section 47. Any interpretation is fraught with grave consequences."

Mr AQM Shafiullah, learned Advocate with all fairness submitted before me that in view of the principle of law enunciated by the Appellate Division, he got no point to be decided in favour of the defendant petitioners.

26. The findings arrived at by the courts below have been rested upon consideration and discussion of legal evidences and materials on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of the legal aspects involved in the suit and the findings are findings of fact which are not liable to be disturbed by this court in the exercise of power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this context the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Durga Choudhrain vs. Jawahir Singh Choudhuri, 17 Indian Appeal, 122 may be profitably referred to. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as far back as in the year 1890 held as follows:

"An erroneous finding of fact is a different thing from an error or defect in the procedure and there is no jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal on the ground of such erroneous finding, however gross or inexcusable the error may seem to be. When there is no error or defect in the procedure, the finding of the first appellate court, upon a question of fact, is final if that Court had before it, evidence proper for its consideration in support of the finding."

Support for this proposition is also sought to be drawn from a series of decisions, both of our jurisdiction and foreign jurisdictions. Some decisions of our Appellate Division in the case of Fokaruddin Mia and another vs. Mohammad Khoda Baksh Sheikh, 29 DLR (SC) 268, Akrab Ali vs. Zahiruddin, 30 DLR (SC) 81, Abdul Matin Chowdhury vs. Chapala Rani Sett and others, 37 DLR (AD) 205, NaintuddinSardar vs. Md Abdul Kalam, 41 DLR (AD) 3, Jasimuddin Kanchan vs. Ali Ashraf, 42 DLR (AD) 289, Mazhurul Borhan vs. Ali Bhuiyan, 15 BLD (AD) 237 and Haider Unnessa and another vs. Monwara & gum and others, 16 BLD (AD) 280 may be also noticed.

27. The preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above is that the finding of fact based on evidence and other materials on record cannot be disturbed by the High Court Division and the same is binding upon it.

28. In view of the discussions made hereinbefore and after giving consideration to all pros and cons and after taking note of the catena of decisions pronounced by the Apex court from time to time; I hold that the Rule is devoid of any substance and the same must be discharged.

29. In the result the Rule is discharged however, without any order as to costs.

Lower court's record be sent down at once.

End.

full_judgment: This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptee who failed to resist pre-emption in both the courts below under section 96 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act (which shall hereinafter be called the Act). 2. Nazamat Ali gifted the disputed land including his homestead measuring 0.70 acres to his daughter-in-law (son's wife) the opposite party 1 Nazuma Khatun for love and for good service rendered by the son's wife to her widower father-in-law in his old ailing age. The gift was made by registered deed (Ext. 3) on 31.1.80. For stamp purchase for the purpose of registration Taka 2000.00 was shown as value of the gifted land. Said Nazuma Khatun thereafter gifted the same land to her husband by another registered deed on 7.4.80 (Ext. A) who is opposite party No. 2 in the pre-emption case, the present petitioner Hafiz Ahmed. The document was endorsed under section 60 of the Registration Act on 17.9.80. The former document was so endorsed on 3.12.80. Opposite party No. 1 Ahamedur Rahman filed the pre-emption case on 30.3.81 claiming himself as a co-sharer in the case holding both by inheritance and purchase and also as owner of the contiguous land. 3. Opposite party No. 2 contested the case by filing a written objection contending, inter alia, that he himself became a co-sharer in the case holding after opposite party 1 had gifted the case land to him before filing of the pre-emption cases, that the transfer in question being a gift in lieu of love and affection and for good services rendered by the son's wife to her father-in-law as per recitals of the document preemption is barred under sub-section (10)(c) of section 96 of the Act; that before filing of the pre-emption case against the opposite party 1 she had already gifted the case land validly and legally to her husband opposite party No. 2 and, as such, at the time of filing of the pre-emption case, the opposite party 1 had not saleable or transferable interest in the case land. For those reasons, the pre-emption case is not maintainable. Parties adduced oral evidence and filed their papers. Both the courts below allowed pre-emption against gift made by Ext. 3 under Mohammadan Law. 4. In the aforesaid circumstances and evidence on record I am to make a decision whether the judgments of the courts below are legal or resulted in an error of law occasioning failure of justice. At the very outset I want to quote the provision of section 96(10) of the Act which is as follows: "96(10) Nothing in this section shall apply to (a) a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase; or (b) a transfer by exchange or partition, or (c) a transfer by bequest or gift (including Heba but excluding Heba-bil-Ewaz for any pecuniary consideration) in favour of the husband or wife of the testator donor, or of any relation by consanguinity within three degrees of the testator of donor." Transfer in question was made on 31.1.80. Opposite party 1 had validly and legally transferred the property in question by way of gift by Ext. A to her husband opposite party 2 on 7.4.80 it was endorsed under section 60 on 17.9.80 that is, long before filing of the pre-emption case on 30.3.81. As such, it is apparent that on 30.3.81 when the case was filed the pre-emptee opposite party 1 had no title or any sa1cable or transferable interest in the case land. According to the recital of the deed, gift was made for love and affection of the son’s wife towards her father-in-law and for the good services rendered to him. For the aforesaid reasons it can be called that the transfer is an exchange not sale as has been illegally found by the courts below. So the transfer is not preemptible. A transfer by bequest or gift or by exchange, as I said, is excluded from the clutch of pre-emption both under sub-sections 10(b) and 10(c) of section 96 of the Act. Provision of section 96 (10)(b)(c) of the Act is no doubt ambiguous. Therefore, I accept the meaning of it which can be given by its interpretation or can be derived, to avoid injustice (Shamsuzzoha Nurul Amin vs, Province of East Pakistan, 22 DLR 377) court can modify the language of statute to effect the manifest and undoubted intention of the legislature. Md. Newjish Khan vs. Md. Amin 21 PLD 622 and Md. Amin Khan vs, Controller of State Duty, 13 DLR (SC) 105. It is well established rule of interpretation that a rule standard be interpreted in such a manner that it should he rather saved than destroyed. Dr. Neelima Ibrahim vs, People's Republic of Bangladesh, 32 DLR 201 and Dr. Nurul Islam vs. Bangladesh, 33 DLR (AD) 201 In view of the above position I find that the intention of the legislature was very clear to exclude transfers made by way of bequest (dictionary meaning will) and gift (Heba) affected in the form and nature as in the present case and also Heba-Bil-Ewaz when it is made without any pecuniary consideration. But a Heba-Bil-Ewaz when made in exchange of monetary consideration even within the three degrees of the donor of testator or beyond that the transfer is embraced within the scope of preemption under sub-section 10(c) of section 96 of the Act and it becomes pre-emptible. The reason is obvious and patent as because right of pre-emption is a right of prior purchase, in Bengali it is called অগ্রক্রয় and by pre-emption the pre-emptor purchases the property at the price at which it is transferred with statutory costs. In that view I hold that transfer by bequest (will or gift) Heba and Heba-Bil-Ewaz without any pecuniary consideration are excluded from pre-emption as the monetary value of those transactions cannot be calculated. 5. For the purpose of registration entailing purchase of requisite stamp paper some value is fixed in the deed but that is not the real consideration, value or price of the property transferred. So pre-emption is prohibited. Therefore, in the instant case the transfer being a gift of 0.70 acres land showing its price at Taka 2000.00 only is beyond the scope of pre-emption. Moreover, the gift in the present case has been made by the father-in-law to the daughter-in-law (son's wife) for love and affection and for good services rendered by the donee to the donor at his old age as averred in the deed of gift. In the case of Kanchan Mala vs, Renu Miah 12 DLR 479 (para 6) it has been held as follows: "love and affection cannot be measured in money and, as such, it cannot be said that the gift in question is a hiba-bil-ewaj wholly for consideration though partly the gift of exchange is for Rs 2000.00. In the aforesaid circumstances the gift in question is not a hiba-bil-ewaz as contemplated by section 96 of Bengal Tenancy Act and, as such, it cannot be pre-empted. Principles both in Bengal Tenancy Act and State Acquisition Act regarding pre-emption are same" In Mulla's Principles of Mohammadan Law in section 138 "gift" has been defined as followed: "A hiba or gift is a transfer of property made immediately and without any exchange by one person to another and accepted by or on behalf of the latter." From this definition I do not find any distinction between gift and Hiba. Hiba is Arabic name of gift So gift or Hiba in whatever name it is called is exempted from pre-emption, according to the provision of sub-section (10) of section 96 of the Act. In the deed (Ext. 3) the portion of the homestead of the donor also has been included and transferred by way of gift which is prohibited from pre-emption. Courts below, because the deed of gift of the opposite party 2 by Which the opposite party I gifted the case property to the opposite party 2, her husband which was endorsed under section 60 of the Registration Act, before the endorsement of the deed of gift in question and because the former deed was registered in a different sub-registrar's office and execution was confirmed on commission, have found that the subsequent transfer was collusive and sham transaction to defeat the right of pre-emption, I say those findings are results of surmise and conjecture without any evidence on record. My considered opinion is that the transfer in question is a gift in the form of exchange for love and affection and for good service and the subsequent transfer of case land by opposite party 1 to opposite party 2 in no way or manner and in any law is illegal or invalid and it was made long before the pre-emption case was filed and when opposite party 1 had no interest in the case land and it cannot be said that the transfer by wife to husband was made in anticipation of filing of pre-emption case. So pre-emption in the instant case should have been refused by the courts below. In the case of Md. Abbas Ali vs, Md. Osman Ali and others reported in 37 DLR 324 in a proceeding under section 96 of the Act (Para 12) it has been held as under: "The vendee is not obliged to provide opportunities to the pre-emptor to be substituted in his place through court or otherwise so far as the sale nor pre-emption is concerned. The vendor and the vendee are at liberty to avoid pre-emption by all lawful means." In 29 DLR (Upendra Chandra Roy vs, Janab Ali, para 7) it has been held as follows: "If the reconveyance takes place before the starting of the proceeding for pre-emption, the pre-emptee's right ceased to exist" Although facts are not same, but spirit of law is same. Similar view has been taken in 18 DLR 317 which is as follows: "What is required is that the Court must examine fairly and soundly, the facts of the case and decide for itself whether the transfer itself is still existing In the case of Gobinda Dayal vs Inayetullah ILR 7 (All.) 775 an eminent Judge Mr. Justice Mahmood has held as under: The right of pre-emption is not a right of 're-purchase' either from the vendor or from the vendee, involving any new contract of sale; but it is singly a right of substitution, entitling the pre-emptor, by reason of a legal incident to which the sale itself was subject, to stand in the shoes of the vendee in respect of all the rights and obligations arising from the sale under which he has derived his title. In the instant case at the time of filing pre-emption case no subsisting right or interest of the pre-emptee existed in the property. In the case of Bishan Singh AIR 1958 (SC) at page 838 (pars 11), it has been held as under: The vendor and the vendee are, therefore, permitted to avoid accrual of the right of pre-emption by all lawful means. The vendee may defeat the right by selling the property to a rival pre-emptor with preferential or equal right. In the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, the discussions and for the reasons above I hold that the transfer in question made as gift by Ext. 3 is beyond the scope of pre-emption. So the judgments and orders of the court below cannot be sustained and are liable to be set aside. 6. In the result, therefore, the Rule is made absolute. The judgments and orders of the courts below allowing the pre-emption are set aside. The pre-emption case is dismissed. No order as to costs. Send down the records at once. End.

lawyer:
MI Farooqui with Saleemullah, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
Farid Ahmed with Emdadul Hoque Azad, Advocates ----- For Opposite Party No.1.

Safar Ali Miah & others ----- Petitioners.
Vs.
Badsha @ Siddique & others ----- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker, J.: This revision case has come to this Bench upon a reference by a learned Single Judge to decide whether, in the event of violation, a decree of prohibitory injunction is enforceable in an execution case for reliefs provided in Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, and if not, what is the remedy available to the decree-holder.

2. Upon an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure a Rule was issued calling upon the Judgment-debtor opposite-parties to show cause why the order dated 8.5.85 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Narayangonj rejecting the application for execution being Title Execution Case No.5 of 1982 as not maintainable, should not be set aside.

3. The petitioners instituted Title Suit No. 57 of 1968 on 14.3.68 in the 2nd Court of Munsif at Narayangonj for permanent injunction restraining the opposite-parties from entering into the suit land and the suit was dismissed on contest on 31.5.1969 but on appeal, being Title Appeal No. 196 of 1969, the suit was decreed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka on 11.4.70. Thereafter, the opposite-parties preferred Second Appeal No. 232 of 1971 to this Court which was dismissed on 6.12.77, whereupon they filed Civil Petition for Special Leave to appeal No. 132 of 1978 which was also dismissed by their Lordships of the Appellate Division on 23.6.78.

4. Thereafter the decree-holder petitioners filed Title Execution Case No.5 of 1981 on 20.6.81 for restoration of possession of the suit land on the allegation that the Judgment-debtors-opposite-parties in violation of decree for permanent injunction dispossessed the decree-holders on 11.11.71; but the said execution case was dismissed on 10.4.82.

5. Thereafter on 18.6.82 the decree-holders filed Title Execution Case No.5 of 1982 praying for detention of the judgment-debtors opposite-parties in civil prison and attachment of their immovable properties on the ground of violation of decree for permanent injunction by dispossessing the decree- holder-petitioners from the suit land on 11.11.71. This application was made under the provision of Order XXI rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Munsif by the impugned order rejected the application for execution as not maintainable.

<u>6. The Revision Case came up for hearing before the learned Single Judge, DM Ansar Uddin Ahmed J. and during the hearing before him the learned Advocate for the petitioners submitted that the application for execution was maintainable for the reliefs prayed for and in support thereof referred to two cases, one in the case of Saleh Ahmed Chowdhury and others Vs. Kabir Ahmed and others reported in 13 DLR 531, and other in the case of Moynul Mia & others V,. Haji Abdus Samad reported in 33 DLR 207. On the other hand, the learned Advocate for the Judgment-debtor opposite-parties supported the impugned order and referred to two cases one in the case of Burhanuddin Ahmed and others Vs. Veda Brata Chakroborti and others reported in 16 DLR 61 and the other in the case of Ajiran Nessa Bewa and others Vs. Md. Abdul Mannan reported in 1992 BLD High Court Division 323. All these four decisions are Single Bench decisions.</u>

7. In the case reported in 13 DLR 531 Siddiky J, as his Lordship then was, made an observation to the effect that sub-rules (1) & (2) of rule 32 of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure were applicable in the case of prohibitory injunction. In the case reported in 16 DLR 61 which was filed for enforcement of the decree alleging violation of the decree of permanent injunction praying for putting the judgment-debtors in civil prison and for attachment of their properties, it was held by Hasan, J that when there was a violation of prohibitory injunction there remained no decree to be enforced and that willful breach of the injunction could not be held to be willful failure to obey the decree as provided in Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code. In the case reported in 33 DLR 207 wherein a Miscellaneous Case under Order XXI Rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by a decree-holder to enforce a decree of permanent injunction Mustafa Kamal J held that the expression "willfully failed to obey" under Order XXI rule 32 (1) denotes not only a negative state of mind but also a positive act of disobedience and as such the decree-holder's remedy lay in the enforcement of the decree under the said provision of the Code. In the case reported in 1992 BLD 323 in similar circumstances Md. Gholam Rabbani J held that if a prohibitory injunction is violated the remedy was not by putting the decree into execution as the decree was not executable and as such the execution case was not maintainable for any remedies under Order XXI rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure. For these conflicting decisions the learned Single Judge made this reference to resolve divergence of views by a larger Bench, The learned Chief Justice, however, sent the revision case to this Bench for hearing and disposal of the matter.

8. We have heard Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate who appeared along with Mr. M Saleemullah for the petitioners and also Mr. Farid Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the opposite-parties.

<u>9. Apart from the above mentioned four cases Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioners has referred to the case of Kad Banu and others Vs. Hajera Khatun and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 183= BCR 1985 (AD) 73 in support of his contention that when a person disobeys a decree of injunction he not only fails to perform an act which he is directed to do but also when he does an act which he is prohibited from doing. The learned Advocate also submitted that the provisions of Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure are identical with the provisions of Order XXXIX rule 2 (3) of the Code and he has referred to the case of State of Bihar Vs. Rani Sonabati Kumari reported in 1964 AIR (SC) 61 in support of his contention.</u>

10. As has been mentioned above the question for determination is whether in the event of violation of a decree for prohibitory injunction the decree is enforceable for the reliefs provided in Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the case reported in 13 DLR 531 same as 1960 PW (Dhaka) 1022, the judgment-debtors were restrained from interfering with the possession of the decree-holders in the suit land from changing the nature of the land. The decree-holders filed an execution case alleging that the judgment-debtors in disregard of the said prohibitory decree excavated certain ditches in the suit land and prayed for enforcing the decree of prohibitory injunction by putting the judgment- debtors in civil prison and by attaching their properties. The learned Munsif found that the judgment-debtors had violated the order of injunction but held that the provision of Order XXI rule 32(5) was not applicable to the case. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge held that sub-rule (5) of rule 32 of Order XXI was applicable. The judgment-debtors thereafter moved the Dhaka High Court in revision and obtained a Rule wherein the learned Advocate for judgment-debtors-petitioner submitted that none of the sub-rules of rule 32 of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure applied to a case of prohibitory injunction and the learned Single Judge observed as follows:

"I am afraid this amounts to going a little too far. I think sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 32 of Order XXI are applicable to cases of prohibitory injunction. I, therefore, do not accept Mr. Mofakhcr's contention in this regard, but I agree with him in his submission that sub-rule (5) of rule 32 of Order XXI of the Code does not apply to a case of prohibitory injunction."

11. In the case reported in 16 DLR 61 same as 1964 PLD (Dhaka) 661 the decree-holders put the decree into execution and sought for reliefs under Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment-debtors praying for their punishment by attachment and sale of some of their properties on the allegation that they were bound by a decree of permanent injunction being transferees pendent lite but they had disobeyed the injunction by interfering with the possession of the decree-holders in the suit land. It was noted by the learned Single Judge that on the pleadings one question arose for determination, namely whether in the circumstances of the case clause (5) of rule 32 of Order XXI of the Code was applicable. The executing Court held that the injunction order being prohibitory one the relief under rule 32(5) was not available. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge relying upon the provisions of section 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure and 52 of the Transfer of Property Act held that clause (5) of rule 32 of Order XXI of the Code was applicable. On a Second Miscellaneous Appeal of the High Court, the learned Single Judge upon a consideration of the provisions of sub-rule (1) of rule 32 of Order XXI of the Code held that the remedy for enforcing the decree has been provided therein in case of willful failure to carry out the injunction by the judgment-debtors and in such a case the decree may be enforced when there is willful failure but not willful disobedience or violation of the injunction order and also held that when there was a violation there remained no decree to enforce. The learned Judge further held that as the prohibitory injunction had been violated the decree was not executable and the execution case was not maintainable.

<u>12. In the case reported in 33 DLR 207 the decree holders obtained the decree for permanent injunction against the judgment-debtors who were permanently restrained from creating any disturbance to the peaceful possession of the suit land by the decree-holders but the judgment-debtors violated the order of permanent injunction and trespassed into the suit land and cultivated Boro paddy therein. The decree holders prayed for enforcement of the decree by putting the judgment-debtors into the civil jail and by attaching their properties under Order XXI rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Munsif allowed the prayer of the decree-holders and committed the judgment-debtors to the civil prison to suffer imprisonment for 15 days each. Thereafter the judgment-debtors moved this Court in revision and obtained a Rule. In course of hearing of the Rule it was submitted on behalf of the judgment-debtors that the Miscellaneous Case was not maintainable on the ground that when a prohibitory order of injunction was violated the decree was not executable and referred to the case reported in 16 DLR 61 in support of their contention. Mustafa Kamal J held that sub-rule(1) of rule 32 of Order XXI was a particular manner or method of enforcing an otherwise in executable decree in case of violation and sub-rule (1) implies that if the prohibitory order is violated then by securing the detention of judgment-debtor in the civil prison or attaching his properties or by both such an in executable decree can be enforced and that sub-rule (5) is an alternative or additional remedy. Secondly, the words "willfully failed to obey" do not imply that it is only a negative act of willful failure that will attract the mischief of sub-rule (1). If a person does exactly the act which he is prohibited from doing then it is very much a willful failure to obey the decree. Thirdly, when a prohibitory order of injunction is violated the decree can be enforced invoking provision of sub-rule (1) of rule 32. Sub-rule (1) of rule 32 is a special penalty reserved for the judgment-debtor if he willfully disobeyed the decree. Fourthly, there is a remedy for every wrong done and if a prohibitory order of injunction cannot be enforced it would be practically useless to obtain such a decree for permanent injunction. His Lordship thereafter referred to the cases of Prag Dutt Vs. Kedar Nath and others 1945 AIR Oudh 81, and the case of Gundila Manjappa Shelly Vs. Manjakke Shedthi and others reported in 1961 AIR Mysore 268 wherein it has been held that a person disobeys an injunction not only if he fails to perform an act which he is directed to do also when he does an act which he is prohibited from doing; and his Lordship also referred to the case of Toon Lal Vs. Soonoo Lal reported in 1938 AlR Pat 522; the case of Nari Chinnabba Chetty Vs. E Chengalroya Chetty and others reported in 1950 AlR Madras 237; the case of Ajabroo Vs. Atmaram, reported in 1954 AlR Nag 245; the case of Muuari Lal Vs. Nawal Kishore reported in 1961 AlR Pur 547 and the case of Saleh Ahmed Vs. Kabir Ahmed reported in 13 DLR (Dhaka) 531 and held, contrary to the views taken in the case reported in 16 DLR 61, that when a prohibitory injunction is violated the decree-holder's remedy lies in the enforcement of the decree under Order XXI rule 32 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure apart from any other remedy that he may have had.</u>

13. In the case reported in 1992 BLD 323 the decree-holder filed a suit for permanent injunction against the judgment-debtors and obtained an ex parte decree restraining the judgment-debtors from permanently entering into the suit land. The decree-holder filed an execution case under Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure alleging that the judgment debtors disobeyed the decree by forcibly entering into the suit land and erecting huts and planting trees therein. The judgment-debtors denied the allegation contending that they were in exclusive possession of the suit land since 26.3.46 when the husband of judgment-debtor No. 1 Azirunnessa transferred the suit land to her by a registered kabinnama. The learned Munsif allowed the execution case directing the judgment-debtors to remove the obstructions like huts, banana trees, etc. from the suit land within 35 days; otherwise the land of schedule No. 2 of the execution petition would be attached and sold to compensate the decree-holder with Tk. 5000.00. The judgment-debtors thereafter moved this Court in revision and obtained a Rule. The learned Single Judge referred to the cases reported in 13 DLR 531, 16 DLR 61 and 33 DLR 207 and differed with the decisions in 13 DLR 531 and 33 DLR 207 and also the other cases of Indian jurisdiction and agreed with the view taken in 16 DLR 61 and held that when a prohibitory injunction is violated the remedy is not by putting the decree into execution but by adopting other measures as provided by the law and further held that when a prohibitory injunction has been violated the decree was in executable and the execution case was not maintainable for any of the remedies under rule 32 of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Judge came to the aforesaid conclusion for the following reasons given by him; firstly, three types of decrees namely for specific performance, for restitution of conjugal rights or for injunction have been grouped together in sub-rule (1) of rule 32, they being of similar nature, The first two being mandatory the other, namely for injunction, must be of similar nature that is mandatory injunction and not prohibitory injunction. Secondly, the expression "failed to obey," "has not obeyed" and "has obeyed" used in sub-rules (1) (3) and (4) of rule 32 and the expression "act required to be done" used in sub-rule (5) must have the same meaning as to obeying the decree. Thirdly, the words "in lieu of or in addition to all or any of the processes mentioned aforesaid" stated in sub-rule (5) prescribed a direct mode of execution indicating that only those types of decrees for specific performance of contract and for injunction all the sub-rules were applicable. As a decree for restitution of conjugal right cannot be executed in accordance with sub-rule (5), rule 33 of Order XXI prescribed another type of execution for that and similarly a decree for execution of document or endorsement may be executed in accordance with rule 34 of Order XXI; but there is no other rule in Order XXI prescribing alternative mode of execution of decree for prohibitory injunction.

14. The only question for determination before us is whether in the event of violation of the decree for prohibitory injunction the decree is enforceable for the reliefs provided in Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure which is in the following terms:

"32.-(1). Where the party, against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction, has been passed, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has wilfully failed to obey it, the decree may be in forced in the case of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction by his detention in the civil prison, or by the attachment of his property, or by both."

15. The first question arises is whether the words "willfully failed to obey" in sub-rule (1) of rule 32 also connote willful disobedience or violation of injunction order. Hasan, J in 16 DLR 61 held that the words "willfully failed" do not imply willful disobedience and opined that when there was violation there remains no decree to enforce. But Mustafa Kamal J in 33 DLR 531 held that the words "willfully failed to obey" do not imply that it is only a negative act of willful failure but also a willful failure to obey the decree. Md. Gholam Rabbani J agreed with the view taken by Hasan J and differed with the view taken by Mustafa Kamal J. But we need not decide the question as their Lordships of the Appellate Division have decided the question in the case of Kad Banu and others Vs. Hajera Khatun and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 183; BCR 1985 (AD) 73 wherein their Lordships held- "a person disobeys an injunction not only when he fails to perform an act which he is directed to do but when he does an act which he is prohibited from doing. There is as much disobedience in one case as in the other 	" Thus there is no doubt for holding that the provision of sub-rule (1) of rule 32 of Order XXI apply to prohibitory injunction.

16. Further it may be noted in this connection that in the Civil Procedure Code 1882 there were the words "for the performance or abstention of any particular act" which were substituted by the words "for an injunction" in sub-rule (1) of rule 32. In the Code of 1882 both for the performance of an act or abstention from performing an act was there for the words "for an injunction". Thus as has been held by Mustafa Kamal J in 33 DLR 207 the words "willfully failed to obey" do not imply only a negative act of willful failure but also a willful failure to obey the decree.

<u>17. As to the observation that when there is a violation of permanent injunction there remains no decree to be enforced, Md. Gholam Rabbani J followed the decision reported in 16 DLR 61 wherein Hasan, J quoted a passage from the case of Angad and others Vs. Madho Ram and others reported in 1938 AIR Allahabad 416 wherein it has been observed that as soon as an act which is restrained from being done under a prohibitory injunction is done, it passes the stage of restraint or prevention. In the Allahabad case the decree-holder brought a suit for removal of certain constructions from a piece of land but the decree which was ultimately passed by the Court did not allow the removal of the constructions from the land but allowed an injunction against the judgment debtors that they should not make any other use of the land beyond keeping those structures. After the decree, the judgment-debtors put up a new structure on the land and the decree-holders made an application in execution department for removal of the said structure. In that case the judgment-debtors contended that the decree-holder was not entitled to any relief in the execution department. Their objection was dismissed and the order of the executing Court was affirmed by the lower appellate Court and by a Single Judge of the Allahabad High Court. The objection taken by the judgment-debtors was that sub-rule (5) of rule 32 of Order XXI did not apply to the prohibitory injunction but their remedy was by a separate suit for removal of the new construction. In a Letters Patent Appeal a Division Bench held that sub-rule (5) of rule 32 does not apply to prohibitory injunction and the remedy of the decree-holders for removal of new construction lies by way of a suit. The Division Bench allowed the prayer of the decree-holders to convert the proceeding into a suit. But there is nothing in this case to show that when there is a violation of prohibitory injunction there remains no decree to be enforced: It may be mentioned in this connection that Mustafa Kamal, J in 33 DLR 531 agreed with the observation that when a prohibitory order of injunction is violated there remains no decree to enforce. Mr. Farid Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite-parties failed to point out anyone case in support of this proposition. Mustafa Kamal, J further observed in 33 DLR 531 that a wrong cannot be alleged to go without any remedy and pointed out that when a judgment-debtor willfully violates a prohibitory order of injunction sub-rule (1) of rule 32 gives the specific remedy to the decree-holder for such violation of the decree. Further, Courts do not grant decrees either for violating it or for being violated with impunity against a decree of prohibitory injunction.</u>

18. It is true that a decree for prohibitory injunction is not to be drawn up specifying the relief granted as required under Order XX rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Unlike other decrees there is no specific relief to be incorporated in the decree drawn up pursuant to a judgment in a suit for permanent injunction. Section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure prescribed the time limit for execution in all kinds of decrees except a decree granting injunction. This was necessary because a decree for permanent injunction need not be executed unless it is violated by the judgment-debtor. Since permanent injunction is the issue as in force in perpetuity the question of execution arises only when the order of injunction is violated. When a decree for permanent injunction is violated the decree-holder can enforce the decree by putting the judgment-debtor in civil prison or by attachment of his property and sale thereof in accordance with sub-rule (1) of rule 32 of Order XXI in order to compel the judgment-debtor to obey the decree. In this connection section 54 of the Specific Relief Act 1877 may be referred to show that when the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of property, the Court may grant a perpetual injunction in the six cases mentioned therein including the case where the injunction is necessary to prevent multiplicity of judicial proceedings. This shows that a decree for permanent injunction can be enforced for violation of it by taking recourse to the provision of sub-rule (1) of rule 32 of Order XXI and not by a fresh suit. It is for this reason of avoiding multiplicity of proceedings that such a decree should be enforced without taking recourse to a separate suit.

19. Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has also submitted that there are similar provisions in Order XXXIX rule 2 sub-rule (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure that in case of disobedience or violation of temporary injunction during the pendency of the suit when the court may order the property of the person guilty of such disobedience to be attached and also order such person to be detained in civil prison for a term not exceeding six months. If violation of an order of temporary injunction can be enforced by an order of attachment or detention in the civil prison for such disobedience there is no reason why violation of an order of permanent injunction cannot be enforced by detention in civil prison or by attachment of property of the judgment-debtor. This view is supported by the decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of State of Bihar Vs. Rani Sonaboti Kumari reported in 1964 AIR (SC) 221 wherein it has been observed that the provision of Order XXI rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure, when a decree for permanent injunction has been passed, is similar to the provision of Order XXXIX rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure for enforcement of violation of an order of temporary injunction.

20. It may be mentioned that our Appellate Division in the case of Sashi Mohan Sen Vs. Ain Ullah reported in 1992 BLD (AD) 8 observed as follows:

"A reference to Order XXI, rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure shows that when against any party a decree for injunction is passed and he has the opportunity of obeying the decree and he willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced by detaining him in civil prison, or by the attachment of his property or by both."

Following the above quoted observations of their Lordships of the Appellate Division Md. Mozammel Hoque, J held in the case of Selimuzzaman Vs. Deputy Commissioner, Shariatpur and others reported in 44 DLR 545 that the judgment debtor having willfully failed to obey the decree, action under Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure was called for in case of violation of permanent injunction.

21. In view of the above discussions we are of the opinion that in the event of violation of a decree for prohibitory injunction the decree is enforceable against the judgment-debtor in an execution case for the reliefs provided in Order XXI rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and accordingly we answer the reference in the affirmative.

22. In the result the Rule is made absolute. The impugned order dated 8.5.85 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Narayangonj is set aside and the learned Assistant Judge concerned is directed to proceed with the execution case.

In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 25.2.1990 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka, in Civil Order No. 579 of 1990)
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, C.J.: In this appeal by special leave, Defendants, Managing Director of Rupali Bank and others, arc the appellants. Plaintiff, an Assistant Cashier of this Bank is the main respondent, (No. 1). The matter arises from a suit filed by the respondent before the Assistant Judge challenging his termination from the appellants' service. He got a decree declaring his "termination" void. The decree has been upheld by the appellate Court and finally, in revision, by the High Court Division. Leave has been granted to consider the question whether the whole proceedings including the decree of the Civil Court suffers from Coram Non Judice in view of the Administrative Tribunals, Act, 1980, which has ousted the Civil Court's jurisdiction in all matters relating to terms and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic or of any statutory authority, like the appellants' Bank.

2. Respondent-plaintiffs service was terminated with all service benefits by the appellants-employer by an order dated 15 September, 1981. He filed the suit (Title Suit No. 26 of 1987) challenging the termination on the ground of malafide action of the employer. Employer- appellants challenged the maintainability of the suit invoking section 4 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980--Act VII of 1981, read with the Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984 which provided for creation of a Tribunal with exclusive jurisdiction on service matters. Alternatively, the appellants contended that the plaintiff being a "worker" his remedy lay only before the Labour Court, in which case also the civil Court's jurisdiction was ousted. This question as to jurisdiction was not given any consideration by the trial Court which decided the suit on merit; the appellate Court considered this question but decided it against the appellants and upheld the decree. The appellants challenged the decree before the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction (Civil Order No. 579 of 1990). A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division summarily rejected the revisional application in a lengthy judgment mainly discussing the merit of the case, brushing aside the question of jurisdiction of the civil Court saying that it was a matter of mere technicality. Some of the observations of the learned Single Judge are:

"technicality as to forums whether the plaintiff is a worker or an employee and in such view, suit or petition should lie should not be sole criterion for interference ----- If the order of termination/removal was found not sustainable, mere technicality as to forum should not afford reasonable ground to interfere under section 115 CPC  But the present position of section 115 has undergone a radical change. The question of jurisdiction is not being replaced by error of law occasioning failure of justice".

3. Mr. Hasan Arif, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the appellants, has assailed this view of the learned Single Judge as totally erroneous and has contended that in view of absence of jurisdiction of the civil Court the plaint should have been rejected outright. Mr. NH Khondker, learned Advocate for the respondent, has argued that when the respondent is not governed by the law of master and servant, the civil Court's jurisdiction is not totally ousted. He has referred to a number of decisions including a decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Managing Director Janata Bank Vs. Hafizuddin Ahmed, 29 DLR (SC) 39 in which it has been held that employees of statutory corporations, such as Janata Bank, are not governed by master and servant law and that they may maintain a suit before a Civil Court. There is no dispute that law of master and servant is not applicable to an employee of a statutory corporation; but this does not mean that all classes of employees of a statutory corporation may file a suit in the civil Court. Maintainability of such a suit depends upon the rank, status and nature of work of the employee concerned. The question therefore is where the matter of "grievance" of an employee, who is a worker, is to be brought for adjudication. First, I shall see whether the case of the respondent falls within the ambit of the Administrative Tribunal Act, as alleged by the learned Deputy Attorney-General.

4. The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 was made by the Parliament under Article 117 of the Constitution to provide for establishment of Administrative Tribunals to exercise jurisdiction on matters relating to terms and conditions of service of persons "in the service of the Republic  any  statutory authority". The words "or any statutory authority", as underlined by me, have been inserted in section 4 of this Act by a subsequent amendment. This Act came into force with effect from the date of a notification under section 1(2), which appears to be 5 June 1981. Section 4(1) of this Act confers exclusive jurisdiction upon the Administrative Tribunal on certain matters. It is quoted below" "

4.—Jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunals.—(1) An Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine applications made by any person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of Republic or of any statutory public authority."

5. "Statutory public authority", as defined in section 2(aa) of the Act, means an authority, corporation or body specified in the Schedule to this Act. The Schedule included, among others, Rupali Bank. This Schedule was brought in by the Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984—Ordinance No. LX of 1984, with effect from 25 September 1984. It is clear that in respect of terms and conditions of service of any person of the Rupali Bank, which is a statutory authority, the Administrative Tribunal got exclusive jurisdiction and that no other court or tribunal shall exercise jurisdiction on such matters. The civil Court's jurisdiction thus stands totally ousted.

6. Respondent, though a person in the service of the appellants' bank, did not, nor could he have, come to the Administrative Tribunal seeking redress against his termination for two reasons. He was terminated in 1981 when no persons in the service of any statutory authority, such as the Rupali Bank, were brought into the ambit of section 4 of the Act; such persons were brought in from 25 September 1984, as pointed out above. Secondly, no application of any person in the service of the Republic or of statutory body shall be entertained by the Administrative Tribunal, as provided in this section itself, unless it is made within six months from the date of the order or decision of the authority complained against. Sub-section (2) of section 4 of course provides that in case the order or decision complained of may be varied, reversed or modified by a "higher administrative authority" under any law in force, then the period of six months' limitation will be counted from the date of decision of the higher administrative authority. This is, however, not the respondent's case. Before filing his suit in 1987 he had spent about six years' time seeking remedies before persons and authorities not contemplated in sub-section (2). His case, therefore, goes out of the ambit of the Administrative Tribunal. His case will be governed by the law which was applicable to him and was in force at the time of his termination in 1981.

7. He is, on his own pleading in the plaint of his suit, an Assistant Cashier of the Rupali Bank. As such, he clearly falls within the definition of a "worker" under the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders Act), 1965, briefly the Standing Orders Act, as well as under the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969. Under section 2(v) of the Standing Orders Act, "worker" means any person employed in any shop, commercial or industrial establishment to do any skilled, unskilled or clerical work but does not include any person who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity. "Under section 2(h) of this Act, any person employed in such an establishment to do "managerial or administrative" functions falls into the class called. "employer". In the corresponding provision of the' Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, worker workman has been defined in almost same terms. An individual worker seeking redress of any grievance, such as redress against" his removal or termination, may file a complaint to the Labour Court constituted under section 35 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance. Similarly, a worker/workman may file an application to the Labour Court seeking enforcement of any right secured to him by law, award or settlement. The Labour Court is the only forum for a worker/workman to seek remedy against grievances relating to his employment. In the instant case of the respondent, who felt aggrieved by his termination remedy lay before the Labour Court under section 25(1) of the Standing Orders Act.

<u>8. Mr. NH Khondker has referred to two decisions of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in "Assistant Manager, Rupaii Bank Vs. Nurul Islam", 39 DLR 167. One such decision is that employees of the Rupali Bank were not workers because there was no Gazelle Notification bringing them into the definition of "worker" under the Standing Orders Act; the other decision is that there was no express provision in the Standing Orders Act excluding the civil Court's jurisdiction over the matters of workers' service conditions. Both these decisions were dissented from by another Single Bench in "Md. Shahabuddin Vs. Janata Bank", 41 DLR, 94. In that case the learned Single Judge. after referring to some previous decisions, such as, in the cases reported in 29 DLR (SC) 39; (1987) BCR (AD) 454 and 35 DLR 151, held that Clerks and Cashiers of the Janata Bank arc workers and that the civil Court got no jurisdiction to entertain a suit for redress of any grievance of those workers in connection with their termination.</u>

<u>9. A Labour Law such as the employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, or the Industrial Relations Ordinance is a special law vis-a-vis the Code of Civil Procedure which is a general law. The latter affects the community at large: all people of the state arc governed by it. While the former relates to and affects particular persons or things; it operates upon a selected class, rather than the public generally. Relation between a general law and a special law is by the principle known as Generalia Specialibus non derogant-which in English means, "general words do not derogate from the special". In other words, if any legal remedy is ordinarily available under both general law and special law the remedy prescribed by the special law must be sought to the exclusion of the remedy otherwise available under the generally.</u>

<u>10. This principle of law had been nicely expounded by Willes, J. in Wolverhampton New Waterworks Co. Vs. Hawkesford (6 CBN 6.336) which was approved by the House of Lords in Nevile Vs. London Express Newspaper (1919 AC 368), where It was observed:</u>

<u>"Where the statute creates a liability not existing at common law, and gives also a particular remedy for enforcing it the party must adopt the form of remedy given by the statute".</u>

<u>This principle has been followed all through by our Courts. Reference may be made to the case of Jogesh Cnandra Dutta Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 30 DLR 219. In that case civil Court's jurisdiction was held ousted by section 188 of the Customs Act. In a recent case, Rafiqul Alam Vs. Mostafa Kamal, 42 DLR (AD) 137 this Court found complete ouster of Civil Court's jurisdiction on election disputes. It was held by this Court that section 26 of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983, ousted, by necessary implication, the civil Court's jurisdiction to entertain a suit for declaration that the rejection of nomination papers by the Returning Officer was invalid, in view of the fact that a separate forum-- Election Tribunal---was created for this purpose by the said Ordinance which is a special law.</u>

11. In the instant case, this principle shall apply. Respondent, admittedly a worker filed this suit, challenging the legality of his termination from service, before the civil Court whose jurisdiction to entertain the suit stood ousted by necessary implication. That is, when the Labour Court was there his remedy lay before that court only. Ouster of a court's jurisdiction may be provided by express words as also by necessary implication. In this case the appellate Court held the suit maintainable relying upon the Single Bench decision in the 39 DLR 167 case, but this decision is palpably erroneous. The decision by the other Single Bench in the 41 DLR 94 case is found to be perfectly correct.

<u>12. Jurisdiction of a court goes to the very root of a matter brought before it. and if the court got no jurisdiction everything shall fall through. We are surprised to find that the learned Single Judge in this case held that the Court's jurisdiction is a mere technicality and that it is the merit of a case that matters. The court which go; no jurisdiction over a matter shall not go into the merit of the matter. The view expressed by the learned Single Judge regarding jurisdiction is grievously erroneous.</u>

<u>Similarly the other view of the learned Single Judge that in the present position of section 115 CPC, the question of "jurisdiction" is replaced by "error of law" is equally faulty. The Assistant Judge having no jurisdiction over the matter the decree passed in the suit is void. The result therefore is that this appeal is allowed; the impugned decree is set aside and the suit is dismissed. No order as to cost.</u>

End.
