parties:
Abdul Muhaimin Khan & another  ----- Petitioners.
Vs.
Bashiruddin & others ----- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
By this rule opposite party No.1 was directed to show cause as to why the order dated 13.8.90 passed by the Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Misc. Case No. 40 of 1990 should not be set aside or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may deem fit and proper.

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the Rule are as follows:

Opposite party No. 1 filed Misc. Case No. 40 of 1990 in the court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the land transferred by document dated 8.3.90 by opposite party No. 2 to the present petitioners claiming that he was a co-sharer. It was further contended that the document sought to be pre-empted was actually a deed of sale but in order to avoid pre-emption by co-sharer it has been given the colour of an exchange and the land shown to have been exchanged for the schedule land was fictitious and non-existent. The present petitioner being the pre-emptee on 20.5.90 filed a petition in the trial Court for rejection of the pre-emption petition on two grounds, namely; (1) the document sought to be pre-empted has not yet been registered under section 60 of the Registration Act and as such the pre-emptor has no cause of action and the case was premature and (2) the document in question is a deed of exchange on the face of it and in a pre-emption case which is a summary proceeding there is no scope for the court to go beyond the document and decide whether it was a deed of exchange or sale document and that exchange not being pre-emptable the pre-emption case was not maintainable. The learned Assistant Judge by his impugned order dated 30.8.90 deferred the decision on both the points till final hearing of the pre-emption case. So far point No. 1 is concerned, the trial Court relied on the decisions reported in 31 DLR (AD) 118 and 34 DLR (AD) 220. As regards point No. 2 as quoted above the court has referred to the ruling reported in 36 DLR (AD) 1. As against the aforesaid order of the learned Assistant Judge the purchaser-opposite party as petitioners moved this court and obtained the Rule.

3. Heard Mr. JN Dev, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, and Mr. SK Sinha, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1.

<u>4. Mr. Dev, in his argument, has referred to the decisions given in the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Mokles Ali reported in 31 DLR (AD) 118, Lebu Mia Vs. Gonesh Chandra Nath reported in 34 DLR 220 and in the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Baser Ali reported in 21 DLR 599. The learned counsel for the petitioners has frankly admitted that as per decisions given by the superior courts including the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh there is no doubt about the fact that right of pre-emption accrues from the date of registration of the document sought to be pre-empted and not from the date of execution or presentation for registration and that the defect of prematurity arising out of filing a case for pre-emption before the registration of the document is complete, can be cured if the document is registered during pendency of the pre-emption proceeding. But his main contention is that pre-emption proceeding may proceed if no objection on the point of prematurity for non-registration of the document in question is raised by the opposite party before the document is registered, but if such objection is raised before registration of the document the pre-emption petition is liable to be thrown out on the ground of prematurity. In other words, according to Mr. Dev, if the cause of action for pre-emption matures before objection is taken the objection must fail but if the objection is raised before such maturity the objection must be sustained. It may be pointed out here that the learned Advocates of both the sides admitted that the document sought to be pre-empted in the instant case was not registered till 20.5.90 on which date the present petitioners filed the petition before the trial Court for rejection of the pre-emption petition on the ground of prematurity and that in the meantime, the registration of the document under section 60 has been completed. In the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Baser Ali reported in 21 DLR 599 a Single Bench of the Dhaka High Court held that right of pre-emption accrues not on the date of execution of the deed but on the date of its registration. It the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Mokles Ali reported in 31 DLR (AD) 118 the Kabala sought to be pre-empted was presented for registration on 29.7.72 and duly registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 11.8.72. Application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act was filed on 8.8.72 i.e. 3 days before the kabala was registered. In that case question that arose was whether the application for pre-emption was liable to be thrown out on the ground that on the date on which the pre-emption application was filed, there is no legal transfer. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that since the document of transfer was registered according to law while the pre-emption application was pending in the trial Court, the Court could act upon it on the ground that the pre-maturity in filing the pre-emption application has been cured by the fact that the transfer legally took place while the application for pre-emption was pending in court. The defect of pre-maturity was therefore fully cured. The court further held: "Apart from this, a simple illustration from the Code of Civil Procedure will clarify the position. If the petitioner would have filed an application for amendment of the petition after registration of the kabala, no objection could be taken and the amended petition would have made it a competent one. We do not see any difference, in substance, when the document is produced before the court and the court acts upon it, and when from the document it is patent that the cause of action accrued from 11.8.72 before the parties have gone on issue or the pronouncement of judgment. The defect of prematurely therefore, was fully cured and in this view of the matter the decision of the High Court cannot be maintained".</u>

5. Mr. Sinha, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 has laid stress on the words "before the parties have gone on issue or the pronouncement of the judgment" and has pointed out that this observation of their Lordships of the Appellate Division indicates that the question whether the pre-emption petition was premature or not has to be decided at the time of the hearing of the case itself and the delivery of judgment and as such there was no scope for rejection of the pre-emption petition under or. 7 rule 11 CPC.

<u>6. Similar view was taken in the case reported in 24 DLR (AD) 220 as referred to above. In the above quoted cases the Appellate Division though has not specifically laid down that the question of prematurity of a pre-emption petition on the ground of non-registration of the document in question should be heard and decided at the time of final hearing of the pre-emption case, yet on perusal of the judgment of the Hon'ble court it appears that the court had in mind that such a point should be decided at the time of final hearing and not earlier, so that the pre-emptor may not be put to the trouble of filing a fresh petition of pre-emption after the registration of the kabala. The matter can be looked at from another angle once a document of transfer after proper execution is presented for registration and the executant admits its execution and the registering authority finds the document in proper form then neither the parties to document nor the registering authority can refuse registration. Completion of registration under section 60 of the Registration Act is mere procedural step which is to be taken by the registering authority. In that view of the matter to reject a petition for pre-emption at the initial stage on the ground of non-registration of the document before filing of the petition would cause unnecessary hardship on the pre-emptor and may lead to further complications. Above these, the learned Advocate for the opposite party has referred to the decision of a Division Bench given in the case of Jatindra Chandra Urang Vs. Shamsuddin and others reported in 34 DLR 264. In that case the document sought to be pre-empted was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act after filing of a revisional application, that is, long after the objection was taken by purchaser pre-emptee as regards prematurity of the pre-emption case and accepted by the trial Court. In that circumstances of the case the Division Bench of this court presided over by Mr. Justice Ranadhir Sen and Mr. Justice Abdul Matin Khan Chowdhury, observed:</u>

<u>"Eventually the endorsement under s.60 of the Registration Act has been made during the pendency of the matter before this Court. It cannot be conceived that pendency of the matter before this court is not a continuation of the original proceeding. In our opinion, it was under the same process of continuation and the matte awaits final adjudication. The learner Subordinate Judge did not adjudicate upon the matter on the merits of the pre-emptors claim. We are therefore of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge fell in error in hurriedly disposing of the matter without waiting for the result of a case resting on similar point before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. It is unfortunate to notice the impatience of the learned Subordinate Judge when it was brought to his notice that the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Mokles Ali was specifically pending before the Appellate Division. Be that as it may, we would discourage the practice adopted by the learned Subordinate Judge in throwing out the pre-emptor's application by the order dated 30.8.78."</u>

7. The facts of the above quoted reported case are completely similar to the present case and as such I find that the above quoted decision is fully applicable in the present case. In that case the court also deprecated the action of the Subordinate Judge in rejecting the pre-emption petition summarily on an application filed by the pre-emptee under Order 7 rule 11 of the CPC. From what has been stated above I hold that the learned Assistant Judge by his impugned order committed no error of law by deferring the decision on the point of prematurity of the pre-emption petition till final hearing of the case itself, So, that portion of the impugned order must stand.

8. As regards the 2nd point that in a pre-emption case under section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act or under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which is a summary proceedings, the court cannot go beyond the document and must act on the document itself. Mr. Dev has contended that the document sought to be pre-empted in the present case is apparently a deed of exchange which is not pre-emptable under the law and the court not being competent to enter into the question of the nature and character of the document should have rejected the pre-emption petition under Order 7 rule 11 CPC. On this point he has referred to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Abdul Wahed Vs. Mst. Jamrat, reported in 19 DLR (SC) 136. In that case it was held that though pre-emption should be allowed where the necessary conditions are satisfied, the Courts have frequently given their approval to certain modes by which title can be acquired which place difficulties in the way of pre-emptors. The parties to a sale-deed can adopt any methods within the limits of law to defeat or delay pre-emption of the land sold. In that case, first a mortgage document was created and thereafter the equity of redemption was transferred in favour of the mortgagee. It appears that in that decision the court took a lenient view in favour of the purchaser pre-emptee and held that in a pre-emptable transaction the parties to the transaction are under no legal obligation to publish their intention to the intending pre-emptors. They may use whatever means and methods as are allowed by law to carry out their intention. The condition precedent is that the purchaser and seller must remain within the limits permissible by law. Giving effect to a transfer first by making a mortgage deed in favour of the transferee and thereafter selling the equity of redemption may be termed as clever. But this is permissible under the law. But to give a deed of sale the colour of an exchange by including a fictitious land is a fraudulent act on the part of transferor and the transferee and this is not permitted by law.

9. Mr. Dev also referred to the decision given by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court reported in 51 CWN. In that case it was held that the matters expressly specified in section 26F are not the only matters within the proper scope of an enquiry under that section of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885. It has been further held that if a question is raised that purported transfer is not a real transfer but a benami transaction in the sense that the transferee holds the property on behalf of the transferor, such a question falls within the proper scope of an enquiry under section 26F. That case also was a summary proceeding under section 26F of the repealed Bengal Tenancy Act. It is difficult to understand how the afore-quoted decision can be of any help to the present petitioner.

<u>10. In the case of Aswan; Kumar Vs. Hori Mohan reported in 36 DLR (AD) I, it has been held that the question of benami nature of kabala on the basis of which pre-emption is claimed cannot be gone into and determined in a proceeding for pre-emption but if the transferee or the transferor takes the plea that no transfer took place under the kabala and the transferor remained in possession of the land the court in a pre-emption proceeding can enter into such question and give a decision. In that reported case the transferor of the kabala which was sought to be pre-empted, took the plea that no transfer took face under the said kabala but it was executed only to clear his title in the land which he had purchased in the benami of his nephew Respondent No. 2 under a previous kabala from respondent No.6. So, it is clear that it has been held in the above quoted case that the question whether a document sought to be pre-empted is a real transaction or not, can be enquired into in a summary proceeding for pre-emption. On the other hand, the learned Advocate for the contesting opposite party has relied on the ruling of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court given in the case of Kazi Mobarak Ali Vs. Mohammad Yeasin Mazumder and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 60. In that case the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration that the unanimous award of a village court was not binding upon him as because it was obtained by fraud alleging that he did not nominate any representative but the Chairman of the Union Parishad, in order to mitigate his previous grudge, included 2 persons as representatives of the plaintiff and obtained the unanimous award. The suit was contested on the plea that an unanimous award was final and could not be challenged and filed a petition for rejection of the plaint. The trial Court rejected the petition under Order 7 rule 11 of CPC. On revision it was upheld by the High Court Division. On appeal their Lordships of the Appellate Division held:</u>

<u>"But at this stage it is the plaint of the suit which is the only record before the civil Court and it is on the basis of that plaint that the civil Court is to see whether the suit is barred by any law or whether it is not otherwise maintainable. The plaint shows that these respondents did not nominate their representatives; but the defendant-appellant pressed for rejection of the plaint. In the face of the allegation in the plaint that the plaintiffs respondents did not nominate their representatives in the Village Court the plaint can not be rejected. To determine the truth of this allegation, evidence is necessary and this can be available only in the course of trial of the suit which is prima facie maintainable.</u>

<u>11. So, in that case an apparently unchallengeable award of the village Court was challenged in the civil Court on ground of fraud. In the present case pre-emption has been sought of a transaction which is apparently not pre-emptable with the allegation that it is a transfer by way of sale and fraudulently has been given the colour of exchange in order to defeat the right of pre-emption of the co-sharers. Under the circumstances I do not find any reason as to why the law enunciated by the highest court of the country should not be applicable in the present case. The question whether the document sought to be pre-empted is actually an exchange deed or a sale deed can be decided only after having evidence of both the parties at the time of hearing of the pre-emption petition and as such there was no scope to reject the pre-emption petition summarily on an application under Order 7 rule 11 CPC. I, therefore, find that the learned Assistant Judge has rightly kept the matter pending till final hearing of the pre-emption case itself. I do not find any error of law on the face of the record resulting in failure of justice in the impugned order.</u>

In the result, the Revision fails. The rule is discharged with cost. The stay order granted by this court on 26.11.90 is hereby vacated. Communicate the order at once.

End.

Md. Amir Hossain, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Party
parties:
Sonali Bank and another ------ Petitioners 
VS 
Chandon Kumar Nandi ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The Rule at the instance of the defendant-petitioner was directed against the judgment and decree dated 4-3-86 and 10-3-86 respectively passed by the District Judge, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 127 of 1985 reversing the judgment and decree dated 8-8-85 and 17-8-85 respectively passed by the Munsif (Assistant Judge) Sadar, Comilla in Title Suit No. 43 of 1983.

2. The short facts necessary for the disposal of this Rule are, that the plaintiff-opposite party, Chandan Kumar Nandi instituted Title Suit No. 43 of 1983 in the Court of Munsif (Assistant Judge), Sadar, Comilla against the defendant-petitioner No. 1, Sonali Bank and another for a declaration that the termination of his service by the defendant Bank vide memo No. PO Corn. EST (PF)/9336 dated 19-9-81 issued by the then Assistant General Manager of Sonali Bank, Comilla is illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiffs case is, that he was an employee of the Sonali Bank posted at Comilla main branch and joined in the service of the Bank as Assistant Cashier on 7-1-81 and performed his duties faithfully to the satisfaction of the authority. But due to a general strike, he could not attend office on 10-9-81 and 11-9-81 and so his service was terminated by the above mentioned letter dated 19-9-81. No notice was served upon him before terminating his service. Hence, the termination of his service is illegal and void and therefore, the plaintiff filed the suit for aforesaid declaration.

3. The defendant-bank contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs suit for simple declaration without consequential relief is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Plaintiff had an objective standard for the valuation of the suit by way of his two years salary at the rate of Taka 1,000.00 per month but he did not give any such objective valuation in his suit and so, on the point of valuation also, the plaintiffs suit is not maintainable. Hence, the plaintiffs suit is liable to be dismissed on the point of maintainability.

4. The learned Munsif (Assistant Judge) after hearing both the parties and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, came to a finding that the suit in the form of simple declaration is not maintainable and on this finding, the learned Assistant Judge dismissed the suit of the plaintiff vide his judgment and decree dated 8-8-85 and 17-8-85. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed an appeal before the learned District Judge being Title Appeal No. 127 of 1985. The learned District Judge after hearing both the parties came to his finding that the suit is maintainable and thus he set aside the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge and sent the suit back on remand for disposal according to law vide his judgment and decree dated 4-3-86 and 10-3-86.

5. Being aggrieved by this judgment and decree of the learned District Judge, the defendant Bank as petitioner has moved this court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr. ABM Khairul Huque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner, has submitted that the plaintiff was a temporary employee of the Bank whose service was liable to be terminated on one month's notice or on payment of one month's pay in lieu thereof. The learned Advocate referred to Regulation No. 11(3) of Sonali Bank Employees Service Regulations, 1981 which provides that "the appointment by direct recruitment of an employee other than an officer, shall be on temporary basis and he shall be eligible for confirmation in the service of the Bank not earlier than twelve months subject to his satisfactory conduct and performance of duties and availability of a permanent post.

7. The Regulation 13 of the same service regulations has provided that the service of a probationer or a temporary employee shall be liable to termination by the competent authority without assigning any reason after giving him one month's notice in writing or on payment of one month's substantive pay in lieu of such notice. Mr. Khairul Hoque submits that the plaintiff joined the Bank's service on 7-1-81 and that his service was terminated on 19-9-81 before completion of twelve months' service while he was still in temporary employment and thus the termination of his service was made according to law by allowing him to receive his one month's salary in lieu of notice vide Bank's Memo. No POC EST (PF) 9336 dated 19-9-81.

8. Mr. Md. Amir Hossain, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party, on the other hand, submits that the definition of probationer as given in Regulation 2(q) is, that a probationer means an officer employed on probation against a substantive vacancy in any post. The contention of Mr. Amir Hossain is, that the plaintiff was not a probationer and, as such, his service was not liable to be terminated in the manner as has been done by the Bank Authority.

9. But it appears that regulation No. 2(q) has given the definition of probationer officer but not the definition of any employee. The plaintiff was not a probationer-officer but he was a temporary bank-employee as per Regulation No. 11(3) and that the Regulation No. 13 has provided for the manner of termination of service both of a probationer-officer and of a temporary employee.

10. Mr. Md. Amir Hossain next submits that the plaintiff was confirmed in his service as per statement made in his plaint. But it is now an admitted fact that the plaintiff joined in the service of the Bank on 7-1-81 and his service was terminated on 19-9-81 before completion of twelve months and, as such, he cannot be said to be a confirmed employee of the Sonali Bank because of the fact that the Regulation itself has provided that he will be eligible for confirmation after completion of 12 months' satisfactory service. His twelve months service was not completed on the date of termination of service. So, the question of his confirmation in service did not arise at that time.

11. In this connection. Mr. Khairul Huq, referred to a decision in the case of Abdul Mannan Sikder vs. Bangladesh Bank and others, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 298. It has been held by their Lordships in that case as under-

"So long an employee is not confirmed, he continues under probation. His services can be terminated under Regulation 10."

That was a Bangladesh Bank's case and the relevant regulation was Regulation No. 10. In the instant case; the manner of temporary employment of Sonali Bank employee is contained in regulation 11(3) of the Sonali Bank Service Regulation and the manner of termination of temporary employment is contained in Regulation No. 13. In view of the principle as laid down in the decision referred to above and in view of clear provisions as contained in Regulation Nos. 11(3) and 13 of the Sonali Bank Employees Service Regulations, 1981. I am of the opinion that the Bank authority was competent to terminate the service of the plaintiff during the period of his temporary employment. Mr. Khairul Huq next argued that the Sonali Bak is a commercial establishment and that the plaintiff being its employee was a worker as per definition of "worker" given in section 2(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 and that a worker has no remedy in civil Court but that his remedy against any grievance lies in the Labour Court. The contention of Mr. Huq is that the plaintiff being a worker, his suit was not maintainable in the civil Court and accordingly, the learned Assistant Judge rightly dismissed the suit as being not maintainable, but that the learned District Judge has committed an error of law in setting aside that judgment of the learned Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment. "Worker" has been defined in section 2(1)(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 as under:

"Worker means any person including an apprentice employee in any shop, commercial establishment or industrial establishment to do any skilled, un-skilled, manual, technical, trade promotional or clerical work for hire or reward, whether the terms of employment be expressed or implied."

The question now arises as to whether Sonali Bank is a commercial establishment and whether the plaintiff being its employee is a worker within the definition of worker as quoted above. In support of his contention that Sonali Bank is a commercial establishment Mr. Huq referred to a decision in the case of State vs. Abdul Awal reported in 35 DLR 151. Their Lordships have held in that case as under :

"The words "commercial establishment" have been defined in section 2(c) of the Shops and Establishments Act, 1965,"

Among other concerns "banking company" and "a bank" was also "included" within the definition of commercial establishment. Before the nationalisation of banks in Bangladesh the National Bank of Pakistan and its branches were included within the definition of commercial establishment. The definition of "commercial establishment" in the said Act has undergone no change after the nationalisation of banks.

12. Mr. Huq, then argued that Sonali Bank is a commercial establishment within the definition of "commercial establishment" as defined in section 2 (d) of the Shops and Establishments Act, 1965 and that the plaintiff being its employee was a worker and, as such, his suit was not maintainable.

13. Mr. Huq relied on a decision in the case of Md. Shahabuddin vs. Janata Bank reported in 41 DLR 94. That was a case regarding the similar termination of service of some Janata Bank employees and in dealing with that matter a Single Bench of his court held that the plaintiffs were workers as defined in labour law having no remedy in civil Court. Labour Court is the proper forum for redress of their grievances/

Mr. Huq referred to another decision in the case of Senior Manager, Dost Textile Mills Ltd. and another vs. Sudhansu Bikash Nath, reported in 1988 BLD (AD) 66 wherein it has been held by their Lordships as under :

"The very moment it is found that the plaintiff is a worker, he is non-suited. His suit under the Civil Procedure Code is not maintainable. Specific remedy of his grievance lies in a separate forum, the Labour Court. There is implied ouster of the jurisdiction of the civil Court as there is forum of Labour Court for remedy by a dismissed worker created by special statute, Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act."

In this connection, Mr. Huq referred to another decision in the case of Managing Director, Rupali Bank Ltd. and others vs. Tafazal Hossain and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260. That was a case regarding termination of service of an Assistant Cashier of Rupali Bank and their Lordships in that case held that the plaintiff clearly falls within the definition of a worker under the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 as well as the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1965. Their Lordships further held therein as under:

"Jurisdiction of a Court goes to the very root of a matter brought before it and if the court got no jurisdiction everything shall fall through. The court which got no jurisdiction over a matter shall not go into the merit of the matter."

In view of all the above principles of law, it will appear that Sonali Bank is a Commercial Establishment and that the plaintiff of the instant case being an Assistant Cashier of Sonali Bank was clearly a worker and that his suit was not maintainable, the civil Court having no jurisdiction to entertain his suit.

14. Mr. Amir Hossain, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party, submits that the case recorded in 41 DLR 94 is relating to an employee of Janata Bank and the case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260 is in respect of an employee of Rupali Bank, but that the plaintiff of the instant case was an employee of Sonali Bank and so he cannot be equated with the employee of Janata Bank or Rupali Bank to bring him within the meaning of worker. But the fact remains that all these banks were nationalised under the same law, namely, the Bank's Nationalisation Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 26 of 1972) and that all the employees of the nationalised commercial banks are guided by the similar pay scale and similar service regulations. Therefore, there is no reason to distinguish between an employee of Janata Bank or Rupali Bank and an employee of Sonali Bank. I am, therefore, unable to accept this contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party.

<u>15. Mr. Md. Amir Hossain next argued that all the employees are not necessarily workers as because the Assistant Cashier or Cashier is not included in the definition of worker and, as such, the plaintiff being an Assistant Cashier cannot be termed as worker. But the fact remains that the definition of worker as given in the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act has not named any employee in its concept. It is a general definition starting with the person employed in any shop and commercial establishment who is not employed in any managerial or administrative capacity is a worker. Bank has already been found to be a commercial establishment and the plaintiff being an Assistant Cashier was not doing managerial or administrative job, but he was doing a clerical work. Therefore the plaintiff can undoubtedly be said to be a worker within the meaning of worker as defined in the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act.</u>

<u>16. Mr. Amir Hossain referred to the schedule-I of the Service Regulations in term No. 2 of category 'B' of the classification of Sonali Bank's employees and said that Assistant Cashier has been classified a "non banking" staff under the broad category of "other employees" and accordingly, the plaintiff being an Assistant Cashier was not within the Bank Staff and, as such, he cannot be said to be a worker. But the classification of officers and other employees as given in schedule I of the Sonali Bank Employees Service Regulations, 1981 is nothing but an internal agreement made by the Bank for staff management for the purpose of their internal administration only. This classification made in the schedule has nothing to do with the definition of worker. The plaintiff being as Assistant Cashier of the Bank was undoubtedly an employee of the Bank taking his salary from the bank having all the incidence of the Bank employees. Therefore, this argument of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party appears to have no substance.</u>

17. The case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260 is in respect of the termination of service of an Assistant Cashier of Rupali Bank. The instant case before us is also in respect of the termination of service of an Assistant Cashier of Sonali Bank. Therefore, the principle of law as laid down in the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260 is exactly applicable to the case of the plaintiff of instant case before us. By a consideration of all the above facts of the instant case together with the principles of law as laid down in the cases referred to above, I find that the plaintiff of the instant case being an Assistant Cashier of Sonali Bank is a worker within the definition of Worker" as given in section 2(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 and accordingly, I hold that the plaintiff is non-suite d the civil Court having no jurisdiction to entertain his suit, his only remedy shall lie before a labour Court. Mr. Amir Hossain next argued that even if the plaintiff is found to be a worker still then, he shall be entitled to come before the civil Court for redress of his grievance under proviso to section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act wherein it has been provided that no complaint shall lie before labour Court against an order of termination of employment of a worker under section 19, unless the service of the worker concerned is alleged to have been terminated for his trade union activities. Mr. Amir Hossain contends that the proviso to section 25 speaks of going to the labour Court for a worker's termination of service for trade union activities and in case of his termination not for any trade union activities, the worker shall be entitled to seek relier under the general law in a civil Court and in that view of the matter Mr. Hossain submits that the plaintiffs suit in the civil Court is maintainable, as because his termination of service was not made for any trade union activities as there was no such allegation in the termination letter. In this connection, the learned counsel for the Bank submits that there is no distinguishing factor for some of the workers going to the labour Court and some others going to the civil Court for their grievance, as it is the provision of the Special Statute for the workers to seek relief of their grievance in the labour Court. He further made a reference to 44 DLR (AD) 260 wherein it has been clearly held that the remedy prescribed by the special law must be sought for in exclusion of one available under the general law. In view of the above facts and circumstances, the contention as put forward by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party is, in my opinion, not acceptable.

<u>18. The learned Counsel for the Bank-petitioner next submits that the learned trial Court rightly came to the finding that the plaintiffs suit was not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and for not giving standard valuation of the suit but that the learned District Judge without proper appreciation of law involved in the matter, has come to an erroneous finding that the suit was maintainable and that this decision of the learned District Judge has occasioned a failure of justice to the defendant-petitioner. In this connection, he has referred to a decision in the case of Manager, Personal Division vs. Sazahan Miah and others, reported in 35 DLR 224 wherein it has been held that "the plaintiffs suit for declaration that his dismissal by the Bank was illegal and not binding upon him was not followed by any consequential relief. Omission to pray for any consequential relief for the purpose of enforcing a declaratory decree would be hit by the provision to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act." Mr. Huq said that this decision has been subsequently confirmed by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the Civil Petition for Special Leave being No. 299 of 1993.</u>

19. It appears that a petition has been filed on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party praying for amendment of the plaint by inserting a prayer for consequential relief in the form of re-instatement of the plaintiff in his service. This is an admission on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party that his suit was not maintainable without a specific prayer for consequential relief.

20. In view of all the discussions as made above, it will appear that the plaintiffs suit was not maintainable not only on the ground of absence of consequential relief under proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but also on the ground that the civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain his suit as because the plaintiff being an Assistant Cashier of Sonali Bank has been found to be a worker within the meaning of 'worker' as defined in the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 and that the remedy of his grievance lies in a separate forum, the Labour Court Hence under such circumstances, the question of amendment of the plaint does not also arise in the civil Court. The amendment-petition is thus rejected.

21. In view of all that has been discussed above, I find that the learned District Judge has committed an error of law resulting in an error in his decision which has occasioned a failure of justice to the Bank-petitioner. The impugned judgment of the learned District Judge suffers from infirmity. I am, therefore, of the opinion that it calls for interference by this court.

22. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge are hereby set aside and those of the learned Assistant Judge are restored.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 10th July 1986 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Writ Petition No. 547 of 1985).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman, J : Respondent No. 2 instituted Industrial Relations Case No. 73 of 1985 before the First Labour Court, Dhaka under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, in brief, IRO, against the appellant Bank and its three officers. He was employed as a Sub-Accountant in the International Division of the Head Office of the Bank. He was also the Organizing Secretary of the Pubali Bank Karmachari Sangha. He was promoted to the rank of an officer by an order dated 14th July, 1984, but he declined to accept that promotion. He was again promoted to the rank of an officer with effect from 18th February, 1985 but he refused to accept that promotion on 30th May, 1985 on the ground of his union activities. The Bank confirmed his promotion, and, by an order dated 23rd September, 1985 transferred him from its Head office at Dilkusha Commercial Area, Dhaka-2 to its Naya Paltan Branch, Dhaka. Respondent No.2 asserted that the transfer was done malafide in violation of the provisions of section 47B of the IRO. He instituted the aforementioned IRO case and prayed for stay of operation of the orders of promotion and transfer till disposal of that case. The Labour Court stayed the order of transfer till disposal of the IRO case. The High Court Division upheld that order in the appellant's Writ Petition No. 547 of 1985.

2. As there are several conflicting decisions of the High Court Division, leave was granted to settle the question whether under the IRO the Labour Court has got the power to grant an ad-interim order for stay of the operation of an order, impugned before it. At the time of the hearing the appellant is allowed to urge further whether in the respondent's application under section 34, not raised as an industrial dispute under section 43 of the IRO the drift unnecessarily for too long a time. As the law declared by the High Court Division is binding on all courts subordinate to it, the High Court Division is to avoid making conflicting decisions on a substantial question of law so that subordinate Courts may not suffer from uncertainty and lack of guidance. If a Single Bench intends to differ from the decision from another Single Bench or if a Division Bench wants to differ from the decision of another Division Bench then the matter should be referred to the Chief Justice for constituting an appropriate Bench for resolving the dispute. In the face of two conflicting decisions on the same question of law a Bench of the High Court has got no "option" but to follow anyone of the two conflicting decisions or to follow the "latest pronouncement".

<u>3. Whether the Labour Court, 'deemed as a civil court', has power under Order IX or under Order XXXIX rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure came up for consideration in two different sets of cases before the High Court/High Court Division. In MIs. MM Ispahani Ltd. 19 DLR 612 it was held that a Labour Court can exercise powers under Order IX. A contrary decision was given in Khulna Tobacco Industries Limited 29 DLR 148. As that decision was made without referring the matter to a Full Bench, a Division Bench in Raj Textile Mills Ltd. 33 DLR 376 held that it had the option to follow either of the aforesaid two conflicting decisions and relied on 19 DLR 612. Following the same reasoning another Division Bench in MIs. Adamjee Jute Mills Ltd. 29 DLR 11 followed the decision reported in 29 DLR 148.</u>

<u>4. In an unreported Division Bench decision. The Chittagong Textile Mills Ltd. Vs. Shafiqur Rahman (Civil Revision Case Nos. 40 and 88 of 1972), noted in Bangladesh Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. 27 DLR 367 it was held that a Labour Court is not a Court subordinate to the High Court Division and as such the High Court Division cannot exercise its revisional jurisdiction in respect of any order of such a court under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code. Another Division Bench, in different contexts, in Bangladesh Fishermen's Co-operative Ltd. 27 VLR 367 and in Management Board, AR Howlader Jute Mills Ltd. 28 DLR 369, held the view that Labour Court is not a civil court.</u>

<u>5. After considering 19 DLR(Dat) 612 and 29 DLR 148 the High Court Division in the instant case followed 33 DLR 376 terming it as "the latest pronouncement" of that Court. The learned Judge, Sultan Hossain Khan, J., who delivered the judgment in this case was a party to 33 DLR 376. Subsequently, another Division Bench held a diametrically opposite view in Chairman, Chittagong Port Authority, Chittagong Vs. Kalipada Dey & ors. 39 DLR 39. It was done again without referring the matter to the Chief Justice for constituting an appropriate Bench for settling the disputed question of law.</u>

6. The uncertainty with regard to the powers of the Labour Court was unfortunately allowed to power to suspend the operation of the order during the pendency of the appeal. It was observed:

"Strictly speaking, the matter does not fall to be governed by Order XXXIX, rule 1, CPC. In our opinion, the power to grant interim relief by suspending wholly or partially, the operation of the order appealed against is reasonably incidental or ancillary to the main appellate jurisdiction. It would be wrong to regard the exercise of this incidental or ancillary power as enlargement of the appellate jurisdiction of the Court."

7. Before we consider the reasons given in the impugned decision let us refer to some cases cited before us from the Pakistani jurisdiction. In Zafar Iqbal Vs. The Province of Sind PLD 1973 Karachi 383, a habeas corpus matter under the constitutional jurisdiction of the Court, it was observed that where a Court has power to pass an order finally it will generally have the power to do so by way of interim measure unless such a power is either expressly or by necessary implication excluded. The observation was made by the same judges who had decided, less than a week before, Brooke Bond (Pakistan) Ltd. PLD 1973 Karachi 189. The observation in Zafar Iqbal's case has no relevance in the instant case where the powers to the Labour Court have been specifically delineated. Observation in a decision, made in general terms, can hardly be used as a curry powder in every case.

8. In Brooke Bond (Pak.) Ltd. Vs. Second Sind Labour Court, PLD 1973 Karachi 189, Tufail Ali A Rahman, CJ held that sub-section (2) of section 36 of the IRO does not confer upon a Labour Court, while adjudicating and determining an industrial dispute, all the powers of a civil Court under the Civil Procedure Code but only such of them as may be described as procedural, i.e. such as are required "for the purpose" of adjudication and determination. Now, it is clearly not necessary in order to be able to adjudicate or determine a dispute, that pending the adjudication or determination, a party be restrained from giving effect to the kind of order of which respondent No.2 complained to the Labour Court.

This view is, I think, further supported by the express conferment of three powers enumerated in this sub-section. This was wholly unnecessary if all the powers available to a civil Court under the Civil Procedure Code had already been conferred. Even without these powers I should have been inclined to hold that the Labour Court has these powers as I think they are clearly "procedural powers" in the sense in which I have used that phrase a little earlier. But the matter could have been in some doubt and, it is in order to avoid that doubt, that the Legislature has, I think expressly conferred these powers, using care at the same time, by employing the words "including the powers of", not to prejudice the generality of powers already conferred."

9. In that decision the use of words "and shall" after the words "civil Court" in sub-section (2) was termed as an example of bad drafting. In view of the use of the two words "and shall" after the words "civil Court", an argument was advanced that the Labour Court shall be deemed to have all powers under the Civil Procedure Code, but it was repelled, as acceptance of such an argument "would render entirely superfluous all the words in sub-section (2) following "civil Court". It was held: "If the Labour Court is to be deemed a civil Court for all purposes while engaged in the determination and adjudication of industrial disputes, a reference to the Civil Procedure Code would be wholly unnecessary."

<u>10. In Sind Employees' Social Security Vs. Adamjee Cotton Mills Ltd. PLD 1975 (SC) 32 a question was raised whether a Social Security Court in seizin of an appeal, under section 59 of the West Pakistan Employees' Social Security Ordinance, 1965 has, in the absence of an express provision for the purpose, jurisdiction to stay execution of order appealed against. It was argued that by that section it was not the intention to bring the Social Security Court on a par with an ordinary civil Court, so as to make it possible to the former to invoke the provisions of Order XXXIX rules 1 and 2, nor it can lay claim to any other provision of law to suspend the execution of the order appealed against. After considering Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Vs. Irving 105 AC 369 and Commissioner of Khairpur Division Vs. Ali Sher Sarki PLD 1971 (SC) 243, the Pakistan Supreme Court held that when the Social Security court has power to reverse the order appealed against in its entirety it will have also Labour Court could exercise its jurisdiction under section 36 and grant an order of stay.</u>

11. This decision relating to the jurisdiction of the appellate forum has got no relevance in the instant case, there being no question of the power of an appellate authority involved in the matter.

12. Respondent No.2 has also relied on a number of decisions of Indian and English jurisdictions in. support of his contention that the Labour Court had jurisdiction to issue an order of injunction but failed to show the decisions are pari materia with regard to the powers conferred on the Labour Court under the IRO 1969.

13. The impugned decision appears to have been based on the following reasonings:

"From a reading of the definition of the word 'industrial dispute' in section 2(xiii) in our view, an application under section 34 of the IRO though not arising out of an industrial dispute as contemplated under section 43 of the IRO or which may be raised under sections 26 to 31 of the IRO it is an industrial dispute as contemplated under section 36(1). If we accept the proposition advanced by the learned Advocate for the opposite-party-petitioner that word 'industrial dispute' as has been referred to in section 36(1), is an industrial dispute as may be raised under sections 26 to 31 and section 43, then the Labour Court would be devoid of any power and jurisdiction or a procedure to hear an application under section 34 of the IRO which, in our view, cannot be accepted. If the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite-party-petitioner that 'industrial dispute' contemplated under section 36(1) of IRO does not include or is not intended to apply to an application under section 34, then it would take us to that a Labour Court has no power to hear and decide an application under section 34 of the IRO. Hence, in our view, the industrial dispute referred to in section 36(1) must be referable to the definition of the word as given in section 2 (iii) which includes all disputes as have been contemplated in the IRO. It would, therefore, be reasonable to hold that the Labour Court constituted under the IRO shall be deemed to be a civil Court and shall have the same power as vested in such court under the Code of Civil Procedure 	and 	.it must have power to grant injunction or stay the operation of impugned order to preserve the subject matter of the dispute until it is finally decided."

<u>14. The above reasonings are tenuous, at best, and advanced without considering this Division's pronouncements made in MIs. Railway Men's Stores Ltd. Vs. Chairman Labour Court, Chittagong 30 DLR (SC) 251 and James Finlay Vs. Chairman, Second Labour Court, Dhaka 33 DLR (AD) 58 that an industrial dispute shall not be deemed to exist unless raised in the prescribed manner by the Collective Bargaining Agent or the employer, and that a case under section 34 of the IRO is not an industrial dispute. The High Court Division's interpretations about an industrial dispute might have been given, as suggested in 39 DLR (HD) 39, "out of the anxiety that in the absence of such interpretation the labour court while deciding the case of individual disputes will have no power and no procedure creating an absurd and unworkable situation". But such a view can hardly be sustained in law. Till the amendment of section 34 of the IRO on 17.10.70 the prevailing notion of an industrial dispute precluded filing of any application before the Labour Court by an individual. Under section 34, as it now stands, after amendment on 17.10.70, any collective bargaining agent or any employer or workman may apply to the Labour Court for the enforcement of any right guaranteed or secured to it or him by or under any law or any award or settlement. But no corresponding amendment was made in section 36 of the IRO and the Labour Court is left to deal with an application under section 34 in consonance with the acknowledged judicial norms of adjudication including the principles of natural justice.</u>

<u>15. In some of the decisions of the High Court Division and in the impugned one a simple thing has been lost sight of. An adjudication on an industrial dispute under section 36(2) or a proceeding on an application under section 34 of the IRO for enforcement of any guaranteed or secured right though a matter of civil nature, is not a suit and does not attract all the panoply of powers of the Code of Civil Procedure. From the plain reading of sub-section (2) of section 36 it is clear that in adjudicating or determining an industrial dispute, the Labour Court acts as a civil Court for limited purpose and it will not exercise the powers like those given in Order IX or Order XXXIX rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure which the civil Court may exercise ina suit, but are in no sense necessary for deciding an industrial dispute. This view is strengthened if we compare the enumerated powers of the Labour Court given in clauses (a), (b), (c) and (d) of sub-section (2) of section 36 with corresponding wider powers of the civil Court while deciding a suit, as provided in sections. 30(b), 31 and 32, Order XI rules 14 and 16, Order XXVI rules 1-8 and 16(b) and Order IX.</u>

<u>16. An order of stay, in the nature of an injunction, under Order XXXIX rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure or under sections 52 and 53 of the Specific Relief Act as available in a suit, is not so available in any proceeding before the Labour Court, despite the provisions of sub-section (2) of Section 36 of the IRO under which it is deemed as a civil court. As in the respondent's application under section 34 only an individual grievance is urged and not an industrial dispute, raised in the prescribed manner, provisions of sub-section (2) of section 36 of the IRO are not at all attracted and hence the question of the Labour Court's granting a stay order does not arise at all.</u>

In view of the above, we hold that the Labour Court's order staying the operation of the order, impugned before it, was passed without lawful authority. The High Court Division erred in upholding that order. The appeal is allowed without costs.

Mustafa Kamal J : I agree with the decision given by my learned brother MH Rahman, J, I would, however, like to add the following in support of his judgment:

19. Leave was granted in this appeal "to consider whether under the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 the Labour Court has got the jurisdiction to grant an ad-interim order for stay of operation of the order impugned before it."

20. The question, to my mind, arises on two occasions, namely, when the Labour Court decides a non-industrial dispute and when it decides an industrial dispute.

21. A Labour Court may decide a non- industrial dispute under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, shortly the Ordinance, or under some other labour legislations, e.g., under section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965, shortly the Act.

22. When the Labour Court decides a non- industrial dispute under section 34 of the Ordinance, it follows the procedure provided in sub-section (1) of section 36 of the Ordinance as follows:

"36. Procedure and powers of Labour Court. -(1) Subject to the provisions of the Ordinance, a Labour Court shall follow as nearly as possible summary procedure as prescribed under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898)."

23. The above provision may be unhappy and inadequate, but that is where the legislature has stopped. If the summary criminal procedure is not good enough or is hardly relevant to the disposal of an application under section 34, the Labour Court will dispose of the matter in accordance with the principles of natural justice, as has been rightly held by a Division Bench of the High Court Division (Judgment by Aminur Rahman Khan, J.) in Chairman, Chittagong Port Authority, Chittagong Vs. Kalipada Dey, 39 DLR 39. In such a case, there is absolutely no sanction of law in treating the Labour Court as a Civil Court or even to deem it to be a Civil Court. The question of granting either an order of ad-interim stay of the order complained of or an order of injunction does not arise in such a case. The Labour Court in such a case acts purely as a statutory Tribunal with all the trappings of a Court, but not a Court proper.

24. Similarly, when the Labour Court decides an individual complaint from a worker under section 25 of the Act, it does not act as a Civil Court, nor shall it be deemed to be a Civil Court. Apart from the procedure provided by sub-section (1) of section 36 of the Ordinance, the Labour Court is also guided by proviso (c) to sub-section (1) of section 25 of the Act as follows:

"(c) On receipt of any complaint under clause (b), the Court, after notice and giving the parties hearing may decide the matter in such summary way as it deems proper;"

25. The question whether the Labour Court is a Civil Court or is deemed to be a Civil Court arises when the dispute brought before it is an industrial dispute raised in the manner provided in sections 26-31 of the Ordinance, for sub-section (2) of section 36 of the Ordinance provides as follows:

"36(1)........

(2) A Labour Court shall, for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute, be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have the same powers as are vested in such Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, (Act V of 1908) including the powers of-

(a) enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath,

(b) compelling the production of documents and material objects,

(c) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents, and

(d) delivering ex parte decision in the event of failure of any party to appear before the Court."

26. The language employed in sub-section (2) of section 36 has to be closely scrutinised. A Labour Court is not a Civil Court at all. It is only by a legal fiction or a statutory hypothesis that it is to be treated as a Civil Court.

<u>27. When the legislature enacts a "deeming" clause, the correct way to interpret the same is to find out for what purpose and up to what extent the legal fiction has been created. It is the function of the Court to find out the limitation of the legal fiction, to delimit its boundaries and not to extend the frontier of legal fiction beyond what has been provided in the statute. As was held in the case of Radha Klssen Chamria and others Vs. Durga Prosad Chamria, AIR 1940 PC 167, "As the analogy only arises by legal fiction, it must be limited to the purposes enacted by the context and cannot be given larger effect". Also it has been held in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax Vs. Vadilal Lallu Bhai, AIR 1973 (SC) 1016, "Legal fictions are only for definite purposes and they are limited to the purpose for which they are created and should not be extended beyond their legitimate field".</u>

28. Keeping this canon of interpretation in mind one must look into the purpose for which and the extent up to which the Labour Court has been deemed to be a Civil Court under sub-section (2) of section 36. The Labour Court shall be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have the same powers as are vested in such Court under the Code of Civil Procedure subject to the limitation provided in the beginning of the sub-section, namely, "for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute". It shall, therefore, not be deemed to be a Civil Court nor shall it enjoy such powers as are available to a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure if the purpose is not to adjudicate and determine any industrial dispute. Even when it decides an industrial dispute, only such powers as are necessary for the said purpose are to be exercised by the Labour Court. The Labour Court is, therefore, a Civil Court of limited procedural powers while deciding industrial disputes. It does not enjoy the generality of procedural powers of a Civil Court provided in the Code of Civil Procedure. Its procedural powers are referable to the purpose of its functioning and so much of the procedural powers contained in the Code of Civil Procedure as are necessary to suit the purpose are available to it, nothing more.

29. It has been argued from the Bar that the enumeration of specified powers in clauses (a)-(d) after the use of the word "including" is indicative of enlargement of the powers of the Labour Court. It has been submitted that the expression "including" is a term of extension. It imports addition. It adds to the subject-matter. It has extended the powers of the Labour Court. It has been submitted that this Court has held in the case of Dira Dockyard and Engineering Ltd., Vs. BSRS 39 DLR (AD) 59 that when a definition clause uses the word "means", it is an exclusive definition, that is, nothing more can be brought within its meaning excepting what followed after the word "means". But the use of the word "includes" does not exclude other possible meanings besides what have been expressly mentioned in the definition clause. It has been urged that the Labour Court be given an extended jurisdiction following our own interpretation of the term "includes".

30. The argument is fallacious. We are not considering a definition clause here. Sub-section (2) of section 36 of the Ordinance is not a definition clause. When the legislature states that a Labour Court shall have the same powers as are vested in a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, it has already stated all the powers that are contained in the Code, but when it further uses the expression "including" and enumerates some specific powers which are to be found in the Code of Civil Procedure itself, then the question arises, is it an extension or a limitation? Clauses (a)-(d) are revealing. The powers of enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath, compelling the production of documents and material objects, issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents and delivering ex parte decision in the event of failure of any party to appear before the Court, as described in clauses (a)-(d), are relatable to corresponding provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and on analysis it will be found that those powers given to a Civil Court under the corresponding provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are much wider. By specific enumeration the power of the Labour Court has been narrowed down to the language of clauses (a)-(d).

<u>31. By specific enumeration of powers in clauses (a)-(d) the legislative intent is clear. All the elaborate powers of the Civil Court in deciding a civil dispute, as contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, are not necessary for a Labour Court to possess in deciding an industrial dispute. Powers mentioned in clauses (a)-(d) are very elaborate in the Code of Civil Procedure but by specific enumeration of some powers, the Labour Court's powers in respect of the specified powers are limited to the restrictive language of clauses (a)-(d), and not beyond.</u>

<u>The question as to whether the Labour Court has the power to grant an ad-interim stay of the order complained of or an injunction is to be decided not with reference to the generality of powers contained in the Code of Civil Procedure but with regard to the stated purpose for which the deeming provision has been enacted. The question will be, is the power to grant an ad-interim stay or an injunction necessary for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute? The answer plainly is no, because preserving the subject matter of the dispute till its final resolution is a power apart from adjudicating and determining any industrial dispute.</u>

End.
