lawyer:
Abdul Aziz with M. Rezaul Karim, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate ------ For Opposite Party No.7.
parties:
Latika Rani Das ------ Petitioner
 VS
Bibhabati Ray Chowdhury & others ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure by the petitioner Latika Rani Das and is directed against an order dated 7-4-84 passed in Title Suit No. 10 of 1976 by the District Judge, Khulna allowing an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Facts giving rise to this Rule may be stated as follows:

The petitioner filed Miscellaneous Case No. 150 of 1975 in the Court of the District Delegate (Subordinate Judge) Khulna under section 278 of the Succession Act 1925 for obtaining letters of administration with a copy of the will executed by her father late Kiron Chandra Roy Chowdhury contending, inter alia. that her father late Kiron Chandra Roy Chowdhury died on 9-6-63 at. Village-Singati within Police Station Fakirhat, District-Khulna leaving behind the petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 1-5 but they are all Indian nationals, except the petitioner that the said Kiron Chandra Roy Chowdhury before his death disposed of all his properties by a will executed on the 2nd Baisakh, 1370 BS in favour of the petitioner. Hence the Misc. Case for letter of administration. In that Misc. Case defendant No. 6, the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Khulna filed a written objection challenging the genuineness of the will and the case thereby became contentious and in such a case the District Delegate had no authority to issue probate or letters of administration of the will. Hence the petitioner filed the present suit being Title Suit No. 10 of 1978 before the learned District Judge, Khulna on 22-4-76 But subsequently opposite party No. 7 the Assistant Custodian of the Vested Property filed an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for being added as a defendant in the suit mainly on the ground that the properties of late Kiron Chandra Roy Chowdhury have already vested with the Government of Bangladesh by operation of law and all his sons and heirs are now Indian nationals except the petitioner and the property is being dealt with as vested property by the Asstt. Custodian opposite party No. 7 by leasing out the same to some lessees and, as such, opposite party No. 7 has direct interest over the case lands and, as such, he is a necessary party. The application was heard by the learned District Judge in presence of both the parties and learned District Judge on consideration of the submissions made at the Bar and the materials placed before him, was pleased to pass the following order being order No. 83 dated 7-4-84:

"Both sides file haziras. The petition dated 12-1-84 filed by Assistant Custodian Vested Property praying for being added as defendant is put up. Heard. The learned Advocate for the petitioner namely, Asstt. Custodian of Vested Property states that the properties described in the village have vested in the Govt. and as such the Asstt. Custodian should be given chance to oppose the probate case. In view of the ruling reported in 33 DLR 175, I find much strength in this contention. Hence the prayer is allowed.

Let the petitioner be made defendant in this suit. Amend the plaint and register accordingly. To 2-5-84 for W/S.

Being aggrieved by the said order, the petitioner has come up with this application and obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr. Abdul Aziz with Mr. M. Rezaul Karim, the learned Advocate, appeared for the petitioner in support of the Rule and Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appeared for the opposite party No. 7 to oppose the Rule.

4. Mr. Aziz, the learned Advocate for the petitioner challenged the impugned Order and contended that learned District Judge committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by allowing the application under Order 1 rule 10 CPC inasmuch as in a probate proceeding or in a proceeding for letters of administration, the Assistant Custodian of vested property is not a necessary party. His contention is that opposite party No. 7 the Assistant Custodian of Vested Property is not claiming any interest through the testator of the will i.e. through late Kiron Chandra Roy Chowdhury and, as such, he has no right to be added as a defendant in the suit for letters of administration. In support of his contention he has cited a decision in the case of Sreemati Charubal Sen Gupta vs. Abul Hashem and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 254. He has also submitted that the learned District Judge has wrongly relied on a decision in the case of Goutam Ranjan Sen and others vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 33 DLR (AD), 175 as the facts of that case are distinguishable from the facts of the present case. The learned Advocate has further contended that if the opposite party No. 7 is not made a party defendant in the suit under Order 1 rule 10 of CPC the doors for relief will not be shut out against him because he will have his right to come with an application for revocation of the grant of the probate or letter of administration under section 263 of the Succession Act and in that view of the matter, the learned District Judge has committed an error of law in not rejecting the prayer of the opposite party No. 7 for adding him as a party in the suit. About the aforesaid additional relief the learned Advocate has relied on a decision in the case of Ujifa Khatun vs. Tulshi Ranjan Roy reported in 37 DLR 268.

<u>5. Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 7, on the other hand, has submitted that the learned District Judge has rightly passed the impugned order and allowed the opposite party No.7 to be added as defendant in the suit and there is no illegality whatsoever in the said order' and the same has not occasioned any failure of justice. Elaborating his arguments, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No.7 has referred to paragraph No. 2 of the application of the Assistant Custodian of the Vested Property under Order 1 rule 10 CPC, which is as under:</u>

<u>"2.That the properties of late Kiron Chandra Roy Chowdhury have vested with the Govt. as vested properties under operation of law as Kiron Chandra and his son have left this country for India before 1965 and this petitioner is dealing with the property by leasing out in L. Case No. 122F/75-76 75/71-2 of Nagerjat SDO 's office. As such this petitioner has interest over the lands of the case and he is a necessary party in the suit. The plaintiff did not make this petitioner a party in the suit in order to obtain the decree on false claim, and submitted that the above citation shows that the property had already vested in the Government by operation of law and through legal process the same has been leased out to some lessees by opposite party No. 7 i.e. the Assistant Custodian, Vested Property. It has been further submitted that the Assistant Custodian has stepped into the shoes of the owner of the property that means the alleged testator of the will Kiron Chandra Roy Chowdhury who is non-resident in this country and allegedly dead; hence the Assistant Custodian has now direct interest in the property in question and so long it is vested property no letters of administration or probate can be issued and thus he is a necessary party in the interest of justice. So far the decision cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner reported in 33 DLR (AD) 254 the learned Advocate for the opposite party has submitted that the facts of the cited case are quite distinguishable from those of this case. In that case the persons who wanted to be added as defendants had claimed their interest in the suit property through their leassor and not through the testator of the will and, as such, it was held in that decision that:</u>

<u>"The 'interest' in the estate of the testator within the words of section 283, Succession Act, means an interest through the testator A person who claims outside or independently of the will or claims adversely to the testator and disputes his right to deal with the property cannot be deemed to claim any interest in the estate of the deceased.</u>

<u>The crucial point in this case is, whether the respondents claim any interest in the estate through testator, and since they do not, they have no locus stanch to be added as a party to the probate proceeding.</u>

<u>The High Court Division clearly fell into an error in taking the view that the respondents have got such locus standi.</u>

<u>But in the instant case the facts are otherwise. The opposite party No. 7 the Assistant Custodian, Vested Property is claiming interest in the property in question directly through the testator and not through any 3rd person or any lessor. Hence, the aforesaid decision in 33 DLR (AD) 254 is not applicable to this case rather the decision reported in 33 DLR 175 very much applies. As regards the submission of the learned Advocates for the petitioner that the opposite party No. 7 will have additional remedy by way of filing an application for revocation of the grant of probate or letters of administration under section 263 of the Succession Act, it is contended by the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 7 that it is true that the door for the relief against any grant of probate or letter of administration is open for the opposite party No. 7 by way of revocation of the grant of such probate or letter of administration, but for that he cannot be kept away from contesting or seeing the probate of letters of administration proceeding as a party defendant in the facts and circumstance of the case and, as such, the impugned order of the learned District Judge adding Party No. 7 as a defendant cannot be set aside merely on such ground of additional relief available to the opposite party No. 7 in future.</u>

6. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned order and the connected papers placed before me and having given my anxious consideration to the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record along with the submissions made at the Bar, I like to hold that the decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 254 is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case and, as such, the same does not help the petitioner in assailing the impugned order which does not suffer from any legal infirmity and it appears that the same has not also occasioned any failure of justice. Rather, in the facts and circumstances of the case as disclosed, the opposite party No. 7 Asstt. Custodian Vested Property should be rightly given a chance to contest the suit in the interest of justice.

7. For the reasons stated above, there is nothing to interfere with the impugned order of the learned District Judge and the same should be upheld and the Rule be discharged.

8. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted earlier by this court is hereby vacated.

9. Let the suit proceed in accordance with law after giving effect to the impugned order of the learned District Judge.

Let a copy of the judgment and order be transmitted to the court of the learned District Judge, Khulna immediately.

End.

lawyer:
Hemayet Uddin Ahmed with Abdul Quayum and Subodh Ranjan Dutta, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
AKM Zahirul Huq, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party No. 1.
parties:
Repco Laboratories Ltd ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Nuruddin Ahmed and ors ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Nurul Huque Bhuiyan J: This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of plaintiffs-petitioners calls in question the order dated 24.11.88 passed by the learned District Judge, Barisal in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 43 of 1987 affirming the order dated 9.6.87 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Title Suit No. 293 of 1981 rejecting an application under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the suit in the said Court of Subordinate Judge against the opposite patty Nos. 2-17 as defendants for a declaration that the decree obtained by the original defendant No. 1 Imanuddin Rari (since deceased) in Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 against Lilabati Das the predecessor of the plaintiffs is void and not binding on them stating, inter alia, that the suit plot Nos. 2205, 2206, 2207, 2211, 2215 and 2216 and some other lands were auction purchased by the Government in revenue sale and Lilabati Das took fresh settlement from the Government on 30.10.59 and had been in possession thereof. The plaintiffs acquired the land by settlement and purchase from Lilabati Das and were possessing the same. They came to know shortly before the institution of the suit that the defendant No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 for part of the above mentioned land claiming that he had taken settlement of the land from one of the original recorded tenants Sudhendu Nath Roy Chowdhury in 1960 B.S. and by fraudulent suppression of the summonses and all other processes obtained an ex parte decree on 9.3.63. They alleged that the decree had clouded their title and hence the suit.

3. The opposite party No. 1 was not a party in the suit and on his prayer he was added as defendant No. 12 in the suit and he filed a written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. and making allegations that Lilabati Das, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, previously filed Title Suit No. 376 of 1963 challenging the decree passed in Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 and lost up to the Supreme Court and therefore the present suit was barred by principle of res judicata. His further case was that defendant No. 1 had valid title and possession over the suit land and he acquired it from defendant No. 1.

4. When the suit was in peremptory hearing stage and heard in part the contesting defendant No. 12 filed an application praying for temporary injunction to restrain the plaintiffs from erecting any new house on plot No. 2205, not to cut any tree from plot No. 2211 and from filling up the pond or changing the nature and character of plot No. 2206 during the pendency of the suit alleging that the plaintiffs were threatening to do such acts.

5. The plaintiffs filed a written objection against the application for temporary injunction stating that they were in exclusive possession of those plots, that the defendant No. 12 had no possession over the land and as such he was not entitled to get any order of injunction.

6. The learned Subordinate Judge by order dated 13.7.86 refused to pass any order of temporary injunction but he passed the following order "in view of the verbal undertaking of the learned Advocate on behalf of the plaintiffs that they would not make any further construction on the disputed suit plot No. 2205 during the pendency of the suit, the application for temporary injunction be disposed of accordingly."

7. Being aggrieved by the order dated 13.7.86 the defendant No. 12 filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 65 of 1986 before the learned District Judge, Bakerganj who by his order dated 8.9.86 allowed the appeal in part and in a modified form restraining the plaintiffs by a temporary injunction from making any new construction on plot No. 2205 till the disposal of the original suit with direction to the learned Subordinate Judge to take up the final hearing of the suit himself immediately on receipt of the record and dispose of the suit within two months from that date.

8. The plaintiffs filed an application before the learned Subordinate Judge under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to modify the order of injunction passed by the learned District Judge in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 65 of 1986 stating, inter alia, that in view of the direction of the Deputy Director of the Department of Environment Pollution Control, Bangladesh dated 30.6.86 the plaintiffs were required to take adequate step to construct a drain and to complete the construction of the 4th storey of the main building on plot No. 2205. The learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 9.6.87 rejected the application with the observation, inter alia, that he had no jurisdiction to change in any way the order of temporary injunction passed by the Appellate Court.

9. Against the order dated 9.6.87 the plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 43 of 1987 before the learned District Judge, Barisal. They also filed an application under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the learned District Judge, Barisal. By two separate orders dated 24.11.88 the learned District Judge rejected the application under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and dismissed the appeal on the observation that the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in holding that he had no jurisdiction to change or sit on the order of temporary injunction by the Appellate Court and the plaintiffs could not get any relief under Order 39 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

10. Against the order dated 24.11.88 passed by the learned District Judge dismissing the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 43 of 1987 the plaintiffs have obtained the present Rule. They have not moved this court against the order dated 24.11.88 rejecting the application under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

11. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, has submitted that because of the delay in the disposal of the suit and the changed circumstances the modification of the jurisdiction order or to accord permission to work as specified in the application under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure it was imperative for the learned Subordinate Judge to do complete justice in the case and he has erred in not modifying the order of injunction under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>12. Mr. Abdul Quayum has further submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge has erred in not at all considering the question of convenience and inconvenience of the parties. He has also submitted that the undertaking given on behalf of the plaintiffs to the learned Subordinate Judge not to make any construction amounts to an injunction and as such the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the order for modification of the injunction order can not be passed is misconceived. The last submission of Mr. Abdul Quayum is that the plaintiffs gave the undertaking to the learned Subordinate Judge not to make any construction during the pendency of the suit on the expectation that the suit would be soon disposed of but the suit having not been soon disposed of and the delay in the disposal to the suit having caused an irreparable loss to the plaintiffs by giving rise to contingencies that was not available at the time of passing the injunction order the learned Subordinate Judge erred in not exercising inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in modifying the order of temporary injunction. In support of his submission he had relied upon the cases namely, Govinda Ramanuja Das Goswami Vs. Vijiaramaraju and another, AIR 1929 Madras 803; Chaturbhujdas Parmanandas Vs. Natvarlal Tribhovandas, AIR 1931 Born 509; AB Gurumurthi Chetty Vs. Sella Perumal Pillai, AIR 1936 Madras 651; Abdul Barek Mia and others Vs. AMM Serajul Islam, 20 DLR 501; Delower Hossain Vs. Saber Ahmed Kutubi Chowdhury and others, 29 DLR 211; Kaysons Vs. National Bank of Pakistan, Karachi, PLD 1972 Karachi 174; Abdul JaIil Munshi and another Vs. Abu Bakr Siddique, 35 DLR (AD) 42.</u>

13. In reply to the submissions of Mr. Abdul Quayum Mr. AKM Zahirul Huq the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, submits that the question of convenience and inconvenience is considered in the disposal of an application for temporary injunction and not in the disposal of the application for modification of the injunction order. He has further submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the instant case Order 39 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no application. He has next submitted that the learned District Judge having passed the order of temporary injunction the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly held the view that he has no jurisdiction to change it under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

14. In AIR 1929 Madras 803 it has been held:

"Order 39 r. 4, is intended to cover two classes of cases : (1) When an urgent order ex parte has been passed under r. 3, r. 4 will allow the party against whom it has been passed to apply to have it discharged or varied or set aside; and (2) when an injunction order already in force has, owing to fresh circumstances, become unduly harsh or unnecessary or unworkable, it would be open to either party to apply under r. 4 to the Court to discharge, vary or set it aside. R. 4is not intended to set at naught the ordinary cursuscurise that, once a Court has decided a matter after giving each side an opportunity of being heard, its order is final and binding on itself as much also the parties, and cannot be re-opened except on the presentation of some new matter not available when the original order was passed."

It is nowhere held in this decision that an order passed by a superior court can be set aside by a court subordinate to it as is the case before us. In this case the application under Order 39 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure was made before the court which passed the order of temporary injunction but in the instant case the application for modification of the order of injunction under Order 39 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure was made before the Subordinate Judge although the order of injunction was passed by the learned District Judge being the Appellate Court and as such Order 39 rule 4 of the Code is not applicable in the instant case even if there is some new matter or contingency that was not available at the time of passing the injunction order namely, the construction of drain and completion of the 4th storey of the main building on the suit plot No. 2205. In these circumstances, it is held that the case reported in AIR 1929 Madras 803 has no manner of application in the instant case. In AIR 1931 Born 509 on an application by the plaintiff for attachment before judgment of the property of the defendant, the defendant gave an undertaking that he would not sell the same till the disposal of the suit and the Court did not pass any order for attachment. But the defendant sold the property before the disposal of the suit. The plaintiff thereafter applied for proceedings for Contempt of Court against the defendant. The application was not granted. In this\case the defendant in violation of the undertaking given by the defendant sold the property before the disposal of the suit and thereupon the plaintiff filed the application, for drawing up contempt proceeding against him but the application was rejected. In the instant case the plaintiffs gave undertaking to the learned Subordinate Judge not to make any further construction on suit plot No. 2205 during the pendency of the suit and the learned Subordinate Judge did not pass the order of injunction as prayed for by the defendant No. 12. On appeal by defendant No. 12 the learned District Judge passed the order of temporary injunction. There is, therefore, no question of violation of undertaking in the instant case. Thus the case in AIR 1931 Born 509 also has no application in the instant case.

15. In AIR 1936 Madras 651 it has been held;

"Where a Court accepts an undertaking given by a party, its order amounts in substance to an injunction restraining him from acting in breach thereof, and the Court has jurisdiction to deal with the breach of such an order." The law laid down in this case obviously does not help the plaintiffs.

16. In 20 DLR (HCD) 501 it has been held :

"In an appropriate case the Court has inherent power to grant injunction under section 151 C.P.C. for the ends of justice even if the matter is not covered by Order 39 rules 1 and 2 on the Code."

It is not disputed that if an application for temporary injunction is made under rules 1 and 2 of section 39 of the Code the court can exercise in here  power in appropriate case under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But the inherent power of the Subordinate Judge under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure can not extend to interference will the order of temporary injunction passed by the Appellate Court namely, a the District Judge. In other words, the Subordinate Judge has no jurisdiction to change or sit on the order of temporary injunction passed by the District Judge in exercise of the inherent power under section 151 of the Code. Therefore, the case in 20 DLR (HCD) 501 is not attracted in the face of the present case.

17. In PLD 1972 Karachi 174 the appellant Kaysons was a pledger and the respondent was a Bank with whom it had pledged its goods. The Bank filed suit for recovery of money. The appellant filed are application for obtaining a general order of the court that the goods which were pledged with the respondent might be disposed of with the consent of the appellant at a price not below their pledged value. This prayer was accepted by consent and order was made accordingly. Thereafter another application was math by the respondent practically for the same purpose an counsel for the respondent said that it was a mistake which resulted from the fact that the same case wall handled by two lawyers in his office. After the application a third application was made which wall dated the 22nd of March, 1971 and was presented or the 26th of March, 1971 in which a reference was made to the order of the 26th of October, 1970. A prayer was also made for nominating the Nazir as the person who would sell the pledged goods at the best offers supplied by the appellant within one month. In the above circumstances it was held in this case:

"Sometimes after consent is given to an order the situation may change and in view of the changed circumstances or consideration which were not originally contemplated it may be necessary to take the stand that the consent order needs to be revised but in that event the proper course is to rely on the changed circumstances or the new considerations and on that basis to justify that the consent order can be modified. In this case such a course was not adopted and if it is correct that only the name of the person who was to effect the sale was to be introduced, then on that plea the substantial modifications that have been obtained could not be justified. We think there was warrant for adopting the course which has been adopted."

18. In this case the application was made under Order 39 rule 6 of the Code which reads as follows :

"6. The Court may, on the application of any party to a suit, order the sale, by any person named in such order, and in such manner and on such terms as it thinks fit, of any movable property, being the subject-matter of such suit, or attached before judgment in such suit, which is subject to speedy and natural decay, or which for any other just and sufficient cause it may be desirable to have sold at once."

The Order 39 rule 6 of the Code relates to movable property, being the subject matter of the suit or attached before judgment in the suit, is subject to speedy and natural decay or for any other just and sufficient cause it is desirable-that the goods be sold at once. But in the instant case subject matter of the suit is an immovable property which is not subject to speedy and natural decay or it is not desirable that the same be sold at once for any just and sufficient cause. Moreover, in the instant case the learned Subordinate Judge held that he had no jurisdiction to change the order of injunction passed by the learned District Judge and that was not the case in the said Karachi case. In the above circumstances the case in PLD 1972 Karachi 174 also has no application in the facts of the instant case.

19. In 29 DLR 211 it was held:

"If an order of injunction has been passed after giving opportunity to both the parties to be heard, it cannot ordinarily be set aside or varied under rule 4; but where there has been no opportunity to a party against whom the order of injunction has been passed to be heard that principle or law will not apply and rule 4 of Order XXXIX of the Code will come to the aid of that party to require the Court to recall the order."

In the light of the case reported in 29 DLR 211 Order 39 rule 4 of the Code would apply in aid of the plaintiffs if they were not given an opportunity of being heard at the time of passing the order of injunction. In the instant case the injunction order was passed by the learned District Judge after giving opportunity to both the parties. Further, the plaintiffs filed the application under Order 39 rule 4 of the Code before the learned Subordinate Judge for modification of the order of injunction passed by the learned District Judge and as such the case reported in 29 DLR 211 is distinguishable from the instant case on facts and as the principle laid down in the said does not apply in the instant case.

20. In 35 DLR (AD) 42 it has been held :

"There is no doubt that in an exceptional circumstance, as for example in the case of an extreme urgency or where the order of injunction is, on the face of it, without jurisdiction, an application under Order 39 rule 4 of the Code may be made for varying an ex parte order made under rule 3 of the Order but such an application can be disposed of only on hearing the parties on merit, which is likely to be almost similar to the hearing of the parties in pursuance of a notice under rule 3."

In the light of the case in 35 DLR (AD) 42 the application of the plaintiffs under Order 39 rule 4 of the Code lies for modification of the injunction order in case of extreme urgency or if the order was on the face of it without jurisdiction and if the application was made in the same court which passed the order. But that is not the case before us and as such the case in 35 DLR (AD) 42 does not apply in the instant case.

<u>21. In the case before us the only question for consideration is whether the learned Subordinate Judge has jurisdiction to change or sit on the order of temporary injunction passed by the learned District Judge under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The answer is, that the learned Subordinate Judge has no such jurisdiction under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code. The order of temporary injunction having been passed by the learned District Judge the learned Subordinate Judge has no scope to consider the question of the balance of convenience of the parties and the learned Subordinate Judge can not be said to have erred in not considering the balance of convenience and inconvenience of the parties as contended on behalf of the petitioners. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has not been able to cite a single authority showing that the Subordinate Judge can sit on an order of temporary injunction passed by the District Judge on appeal.</u>

22. I fully agree with the learned District Judge that the learned Subordinate Judge was quite correct in holding that he had no jurisdiction to change or sit on the order of injunction passed by the learned District Judge and the learned District Judge having correctly passed the order affirming the order of the learned Subordinate Judge rejecting the application under Order 39 rule 4 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure there is no scope for me for interference with his order.

Accordingly, the Rule is discharged but without any order as to costs.

End.
